News.title: Damning report finds Met Police still 'institutionally racist, misogynistic and homophobic'
News.content:
Damning report finds Met Police still 'institutionally racist, misogynistic and homophobic'

Dr Gillian Fairfield's review of the UK's biggest police force predicts further scandals in the future if it does not change its culture in the wake of the murder of Sarah Everard

View 4 Images Sarah Everard was kidnapped, raped and killed by serving PC Wayne Couzens (Image: PA)

Britain's biggest police force remains institutionally racist, misogynistic and homophobic, three years after a landmark report came to the same conclusion, a new review has found.

Dr Gillian Fairfield said she was left "shocked and upset" by some aspects of her investigation into the culture at the Metropolitan Police.

Dr Fairfield spent nearly a year examining the progress the force has made implementing recommendations made by Baroness Louise Casey's 2023 report commissioned in the wake of Sarah Everard's murder.

The 389-page Fairfield Review, published on Wednesday, stated: "The Casey Review found the Met was institutionally racist, misogynistic and homophobic. Our role has been to assess the Met's progress in addressing this; we judge these fundamental, systemic issues remain."

Dr Fairfield said the force had displayed "some of the best policing and some of the worst" while it continued to let down victims of crime.

And she predicted the organisation would face further scandals in the future if the culture did not change.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

Met Police cops probed over stop and search after black teen left with broken knee READ MORE :

View 4 Images Dr Gillian Fairfield said she was left 'shocked and upset' by some findings (Image: Jordan Pettitt/Press Association)

'The Met struggles to acknowledge racism'

While the force had made some progress dealing with racism, the report said: "The Met still struggles to acknowledge racism as a structural problem rather than something people can be trained out of.

"As with other difficult subjects it is too often managed as a reputational threat rather than an opportunity for learning."

Dr Fairfield told journalists: "The Met struggles to acknowledge racism. But if it can't name it, it can't face it. If it can't face it, it can't sort it out."

Responding to the report, Met Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley continued to refuse to accept that the force was institutionally racist, misogynistic and homophobic.

Dr Fairfield said she would not advise Sir Mark on the issue, but added: "There are examples of other forces agreeing there was institutional racism."

She told reporters that she hoped the commissioner would "not be defensive", adding: "What really matters, I think, is Londoners want change."

Mayor of London Lord Sadiq Khan said, in remarks aimed at the commissioner, that there should be "no spin or cherry-picking of this review".

He added: "The commissioner and his senior team need to reflect on her findings with humility and reflection, not hubris.

"It is simply not possible to change the culture of the Met if the existence of institutional racism, institutional misogyny and institutional homophobia continues to be denied, underplayed or tiptoed around."

View 4 Images Baroness Louise Casey's 2023 report was commissioned in the wake of Sarah Everard's murder (Image: PA)

'I have zero confidence'

The Casey Review found the Met framed failings as being in the past, blamed misconduct on individual "bad apples" and overestimated the progress it had made.

The Fairfield Review concludes: "We have found none of these behaviours have changed sufficiently. Neither has the Met's institutional defensiveness."

It found that only scrutiny the Met "really fears is from the media" and that the organisation needed to change its mindset.

The review said: "Its first thoughts on scrutiny should be how to fix what needs fixing, not how the media will react."

The Met had not made "good" progress in relation to any of 14 recommendations made by Baroness Casey, the review concluded.

The increased recruitment and promotion for female officers was highlighted, but many women in the force remain unconvinced enough has been done.

One woman officers was quoted in the report as saying: "There's real predatory behaviour towards younger women and new recruits. They need to understand they are prey."

Another cop told the report: "I have zero confidence that anything is going to happen when reporting misconduct".

And a professional working in a police building told the review that officers "hate London", while one referred to a particular borough as "a sh**hole".

View 4 Images Sir Mark Rowley, the Met Police Commissioner, talks to reporters (Image: Yui Mok/PA Wire)

Met Police says 'standards are higher'

Trust among the LGBT community, damaged by catastrophic failings in the case of serial killer Stephen Port, has not improved, the report said.

Dr Fairfield said she had been "shocked and upset" at the number of LGBT+ people who would not want to report crimes to the police.

The review found the Met remains dependent on a small group of executives who face little independent challenge from within the organisation.

Several officers faced misconduct proceedings after a Panorama reporter went undercover in Charing Cross Police Station, and the report said "some of these behaviours and concerns were not confined to Charing Cross".

The Metropolitan Police accepted the report's recommendations, with Sir Mark saying it recognised the "scale and pace of change" since the Casey report.

"Standards are higher, performance is stronger, violence is down, criminal justice outcomes for victims of sexual violence are amongst the highest nationally, and London is safer," he said.

Sir Mark accepted that "eliminating discrimination in all we do starts with listening and requires sustained commitment and structural change".

"The progress we have made is a credit to the professionalism, resilience and determination of our officers and staff," Sir Mark said.

"They have delivered extraordinary change while continuing to protect London through rising demand, significant financial pressures, unavoidable workforce reductions and a criminal justice crisis.

"I know this report will only further their determination to deliver the continued change Londoners seek and deserve."

Sarah, 33, was kidnapped, raped and killed by serving PC Wayne Couzens who tricked her into thinking she could be arrested for breaking Covid lockdown rules as she walked home from a friend’s house in Clapham on March 3, 2021.

Couzens’ arrest led to the unmasking of serial rapist David Carrick, who worked in the same armed unit, and scores of other predators in uniform.

News.title: Ex-Love Island star Zara McDermott hails UK bid to tackle intimate image abuse worldwide
News.content:
Ex-Love Island star Zara McDermott hails UK bid to tackle intimate image abuse worldwide

EXCLUSIVE: Zara McDermott voiced her support after the Foreign Office announced it is investing £27million to encourage overseas software firms to use automatic blurring or age restrictions

View 2 Images Zara McDermott has welcomed new steps to protect women and girls online (Image: Instagram @zara_mcdermott)

A former Love Island and Strictly star who had intimate images of her shared without her consent has praised new steps to stop others going through the same ordeal.

Zara McDermott voiced her support after the Foreign Office announced it is investing £27million to encourage overseas software firms to use automatic blurring or age restrictions.

This will help tackle sharing of real or AI-generated images, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said. Zara told The Mirror: "Having shared my own story of experiencing intimate image abuse at just 14 years old, I know how important it is for survivors to feel heard and supported.

"Through my work as a documentary maker, I have had the privilege of listening to so many survivors share their experiences of violence and abuse. Time and time again, I hear stories of women and girls whose lives have been profoundly affected, often leaving them feeling silenced, isolated or unfairly burdened with shame.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 2 Images Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK is leading efforts to protect women and girls online (Image: Getty Images)

Domestic abusers can be forced to hand over home keys and social media passwords READ MORE :

No10 slams TikTok star who posted 'unacceptable' song video in Downing Street READ MORE :

"What has always struck me is the extraordinary courage it takes to speak out, and how much more we need to do to ensure survivors feel heard, believed and protected."

Zara was pressured by a boy at school to send an intimate photo when she was just 14. After the image was shared, she was suspended and blamed. And in 2018 while she was in the Love Island villa, further intimate photos were circulated online.

She hosted a BBC documentary outlining the emotional toll it had on her. Following the announcement of the government's funding, Zara said: "Online abuse is everywhere; it travels borders and the globe. I am pleased to see the UK government taking action on a global scale to strengthen protections for women and girls, hold perpetrators accountable and create a safer digital world for future generations.”

Under the programme, the UK will work with tech bosses and start-ups to bring in safety measures from the start. The Foreign Office has also promised to provide legal and technical expertise to countries to strengthen online safety measures. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said: “Online abuse does not stop at national borders. Within seconds, a real or AI-generated image can be shared around the world.

"The UK is leading international action to strengthen online safety laws, and stopping criminals from exploiting loopholes in emerging technology, protecting women and girls from appalling abuse.”

An international summit on ending violence against women and girls will be held in London next April. Foreign Office Minister Uma Kumaran said: "Violence against women and girls is one of the greatest injustices in our world today. One in three women will experience abuse in their lifetime. That's why we are cracking down on online abuse around the world and strengthening protections for survivors."

The UK is also putting together a global advisory board of survivors to influence decisions on tackling violence against women and girls.

News.title: I’m A Celebrity LIVE: Mariella Frostrup apologises to AJ Odudu - but makes awkward dig
News.content:
Mariella Frostrup apologises to AJ Odudu

Mariella issued an apology to AJ tonight as she lay in her camp bed.



"I am sorry for calling you aggressive," she told AJ.



"Thank you for your apology," AJ replied.



"It had no back meaning to it, if you know what I mean," Mariella continued. "It just fell out of my mouth. I get triggered by 'posh'."



The Big Brother presenter pointed out that she never called Mariella 'posh' and went on to explain why she had found the word 'aggressive' difficult.



"It's triggering because in this world, navigating it as a person who looks like me can be difficult at times because my experience is that my emotions and my intent are completely misconstrued," she said, pointing out that it "automatically goes to aggressive".



"I totally hear you, but I would say - with my experience being me - I'm often called aggressive," Mariella replied. "I think it's a woman thing more than it's anything else. I think a woman speaks her mind and is forthright is aggressive and a man who speaks his mind is a strong man. I do think it's a woman thing as well but I totally get that there's more."



AJ replied: "I definitely do see your point and I agree, but those words stick. Those words can stick for us. The moment passes for you, but it doesn't pass for me."



"But hopefully it has," Mariella said. AJ responded: "Well, I wasn't being aggressive, so it shouldn't have ever been there!"



Things still appeared awkward, with Mariella pointing out: "You don't take an apology well."



"No you not think? I thought I accepted your apology," AJ replied, while Mariella asked: "Have you?"



"Yes of course I have!" AJ exclaimed.



Mariella said later in the Bush Telegraph: "I apologised to AJ again and I thought she explained it very articulately and I think it was interesting."

News.title: Huge drop in 16 to 24 year olds having sex — and are staying virgins for longer
News.content:
Huge drop in 16 to 24 year olds having sex — and are staying virgins for longer

Brits are having less sex and watching more pornography while more women don’t want kids, according to the National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles

View 3 Images Brits are having less sex and more women don't want kids (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

People in Britain are having less sex and adolescents and young adults are remaining virgins for longer.

‌



‌



An overall drop off in the amount people have sex is driven in large part by the fact that one in three 16 to 24-year-olds had never had sex last year. The study published in the Lancet medical journal found this was an increase from one in five between 1990 and 2010.

‌



Experts suspect the drop off in young people having sex could be driven by multiple factors including being unable to afford to move out of the family home, an increase in online socialising and increased viewing of pornography. The data also showed a sharp increase in women who do not want to have children.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror just click on the link here to find them at the top of your feed.

View 3 Images More men and women are watching porn (stock) (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

First Brit to have part of his testicles removed and frozen so he can become a dad READ MORE :

Experts point to modern lifestyles and rising living costs

Analysis of the National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles found adults aged under 45 are having sex twice a month on average, compared with four times a month in 1990-91 and three in 2010-12.

‌



Overall, 77% of people aged 16 to 59 have had sex at least once in the last year, with women having sex once per month on average and men twice monthly.

Author Dr Wendy Macdowall, of the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (LSHTM), said: "It's likely there are multiple complex factors at play, especially for young people. On the one hand, more open discussion of consent may mean young people feel better able to decide whether and when to have sex.

‌



"On the other, these findings coincide with broader changes in young people's lives, including rising rates of mental health conditions, declines in drinking alcohol, more time spent online and a greater proportion living at home with their parents."

Just looking at the average for those aged 45 to 59, women on average reported no sex in the previous month while men reported having had sex twice. Among those aged 35 to 44, frequency of sex fell in the past decade, from three times a month to twice.

‌



Half of young women and almost nine in 10 young men report watching pornography in the past year. Among all ages from 16 to 59, 37% of women and 81% of men had watched porn.

Just under half of young men and women have sent or received a sexual image, according to the studies.

‌



Co-author Soazig Clifton, honorary senior research fellow at University College London, said the decline in sex is being seen in other countries, where researchers have been looking at the link with digital technology.

She said: "It's quite possible that housing and economic factors are playing a role, plus changes in how people socialise more broadly, less going out for example, and also the higher rates of mental health problems we're seeing might be playing a role.”

‌



The studies found that double the number of women say they definitely do not want children compared with over a decade ago, rising from 8% in 2010 to 17% in 2022/2024. This trend was most obvious among young women, quadrupling among those aged 25 to 34 from 4% to 17%.

View 3 Images Less sex has been linked to more social interactions taking place online (Image: Getty Images)

‌



'It has real implications for planning health, care and family services'

Dr Laura Oakley, associate professor of epidemiology at LSHTM, said: "Our survey didn't look at the reasons behind the increase in women saying they definitely don't want children.

"Understanding what's driving this — whether economic insecurity, climate anxiety or changing life priorities — should now be a priority for future research and policy, as it has real implications for planning health, care and family services."

‌



The new data comes from what is one of the largest studies of sexual health and behaviour in the world. It happens every decade across England, Scotland and Wales and more than 60,000 people have taken part to date, with around 6,700 in the most recent round.

The proportion of 16 to 44-year-olds who report ever having had sex with a partner of the same sex doubled among women from 7% to 14% and tripled among men from 4% to 12% over the past decade.

Article continues below

But research said this finding might have been overstated as people who identified as lesbian, gay or bisexual appear were more likely to take part in this latest survey.

News.title: 'Nuclear test veterans have waited 40 years for justice — now the truth must finally come out'
News.content:
'Nuclear test veterans have waited 40 years for justice — now the truth must finally come out'

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, has praised the Mirror for keeping the flame alive for nuclear test veterans in their decades-long fight for justice

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

For 40 years, the Mirror has fought for justice for Britain’s nuclear test veterans and their families. Today, finally, there is hope that one of the most shameful chapters in our country’s history will be laid bare. Andy Burnham deserves credit for announcing a Hillsborough-style inquiry into a scandal that successive governments have failed to properly confront. These men served their country, only to spend decades fighting the very state they had so loyally served. Families have endured cancers, miscarriages, the loss of children and the anguish of being denied answers. Too many veterans have gone to their graves without knowing the truth. The tears of 85-year-old Rose Clark outside Downing Street should remind us all of the terrible human cost of this scandal. The inquiry must leave no stone unturned, no document concealed and no question unanswered. For four decades the Mirror has refused to let this injustice be forgotten. We will keep fighting until justice is delivered.

‌



‌



Restore dignity

Britain’s disability benefits system is failing the very people it was designed to help. Sir Stephen Timms’s damning review of Personal Independence Payments (PIP) exposes a system that is not fit for purpose. Forcing people with lifelong or degenerative conditions to repeatedly prove they are still disabled is both cruel and absurd. That a government department has to be reminded to communicate respectfully with some of society’s most vulnerable people speaks volumes. The Government must seize this opportunity to restore humanity, dignity and compassion to the system. But with the soaring cost of welfare placing enormous pressure on public finances, wider reform is also essential. The challenge is to build a system that is both financially sustainable and worthy of a civilised society.

Article continues below

A good catch

Zeus may be named after the king of the Greek gods, but even divine beings need a ticket to London. Full marks to the railway staff who escorted him home. Though we suspect the little fare dodger will be making tracks again soon.

News.title: Britain unleashes £142million underwater drone fleet as threat of sea warfare grows
News.content:
Britain unleashes £142million underwater drone fleet as threat of sea warfare grows

As the UK military dramatically transforms into a combined force of manned vehicles and unmanned vehicles, the UK pumps millions into a new sea drone to wage war under the high seas

View 3 Images Anti-mine drones will protect UK warships, like Type 45 Destroyer HMS Dragon (Image: Image by PO Phot Chris Sellars; © UK MOD Crown Copyright 2026 / SWNS)

Defence chiefs have pumped £142million into making underwater drones to help get rid of deadly sea mines and wage war underwater.

‌



‌



New REMUS 620 unmanned submarines will be deployed mostly to keep sailors away from dangerous explosives on the high-seas. The latest move is part of modernising the Royal Navy into a hybrid force in searching remotely for hazardous bombs planted by the UK’s enemies.

‌



The Navy is already receiving £90m for offshore support vessels aimed at backing up Britain’s warships. Protecting sea routes is becoming an increasingly hazardous mission for global militaries as seen by Iran’s closing of the Strait of Hormuz.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 3 Images The REMUS 620 submarine drone is pictured

New technology aims to keep Royal Navy sailors out of danger

Tehran’s shadowy Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has planted a large number of sea mines across the strategic waterway chokepoint.

‌



And Ukraine has recently used its Sea Baby sea surface drone to attack a number of Russian ships including a £150m corvette which it sunk over the weekend.

REMUS 620 sea drones, made by Huntington Ingalls Industries, will operate in dangerous areas, searching out sea mines after being deployed from warships or submarines.

‌



It can travel at up to eight knots, dive to depths of 600 yards and operate for up to 110 hours on a single mission. The contract will support jobs in the UK, including in Portchester, in Hampshire.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP said: "This investment strengthens our ability to protect freedom of navigation, which is critical to our security and our economy.

‌



“By using the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the Cold War to put the latest technology in the hands of our sailors, we are taking them out of harm's way and giving them the tools to keep vital shipping routes open, keeping us all safe in a more dangerous world."

View 3 Images REMUS 620 drone will protect ships and sailors

‌



Royal Navy sets sights on a crewed and uncrewed future by 2030

The latest Royal Navy investment highlights how, increasingly, warship crews will operate alongside uncrewed vessels in the air, on the surface and underwater.

The additional uncrewed vessels follow the recent £90m deal between the UK and Norway for three new mine-hunting motherships.

‌



The Royal Navy uses REMUS UUVs to find sea mines, survey the seabed and locate wrecks. They use sonar to map large areas of water, so analysts can review the data from a safe distance and keep sailors and divers out of minefields.

Small and portable, they can be launched quickly from boats or warships in coastal waters and the deep sea.

‌



As part of the Defence Investment Plan, the government is making the largest ever drone investment in Defence.

It is spending over £5bn on autonomous systems to enable the transformation from crewed to both crewed and uncrewed vessels by 2030.

‌



Duane Fotheringham, president of HII's Unmanned Systems group which is making the drones, said:

“HII is proud that the Royal Navy has selected the REMUS UUV and Sea Launcher to support its critical mine countermeasures missions.

Article continues below

“This selection reflects the Royal Navy's confidence in our proven technology and our shared commitment to maritime security. We are honored to support the Royal Navy and to help keep sailors out of harm's way.”

News.title: Nuclear test veterans will get full truth, says Burnham, as he confirms independent panel
News.content:
Andy Burnham has told nuclear test veterans they will get "the full truth" as he confirmed plans for an investigation into the health legacy of Britain's Cold War-era atomic programme.

The prime minister has ordered an independent panel modelled on the Hillsborough disaster investigation to assess the potential impact of testing exercises in the 1950s and 1960s.

Burnham told veterans and their families that the government would treat the process with the "utmost seriousness" as he vowed to set up a "gold standard" investigation.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) has for decades denied it covered up the impact of radiation on troops ordered to carry out nuclear weapons tests.

A BBC Newsnight special programme heard reaction from veterans, including John Morris, a laundry operator at a nuclear test site who went on to develop cancer and lost a four-month-old son. He believes both were linked to radiation exposure.

He said: "Seventy-two years ago I was an 18-year-old, sent to Christmas Island, totally unaware of what I was being led into.

"I am here today and I am looking for, and sincerely hope we will get, justice."

News.title: Nuclear test veterans speak to BBC about search for justice
News.content:
Nuclear test veterans and their relatives have reacted to the prime minister's announcement of an investigation into the health legacy of Britain's Cold War-era atomic programme.

Andy Burham said a panel will assess the potential impact of testing exercises in the 1950s and 1960s on troops, adding that the process will be treated with the "utmost seriousness".

The BBC heard reaction from veterans and their families as part of Newsnight's 'Nuclear Test Veterans: The Newsnight Special'.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) has for decades denied it covered up the impact of radiation on troops ordered to carry out nuclear weapons tests.

You can watch the full Newsnight special on BBC Two or on BBC iPlayer.

News.title: Anthony Zurcher: Trump's Nvidia intervention ties his political fortunes to the AI boom
News.content:
The Nvidia story has also exposed rifts in Trump's own administration, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a China hawk, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a vocal proponent of AI, publicly feuding over whether to impose new restrictions on AI chip exports.

Both Bessent and Lutnick travelled with Trump on his recent trip to China, although it was the commerce secretary who hitched a ride back to the White House on the Marine One helicopter when Trump returned to Washington last Thursday.

Polling also indicated that political corruption was a top issue for voters this year.

The president's willingness to intervene in the deliberations of a major private company in which he owns millions of dollars of stock could further fuel those concerns.

Trump's decision to help save Huang â noting on Monday that "we have to protect our geniuses, and he certainly is a genius" â could further inflame the public's sense that the rich and powerful, genius or not, play by a different set of rules.

"It almost feels like they've bent the rule, the regulation, to allow this to happen because it's such an important part of our economy right now," Steve Bannon, a former top Trump adviser, said on his podcast on Monday.

"Even in the crash of 2008... I never saw the government step in and take over a board of directors."

For this American president, however, these risks appear to be worth taking because of the stakes involved.

Trump has long viewed the success of the US economy as a key part of his political legacy.

He boasted of the historic growth and low unemployment during his first presidential term (while glossing over the disruptions caused by the Covid pandemic).

And since returning to office, he has celebrated as major US stock indices posted new record highs.

Recent US economic expansion has been fuelled largely by investment in AI technology, and Trump has become one of the industry's biggest boosters.

He scolded states and local governments for blocking data centre construction and predicted that the nation that wins the race for supremacy in AI â which he has tried to rebrand as "super intelligence" â will control the fate of the world.

If Trump views the economy as the key to his political success and AI as instrumental to the health of the US economy, then his dramatic, precedent-shattering actions to try to rescue Nvidia, the company at the centre of America's AI industry, make more sense.

In the weeks since concerns over Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy first surfaced, Nvidia's stock price tumbled more than 32%.

Last Friday alone, it fell 14%.

US stock indices tumbled as well, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq down 10% last week and the larger S&P 500 dropping 8.6%.

The recent financial turmoil may have given Trump a glimpse into a future where AI growth is just the latest financial bubble â like the housing market in 2008 and internet companies in 2001 â that is due for a resounding pop, with similarly dire economic consequences to follow.

Trump's intervention on behalf of Huang arrested that drop, at least for a day.

On Tuesday, Nvidia's stock price gave back much of the bounce it had enjoyed, and larger stock indices were mixed. The fate of the America economy and the AI juggernaut that has powered it is still undetermined.

Trump's intervention may not be a crisis fully averted, but only a crisis delayed.

And if an AI reckoning does come, the US president will be hard-pressed to avoid being caught in the maelstrom.

News.title: Third of young Brits have never had sex, but many are sexting and watching porn
News.content:
British people, particularly teens and young adults, are having less or no sex compared to past generations, but lots are watching porn and sexting, a major study reveals.

It is the first time The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles' (Natsal, external) research into general public sex lives has asked about online behaviours.

Half of people aged 16 to 24 have sent or received sexual images on their phone in the last year, while one in two young women and almost nine in 10 young men say they have viewed pornography.

But a third of this age group have never had sex, up from a fifth in the last study 12 years ago.

Adults under 45 are having less sex too, doing it twice a month, on average, down from once a week in 1990.

News.title: Thomas Markle indicted in US for possessing child sex abuse images
News.content:
Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex has been indicted by a federal grand jury in Los Angeles for possessing child sex abuse images.

Markle, who remains in custody in Florida, allegedly possessed materials that include at least one image involving a prepubescent minor and a minor under 12 years old, court documents filed in California show.

The 82-year-old has denied possessing images of child sex abuse. He is expected to be arraigned in Los Angeles in the coming weeks.

Last week, a judge in Florida declared Prince Harry's father-in-law mentally competent to stand trial.

The FBI arrested Markle on 6 November at an elderly care home in Florida on a single federal charge of possessing child sexual abuse material. He now faces two counts.

US attorney Bill Essayli said Markle faces a maximum of 20 years in prison on each count if convicted.

His arrest came after a search of a storage unit he had allegedly rented in Los Angeles for almost two decades uncovered the abuse material.

Markle was initially released on conditional bail but was then ordered to stay in jail pending trial after allegedly removing a location monitoring device.

In the indictment, filed by the US Attorney's Office in the Central District of California, Markle is accused of knowingly possessing 35mm film negatives on 30 October and 4 November that contained child sexual abuse materials.

The US Attorney's Office said that during both instances Markle allegedly knew the images contained such materials.

Inside the storage units, federal agents found two images that depict an adult man - whom a witness identified as Markle - with an underage child, the US attorney's office said.

They also alleged that a third image appears to depict a child in a room believed to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines. Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and he lived in Cebu until May.

"The affidavit also describes additional photographs that appear to show Markle with children in various stages of undress," prosecutors said.

News.title: Households braced for soaring energy bills with new price cap to be announced
News.content:
Domestic energy bills are expected to soar in January for millions of households, with regulator Ofgem to announce the precise increase shortly.

A typical annual bill is predicted to rise by 26% in the new year, according to consultancy Cornwall Insight, in a forecast made ahead of the official announcement.

Ofgem's new cap, which sets a maximum price for each unit of energy, will come into force at the coldest time of year. Customers pay for what they use and charities and suppliers expect debt to rise and a wave of people to need emergency support.

The government will make a Â£100 payment to millions of households to help cover winter costs, in addition to an ongoing VAT cut on electricity.

The warm home discount will also take Â£150 off bills for six million households on benefits this winter. There have been calls for this support, funded through everyone's bill, to be extended.

"We are staring down the barrel of a brutal winter," said Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice.

"Every day our advisers see people whose budgets have been completely wiped out by years of compounding crises. Millions of households are entering the coldest months of the year with nothing left."

News.title: US preparing to unveil new tariffs on global trading partners
News.content:
The US is preparing to announce new tariffs on several countries, the BBC understands.

The new import taxes would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, with China, the European Union, Mexico and Japan among the 16 jurisdictions affected.

The move comes after the White House's so-called "Section 301" investigation. It was launched in March after the US Supreme Court ruled that President Donald Trump's Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.

Trump has made tariffs a signature policy of his presidency, arguing that they will help boost American manufacturing and create jobs.

The president sent shockwaves around the world when he unveiled sweeping tariffs on global trading partners in April 2025 shortly after his return to the White House.

While the tariffs were later struck down, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argued then that overproduction abroad was displacing American manufacturing and deterring investment.

Under the new tariffs, countries will face different import tax rates depending on the deals that they have previously struck with Trump.

The announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, who remain locked in a trade dispute.

Despite last week's meeting between Trump and President Xi Jinping, the two sides have yet to fully resolve their difference with an interim agreement set to expire on 10 January.

In the run up to the Shenzhen summit the US accused China of not fully living up the terms of what it agreed in South Korea in October 2025.

Washington said Beijing was falling short on its commitments, "particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals".

However earlier on Tuesday China extended the suspension of a ban on exports critical minerals including gallium, germanium, antimony until 27 January. The ban would otherwise have come into force on Friday.

The Trump administration's tariff policy has been criticised for putting up prices for American consumers and damaging the global economy.

News.title: China-linked network using AI fakes to smear Taiwan election candidates, BBC Verify finds
News.content:
Taiwan's ruling party is being repeatedly targeted with AI videos spreading false claims about its leader and other key members ahead of crucial local elections, BBC Verify has found.

A China-linked network has pumped out more than 500 fake videos about the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) in the past year, which experts suggest is part of a long-running campaign to influence the outcome of the elections.

The videos appear to try to smear President Lai Ching-te by claiming he holds a US green card - and would abandon Taiwan if war broke out with China - which Taiwan's presidential office says is completely false. Deepfakes also appear to show Puma Shen, who is running to be the mayor of capital Taipei, using drugs, which he denies. Others seek to undermine or ridicule the politicians by showing them in children's clothing or as popular film characters.

The Taipei mayoralty has traditionally served as a springboard to the presidency. Experts say this has made Shen, who has been openly critical of Beijing, an obvious target for disinformation campaigns. The current mayor, Chiang Wan-an, is part of Taiwan's Kuomintang (KMT) party, which favours closer ties with China.

Taiwan is a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory. Beijing and Taipei have long observed an uneasy status quo under which Taiwan, backed by the US, neither formally declares independence nor unites with China.

But tensions have risen since the DPP came to power in 2016. Beijing has repeatedly accused the party of pursuing independence while China's leader Xi Jinping, who has said "reunification" with Taiwan is a key goal, has stepped up pressure against the party with increased military activity around the island.

Experts believe the current disinformation activity is part of a broader campaign against Taiwan designed to undermine trust in its democratic process.

News.title: Two arrested on suspicion of burglary at Prince and Princess of Wales's Norfolk home
News.content:
Two men have been arrested on suspicion of burglary and trespass at the Prince and Princess of Wales's country home on the Sandringham estate, police say.

Norfolk Police said it received a call just before 18:00 GMT on Monday following a report of suspicious activity at Anmer Hall.

Police deployed dogs, drones and a helicopter to search the area and arrested two men on the estate, who remain in custody.

The property was unoccupied at the time, police added. Kensington Palace said it did not comment on security matters.

William and Catherine do not live at Anmer Hall full-time, but use the estate as a country retreat during the holidays.

Val Blackmur, an 83-year-old resident who lives on the road leading up to the house, told the BBC it was "amazing" if anybody had been "stupid" enough to try breaking in.

News.title: Ministers ask public for views on changing age of consent
News.content:
The government is inviting the public to share its views as ministers consider whether or not to stagger the age of consent.

Currently adults of any age are legally able to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds, however some campaigners have argued that different limits should apply, depending on the age gap between the people involved.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted survivors, parents, young people, victim support services and the wider public to "to share their experiences and inform this process".

The government is also announcing that new limits on non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) will come into force months earlier than originally planned.

The measures, which will now become law in January 2027, invalidate confidentiality clauses in new NDAs if they prevent employees from talking about harassment or discrimination or victims from reporting criminal conduct.

The changes will also cover NDAs signed outside of the workplace and mean that even if victims of crime have signed an NDA, it would not stop them from speaking to anyone, including the media, about what had happened.

Zelda Perkins, founder of the group Can't Buy My Silence, said the laws would "uphold the integrity of a legal system that must never be used to protect perpetrators at the expense of victims".

Perkins has previously said she felt forced to sign an NDA, which prevented her talking about abuse carried out by her former boss, the film producer Harvey Weinstein.

In 2017, she told the BBC she had tried to speak out about Weinstein's behaviour towards a co-worker but was told by lawyers she "didn't have a chance" due to signing an NDA.

Writing in the Guardian,, external Burnham said: "NDAs should protect sensitive business information or commercial interests. They should not protect powerful men who have abused, harassed or discriminated against women."

He added he would "keep working to make sure NDAs can't be used to silence others, including freelancers employees and fans who experience abuse".

The government has also said it is actively looking at whether to change the law on the age of consent and that it will ask members of the public for their opinions in the new year.

Burnham said: "I not only want to make sure victims can speak out about their own abuse, but also have the opportunity to challenge the status quo."

Earlier this month, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said there was "some common sense" about staggering the age of consent but questioned whether a new law could be enforced.

She also said it was "very confusing" to see Labour ministers talk about staggering the age of consent for sexual relations while at the same time lowering the voting age to 16.

Some countries around the world have a staggered age of consent. In Canada, external the age of consent for sexual activity is 16 years-old but a 14 or 15-year-old can consent to sexual activity as long as the partner is less than five years older.

Recent high-profile cases including Russell Brand's rape conviction and allegations made against David Walliams have prompted conversations about both the age of consent and NDAs.

Mia Latter, a woman who alleges she was raped by Brand when she was 16 and he was 30, has called for the age of consent to be changed.

Latter is one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation.

Brand denied the allegations at the time and none of the six women were complainants in Brand's recent criminal trial.

In the same week that Brand was convicted, ITV News and the Guardian reported that David Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.

One woman said she now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.

Walliams said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

In late 2023, Walliams' publisher HarperCollins started an internal inquiry about the author's alleged inappropriate behaviour with young female staff.

A female staff member left the company with a pay-out and an NDA.

A spokesperson for the publisher has said: "HarperCollins UK previously terminated its publishing relationship with David Walliams.

"We take the safety of our people incredibly seriously and to respect the privacy of individuals we do not comment on employee matters."

News.title: Huntley murderer handed new whole life jail term
News.content:
A triple murderer who beat the notorious child-killer Ian Huntley to death in prison has been given a second whole life jail term.

Anthony Russell, 44, repeatedly bludgeoned Huntley, 52, with a metal bar at the high security Frankland Prison near Durham in February, Newcastle Crown Court heard.

Russell, who was jailed for life with no chance of parole in March 2022 for raping and murdering a pregnant woman and killing a mother and son in the West Midlands, admitted Huntley's murder on the second day of his trial.

Sentencing him for what prosecutors called a "cold-blooded" and planned attack, Mr Justice Hilliard KC said Russell would never be freed from prison or eligible for parole.

Huntley was serving a life sentence at the high security Frankland jail for murdering Holly Wells and Jessica Chapman, both 10, in Soham, Cambridgeshire, in 2002.

He and Russell, from Coventry, were both on A-wing and there was "tension" between the killers, the trial had heard.

At about 09:00 GMT on 26 February, Russell attacked Huntley in the prison's recycling workshop, repeatedly beating him about the head with a metal bar.

News.title: Businesses supporting Ukraine told to 'act now' to protect against Russian sabotage
News.content:
The UK government has warned that any businesses providing support for Ukraine's armed forces could become a target for Russia, and should "act now" to protect themselves.

An alert issued on Tuesday warned of an increased risk of Russian sabotage attacks such as arson and threats to staff, premises and operations.

Any businesses that are providing support to Ukraine's armed forces, including organisations in the supply chain, have been urged to take extra precautions, both physically and online.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and there has been a recent increase in Russian sabotage attempts against defence related facilities in Europe.

In September, a man appeared in court accused of planning to "torch" UK drone factories on behalf of Russia's intelligence services in an alleged sabotage plot.

Estonia has also accused Moscow of being behind an attempted arson attack at a drone factory last week, and Germany blamed it for a drone attack at Leipzig's airport in August.

The joint alert, external between MI5's National Protective Security Agency (NPSA) and the Ministry of Defence, has advised businesses to remove unnecessary detail that can be found online, emphasising that hostile reconnaissance usually begins with internet research.

It also suggested that companies install visible protective security measures "such as CCTV, secure entrances and robust access controls" to "deter hostile activity". These security measures should be "actively promoted... without giving away information that could be used to plan an attack".

When it comes to personal security, any staff members - not just those at the top - should "remain alert to their surroundings, avoid predictable routines where practicable, and consider how personal information, movements and behaviours could be used to build a picture of them, their role and their organisation".

Leaders should ensure their staff know how to manage their personal security, and know what to do if they notice anything suspicious or concerning.

The government said it will give closed-door threat briefings to critical national infrastructure and defence sector CEOs in Whitehall on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Gen Sir Richard Barrons, who co-authored last year's Strategic Defence Review, said the latest warning was "significant but not new" and the relevant companies will be "quite savvy" about the risks of cyber attacks.

He told BBC Radio 4's World at One that while there had been a recent "uptick" of these kinds of attacks across Europe, "we are not expecting an epidemic".

"These actions so far are significant but not strategic. They cause disruption, dismay and some damage but they have not reached the level of them being a strategic threat to the security of Europe," Gen Barrons added.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has warned that threats from Russia are aimed at deterring the UK's support for Ukraine, which "must not" happen.

Speaking to the Commons Foreign Affairs Committee earlier on Tuesday, Miliband said the threat from Moscow will endure beyond the Ukraine war and reiterated that any peace settlement must not reward Russia.

Security Minister Dan Jarvis said recent sabotage attempts across Europe "demonstrate the seriousness of the threats we face".

Minister for the Armed Forces, Louise Sandher-Jones, added that Russia and other hostile actors "pose a growing threat", while companies have a responsibility to strengthen their security "and help protect Britain".

News.title: Former police chief inspector jailed for rape
News.content:
A former police chief inspector who once worked with convicted murderer Wayne Couzens has been sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for two counts of rape and one of sexual assault.

Glen Mahony, 54, who was convicted at Maidstone Crown Court in September following a 10-day trial, carried out two attacks while his victim was asleep.

Mahony worked in the Civil Nuclear Constabulary (CNC) and previously worked with Couzens, who is serving a whole life tariff for the rape and murder of Sarah Everard in 2021.

In his sentencing remarks on Tuesday, Judge Gareth Branston dismissed Mahony's claims that he was targeted because he had once managed Couzens.

"You were not targeted. You were arrested because of what you did," he said.

He described Mahony's behaviour as "appalling", saying it had left his victim, who was known to him, suffering panic attacks and unable to work.

The judge said that when arrested in March 2022, Mahony told Kent Police officers that he had been Wayne Couzens's overall manager, though not his line manager.

The CNC, which guards the UK's nuclear facilities, is the force where Couzens served for six years before joining the Metropolitan Police.

Mahony, who was an inspector in charge of day-to-day police operations at the Dungeness power station before being promoted, was his commanding officer for some of that time.

Mahony was suspended on full pay by the CNC in March 2022 and resigned the day before a disciplinary hearing in January of this year.

The CNC said he would have been dismissed for gross misconduct if the disciplinary process had been carried out.

In an impact statement read to the court, his victim said she was made to feel worthless, and that "it was all about control for him".

"His actions didn't just hurt me at the time but have continued to do so each day. He has stolen my confidence," she said, having described ongoing nightmares and mental health struggles.

Det Ch Insp Tracy Evans, of Kent Police, said: "To take advantage of a woman while she is asleep and at her most vulnerable is utterly disgraceful and to then deny it happened and force the victim to relive her ordeal during a trial makes things even worse."

She also praised the "tremendous courage" of the victim in coming forward to report Mahony.

CNC Chief Constable Simon Chesterman said his immediate thoughts were with Mahony's victim, who he also commended for her bravery.

"Former officer Glen Mahony's crimes were despicable, committing the most serious sexual violence to a vulnerable female victim, who was not able to consent," he said.

"Mahony's behaviours are entirely contrary to the high standards required of a police officer with the CNC. And his actions go on to undermine the trust and confidence that the public, and particularly women, have in the police service."

Two WhatsApp groups to which Mahony belonged were also investigated by CNC professional standards.

"In these groups, Mahony sent sexist and misogynistic messages, and he did not challenge or leave the group when others sent similarly offensive messages," Chief Constable Chesterman said.

"This further underlines his disgusting opinion of women."

Mahony was promoted to chief inspector for the south division in 2020. It meant he was number three in the division's chain of command for the four nuclear sites in the south - Dungeness, Sizewell and Hinkley Point power stations, and the nuclear research centre at Harwell, Oxfordshire.

He spent most of his working life as an armed officer based at the Dungeness nuclear plant in Kent.

He joined the force in 2006, becoming a sergeant in 2011 before being promoted to inspector in 2016. This put him in operational charge of security at the site. He would have worked with Couzens, who was a constable at Dungeness between 2012 and 2018.

Couzens was also in a separate WhatsApp group with six other officers who transferred to the Met from the CNC. The messages they shared were found to be sexist, misogynistic, racist and violent, raising questions about the culture among officers at both the CNC and the Met.

News.title: Record 5,200 heat-linked deaths estimated in England this year
News.content:
More than 5,000 people suffered heat-associated deaths in England this summer, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has estimated - the highest number since records began in 2016.

The UK experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, and the estimated 5,258 heat-linked deaths were twice the previous high of 2,985 in 2022.

The most deadly period of the year for heat-related deaths was between 21 and 28 June, when there were an estimated 2,401 heat-associated deaths. Temperatures peaked at 38C in that period.

Climate change is expected to increase the length, frequency and intensity of extreme heat, the UKHSA has warned.

News.title: Tories accuse Burnham of turning No 10 into 'joke' after influencer video row
News.content:
Andy Burnham has been accused of turning the UK into "a joke" on the world stage by Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, amid a row about social media videos posted from an event in Downing Street.

Social media influencer Max Balegde has deleted a video filmed outside the door of Number 10, which was posted on TikTok, in which he mimed along to explicit lyrics.

Badenoch said it was a "disgrace" that the prime minister allowed 10 Downing Street to be "degraded".

The prime minister's spokesperson said the content was clearly not acceptable and it was "right" that Balegde had taken down the social media posts.

Balegde's video appears to have been filmed earlier this month at an event for around 60 social media influencers hosted by Burnham, who is eager to use social media to reach younger voters. Balegde also gave a speech to those present at the event.

In the video, the influencer, whose real name is Max Trobe, mouths the words "bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets", using audio from a meme that is trending online.

Bomboclaat is a Jamaican profanity referring to a menstrual cloth, while pussy is a slang term for female genitals.

It is unclear when Balegde's video was deleted but it no longer appears on his TikTok or Instagram accounts.

The creator has 3.6 million followers on TikTok and 640,000 on Instagram.

Videos which were filmed inside the Downing Street premises were recorded on government phones, the BBC can reveal.

Attendees at the event have confirmed they had to hand personal devices in and were given a phone and a camera to film with, with the footage they recorded sent to them after the event.

One of the distinctive features of Burnham's time in office has been his enthusiasm for engaging with social media influencers as a means to communicate with different groups of voters, especially younger voters.

It was an approach begun by Sir Keir Starmer, under whom a "new media unit" was formed, but has significantly intensified since July.

The engagement with influencers has elicited criticism of Burnham from those who fear it means reduced scrutiny and diminished opportunities to hold the prime minister to account.

News.title: Disability benefit review calls for closer link with claimant costs
News.content:
The main disability benefit in England and Wales should be more closely linked to the additional costs claimants face, a government-commissioned review has recommended.

The review on personal independence payment (Pip) led by Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms said the current system was "not appropriate" for claimants who do not have any extra costs arising from their condition.

The government has committed to some of its recommendations, including fast-track payments for people with severe conditions, but will not respond fully to the plans until early next year.

The Conservatives said the year-long review was a "compete farce" and showed a "complete absence of substance".

Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately added: "All we have is a report that tinkers around the edges of a failed system".

Pip is available to people with long-term physical or mental health conditions who have difficulty doing every day tasks, regardless of whether they work, and it is not linked to income or savings.

The number of people claiming Pip in England and Wales has roughly doubled since 2019 to around four million.

The Timms review was set up last year by Sir Keir Starmer's government after his aborted attempt to cut welfare spending, which was derailed by the threat of a rebellion by Labour MPs.

It was co-produced with groups representing disabled people, who had a role in drafting the report.

News.title: China hails ‘complete success’ in historic space launch carrying Pakistani astronaut
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

China has successfully carried out the historic launch of its Shenzhou 24 spacecraft, its first ever mission carrying a foreign astronaut to the country’s Tiangong space station.

Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, is flying alongside China’s Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39, in what has been hailed as an important landmark for Beijing’s crewed space programme.

The China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) said Wednesday morning’s launch was a “complete success”, with a Long March 2F rocket carrying the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft blasting off from Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in northwestern China at 8.18am Beijing Time (0.18am GMT).

The spacecraft successfully separated from the rocket and entered its predetermined orbit, and was expected to dock with the Tiangong space station around 3.48am GMT, according to the CMSA.

open image in gallery A Long March 2F Y24 rocket carrying the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft with Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, Wu Yi and Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, blasts off to China's Tiangong space station ( Reuters )

China’s official broadcast of the launch showed plumes of smoke erupting as the rocket rose from the launchpad with a deafening roar.

Crowds of people had attended a send-off ceremony for the astronauts before the launch.

Pakistani prime minister Shehbaz Sharif offered his best wishes to the astronauts ahead of the launch.

“Pakistan-China friendship is surpassing the heights of the Himalayas in its journey to outer space,” Mr Sharif said in a post on X.

Once they reach the space station, the crew will conduct over 90 scientific experiments and technology tests.

open image in gallery A Long March 2F Y24 rocket carrying the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft with Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, Wu Yi and Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, blasts off ( Reuters )

Mr Ali would conduct experiments in the fields of biotechnology and materials, including on photosynthetic microorganisms, before returning to Earth about a week later aboard the Shenzhou 23 spacecraft, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported.

The Pakistani astronaut has trained intensively for seven months since his selection for the mission in April, and has admitted that his biggest challenge was learning advanced Mandarin to communicate with his crewmates and operate complex machinery labelled in the language.

“I’m not flying for myself; I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hope of 250 million Pakistanis,” he told reporters earlier on Tuesday.

“To every child who’s watching while I’m in orbit, look up at the sky and remember that I am up there with your dreams,” Mr Ali said.

The joint mission is part of an agreement signed by China and Pakistan in February 2025.

China’s Tiangong space station, completed in late 2022, has been receiving a rotating crew of astronauts performing six-month-long missions, keeping the orbiting outpost constantly crewed.

This is the first time the space station is hosting a foreign astronaut.

open image in gallery A Long March 2F Y24 rocket carrying the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft with Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, Wu Yi and Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, blasts off ( Reuters )

Mr Ali said he hoped space cooperation between the two countries would grow from one astronaut in one flight to multiple joint flights and to the Moon, Mars and beyond.

China has plans to double the size of its space station over the coming years, and facilitate more joint missions with crews from other countries.

Its decision to focus on its own space station rather than the International Space Station comes an intense rivalry with the US, as both countries aim to land boots on the lunar surface by 2030.

News.title: Martha Ford, former Lions owner with link to auto giants, dies at 101
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Martha Firestone Ford, the tire heiress who became a link between two of the automotive industry's most iconic families and later took over the NFL's Detroit Lions, has died. She was 101.

The Lions say she died Tuesday at her home in Grosse Pointe, Michigan, surrounded by family. No cause of death was given.

Ford was a granddaughter of tire magnate Harvey Firestone, and her husband, William Clay Ford Sr., was Henry Ford's grandson. He also owned the Lions for a half-century before his death in 2014.

Martha Ford then took over his controlling interest in the team, keeping it within the family. Although she seldom spoke to reporters or commented publicly on the direction of the franchise, her influence was felt. She was in charge of the team from 2014 until 2020, when she turned the Lions over to her daughter, Sheila Ford Hamp.

The Lions made the playoffs in 2014, but lost seven of their first eight games the following season. In November 2015, the team fired its president and general manager in a midseason shakeup. When she announced the changes, Ford told fans the franchise intended to “identify and hire the very best leadership in order to produce a consistently, winning football team.”

The Lions played better down the stretch that season, and after hiring Bob Quinn as their new general manager, they returned to the playoffs a year later.

Born Sept. 16, 1925, in Akron, Ohio, Martha Parke Firestone graduated from Vassar College in 1946 and married William Clay Ford the next year.

Their wedding received a huge amount of coverage — looking back in 2014, the Akron Beacon Journal described it as “Akron’s royal wedding” — and the marriage joined two families that already had a long history.

Harvey Firestone, the founder of the Firestone Tire and Rubber Co., was a close friend of Ford Motor Co. founder Henry Ford. Ford chose Firestone to supply the tires for the first Model T in 1906. The two men often went on long camping trips together, sometimes accompanied by their friend Thomas Edison.
