World.title: Poll finds US voters want government to end Iran war regardless of terms
World.content:
New survey finds that 55 percent of voters, including 80 percent of Democrats, want the Iran war brought to an end immediately.

Share Poll finds US voters want government to end Iran war regardless of terms on social media

A new poll has found that a majority of voters in the United States want an end to the US-Israel war on Iran immediately, even if it means accepting less favourable conditions.

Overall, 55 percent of those surveyed agreed with an “end to the war now, regardless of the terms”.

That number was even higher among Democrats and independents, who agreed with the statement at a rate of 80 percent and 59 percent, respectively. About 25 percent of Republicans said the same.

A majority of Democratic voters also supported steps to pressure the administration of President Donald Trump to stop the conflict.

Fifty-three percent of party members said they would favour Congress withholding funding for military operations, and 51 percent would back an “an Iran war-funding cutoff” in upcoming budget negotiations, even if the manoeuvre risked a government shutdown.

The numbers were published on Tuesday as part of the latest Critical Issues Poll, released by the University of Maryland and the research firm Ipsos.

Shibley Telhami, the poll’s principal investigator, said he was surprised by the level of support for ending the war, regardless of the terms.

“We knew that people were strongly opposed to this war and wanted it to end,” he told Al Jazeera in a phone call. “What we were less sure of is what they would be willing to accept to achieve this.”

The survey asked 1,022 US adults about their perspectives on the war.

In one question, they were tasked with assessing with three options: whether to end the conflict immediately, escalate militarily, or continue on the current path in order to extract concessions from Iran.



Just 21 percent of all respondents favoured the current path, and 18 percent supported escalation.

“Clearly, the public mood is to end it now, whatever it takes,” said Telhami.

Questioning the rationale for war

Voters also appear sceptical about the US government’s arguments in favour of the war, which include dismantling Iran’s nuclear programme.

The Critical Issues Poll found that only 28 percent of those surveyed believed that the war had left Iran in “worse position” to develop nuclear weapons.

While the US has long voiced concerned that Iran could pursue nuclear arms, intelligence assessments have not found evidence that Tehran has authorised such a step since abandoning its nuclear weapons programme in 2003.

The Strait of Hormuz has also emerged as a key issue, with Iran closing the waterway to commercial traffic early in the war. The Trump administration has responded with a naval blockade in the strait.

Some 20 percent of the world’s oil supply passes through the maritime artery, and fuel prices have spiked as a result of the war.

About 35 percent of respondents in Tuesday’s poll said that they believe Iran is now in control of the strait, while just 12.7 percent said the US is in control.

The poll comes as the Democratic Party is debating how far it should go to end the unpopular war.

In the recent midterm elections, backlash against the war — and as well as related issues like rising fuel prices — contributed to big gains for the Democratic Party.

Trump’s Republican Party, meanwhile, suffered one of its most bruising setbacks in modern US history, losing control of both chambers of Congress.

Members of the Democratic Party’s anti-war left have pointed to the results as proof that voters want an end to the war and an end to US support for Israel.

But that position has brought them into conflict with members of the party’s more hawkish establishment wing.

While leaders such as Representative Hakeem Jeffries and Senator Chuck Schumer have both expressed support for ending the war, they have yet to commit to aggressive strategies to reach that goal.

That includes potentially cutting off funding for military operations against Iran, or using an upcoming funding battle in December to demand that the White House end the war.

“A lot of Democratic figures are dismissing the intensity of public feeling on this issue,” said Telhami. “If they don’t adapt, they will be left behind.”

He added that progressive figures such as Senator Bernie Sanders and Senator Chris Van Hollen have been among those pressing for a more assertive stance.



Van Hollen, who is challenging Schumer to lead the Democratic majority in the US Senate, has used the war to portray the party’s moderate leadership as out of step with voters.

The poll found that Democratic voters prefer Van Hollen over Schumer by a ratio of nearly three to one.

World.title: Alaska ends deal to give voter records to US Justice Department
World.content:
The decision follows the conclusion of the 2026 midterm elections and an effort under Trump to collect state voter rolls.

Share Alaska ends deal to give voter records to US Justice Department on social media

Alaska has terminated a memorandum of understanding that granted the United States Department of Justice (DOJ) access to the state’s voter rolls.

On Monday, outgoing Lieutenant Governor Nancy Dahlstrom, who oversees the state’s elections, announced she had notified the Justice Department that Alaska was withdrawing from the 2025 memo, effective immediately.

In a statement, Dahlstrom said her state had entered the agreement “in good faith to cooperate with our federal law enforcement partners”. But she acknowledged a shift had taken place after the 2026 midterm elections.

“The circumstances have now changed,” Dahlstrom wrote. “The election has concluded and the agreement no longer serves a continuing purpose.”

The reversal comes after months of pressure from the administration of President Donald Trump for states to surrender their voter rolls to federal authorities.

Trump has argued that such information was necessary to root out fraud during the November 3 midterms.

But officials in certain states argued that the federal government was encroaching on their constitutional authority. Under the US Constitution, only states have the power to administer elections.

Experts have also called Trump’s claims of “rigged” elections unsubstantiated.

No voters flagged for removal

The memorandum, signed last December at the Justice Department’s behest, established terms under which federal officials could flag potentially ineligible voters on Alaska’s voter rolls.

“Since that time, the DOJ has not identiﬁed any potentially ineligible voters or raised concerns regarding Alaska’s voter registration records,” the state Division of Elections said.



“No voters were removed from Alaska’s voter rolls as a result of the agreement.”

The announcement came as the state certified its November 3 midterm election results, in which Democrats flipped a Senate seat and won the governor’s office.

Alaska was one of several surprise battlegrounds during the midterms.

Democrat Mary Peltola unseated two-term Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in a fiercely contested Senate race marred by allegations of a spoiler candidate recruited to sabotage the senator’s re-election bid.

Meanwhile, Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won the state’s governorship, ending nearly three decades of Republican control in that office.

Democrats nationwide made significant gains, flipping both chambers of Congress in the midterms.

That result was largely fuelled by voter frustration under Trump, whose Republican Party suffered defeats in former strongholds like Texas.

A legal battle over voter rolls

Faced with drooping approval ratings in the lead-up to the election, Trump had falsely claimed that many non-citizens were registered to vote across the country.

His administration sued some 30 states as well as Washington, DC, after they declined to hand over their unredacted voter rolls for review.

Twenty-eight of those cases were ultimately dismissed in court, according to the Brennan Center for Justice, a public policy institute at New York University.

The Justice Department suffered a further setback last month when a federal judge struck down its nationwide voter-list maintenance programme, ruling that it lacked legal authority to collect and assess state registration lists. The administration has appealed the ruling.

Alaska was one of at least 16 states that complied with the administration’s demands for voter roll access.

But it was sued by voting rights advocates for surrendering voter information, in violation of the Alaska Constitution.

In its Monday statement, Alaska’s Division of Elections said it had directed the Justice Department to destroy Alaska’s confidential voter information in accordance with the 2025 memo — a move that could have implications for the pending lawsuit.

On Tuesday, Democratic State Senator Bill Wielechowski suggested the latest termination was timed to prevent further scrutiny from the lawsuit.

“The real reason they did this is to try to make the lawsuit over this release go away before the incoming Gov. Kreiss-Tomkins Administration could settle or produce discovery,” Wielechowski wrote on social media.

Kreiss-Tomkins is set to be sworn in as governor on December 7.



Wielechowski also noted that Alaska’s request for the Trump administration to delete the records is “likely meaningless”, since federal authorities have “undoubtedly already loaded it” onto government databases.

In its Monday statement, Alaska’s Division of Elections said its decision to end the memo did not constitute an admission of wrongdoing.

The state’s interests, it added, were “best served by terminating the agreement and continuing to rely on its established voter list-maintenance procedures”.

A Justice Department spokesperson told The Associated Press on Tuesday that the department would issue a formal response to the state.

World.title: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
World.content:
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.

Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.

Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."

Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged China spy who led Megaspeed, a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.

The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping to divert advanced chips to China.

In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".

But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.

"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.

Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with any efforts to get to the bottom of whether the company or Huang potentially knew about any chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.

"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.

"It shouldn't be what my message would be either."

While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.

The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return.

World.title: French ex-President Sarkozy and wife Carla Bruni to face trial
World.content:
Nicolas Sarkozy and his wife Carla Bruni-Sarkozy are to face trial next year over charges stemming from the former French president's conviction for conspiring to fund his election campaign with money from late Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi.

The charges centre on the retraction of the testimony of a key witness who had initially said he had evidence that could incriminate Sarkozy.

The pair deny any wrongdoing.

Sarkozy was given a five-year sentence in the case last September and became the first French ex-president to go to jail, even though he only spent 20 days behind bars. He has always denied doing anything wrong in the case and the appeals verdict is expected next Monday.

Since losing his re-election bid in 2012, Sarkozy has faced several criminal investigations.

In 2024, he was handed a one-year sentence â of which six months were suspended â over the illegal financing of his 2012 re-election campaign.

In 2021, he was found guilty of trying to bribe a judge and sentenced to three years in jail â two of them suspended â and thus became the first former French president to get a custodial sentence. He was allowed to serve his time at home wearing a tag instead of going to jail.

The new case centres on a Libyan businessman, Ziad Takieddine, who had said he had written proof that Sarkozy's 2007 campaign bid was "abundantly" financed by Tripoli, and that the â¬50m (Â£43m) in payments continued after he became president.

Takieddine, who died last year, withdrew his accusations in an interview in 2020.

At the time, Sarkozy was said to have stated: the "truth is finally coming out", but officials found the retraction to be "insincere" and a new investigation was launched into the "Save Sarko" file â the nickname the alleged perpetrators had used for the operation, according to French media.

So the former head of state and his wife, an Italian-born former supermodel and singer, will now face charges of "criminal conspiracy with intent to commit fraud" and benefiting from witness tampering. They deny any wrongdoing.

World.title: Indian government has 'lost the plot', says 'cockroach' leader barred from UK flight
World.content:
One of the leaders of India's "cockroach" movement has said the Delhi government has "completely lost the plot" after he was stopped from leaving the country for the UK.

Saurav Das said he was meant to board a flight on Tuesday morning but was told by immigration officers his passport had been "flagged" because of discrepancies involving his date of birth.

In an interview with the BBC, Das said there were no discrepancies in his documents, accusing the Indian government of using cheap tactics to stop activists from travelling and speaking on issues that matter to young people.

The BBC has reached out to the federal home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment.

Saurav told the BBC World Service's Newshour programme the incident showed the government was "scared".

"They are scared of the cockroach movement. They're scared of young people asking them questions because they have never had to deal with a generation that wants to ask questions so head on. So that jitters them."

By not allowing him to travel, he said the government had lowered India's stature in the world.

"It's international news that I am unable to travel to the UK," he said. "And this shows Prime Minister Modi in such poor light.

"It's a way to harass, to target activists, young voices in India by the Modi government."

Das said he had been invited by the Oxford Union, as well as universities including Cambridge and Edinburgh, to speak about the movement.

Ratna Singh, another leader of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), wrote: "The manner in which Saurav was not allowed to board today raises deeply troubling questions about the state of freedom of expression and the space being allowed for young voices in this country."

On Tuesday, the London School of Economics Student Union's Amnesty International Unit, a student-led charity group, shared a post on Instagram saying that an event featuring Das had been "indefinitely postponed".

World.title: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
World.content:
Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US.

In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.

Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.

Huawei said, external the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis", adding that it would "take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests".

Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.

However, the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.

Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.

Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors.

During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge.

"For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in statement, external.

"Thanks to the work of the FBI and our federal prosecutors, those who engaged in these criminal activities will be held accountable."

However, defence attorney Brian Heberlig said it was by dint of hard work that Huawei's business had expanded with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff.

Following the verdict, Heberlig told the BBC that Huawei was gratified that the jury had rejected the racketeering charge.

"The RICO [Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act] count that alleged that Huawei was a corrupt organisation, with a corporate culture and policy of committing crime. That was, in our view, a significant overreach, and the jury soundly rejected it," he said.

"Of course, we have mixed emotions about the rest of the verdict ... [we] thought that Huawei was deserving of acquittals across the board."

Sentencing is planned for September 2027. Heberlig said there will be "significant advocacy" to achieve the lowest sentence possible. Following that, he said he fully expects Huawei to appeal.

"If I know Huawei, that fight will continue, and the company's not going to rest until it's pursued every last argument it can through appeal, and hopefully, ultimately toward vindication," he said.

World.title: Land mine casualties soar in Syria, two years after war
World.content:
Eleven-year-old Alaa was tending her family's goats with her siblings in a field behind their home in Umm Khuzaym, north-west Syria, on Sunday when there was a flash and a deafening bang.

"Then we heard people screaming," Alaa's father, Walid Mohammed Al-Ghafar, told the BBC.

Walid ran outside to find his daughter lying face down, killed, and her 10-year-old brother, Mahmoud, seriously injured.

Unwittingly, the children had triggered a landmine.

The incident and others this week bring to nearly 1,000 the number of children killed or injured by explosive ordnance in Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, according to the UN Mine Action Service (Unmas).

The village is one of many where families have returned to homes and farmland that were once on the front lines of Syria's 13-year civil war.

Alaa's father said demining teams had visited several times to clear the fields. He and other residents believed it was safe for farmers and children to move around.

But mines and other explosives can lie far beyond former battle lines, making it difficult to establish which areas are safe.

"Remnants of war from today's conflicts are often very widely and broadly scattered, often without patterns, which makes it extremely difficult to do clearance," Katrin Atkins, research lead at Landmine Monitor, a global mine monitoring initiative, told the BBC.

The dangers are reflected in a sharp rise in casualties across Syria.

A total of 1,602 people were killed or injured by landmines and explosive remnants of war in 2025 alone, an increase of more than 50% on the previous year, according to the Landmine Monitor report, published by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines on Tuesday.

Only Myanmar, with 1,891 casualties, recorded more.

The report attributes the rise in Syria partly to the large-scale return of refugees and internally displaced people following Assad's overthrow.

"When you look at population movement, a couple of months later you see an increase of incidents in these areas, because that's exactly where people go and start to use the fields again," Atkins said.

More than 60% of casualties recorded by the world's largest landmine clearance charity, the Halo Trust, involve farming, agriculture or shepherding, according to its Syria programme manager, Simon Jackson.

"They're not going to wait for the government or for organisations like us to come and tell them that everything is safe and clear," he told the BBC. "People are taking risks out of desperation."

Since Assad's fall on 8 December 2024, Unmas has recorded at least 1,556 incidents in Syria involving explosive ordnance.

They have caused 2,701 casualties: 935 people killed and 1,766 injured. Children account for 995 of those victims, or about 37%.

But the toll is likely to be higher, with experts estimating that overall casualties could be under-reported by 25-50%.

World.title: Nigerian monarch, 92, suspended after sexual assault claims
World.content:
One of Nigeria's best-known monarchs, the Emir of Daura, has been suspended from all official engagements and travel following allegations of sexual assault by a Polish tourist.

The visitor said Umar Farouk Umar, 92, had grabbed her chest during a tourism encounter and that she felt disgusted by the experience.

The allegation sparked widespread discussion across social media platforms, with many calling for the suspension of the emir and an investigation - calls the Katsina state government has now heeded.

Umar has not commented on the allegations or his suspension.

He is one of several emirs - a traditional role dating back to pre-colonial times - who still wield great cultural and religious influence in northern Nigeria, although they have lost their political power.

Daura, where Umar serves as emir, holds an extremely important position for the Hausa people who dominate northern Nigeria. It is widely regarded as their spiritual homeland and the origin of the Hausa royal lineage, serving as the core of Hausa origin mythology and the legitimate foundation of traditional authority.

Politicians routinely visit his palace for royal prayers and to gain his support.

On her Instagram page, the tourist said she had spent 30 days travelling around Nigeria before visiting the Emir's palace on 14 November.

She posted a video, which has since been deleted, in which a man who appears to be the emir is holding her hands in his lap.

After some moments she was heard saying: "Stop, stop" as the hands reached for her chest.

According to a statement, Katsina Governor Dikko Umaru Radda directed the immediate constitution of a committee to investigate the allegations.

The statement said the state government was taking the allegations seriously and would rely on the committee's findings to determine the appropriate course of action.

It said the committee's findings and recommendations would be fully implemented, stressing that justice would be served.

However, it did not disclose the membership of the investigative committee, its terms of reference or the timeline for submitting its report.

The emir has been on the throne since 2007, succeeding his brother Bashar dan Umaru, who reigned for 41 years.

World.title: Israeli air strike kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza
World.content:
At least seven Palestinians, including a senior Hamas security official, have been killed in Israeli air strikes in the Gaza Strip, health officials and first responders say.

Naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas's internal security service, was targeted in western Gaza City, Gaza's Hamas-run interior ministry said. The 50-year-old had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid by Israeli special forces.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz announced that Abu Nahel was "eliminated" by the Israeli military.

The six other people were killed in two earlier air strikes elsewhere in Gaza.

Three people, including a teenage boy, were killed in the Wadi Gaza area, south of Gaza City, according to the health officials and first responders. The other three were killed at a police station in the al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Younis, they added.

Gaza's police force, which operates under the interior ministry, said two of its officers were among those who died in the second attack. It also accused Israel of "an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus aimed at sowing chaos" in the territory.

The Israeli military said it struck "military operatives" in both areas.

Witnesses said an Israeli drone targeted Naeem Abu Nahel as he was walking on a side street near a tent camp for displaced people in Gaza City.

Several other people were reportedly seriously injured in the strike.

The Israeli military said Abu Nahel had "possessed extensive institutional knowledge" about Hamas's internal security service - which is responsible for enforcing discipline, protecting infrastructure and rooting out informants - and that his death constituted "a blow to the apparatus's management capabilities".

It also alleged that he had advanced attacks on Israeli troops and civilians during the war and that it killed him "to remove the threat he posed".

Gaza's interior ministry said Abu Nahel's killing followed what it described as the internal security service's "important achievements in combating gangs collaborating with the occupation [Israel] and operating in areas under the control of its military".

World.title: Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports
World.content:
Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after German reports that Russia is preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.

Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media. It was not clear which country had authored the reports.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said such reports were "not new, yet they remain no less shocking", and a government spokesman said the reports were being taken "very seriously".

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he had not seen the reports but dismissed stories citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously".

The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and said the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign".

Citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, public broadcasters NDR and WDR and newspaper SÃ¼ddeutscher Zeitung, said the Russian satellite was dubbed "Sputnik-S" and was equipped with a nuclear warhead. It could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, including important communication and observation satellites.

Asked about the reports, the Nato secretary general told a press conference in Berlin alongside Merz: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element."

The Western defensive alliance had a variety of response options, said Rutte.

"When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary."

Merz did not confirm or deny the reports of Russia's plans, but said they "reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue".

German government spokesman Stefan Kornelius warned against causing "excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers".

Josef Aschbacher, the head of the European Space Agency, told the Handeslblatt newspaper that having nuclear weapons in space was "the ultimate nightmare scenario".

Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit.

Bleddyn Bowen, co-director of the Space Research Centre at Durham University, said that exploding a nuclear weapon in space would have "massive infrastructural effects" as there were now more than 15,000 active satellites. But he told the BBC's Today programme that "the effect of these weapons would be extremely indiscriminate and also take out a lot of Russia's own space infrastructure".

Other countries, including the US and China, have deployed or plan to deploy other weapons in space, exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.

In 2024 the US accused Russia of developing a "space-based" anti-satellite weapon armed with a nuclear warhead. Russia denied the accusation.

"Our position is clear and transparent. We have always been categorically against the deployment of nuclear weapons in space and we are still against it," President Vladimir Putin said at the time.

In September the US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the US had "on-orbit, space-control weapons" circling the planet, but did not provide specifics. In response to the announcement, the Kremlin's Peskov told Russian media that space "must be free of any weapon".

World.title: Disability groups, others demand representation, funding ahead of 2027 polls
World.content:
The Joint National Association of Persons with Disabilities (JONAPWD) has called on political parties and aspirants seeking elective offices in 2027 to engage persons with disabilities and commit to policies that guarantee their representation in governance.

The association said persons with disabilities must move beyond being included in political activities as voters to occupying leadership positions and influencing decisions that affect their lives.

JONAPWD President, Abdullahi Usman, made the call on Tuesday at the third Conference of Stakeholders on Disability Inclusion in Nigeria (COSDIN 3.0), themed Beyond Participation: Advancing Disability Leadership and Accountable Governance in Nigeria.

Mr Usman said the disability community could influence the outcome of the 2027 elections if its members recognised their collective political strength and negotiated with political parties and candidates.

“Any political party, any aspirant who wants the vote of persons with disabilities in this country needs to come and sit down with the community of persons with disabilities to tell us the promise you have for the inclusion of persons with disabilities in this country,” he said.

He criticised political parties for treating persons with disabilities as symbolic representatives rather than giving them meaningful opportunities to participate in decision-making.

Mr Usman also called for adequate funding for the National Commission for Persons with Disabilities and similar state institutions, arguing that establishing disability commissions without providing the resources to function undermines the implementation of the law.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Nigeria enacted the Discrimination Against Persons with Disabilities (Prohibition) Act in 2018, which was signed into law in January 2019. The legislation established the National Commission for Persons with Disabilities to promote and protect the rights of persons with disabilities.

However, Mr Usman said the law and disability commissions had not translated into effective inclusion, urging the federal and state governments to provide adequate funding and strengthen accountability mechanisms.

He also insisted that persons with disabilities should lead conversations about their rights rather than have people without disabilities speak on their behalf.

“Being a person with disability only means that I cannot walk without crutches. It does not mean my brain also cannot work without crutches,” he said.

Inclusion must translate into decision-making

In her keynote address, the Deputy Director of MacArthur Foundation, Amina Salihu, said the passage of the disability law was only the beginning of the struggle, warning that legislation without accountability would do little to change everyday experiences.

She questioned how government institutions were enforcing the law, monitoring compliance and ensuring that public resources matched their commitments to disability inclusion.

Ms Salihu cited Section 29 of the Act, which requires persons with disabilities to make up at least five per cent of the workforce in public organisations, as one measure for assessing implementation.

She also highlighted barriers confronting persons with disabilities in accessing employment, healthcare and public infrastructure, including the absence of sign language interpreters during recruitment and inaccessible public buildings.

“The law is really the floor and not the ceiling of our ambition,” she said, arguing that government agencies must demonstrate measurable improvements rather than rely on policies and declarations.

She further urged disability organisations to strengthen internal accountability and ensure that women, young people and other marginalised groups within the disability community influence decisions.

Similarly, Yunusa Ya’u, convener of the Nigeria Civil Society Situation Room, said establishing disability commissions across several states was insufficient without sustained advocacy and implementation.

He urged persons with disabilities to develop an inclusion agenda ahead of the 2027 elections and use it to engage political parties and candidates.

“If people with disabilities do not participate, then we would always have a deficit between promises and actual implementation,” he said.

Mr Ya’u argued that persons with disabilities are better positioned to identify and address the barriers they face, making their participation in governance essential.

Meanwhile, Omar Alihashi, head of Political Affairs at the Canadian High Commission in Nigeria, said political inclusion must extend beyond the ability to vote independently and safely to contesting elections, influencing public policy and holding public office.

He reaffirmed Canada’s support for Nigerian organisations working to advance disability rights and strengthen democratic participation.

Abimbola Oyelohunnu, a programme officer for social development at the ECOWAS Commission, also called for investment in technology, disability data collection, training and early identification of children with disabilities.

She urged governments to recognise the economic burden on families caring for children with disabilities and incorporate the care economy into social protection policies.

World.title: Nigerian govt identifies 268 obsolete laws, asks NASS to approve revised compendium
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu has asked the National Assembly to approve a revised edition of the Laws of the Federation of Nigeria after a government audit identified 268 of the country’s existing laws as either obsolete or repealed.

Mr Tinubu said a specialised committee, supervised by the Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, Lateef Fagbemi, reviewed 932 laws and recommended that 664 of them be included in the 2025 edition of the Laws of the Federation of Nigeria.

The request was in an executive communication read by Senate President Godswill Akpabio during Tuesday’s plenary.

In the letter, Mr Tinubu explained that the committee was mandated to review the existing laws to reflect legislative, constitutional, institutional and technological changes that had occurred over the past two decades.

The president said updating the laws would make them more accessible and provide a comprehensive reference for Nigeria’s legal framework, thereby strengthening the country’s democracy.

He urged the lawmakers to consider and approve the revised compendium, which would constitute an updated edition of the Laws of the Federation of Nigeria 2025.

The president noted that the compendium would serve as a reliable legal reference for the judiciary, legal practitioners, government institutions, domestic and foreign investors, and the general public.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“An updated, accurate, and easily accessible compendium of federal laws is indispensable to our democratic and economic growth.

“Upon enactment, the Laws of the Federation of Nigeria 2025 will serve as a reliable legal reference for the judiciary, legal practitioners, government institutions, domestic and foreign investors and the general public, thereby enhancing legal certainty, institutional efficiency and public confidence in our justice system,” the president said.

After reading the letter, Mr Akpabio referred it to the Senate Committee on Judiciary, Human Rights and Legal Matters, in collaboration with the Committee on Rules and Business, for detailed examination and further legislative action.

Mr Akpabio, however, urged his colleagues to ensure that no provisions were altered during the review process.

“This is a very excellent exercise. However, as lawmakers, it will be good for you to also take a second look at it to be sure that, particularly, the amendments are well reflected and that line-by-line consideration of the laws is well reflected, and no clauses have been tampered with by those who transmitted the laws as passed by the National Assembly.

“And thereafter, we will do the needful of giving formal approval to these Laws of the Federation 2025, for it to be immediately circulated and in use,” he said.

Similarly, Yahaya Abdullahi (APC, Kebbi North) cautioned his colleagues against rushing the exercise, given its implications for the country’s legal system.

“After close to 21 years, I think this exercise is very important and consequential. This is not something we can rush into because of the consequences that will follow in our justice system.

“We need to forward this to the Committee on Judiciary, Human Rights and Legal Matters before we lend our voice to this important matter. The laws touch different facets of justice delivery in Nigeria,” he said.

The Deputy Senate President, Barau Jibrin, also suggested that the National Assembly could engage consultants to prepare a summarised version of the compendium to make it easier for lawmakers to review.

Nigeria’s outdated laws

The last official consolidation of the Laws of the Federation of Nigeria was undertaken in 2004 and covered federal statutes in force as of 31 December 2002. The 16-volume compilation, known as the Laws of the Federation of Nigeria 2004 (LFN 2004), was subsequently approved by the National Assembly through the Revised Edition (Laws of the Federation of Nigeria) Act, 2007, which came into effect on 25 May 2007.

The compilation brought together existing federal laws in an organised format, but it has not undergone another official consolidation since then. Consequently, several laws enacted after December 2002, as well as amendments and repeals introduced over the years, have not been incorporated into the official compendium.

Although there was an attempt to revise the compilation in 2010, the exercise did not receive the necessary legislative approval to give it legal backing.

The absence of an updated compilation has created difficulties for lawyers, judges, lawmakers, researchers, government institutions and members of the public in identifying the current status of federal legislation. It has also meant that repealed or outdated provisions could remain in older compilations, while subsequent amendments and new laws have to be consulted separately.

The National Assembly had previously acknowledged the problem. In November 2023, the Senate adopted a motion directing its Committee on Judiciary, Human Rights and Legal Matters to engage the Office of the Attorney-General of the Federation to initiate the revision of the 2004 compendium.

The federal government subsequently inaugurated a 46-member committee on 24 October 2024, under the supervision of the Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, to review, update and consolidate the country’s federal laws.

The committee was mandated to identify laws that had become obsolete, spent, or repealed; harmonise conflicting provisions; incorporate subsequent legislation and amendments; and produce an updated, accessible compilation of federal laws.

Legislative approval process

The revised compendium will require legislative scrutiny and approval by the National Assembly before it can become the officially recognised revised edition of the Laws of the Federation of Nigeria.

Under the existing legal framework, the compilation of federal laws is undertaken under the authority of the Attorney-General of the Federation, subject to approval by the National Assembly through an Act.

The request transmitted by President Tinubu will therefore require lawmakers to examine the proposed compilation, particularly to ensure that the amendments made to existing laws accurately reflect legislation passed by the National Assembly and assented to by the President.

The Senate has referred the request to its Committee on Judiciary, Human Rights and Legal Matters, in collaboration with the Committee on Rules and Business, for detailed examination. The House of Representatives will also have to consider the presidential request.

If the proposed revision is to receive statutory approval, the necessary legislative instrument must be considered and passed by both chambers and assented to by the President. This would provide the legal backing required for the new edition to replace the existing official compilation.

Implications for Nigeria’s legal system

The approval of the revised compendium could improve the administration of justice by providing judges, lawyers and other legal practitioners with a more current and consolidated reference for identifying applicable federal laws.

It could also reduce confusion from reliance on outdated statutory provisions, particularly where laws have since been amended, repealed, or replaced. This would help courts and legal practitioners establish the current state of legislation when interpreting laws and determining disputes.

For lawmakers, an updated compilation would make it easier to identify existing legislation, assess areas requiring amendments and avoid duplicating laws that already address particular issues.

The exercise could also improve access to justice by making it easier for citizens, researchers, law students and other interested parties to identify the laws governing their rights and obligations.

For businesses and investors, an accurate and accessible compilation could improve legal certainty by providing clearer information about the regulatory framework governing economic activities in the country.

However, the exercise’s success will depend on the accuracy and completeness of the revised compilation, as well as the public’s access to the updated laws.

Also, removing a law from the compendium does not, by itself, repeal that law or amend its provisions. The legal status of each enactment must be determined by the relevant repealing legislation, expiration, judicial decision or other applicable legal process. Similarly, the consolidation exercise must not be used to introduce amendments that were not lawfully enacted by the National Assembly.

World.title: APC mourns 15 supporters killed in Zamfara road accident
World.content:
The All Progressives Congress (APC) has mourned 15 of its members and supporters killed in a road accident in Zamfara State while travelling to attend the party’s governorship campaign flag-off in Talata Mafara.

In a statement on Tuesday by its National Publicity Secretary, Felix Morka, the party described the incident as a painful loss to its members and supporters in the state

The victims were reportedly travelling from Gummi Local Government Area of the state when the accident occurred. Several other passengers sustained injuries.

Mr Morka said the party received the news of the accident with profound sadness, adding that the incident had affected the entire APC family.

“We extend our heartfelt condolences to His Excellency, Governor Dauda Lawal, the bereaved families, the government and people of Zamfara State, and the leadership and members of our party. This is a painful loss to the entire APC family,” the statement said.

The party also commended the decision to postpone its scheduled governorship campaign rally in Maru Local Government Area following the accident.

According to the APC, the postponement was a mark of respect for those who lost their lives and an expression of solidarity with their grieving families.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The party prayed for the speedy recovery of those injured in the accident and called for divine comfort for the bereaved families.

“May Almighty Allah forgive the shortcomings of the departed, grant their souls eternal rest in Aljannatul Firdaus, and comfort their families and loved ones,” the statement said.

World.title: Police declare Nestoil chair, Sahara Group’s ED, seven others wanted
World.content:
The Nigeria Police Force (NPF) has declared nine business executives, including Nestoil Chairman Ernest Azudialu-Obiejesi and Sahara Group’s Executive Director Tope Shonubi, wanted over an alleged threat to the life of First Bank of Nigeria Managing Director (MD), Olusegun Alebiosu.

The police said that the executives were declared wanted after they failed to honour a police invitation to appear for questioning as part of an investigation into the alleged delivery of a dangerous parcel to Mr Alebiosu.

In an investigation update shared with PREMIUM TIMES on Tuesday, the Assistant Inspector-General of Police in charge of Zone 2, Moshood Jimoh, disclosed that 10 people were invited for questioning, but only one, Eze Emmanuel of Energy Shield Petrochemical Limited, appeared on 12 November.

“The remaining suspects have up till date refused to honour the police investigation. The investigation into the serious threat on the life of the complainant and his family cannot be left unresolved; therefore, all the remaining nine (9) suspects… are hereby declared wanted,” Mr Jimoh wrote.

The others declared wanted are Henry Ojogho of Broron Limited; Emmanuel Iheagwazi of Necit Nigeria Limited; Eze David of Energy Shield Petrochemical Limited; Mr Shonubi of Sahara Group; Mr Azudialu-Obiejesi and Nnenna Azudialu-Obiejesi of Nestoil; Emmanuel Orim and Victoria Orim of Luzen Plaza; and Nduka Obaigbena of General Hydrocarbon Limited.

The police asked anyone with information about their whereabouts to report to the nearest police station.

How the investigation began

According to the statement, the case arose from an incident on 7 May, when a parcel disguised as a gift package was delivered to Mr Alebiosu’s official residence.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The police said that the package was brought by a dispatch rider whose identity and that of the sender were unknown. When it was opened the following morning, two rounds of 7.62mm ammunition and what investigators described as a live explosive were found inside.

The statement noted that Mr Alebiosu reported the discovery to the police, who began an investigation involving detectives, ballistic experts and forensic specialists.

Mr Jimoh explained that the police linked the incident to disputes arising from First Bank’s efforts to recover loans from customers whose debts ran into billions of naira and dollars.

He alleged that some customers had confronted Mr Alebiosu and other bank representatives and threatened them during meetings attended by personnel of other security agencies involved in the debt recovery process.

The police said the threats preceded the delivery of the parcel and that the 10 individuals were invited to establish whether they had any connection with the incident.

The statement noted that the police sent invitation letters dated 5 November to the wanted individuals and asked them to appear on 12 November.

Citing Section 8 of the Firearms Act, which prohibits the possession or control of ammunition without a licence, the police said they would continue the investigation and bring anyone found culpable to justice.

However, the statement did not identify the individuals who allegedly made the threats or explain the evidence linking each of the nine executives to the incident. It also did not establish whether all of them were among the customers involved in the loan recovery disputes.

Earlier police account

When PREMIUM TIMES first reported the incident, the Lagos State Police Command confirmed that it was investigating the parcel.

The Commissioner of Police in Lagos State, Tijani Fatai, disclosed this during a press briefing at the police headquarters in Ikeja.

He noted that no suspect had been arrested.

“Well, there is a case like that which we are presently investigating… when he opened the parcel, he saw two live rounds of ammunition,” Mr Fatai said.

“Presently, no suspects in custody… we are still working on it.”

Mr Fatai also stated that Mr Alebiosu had given investigators the names of people he suspected, although the police had yet to establish their involvement.

At the time, security sources revealed that domestic security personnel at the Ikoyi residence received the package before it was opened. The parcel reportedly bore the managing director’s name but had no identifiable details of the sender.

A senior police officer at the State Criminal Investigation Department, Panti, also said investigators were reviewing closed-circuit television footage around Ikoyi to identify the dispatch rider and trace the delivery.

The Lagos State Police Command spokesperson, Abimbola Adebisi, subsequently confirmed that the SCID had taken over the investigation.

The police have yet to publicly identify the sender of the parcel or establish who was behind the alleged threat.

The individuals declared wanted by the police have yet to issue statements at the time of this report.

World.title: Premium Times Academy trains journalists on conflict reporting
World.content:
The Premium Times Training Academy (PTTA), the capacity-building arm of PREMIUM TIMES Group, has held a two-day workshop in Lagos to strengthen journalists’ capacity for ethical, responsible and conflict-sensitive reporting.

The workshop, held on 23 and 24 November, brought together more than 30 journalists from different media organisations for sessions on conflict dynamics, hate speech, misinformation, verification, humanitarian reporting and ethnic profiling.

It is the second edition of the academy’s peace and conflict-sensitive reporting workshop, following an earlier session held in Abuja in September.

Understanding conflict, media role

Tunde Akanni, a professor of journalism and development communication at Lagos State University, opened the discussions by examining the nature, causes and dynamics of conflict.

Mr Akanni defined conflict as a relationship in which two or more parties perceive incompatible goals, interests, values or needs. He explained that conflict was not necessarily destructive, noting that it could also catalyse social change and pressure for government accountability.

He urged journalists to distinguish between conflict, violence and mere disagreement, stressing that their responsibility went beyond reporting events to explaining their wider implications.

“Journalists act as observers and interpreters who must explain the implications of developments to the public,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Abigail Ogwezzy-Ndisika, a professor of mass communication at the University of Lagos and director of the Institute of Continuing Education, also examined the relationship between journalism ethics and conflict-sensitive reporting.

She warned that the way journalists frame stories could either help de-escalate tensions or worsen divisions, particularly amid the spread of hate speech and information disorder.

“The way a story is framed can either reduce tension or act as a megaphone for hate speech,” she said.

She urged journalists to apply professional and ethical standards that promote social stability rather than amplify tensions.

Lessons from conflict reporting

PREMIUM TIMES publisher Dapo Olorunyomi examined the consequences of insensitive and injurious reporting, drawing lessons from Rwanda, Sierra Leone and Kenya.

Mr Olorunyomi, represented by the newspaper’s Editor-in-Chief, Musikilu Mojeed, distinguished between disputes and conflicts, explaining that conflicts often involve deeper, more enduring issues relating to identity, belonging, historical grievances, and state legitimacy.

He highlighted the devastating consequences of inflammatory media coverage, citing the role of a radio station in Rwanda whose broadcasts contributed to the genocide in the country.

The session examined how irresponsible reporting and inflammatory language can deepen existing divisions and contribute to violence.

Reporting conflict without causing harm

Idris Akinbajo, PREMIUM TIMES’ managing editor, led sessions on applying conflict-sensitive principles to practical reporting situations and gathering and writing news in an era of hate speech.

Mr Akinbajo urged journalists to look beyond the visible manifestations of violence, such as protests and armed conflicts, to investigate the underlying grievances and conditions that fuel them.

He warned that failure to understand these root causes could turn media organisations into instruments of propaganda.

He also stressed the importance of minimising harm to the public, journalists, their colleagues and their families.

During the practical sessions, he examined how journalists could unintentionally amplify hate speech through their reporting and discussed ways to avoid doing so.

Sourcing, verification on social media

Oladeinde Olawoyin, an award-winning journalist and editor with PREMIUM TIMES, addressed the challenges of identifying, sourcing and verifying news in the rapidly changing social media environment.

He noted that the growing volume of information on platforms such as TikTok and Instagram had made it increasingly difficult to distinguish news from ordinary online content.

He urged journalists to assess potential stories using factors such as timeliness, prominence, significance, novelty and localisation while maintaining professional standards.

David Ajikobi, an editor with Africa Check, also demonstrated techniques and tools for verifying social media posts in the age of artificial intelligence.

He outlined steps journalists could take within the first 15 minutes after a claim emerges to establish its authenticity and prevent the spread of false information.

Humanitarian reporting

Mr Mojeed, in another session, examined the role of journalists in reporting humanitarian crises through accurate, contextual and data-supported journalism.

He cautioned that conflict sensitivity should not come at the expense of factual accuracy, warning journalists against compromising the truth to appear sensitive.

He also questioned the reliability of some official figures released by law enforcement agencies, urging journalists to present independently established findings alongside official accounts.

For instance, he said that if a reporter independently counted 20 bodies while the police reported six, the story should reflect both accounts.

Mr Mojeed also drew attention to underreported issues, including internal human trafficking and the effects of inadequate education on vulnerable young people.

Kadaria Ahmed, a journalist and founder of Radio Now, examined how media reporting can shape public perceptions, reinforce fear and contribute to the dehumanisation of particular groups.

She identified several ways ethnic profiling could manifest in newsrooms, including story framing, sourcing, attribution, bias, ownership structures and the use of labels.

She cautioned against descriptions such as “killer herdsmen” when the identities or affiliations of suspected perpetrators had not been sufficiently established.

Ms Ahmed said journalists must report crimes such as kidnapping and killings without attributing the actions of individuals to entire ethnic groups.

She argued that identity politics often reduces people to their group affiliations instead of addressing the underlying issues.

Participants share experiences

Participants described the training as an opportunity to strengthen their professional practice and improve their understanding of conflict-sensitive reporting.

Evelyn Usman, an editor at Vanguard newspaper, said the sessions had provided useful lessons that would improve her reporting.

“I acquired knowledge that will assist my reporting and also help me be a better gatekeeper in peace and conflict-sensitive reporting,” she said.

Ms Usman added that she planned to share the lessons at her newspaper’s board of editors’ meeting.

Toliat Musa, a journalist with the Nigeria Television Authority, described the workshop as an eye-opener, noting that journalists should recognise their role in managing conflict through responsible reporting.

Opeyemi Lawal of the Foundation for Investigative Journalism said discussions on conflict-sensitive reporting were important because they shaped how journalism was received by the public.

“There are a lot of latent conflicts in our society, as the training stated. So the training is important for us to learn how to stem and nip issues like this in the bud,” he said.

Eniola Daniel, a journalist with The Guardian, commended the organisers and described the workshop’s lessons as invaluable.

“We have learned something that cannot be quantified,” he said.

World.title: 26% of pregnant women in Nigeria do not access antenatal care – WHO
World.content:
The World Health Organisation (WHO) has disclosed that about 26 per cent of pregnant women in Nigeria do not access antenatal care, raising concerns over missed opportunities to prevent mother-to-child transmission of HIV.

The WHO Regional Office for Africa’s Team Lead for HIV, Tuberculosis, Hepatitis and Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs), Akudo Ikpeazu, said Nigeria continues to record approximately 10,000 new HIV infections among children annually, highlighting the need to improve access to maternal healthcare services.

Ms Ikpeazu disclosed this on Tuesday while virtually delivering the keynote address at the 2026 Nigeria HIV Prevention Conference in Abuja.

The three-day conference, themed “Building to Last: Re-imagining HIV Prevention Strategies in Nigeria,” was convened by the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare and the National Agency for the Control of AIDS (NACA).

“About 26 per cent of pregnant women in Nigeria do not access antenatal care. As such, they cannot receive essential services including HIV testing, treatment, follow-up, and follow-through existing antenatal services,” she said.

“But every door a pregnant woman walks through must be a door to prevention.”

Gaps in antenatal care coverage

Ms Ikpeazu identified 20 states with low antenatal care coverage and called for stronger collaboration between health authorities and community leaders to improve access to maternal healthcare services.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

She said ward development committees in the affected states could engage traditional authorities, religious leaders and women leaders to facilitate access through nearby health facilities, outreach clinics and other community-based arrangements.

The WHO official advocated the integration of HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis services into routine maternal healthcare, with local government primary healthcare teams responsible for service delivery, linkage and reporting under state supervision.

She also called for the integration of HIV prevention into reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health services through existing primary healthcare structures.

Disparities in maternal healthcare

Findings from the 2024 Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey (NDHS), released in October 2025, corroborate the WHO official’s disclosure.

The survey showed that 26 per cent of women aged 15 to 49 who had a live birth within the two years preceding the survey did not receive any antenatal care during their most recent pregnancy.

Nationally, 63 per cent received antenatal care from skilled health providers, with significant disparities across geographical locations, income groups and educational levels.

While 82 per cent of women in urban areas received antenatal care from skilled providers, only 51 per cent of their rural counterparts received such services.

Coverage ranged from 12 per cent in Kebbi State to 97 per cent in Imo State.

Economic status also influenced the utilisation of maternal healthcare services, with 48 per cent of women from the poorest households receiving no antenatal care.

Similarly, only 41 per cent of women without formal education received antenatal care from skilled providers, compared with 95 per cent of those with education beyond the secondary level.

The survey further showed that only 52 per cent of women attended at least four antenatal visits, while 18 per cent had their first visit within the first three months of pregnancy.

More than half of live births, representing 56 per cent, occurred at home, compared with 43 per cent in health facilities.

Eliminating mother-to-child transmission

Ms Ikpeazu said Nigeria must intensify efforts to prevent HIV transmission during pregnancy, childbirth and breastfeeding.

“Children must remain visible as well. New infections among children have held at about 10,000 a year, demanding stronger action against vertical transmission during pregnancy, childbirth, and through the breastfeeding period,” she said.

She explained that WHO validation of the elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV in breastfeeding populations requires a transmission rate below five per cent and no more than 50 new paediatric HIV infections per 100,000 live births.

The requirements also include 95 per cent antenatal care coverage, 95 per cent HIV testing coverage among pregnant women and 95 per cent treatment coverage among pregnant women living with HIV.

Ms Ikpeazu encouraged states with high antenatal care coverage to strengthen their HIV testing, treatment and follow-up services and seek recognition through established WHO regional mechanisms.

She noted that progress at the state level could support Nigeria’s efforts towards national validation while providing lessons for states with lower coverage.

Government’s prevention priorities

The Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare, Iziaq Salako, also identified the prevention of mother-to-child transmission as one of four priority areas for Nigeria’s HIV response.

Represented by the National Coordinator of the National AIDS, Viral Hepatitis and STIs Control Programme (NASCP), Adebobola Bashorun, the minister said Nigeria must strengthen interventions to ensure that no child is born with HIV.

Mr Salako also called for expanded access to prevention services among adolescents, young women and key populations.

He advocated the adoption of innovative prevention options, including long-acting pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and HIV self-testing kits, alongside behavioural and structural interventions.

The minister emphasised the need to address stigma and discrimination, noting that fear of discrimination could discourage people from accessing essential healthcare services.

He further called for increased domestic financing by federal and state governments, alongside greater private sector participation, to guarantee uninterrupted access to HIV prevention commodities and services.

In her welcome address, the Director-General of NACA, Temitope Ilori, called for increased investment in prevention services, particularly for women, adolescents and vulnerable populations.

“We must invest in adolescents and young people, ensure that women and vulnerable populations have access to appropriate prevention services, and strengthen community-led approaches that respond to the realities of those most affected,” she said.

Also speaking, a former NACA Director-General, John Idoko, identified inadequate investment in prevention, stigma, limited access to prevention services and inequalities in healthcare access as major challenges confronting Nigeria’s HIV response.

Mr Idoko, a professor, called for HIV prevention to be repositioned as a national priority, alongside improved surveillance, greater use of epidemiological data and stronger domestic financing.

He urged stakeholders to ensure that the conference produced a clear national prevention agenda with defined responsibilities, measurable milestones and mechanisms for monitoring progress.

World.title: Northern governors dissolve NNDC board, order comprehensive overhaul
World.content:
The 19 northern state governments have dissolved the Board of Directors of the New Nigeria Development Company (NNDC), in a fresh move to restructure the regional investment institution and reposition it to serve the economic interests of the region.

The decision was taken on Tuesday at a special general meeting in Kaduna, attended by the secretaries to the governments of the 19 states, who represented their respective governments in their capacity as shareholders’ representatives.

The shareholders resolved to undertake a comprehensive reorganisation of the company, including the constitution of a new board, a review of its management structure and a comprehensive audit of its financial, administrative and operational activities.

However, the dissolution of the board will take effect upon the valid adoption of the relevant ordinary resolutions at a general meeting and compliance with applicable statutory requirements.

Addressing journalists after the meeting, the Secretary to the Gombe State Government, Ibrahim Njodi, said the decision was informed by the need to strengthen the company’s institutional capacity, improve corporate governance, enhance operational efficiency and reposition it as a viable investment and development institution.

He said the objective was to ensure that NNDC effectively serves the collective economic interests of the 19 Northern states.

New board to provide strategic direction

Mr Njodi said a new board of directors would be constituted to provide strategic leadership, effective supervision, policy direction and corporate oversight for the company.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He explained that the composition, nomination and appointment of the new board would reflect the ownership interests of the participating states, the provisions of the company’s Memorandum and Articles of Association, and the requirements of the Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA) 2020.

The shareholders, he added, would subsequently approve the nominations and appointments of the new directors in accordance with the company’s constitutional documents and applicable laws.

According to him, the incoming board will undertake a comprehensive review of the existing management structure, personnel, administrative arrangements, operational framework and overall performance of the company.

Mr Njodi said such measures must be implemented in accordance with the board’s statutory and fiduciary responsibilities, the company’s Articles of Association and applicable employment laws.

Comprehensive audit of finances, investments

The incoming board will also conduct a comprehensive corporate governance, financial, administrative and operational audit of NNDC, covering its activities for a period to be determined by the board.

Mr Njodi said the exercise would examine the company’s financial position, assets and liabilities, existing investments, subsidiaries, joint ventures and other commercial interests.

The audit will also assess the performance and profitability of the company’s investments, its compliance with statutory, regulatory and corporate governance obligations, as well as existing contractual commitments and outstanding liabilities.

The effectiveness of the previous board and management structure will also be reviewed, alongside any other matters considered necessary to protect and advance the interests of the shareholders.

Handover, protection of company assets

Mr Njodi said the outgoing board and management would be required, upon the lawful assumption of office by their respective successors, to facilitate an orderly handover of the company’s affairs.

The handover will cover records, books of account, statutory documents, financial records, assets, properties, contracts and other relevant institutional materials.

He added that the incoming board would be responsible for ensuring that all the company’s assets and interests were adequately protected during the transition.

The new board must also ensure that there is no unauthorised disposal, transfer, encumbrance or alienation of the company’s assets.

Shareholders cite governance concerns

Mr Njodi said the shareholders had earlier reviewed the company’s state of affairs, including its corporate governance structure, operational performance, management arrangements and the effectiveness of the existing board of directors.

He said the shareholders considered a comprehensive reorganisation necessary in the overriding interest of the company, its owners and the economic development aspirations of Northern Nigeria.

The Secretary to the Gombe State Government said the shareholders recognised their statutory powers under the Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020, particularly Section 288, which provides for the removal of directors through an ordinary resolution, subject to compliance with the prescribed statutory procedures and the company’s Articles of Association.

He added that the shareholders were determined to restore confidence, accountability, transparency, professionalism and effective corporate governance in the administration of NNDC.

Background: NNDC’s mandate

The New Nigeria Development Company is a regional investment institution jointly owned by the 19 northern state governments. Its origins date back to 1949, when it was established as the Northern Regional Production Development Board.

It was subsequently restructured in 1956 as the Northern Regional Development Corporation before being incorporated as a private limited liability company in 1965.

It became known as the New Nigeria Development Company following the creation of states from the former Northern Region in 1976.

The company’s founding objective was to promote economic development across Northern Nigeria through investments, industrialisation, enterprise development and the creation of economic opportunities.

Over the decades, NNDC developed interests in several sectors, including agriculture, manufacturing, real estate, hospitality, construction, solid minerals, information technology and telecommunications, among others.

However, concerns about the performance of some of its investments and the need to strengthen its corporate structure have featured prominently in recent efforts by the Northern Governors’ Forum to revitalise the institution.

Northern governors intensify NNDC revival efforts

In September 2025, Borno State Governor, Babagana Zulum, reaffirmed the governors’ commitment to revitalising the company, describing it as an important instrument for stimulating commercial and industrial growth across the 19 Northern states.

Mr Zulum, who chairs the governors’ implementation committee on the NNDC restructuring initiative, said the company needed to be transformed into a stronger institution capable of driving strategic investments and regional economic development.

The committee also involved the governors of Kwara, Zamfara and Plateau states.

During a visit to NNDC’s headquarters in September 2025, Mr Zulum assured workers that the Northern governors were committed to strengthening the company and improving its operations.

Before Tuesday’s decision, NNDC was led by a board chaired by Lamis Dikko, while Shehu Mai-Bornu served as its Group Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer.

World.title: ADC demands Tinubu’s resignation or impeachment over Kano governor’s claims
World.content:
The African Democratic Congress (ADC) has called on President Bola Tinubu to resign or face impeachment after Kano State Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf claimed a political agreement with the president during the legal battle over the 2023 Kano governorship election.

The opposition party also urged the National Assembly to initiate impeachment proceedings against Mr Tinubu and investigate the circumstances surrounding the alleged agreement.

In a statement on Tuesday, signed by Bolaji Abdullahi, spokesperson for its David Mark-led leadership, the ADC alleged that the governor’s account raised serious questions about presidential interference in the judiciary.

The party was reacting to an interview Mr Yusuf granted BBC Hausa, in which he claimed that his former political mentor, Rabiu Kwankwaso, sent him to negotiate an agreement with Mr Tinubu while his governorship election dispute was pending before the Supreme Court.

According to the governor, the proposed arrangement involved a request that the president refrain from interfering in the litigation and a commitment to join the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) if the court upheld his election.

The ADC, however, argued that the governor’s account suggested that the president may have influenced the outcome of the litigation in exchange for a political commitment.

“No conduct can be more heinous on the part of a democratically elected President than to make the administration of justice an instrument of political bargaining. No betrayal of the presidential oath can be more profound than to pervert the cause of justice in pursuit of personal political advantage,” the party said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The ADC argued that the alleged arrangement could constitute gross misconduct warranting the president’s removal from office.

“The Supreme Court is not an extension of the APC national secretariat, and the President of Nigeria is not the proprietor of the Nigerian judiciary,” it said.

The party also demanded that those involved in the alleged arrangement be made to provide evidence before the National Assembly.

However, the ADC provided no evidence in its statement that Mr Tinubu contacted Supreme Court justices or influenced their decision.

As of Tuesday evening, neither the presidency nor the Supreme Court had issued a public response to the allegations that PREMIUM TIMES could independently establish.

What the Kano governor said

PREMIUM TIMES reported on Monday that Mr Yusuf, while defending his defection to the APC, claimed that Mr Kwankwaso initiated the political arrangement with Mr Tinubu.

The governor said Mr Kwankwaso instructed him to meet the president and pledge that they would join the APC if he retained his mandate at the Supreme Court.

He also claimed that his former political mentor was prepared to have him swear on the Qur’an to demonstrate their commitment to the arrangement.

Mr Yusuf said he conveyed the proposal to the president, who, according to him, received it positively.

The governor said he subsequently informed Mr Kwankwaso of the outcome of the meeting.

According to Mr Yusuf, Mr Kwankwaso’s later remarks criticising the president frustrated plans for their joint defection to the ruling party.

The governor maintained that his eventual move to the APC was intended to honour the earlier agreement.

His account concerned a request for presidential non-interference in the judicial proceedings, rather than an explicit claim that Mr Tinubu directed the court to rule in his favour.

Kwankwasiyya Movement denies alleged agreement

The Kwankwasiyya Movement has denied that Mr Kwankwaso sent the governor to negotiate such an arrangement with Mr Tinubu.

Mr Kwankwaso, a former governor of Kano State, is now the vice-presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) and running mate to Peter Obi.

In a statement issued on Monday by its spokesperson, Habibu Mohammed, the movement accused Mr Yusuf of attempting to shift responsibility for his defection to the APC.

It challenged the governor to disclose details of the purported agreement, including when it was reached, who was involved, and any evidence that could substantiate his account.

The movement maintained that major political decisions involving Mr Kwankwaso and his followers were taken through consultations with relevant stakeholders.

What the Constitution says about impeachment

Although the ADC cited Section 413 of the Constitution in its statement, the provision governing the removal of a Nigerian president for gross misconduct is Section 143 of the 1999 Constitution, as amended.

Subsection 11 defines gross misconduct to include a serious breach of the Constitution or conduct that the National Assembly considers sufficiently grave to constitute gross misconduct.

Under Section 143, impeachment proceedings require a written notice detailing the allegations, signed by at least one-third of the members of the National Assembly and presented to the President of the Senate.

A motion to investigate the allegations requires the support of at least two-thirds of all members of each chamber of the National Assembly.

The Chief Justice of Nigeria would then, at the President of the Senate’s request, appoint a seven-member panel to investigate the allegations.

The President has the right to defend himself before the panel, either personally or through legal representatives of his choice.

If the panel finds that the allegations have been proved, the President can be removed from office only if at least two-thirds of all members of each chamber vote to adopt its report.

The ADC’s demand does not, by itself, constitute the commencement of impeachment proceedings.

Background
