Omollo warned that anyone suspected of destroying property would be taken to court in accordance with the law, where the judiciary would determine their cases.

He maintained that political differences should not be used to justify vandalism, endanger lives or disrupt public services.

“The Constitution protects the right to express ourselves peacefully and unarmed. Political differences cannot be an excuse to vandalise property, endanger lives or disrupt the services our communities depend on,” he said.

Those present included Public Service, Human Capital Development and Special Programmes Cabinet Secretary Geoffrey Ruku, Embu Governor Cecily Mbarire, Senator Alexander Munyi and Deputy Governor Kinyua Mugo, among others.

World.title: Narok Senator under fire after threatening to shoot auctioneers in Sh1.2m dispute
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Narok Senator Ledama ole Kina is at the centre of a national uproar after a viral video captured him threatening to shoot individuals during a volatile confrontation involving auctioneers and a former Senate office employee.

The dramatic standoff erupted when court-backed agents attempted to seize a milk delivery truck over an unresolved legal dispute and has since ignited intense public debate regarding political accountability and the rule of law.

The controversy surrounds long court battle after Zakayo Rotiken, who served sacked as Narok North Constituency Coordinator between 2017 and 2020, was sacked.

According to records, the claimant was illegally dismissed amidst unpaid salary arrears.

On October 31, 2023, the Employment and Labour Relations Court ruled in Rotiken's favour , a decision that was subsequently upheld when the Senator lost his appeal.

With accrued interest, the court decree now stands at Sh 1.2 million.

Consequently, when the debt remained unsatisfied, licensed auctioneers moved in to execute lawful warrants which in turn provoked a furious reaction from Senator Ole Kina, who fiercely framed the entire episode as a political witch-hunt.

The lawmaker argued that Rotiken was hired by the Narok Senate office rather than his personal capacity, maintaining that any resultant liabilities ought to be handled by the Parliamentary Service Commission (PSC) rather than attaching his private property.

Defending his harsh words in the widely circulated footage, the senator dismissed the agents as trespassers and asserted action against them.

"Anybody who trespasses will get a bullet in their head or leg because that is trespass," said Ole Kina.

“Nitakupiga Risasi!” Senator Ledama Ole Kina embroiled in confrontation with alleged auctioneers over unpaid car loan https://t.co/k4OSXpNsdi November 21, 2026

The claimant's legal team condemned the threats made against statutory court officers emphasizing that a court judgment is an enforceable command rather than a mere suggestion, calling upon the Inspector General of Police of Police and the Director of Criminal Investigatons to urgently investigate the alleged death threats.

Rotiken noted that he merely sought justice through proper judicial channels and should not be penalized or intimidated for pursuing his lawful entitlements.

"When I was illegally dismissed with unpaid salary arrears, I did not resort to violence or politics—I went to the Employment and Labour Relations Court. Nobody is above the law, and I appeal to the police to protect the officers doing their job so that justice can finally be served," he said.

Ultimately, as pressure mounts on security agencies to look into the firearm threats, the unfolding saga highlights a tense intersection between public office obligations and the absolute sanctity of judicial decrees.

While the senator maintains that his assets were unjustly targeted by political rivals, legal experts and the public continue to demand that the rule of law must prevail without exception.

World.title: Ruto defends IEBC, challenges rivals to present alternative policies
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto during his tour of the Western region. [PCS]

President William Ruto has launched a scathing attack on opposition leaders over their demands on the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC), accusing them of attempting to interfere with the electoral agency because they fear losing the 2027 General Election.

The President challenged opposition leaders to allow IEBC to prepare independently for next year's elections, saying they should instead focus on identifying their presidential candidate, developing a manifesto and presenting alternative policies to Kenyans.

Ruto accused his competitors of attempting to play the roles of both contestants and referees by seeking to influence decisions on the procurement of election materials and equipment.

He spoke a day after opposition leaders walked out of a meeting convened by IEBC, alleging bias by the commission.

“Please give IEBC a chance to arrange the elections next year. The people of Kenya will decide. You go and first look for your candidate, find your policies, agenda and plans and sell them to the wananchi. We shall meet at the ballot,” said Ruto.

Speaking during his development tour of Western Kenya, Ruto questioned why opposition politicians were concentrating on determining how IEBC should procure election materials instead of preparing to face voters.

“How can somebody who is in a competition want to decide where the pitch will be, who the referee will be and where the ball will be placed? Leave IEBC alone. Those who will vote are the citizens, and they are the ones who will decide,” he said.

The President accused his opponents of lacking a clear political agenda and capacity to deliver, claiming their campaigns were centred on slogans and personal attacks against him.

He challenged them to explain what they would do differently in agriculture, education, healthcare, infrastructure and employment rather than mobilising Kenyans around the slogan 'Kasongo Must Go'.

“The reason why my competitors cannot develop a plan is that they have no capacity. The reason why they have no agenda is that they have no knowledge. The reason why they cannot develop anything is that they know they have no capacity to deliver on anything that they will say,” he said.

His remarks were echoed by Kakamega Governor Fernandes Barasa and National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang'ula, who rallied Western Kenya leaders behind his re-election bid and defended IEBC against what they termed unnecessary political pressure. President William Ruto during his tour of the Western region. [ Benjamin Sakwa, Standard]

Speaking in Butere, Barasa said the region's political leadership, including Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi, Cabinet Secretary Wycliffe Oparanya, Wetang'ula and trade unionist Francis Atwoli, was united behind Ruto's development agenda.

“IEBC will conduct the elections according to the law. Opposition leaders should leave IEBC alone and allow it to do its work,” he said.

Wetang'ula maintained that IEBC was independent of both the government and the opposition and should be allowed to conduct its work without interference.

“IEBC is independent of the government and independent of the Opposition. You stand there to do your work fairly, truthfully and equally,” he said.

He added: “Just as Arsenal supporters cannot dictate what uniform the referee should wear, the referee's responsibility is to ensure the game is played fairly and the winner emerges through a legitimate process.”

The exchanges underline the growing political contest over the management of the 2027 elections, with the government side accusing the opposition of undermining the electoral agency before campaigns gather momentum.

Beyond the political exchanges, Ruto used his Western Kenya tour to highlight development projects, saying his administration was committed to correcting years of neglect and unequal distribution of national resources.

He also announced plans for a second phase of the Nyota programme targeting an additional 200,000 young people, each expected to receive Sh50,000 to establish or expand businesses.

The government is also targeting 100,000 college graduates for internships from January, with each expected to receive a monthly stipend of Sh20,000.

Ruto's tour comes amid growing competition for Western Kenya's support ahead of the 2027 General Election, with emerging opposition alliances seeking to challenge his influence.

World.title: Ruto sustains attacks on Gachagua, dares Opposition to name 2027 flagbearer
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto launches Matisi-Bokoli-Milani-Teremi road in Webuye West on November 19, 2026. [Benjamin Sakwa, Standard]

President William Ruto has challenged Opposition leaders to name their presidential candidate and unveil a clear political agenda, accusing them of wasting time hopping from one hotel to another and holding meetings in private residences in search of a flagbearer and campaign manifesto.

The President said the Opposition was yet to settle on a flagbearer or agree on a common agenda despite the clock ticking towards the 2027 General Election.

He dismissed the rival camps' political engagements as endless consultations and manoeuvres, arguing that their leaders were more preoccupied with political meetings than developing policies to convince Kenyans.

Speaking in Bungoma during his development tour of Western Kenya, Ruto challenged his opponents to stop what he termed political confusion and present an alternative development agenda, insisting he was ready to face them in the 2027 contest.

"These people do not have a candidate. They are struggling, moving from one hotel to another and from one person's house to another, trying to find an agenda and a manifesto before they can start campaigning. Time is running out, yet they are still struggling to agree on an agenda," he said.

Ruto also launched a fresh attack on former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua, accusing him of promoting tribalism and hatred while questioning his remarks about relocating to Texas, United States.

The President mockingly referred to Gachagua as "Mr Chuki wa Texas", questioning why he would allegedly acquire a house in the US while engaging in politics that could divide Kenyans and fuel hostility.

"Mr Chuki wa Texas has gone to buy a house in Texas. He wants to know whether he will flee our country after spreading tribalism and hatred, dividing people and turning them against each other, before boarding a plane to Texas and leaving others to deal with the consequences," Ruto said.

He accused the former Deputy President of attempting to turn communities against one another for political gain, warning that he would not allow anyone to undermine national unity through ethnic mobilisation.

Ruto said he was ready to confront his political opponents directly but insisted that political competition should not become an avenue for spreading hatred and inciting Kenyans against one another.

The President also questioned Gachagua's allies over their reported visit to the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) offices in Kizirani, accusing the Opposition of picking unnecessary fights with the electoral agency ahead of the 2027 General Election.

He suggested that politicians who begin questioning the electoral commission before elections could be preparing grounds to reject the results should they lose.

"Whenever you see someone picking a fight with IEBC, that person is already looking for an excuse to fail. Now they are coming up with all sorts of excuses, asking whether it is IEBC that votes. Is IEBC responsible for the votes?" He posed.

Ruto urged politicians to stop harassing the electoral agency, maintaining that the power to elect leaders rests with Kenyans and not the commission.

"I want to tell Kenyans to stop harassing IEBC. IEBC does not have votes. The votes belong to the people of Kenya," he said.

The President maintained that his administration was focused on delivering development, challenging the Opposition to explain its alternative plans on electricity connectivity, education, healthcare and infrastructure.

He questioned what the Opposition considered its development agenda, dismissing what he described as recycled political slogans and simplistic promises.

The President particularly took issue with promises centred on providing porridge to Kenyans, questioning whether such pledges could constitute a credible national development agenda.

He urged voters to interrogate the policies and development track records of politicians seeking their support instead of being swayed by political rhetoric and personal attacks.

The latest attack marks an escalation in political exchanges between Ruto and his rivals as competing camps intensify mobilisation ahead of the 2027 General Election.

It also comes amid efforts by Gachagua and other Opposition figures to consolidate their political formations and build a formidable challenge to Ruto's re-election bid, with Western Kenya emerging as a key battleground.

World.title: Ruto lists measures to lower cost of living, put more money in Kenyans' pockets
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto during his State Of The Nation Address at Parliament, Nairobi. November 18th, 2026. [Elvis Ogina, Standard]

President William Ruto has outlined a raft of government interventions aimed at reducing the cost of living, increasing household incomes and creating more employment opportunities for Kenyans.

Addressing Parliament during the 2026 State of the Nation Address on Wednesday, Ruto said his administration had prioritised lowering the cost of essential goods and services while increasing earnings across key sectors of the economy.

“Our economic proposition was simple: Reduce the cost for families and increase the income from what they do,” he said.

On food prices, the President cited the government’s fertiliser subsidy programme, which has reduced the price of a 50-kilogramme bag of fertiliser from Sh7,500 in 2022 to Sh2,000 this year.

He said the government had distributed 38.5 million bags of subsidised fertiliser to farmers, contributing to an increase in maize production from 44.3 million bags in 2022 to 71 million bags last year.

Consequently, maize imports declined from 9.9 million bags to 3.3 million bags, while the average price of a two-kilogramme packet of sifted maize flour dropped from a high of Sh230 in September 2022 to Sh152 in September this year.

Ruto also highlighted gains in the tea, coffee, dairy and sugar industries, saying government interventions had helped improve production and increase farmers' earnings.

He said the Cherry Advance Revolving Fund had disbursed Sh15.07 billion to 684,000 coffee farmers, while tea export earnings increased from Sh163 billion in 2022 to Sh187 billion in 2025.

In the dairy sector, milk production rose from 4.5 billion litres to 5.52 billion litres, while average earnings for farmers increased from Sh32 to Sh60 per litre last month.

Sugar production, he added, increased by 60 per cent between January and October, with cane crushing rising by 57 per cent. The industry is projected to produce more than 900,000 tonnes by the end of the year, with Sh1.2 billion in bonuses expected to be paid to sugarcane farmers.

On healthcare, Ruto said the Social Health Authority (SHA) was designed to ease the financial burden of medical expenses on households through a shared health financing system.

In education, he said the government had employed 100,000 teachers and was preparing to recruit an additional 20,000 to address staffing shortages and reduce the burden on parents who pay teachers hired through Boards of Management.

He added that 23,000 classrooms had been constructed, while 1,600 laboratories were being built and equipped.

The President said the annual education allocation had increased from Sh521 billion in the 2022/23 financial year to Sh784 billion in the current financial year.

"These investments improve the quality of education while progressively reducing the need for Kenyans to finance education," he said.

On affordable housing, Ruto said more than 313,000 homes were at different stages of construction across the 47 counties, with over 1.37 million Kenyans registered on the Boma Yangu platform and more than 18,000 homes already allocated.

He said households could work towards homeownership through monthly payments starting at Sh4,000, which he argued would help ease the burden of rent.

The housing programme, according to the President, had also generated more than 1.1 million employment opportunities and reserved orders worth over Sh61 billion for Jua Kali artisans.

On employment, Ruto said 350,000 Kenyans had secured jobs through the digital economy programme, while another 707,000 had obtained employment abroad through international labour mobility initiatives.

He also cited the Hustler Fund, saying more than seven million Kenyans had established credit records through the programme, with cumulative borrowing reaching Sh94 billion.

Under the NYOTA programme, more than 133,000 young entrepreneurs had received training, mentorship and Sh50,000 each in start-up capital, he said.

The President further announced proposed tax measures aimed at increasing disposable incomes, including exempting workers earning Sh32,333 or less per month from Pay As You Earn (PAYE).

Other proposals include scrapping stamp duty on land transactions valued at Sh1 million or less and removing the 25 per cent import duty on mobile phones.

On pending bills, Ruto said the government had approved the settlement of 28,726 verified claims amounting to Sh27.8 billion, covering debts of Sh50 million and below dating back to 2005.

He added that Sh18 billion owed to public universities and another Sh16 billion owed to public and private hospitals under the former National Hospital Insurance Fund (NHIF) had been approved for payment and were undergoing Treasury processing.

“These are not isolated interventions, but parts of one comprehensive undertaking,” Ruto said.

He maintained that the government's economic strategy was anchored on reducing household expenditure, increasing incomes and expanding opportunities for Kenyans.

World.title: Haaretz reports 23 Israeli soldiers commit suicide, highest toll since 2010
World.content:
The Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported on Monday that 23 Israeli soldiers and officers on active duty have committed suicide since the beginning of this year.

This marks the highest annual figure recorded by the Israeli military since 2010, amid growing concerns regarding the psychological toll of the war and inadequacies in the mental health support system for military personnel.

The newspaper reported that at least 17 other individuals, who had served in the regular or reserve forces during the war, also died by suicide this year after leaving active duty.

Additionally, five suicides were recorded among police personnel, and six among individuals receiving care through the Rehabilitation Department of the Israeli Ministry of Defense.

According to Haaretz, the statistics reveal a persistent rise in suicides within the Israeli military since the outbreak of the war.

While the average number of these cases stood at approximately 12 per year during the decade preceding the conflict, the figure rose to 21 in 2024, reached 22 in 2025, and has now climbed to 23 since the start of the current year.

An upward trend

The newspaper explained that this upward trend has persisted despite a decline in the number of soldiers called up for military service compared to the initial months following the October 7, 2023 attack.

It noted that official military data does not reflect the full scale of the phenomenon, as it previously excluded service members who took their own lives after leaving the military.

Haaretz cited an officer from the army’s Manpower Directorate as saying that the actual figures in previous years may have exceeded the reported tallies.

The officer confirmed a clear increase in suicides, particularly among soldiers who return home without receiving an adequate response to their psychological distress.

The newspaper indicated that while the military has been unable to identify a single, clear common factor among the suicides, it has observed higher rates among “lone soldiers”—those who moved to Israel specifically to enlist—as well as among service members of Ethiopian descent.

It added that some cases were linked to the loss of relatives or friends, or to participation in intense combat; meanwhile, most of the service members who took their own lives this year had not sought mental health treatment prior to their deaths.

Testimonies from struggling soldiers

Citing testimonies from soldiers, Haaretz revealed a decline in the presence of mental health officers in the field, as well as a reduction in the time allocated for addressing the combat-related experiences of reservists before they return to civilian life.

The report further noted that, during the war, the military called up service members who were already suffering from psychological trauma and receiving treatment through the Ministry of Defense—in some instances, without conducting evaluations to determine their fitness for service.

Soldiers also reported that some commanders prevented them from accessing mental health care—either due to manpower shortages or because of persistent, outdated attitudes toward psychological distress.

This raises questions regarding the Israeli military establishment’s capacity to address the mounting psychological repercussions of the war.

World.title: Egypt’s mobile phones surge in price by up to 60%
World.content:
Mobile phone prices in Egypt have seen successive hikes recently, affecting all price categories.

The increases were not limited to high-end, feature-rich devices; they also extended to budget-friendly phones—the primary choice for those with limited income.

During a field visit to Abdel-Aziz Street in Cairo, Al-Masry Al-Youm documented complaints from several merchants regarding a slowdown in sales, driven by repeated price hikes across all types of mobile phones.

This has made the decision to purchase increasingly difficult for consumers.

Retailers reveal dire situation

A street phone retailer, Abdel-Nasser Gad, said that device prices have been rising repeatedly for over a year.

Gad noted that these continuous increases have become a significant burden on buyers, especially those looking for affordable, entry-level phones.

Another retailer, Hafez, said that the prices of some entry-level, limited-capability phones have reached high levels—well above what consumers in the budget-friendly segment are accustomed to.

Regarding the impact of these price hikes on demand, Hafez explained that the rising costs have affected sales activity; some consumers have begun looking for used phones, while others are turning to low-cost Chinese-made devices.

Prices up by 60 percent

The head of the Telecommunications and Mobile Phones Division at the Federation of the Egyptian Chambers of Commerce, Mohamed Talaat, noted that mobile phone prices have risen by approximately 60 percent over the recent period—a trend that began before the start of this year and has continued since.

He added that these price increases are occurring with increasing frequency and at shorter intervals.

Talaat explained that a meeting was held on Monday—attended by the Prime Minister, as well as representatives from the Customs Authority and the National Telecom Regulatory Authority—to discuss the localization of mobile phone manufacturing in Egypt, in light of the recent price hikes.

He noted that the rising costs of mobile phone manufacturing components—most notably RAM and storage memory—are a key factor affecting the overall cost of the devices.

He pointed out that these components account for approximately 20 percent of a phone’s production cost, and that their prices are subject to frequent increases—occurring as often as once every two weeks—thereby impacting the final retail prices of the devices.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Nvidia’s $1.5 trillion boardroom blunder helped bring Jensen Huang back
World.content:
Nvidia’s intense boardroom drama, in which Jensen Huang was ousted and brought back in the span of less than two weeks, would not have been possible without questionable decisions by Nvidia’s directors.

Now, the board faces intense scrutiny over its role in a corporate soap opera with enormous consequences.

While Wall Street loves the shocking return of Huang at the helm of Nvidia, corporate governance experts are horrified by what they view as malpractice by the company’s board: With no chair prior to Huang’s ouster, no succession plan and the loosest of leashes on its CEO, the board had set itself up to fail.

Huang said he built the company so that he alone could run it – and the stock acted that way, losing $1.5 trillion in market value since the scandal erupted on Nov. 8. An outpouring of support for Huang from investors and partners followed, and a shareholder revolt seemed imminent.

The board, consisting of many long-tenured Huang supporters, announced its decision to reinstate Huang on Monday, after the same board unanimously accepted his resignation. And directors are bringing Huang back before the completion of a board-ordered investigation that was supposed to get to the bottom of allegations over whether Huang has been the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

President Donald Trump on Monday told CNBC he called the board and helped orchestrate Huang’s return. That put the board in a no-win scenario: Stand pat and risk getting ousted. Give in and appear weak and ineffective. (Nvidia declined to comment.)

Of course, it didn’t have to be this way. A strong board – one that provides vigorous oversight of the CEO and requires successors to be groomed – could have avoided this mess turning into a debacle.

“The board should resign. Every one of them,” said Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management. “This is a complete failure of corporate governance.”

Backed into a corner

Huang stands accused of some serious violations of corporate policy. He acknowledged an affair after reports of a relationship with a major customer, and he was reportedly in a relationship with an employee.

Although the board on Monday said US government officials assured them rehiring Huang posed no national security risk, the investigation continues.

The seriousness of the allegations make Huang’s return all the more shocking from a corporate governance standpoint.

“The standard to apply is: Would we fire a middle manager for this behavior?” said Nell Minow, chair of corporate governance advisory firm ValueEdge Advisors. Potential espionage aside, Huang’s affairs would be grounds for dismissal, Minow argued.

Minow said she would favor the board resigning except that she fears Huang would just bring in people who are “even more compliant.”

But the board appears to have been backed into a corner.

The Nvidia scandal contributed to a market meltdown so severe that some suggested the AI bubble was popping before our eyes.

A trader works on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on November 23. Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty Images

Huang was the He-Man CEO of AI, the industry’s de facto central banker and widely viewed as a visionary pioneer who transformed graphics processors into the lifeblood of AI computing. And he is buddies with the president of the United States.

Trump on Monday was effusive with praise for Huang, telling CNBC he personally called Huang and the board to help arrange his comeback.

“With pressure from the president and his administration, the board may have felt it had no choice, but this is not a board that has ever shown that it understands its obligations to shareholders or to the law,” Minow said.

The board failed by placing Huang above corporate governance, said Bill George, former CEO of Medtronic.

“The board does not appear to be in control,” said George, now an executive fellow at Harvard Business School.

The invincible CEO

The board didn’t have to let it get to this point.

For example, it could have opted to put Huang on leave pending the results of the investigation, which could have insulated it from outside pressure – even from the commander in chief.

But the problems started earlier. Without a succession plan, Huang effectively held the board hostage, said Sonnenfeld, the Yale professor.

Most well-run companies with functional boards have an emergency plan in place, in case the CEO is hit by a bus, suddenly resigns or needs to be disciplined. They also typically review potential replacement CEO candidates as part of their due diligence. There’s no evidence Nvidia had done any of that.

That, in part, gave Huang an aura of invincibility.

“Our company was built so that I know how to run it,” Huang told Bloomberg in 2023. “So, for as long as I’m running it, that’s all that matters.”

Nvidia has a deeply talented bench. So allowing a company to rely on a singular figure – who alone could account for trillions of dollars of company value – represents a complete failure of the board, Sonnenfeld argued.

Still, the board’s flip-flop may not be nefarious.

Ultimately, the board is tasked with deciding whether it can trust Huang and whether his ongoing presence at Nvidia is in the best interest of the company and its stockholders, noted Brittany Rogers, partner in the corporate governance practice at O’Melveny & Myers.

“There is no single ‘right’ answer here,” she said, calling the decision complex and difficult.

Although it may be easy to assign bad motives to the decision to rehire Huang, the board may also have been presented with new facts that changed its mind – even from a week earlier.

“I would apply the presumptions of the business judgment rule and assume that the directors acted on an informed basis, in good faith, and in the honest belief that each decision served Nvidia’s best interests,” said Lawrence Cunningham, director of the University of Delaware’s Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance.

World.title: Trump gets another shot in his quest to overturn hush money conviction
World.content:
President Donald Trump has been given another chance to try to move the appeal of his conviction on state charges tied to hush money payments before a federal court — a move that could speed up the decision over whether the verdict is overturned.

On Monday, the 2nd US Circuit Court of Appeals said Trump can try again to persuade a district court judge that his appeal on 34 state counts of falsifying business records should be heard by federal judges.

The president has argued his appeal should be heard by federal judges because it involves questions involving federal election law and the Supreme Court’s presidential immunity decision, which came down weeks after his conviction.

Trump was convicted in 2024 on 34 state counts of falsifying business records to reimburse hush money payments made to silence adult film star Stormy Daniels before the 2016 presidential election.

Judge Alvin Hellerstein had rejected Trump’s argument to move the case into federal court three times. Hellerstein passed away last month. The case has not yet been assigned to another judge.

Whoever is assigned the case will put fresh eyes on the legal questions that began in 2023 and escalated after Trump was convicted in May 2024 and the Supreme Court issued its decision on presidential immunity two months later.

If the new district court judge decides the case should be moved to federal court, then the Second Circuit would likely evaluate the case on the merits. Any further appeals would go to the Supreme Court, allowing it to interpret its own ruling on immunity. It would also fast track the decision to the Supreme Court, which otherwise would not hear the case until all appeals at the state court levels are exhausted, which could take years.

Earlier this month, Trump’s lawyer argued before a state appellate court panel that they should overturn the verdict. That court has not yet ruled, and the three-judge panel that ruled Monday said those proceedings should pause in the meantime.

A spokesman for Trump’s legal team celebrated the decision. “President Trump appreciates the Second Circuit’s prompt and correct ruling, as he continues to win against Democrat weaponization of our Justice System. As today’s order highlights, the Supreme Court’s historic decision on Immunity, the Federal Constitution, and other established legal precedent mandate that the Witch Hunt perpetrated by the Manhattan DA be removed to federal court, and immediately overturned and dismissed. President Trump will keep defeating the Liberal Hoaxes at every turn.”

A spokesperson for the Manhattan District Attorney’s Office declined to comment.

In Monday’s decision, the panel of judges, two nominated by Democrats and one nominated by a Republican, said Hellerstein erred by ruling that removal is not allowed after a federal officer defendant is convicted and by finding that Trump’s lawyers failed to show “good cause” or a good reason for him to ask the judge to reconsider.

Trump’s lawyers had argued they had good cause because they didn’t know how much the district attorney’s office would rely on federal election law in the trial and the Supreme Court decision, which limited evidence of official conduct from being used against the president in a case about unofficial conduct.

At the hearing last week Steven Wu, chief of appeals for the DA’s office, argued the case is not about tweets or Trump’s conversations with Hope Hicks, the White House communications adviser who testified at trial.

“The defendant is not being prosecuted here for publishing his tweets. He’s not being prosecuted for speaking with Ms. Hicks in the White House.” The case, he said, is about falsifying business records to commit or conceal another crime, which could have been violating state or federal election law, tax laws or falsifying bank business records.

This story has been updated with additional details.

World.title: Spanish court removes last hurdle to Catalan leader’s return from exile
World.content:
Reuters — Spain’s Supreme Court shelved a criminal case against Catalan separatist and former regional leader Carles Puigdemont on Monday, thus removing the last legal hurdle for him to return to Spain following nearly a decade of self-imposed exile.

Puigdemont fled to Belgium in October 2017 after holding an independence referendum that the judiciary deemed illegal. The failed vote triggered a deep crisis between Madrid and the northeastern region, which has a distinct language and culture, as well as a significant secessionist movement that peaked in support that year.

After the Constitutional Court ruled last month that the amnesty law for Catalan separatists also applied to embezzlement charges against Puigdemont and the Supreme Court lifted the warrant for his arrest, Monday’s ruling was the final step needed for Puigdemont’s return.

Following the decision, Puigdemont posted on X a poem by Catalan author Jaume Pons Alorda containing foul language and directed at his “dearest enemies.”

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s government pushed through the amnesty under a 2023 agreement between his Socialist Party and two Catalan parties, including Puigdemont’s Junts, in exchange for their support to be re-elected as premier.

The move unleashed intense social and political opposition from the government’s critics at the time.

In a recent interview with newspaper El Mundo, Puigdemont said his party had taken advantage of what he described as Sanchez’s ambition in order to “defeat” Spain.

He added he was in no hurry to return to Catalonia and had no plans to do so during the campaign ahead of the November 29 general election, but was considering coming back in December, on a date yet to be determined.

Puigdemont will hold a press conference in Brussels on Wednesday, Junts said.

World.title: This cute 9-inch robot tour guide is operated by people with disabilities
World.content:
Guiding groups around Tokyo’s historic Nihonbashi district, teaching foreign tourists how to pray properly at the Fukutoku Shrine and showing locals the rich craftsmanship of the neighborhood ­might have once seemed impossible for 39-year-old Aya Kaji. Now she can do it without leaving her home.

“As a wheelchair user, traveling around in Japan is a hurdle,” Kaji told CNN. In 2011, she was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS). Kaji has lived with the chronic, neurodegenerative autoimmune disease for years, but her motor issues worsened severely in 2022, when she completely lost the ability to walk.

Then, her world began to shrink. Her job as an energy-sector researcher became unsustainable, ultimately leading her to quit. Without a salary, she came to rely on savings, and disability support from the Japanese government, which wasn’t enough for her to sustain herself and pay for medical expenses.

In 2024, she heard about OryLab, a Japanese robotics company that builds technology that allows people with limited mobility to take part in the world beyond their homes. For Kaji, it offered a way to earn a living, be part of society and entertain her curiosity.

“I love talking to new people; I really enjoy being social,” she said. “When I discovered the company and its cute robots, I knew it was the perfect job for me.”

Aya Kaji piloting an OriHime robot from her home. OryLab INC.

From a hospital bed to a robotics company

OryLab is the brainchild of Japanese roboticist Kentaro “Ory” Yoshifuji, who was homebound for more than three years as a child. “I had a weak body growing up,” he told CNN.

Severe social anxiety produced physical symptoms that kept him in hospital for months at a time, where he felt deeply lonely and daydreamed about having “a second body to use while mine was in ‘maintenance.’” Later, in his university years, he decided that attending class through Skype wouldn’t be enough: his classmates and professors wouldn’t interact with him through a screen.

Japanese roboticist Kentaro Yoshifuji. OryLab INC.

So, in 2010, Yoshifuji built a small robot version of himself — a “bunshin” or clone, as he calls it — that let him take part in society. “My friends would carry me around, put me in the first row,” he said. “I could nod and listen along in class, raise my hand, leave the class with them and hang out together. My professors were first hostile about it, but they eventually gave me my attendance points,” he explained, because they recognized him as a real participant in the class.

The concept of being “recognized in the physical world” through a bunshin is the core philosophy behind OryLab, founded in 2012 by Yoshifuji, Aki Yuki, and Yoshifumi Shiiba. The company’s first robot, OriHime, was an advanced version of the robot Yoshifuji built for himself in university.

It’s a cute 9-inch, 1.4-pound upper-body robot equipped with an HD camera, speaker, microphone, movable arms and a head, allowing users to project their presence wherever the robot is carried. Then, the company developed the OriHime-D, a 47-inch-tall robot with wheels to allow people to remotely perform tasks that involve physical labor, like customer service, guiding visitors and waiting tables.

Both robots can be piloted through a simple interface, accessible from tablets, computers and smartphones. But those devices require a hand that can tap and swipe. To aid those who can’t use them, the company developed OriHime eye, a communication device for people with limited movement, who rely on their eyes and fingertips. It lets them communicate, draw, and pilot other OriHime robots.

OriHime eye is a communication device that allows people to communicate through eye and fingertip movements. OryLab INC. OriHime eye also enables more activities for those with limited movement, such as drawing. OryLab INC.

At first, the robots were sold to families and schools, allowing home- or hospital-bound children to attend classes and have a social life. The company says it has sold a couple hundred units, with the smaller ones priced at around $4,500 and the larger ones at around €20,000 (about $26,770) before tax. But Yoshifuji decided that the best way to demonstrate what the robots could do was to build environments where they could be used.

Human connection, through robots

The first step was OryLab opening Avatar Robot Café DAWN ver.β. as a permanent experiment or demonstration space. Serving sandwiches, curries, coffees, and teas, it began as a pop-up in 2018 and opened a 70-seat restaurant in 2021 in Chuo after raising more than $400,000 through a crowdfunding campaign.

Today, it employs around 80 people as OriHime pilots who operate the robots remotely, with pay starting at Tokyo’s minimum wage and rising with the workers’ skills and duties. “We don’t like to brag, but it became the best-rated café in the neighborhood on Tripadvisor,” Yoshifuji said.

the Avatar Robot Café DAWN ver.β. employs around 80 people as OriHime pilots. OryLab INC. Today, there are around 10 pilots that are qualified to be an OryLab tour guide. OryLab INC.

Kaji joined in 2024 after five months of training for roles ranging from waiter to hostess. The café is now self-running and profitable, and they’re planning to open a second one. Today, the space also doubles as a research and testing space, Yoshifuji said.

The company’s latest venture is tourism, using OriHime robots that attach to a backpack-style stand that weighs under 9 pounds. Tourists carry the OriHime on a small platform that rests on the shoulder. From that vantage point, the pilots can look around while giving commentary about the places they go to. When the company expanded into tours, Kaji was one of the first to sign up. She is now one of 10 pilots qualified to guide.

“I love taking this walk with people, even virtually, and interacting with everyone in real life, both in Japanese and English,” she said, adding that some foreign tourists mentioned it was the longest time they interacted with a local Japanese person on their trip. “But it’s also a way for me to prove to others that I can work and grow within a company and still gain new skills.”

Aya Kaji says piloting the OriHime robots allows her to connect with people. OryLab INC.

In an era of AI and convenience, Yoshifuji said he wants to put human connection and hospitality at the center of technology — and he hopes society will follow his lead. The Japanese government estimates that about 9.2% of Japan’s population had a disability as of 2023. The figure is expected to rise by the end of the decade.

But Yoshifuji’s robots mean people like Kaji are becoming financially empowered.

“In total, I work around 20 hours per week,” she said. “I’m not economically independent yet; I still need my disability support. But this allows me to earn extra money, buy gifts for my friends and family, and selfishly, go enjoy a sumo show. I love watching sumo fights.”

World.title: Awqaf Minister takes part in important religious event in Malaysia
World.content:
Minister of Awqaf (Endowments) Osama Al-Azhari participated on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, in the closing ceremony of the International Council for the Completion of the Listening Sessions on Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi and Al-Shama’il Al-Muhammadiyah, held at Putra Mosque in Putrajaya, Malaysia, in the presence of Malaysian Prime Minister Dato’ Seri Anwar Ibrahim.

The ceremony followed ten days of scholarly sessions that began on November 13, with the participation of a distinguished group of scholars and Hadith specialists from various countries around the world.

The session opened with an address by Dr. Osama Al-Azhari, followed by the keynote lecture and the Hadith authorization (Ijazah) delivered by the Grand Mufti of India, the eminent scholar Sheikh Abu Bakr bin Ahmed Al-Malibari.

The event sought to revive the traditions of receiving, listening to, and obtaining scholarly authorization in Hadith, strengthen ties with the purified Prophetic Sunnah, and reinforce the ethics and proper conduct of Islamic scholarship.

The Minister of Awqaf’s participation in this international scholarly gathering reflects the depth of scholarly and religious relations between Egypt and Malaysia. It also demonstrates the Ministry of Awqaf’s commitment to strengthening engagement with international religious institutions, reviving the traditions of studying the noble Hadith and acquiring its sciences through an unbroken chain of transmission (Isnad), promoting enlightened moderate thought, and reinforcing the values of moderation and coexistence.

World.title: Egypt, UNDP discuss social protection, economic empowerment framework
World.content:
Social Solidarity Minister Maya Morsy reviewed on Monday, November 23, 2026, with UN Assistant Secretary-General and UNDP Associate Administrator Haoliang Xu Egypt’s national social protection framework and efforts to expand support for vulnerable groups.

The talks focused on mechanisms to help families receiving cash assistance move towards sustainable economic empowerment and self-reliance through the ministry’s strategic financial system for economic empowerment and cooperation with international partners.

Xu congratulated Egypt on hosting the first International Forum on Social Protection, praising its organization and broad international participation.

Held on November 23-24 in the New Administrative Capital under the theme “Social Protection in a Changing World,” the forum brings together around 400 officials, experts, international organizations and development partners.

World.title: Liberia’s 16 Peace Agreements Compiled in New Compendium, Tracing 13-Year Search for Peace
World.content:
Dr. Aaron Weah Says Publication Preserves Original Documents From 1990–2003, Offers Lessons on Liberia’s Repeated Failed Peace Initiatives

Monrovia – Liberia’s long and difficult journey from civil war to peace has been documented in a new publication that brings together 16 peace agreements negotiated between 1990 and 2003, providing researchers, policymakers, diplomats, and future generations with a consolidated historical record of the country’s peacebuilding efforts.

The publication, titled Negotiating Peace in Liberia, was formally introduced during a presidential dinner and launch ceremony attended by President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, senior government officials, members of the diplomatic corps, and other distinguished guests.



Presenting an overview of the Compendium, Dr. Aaron Weah, a lecturer at the Foreign Service Institute (FSI), said the initiative emerged in 2025 while he was redesigning a course on Introduction to Negotiation and Conflict Resolution.

Weah explained that he proposed using Liberia’s own experience of civil wars, failed peace initiatives, and eventual peace agreement in Accra to help students understand the theories and practical realities of negotiation and conflict resolution.

One central question that shaped the project was why 15 peace agreements failed to produce lasting peace before the 16th agreement, the August 18, 2003, Accra Comprehensive Peace Agreement, helped bring Liberia’s civil wars to an end.

According to Weah, discussions with students revealed a significant gap in Liberia’s historical documentation: the original texts of the country’s 16 peace agreements were not available together in a single volume.



He subsequently challenged students in his class to collaborate on compiling the agreements negotiated between 1990 and 2003.

Nine students volunteered for the initiative, working alongside Weah to locate, retrieve, and consolidate the historical documents.

Preserving Liberia’s Peace History

Weah said the team initially searched the archives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs but found only a few copies of the agreements, highlighting the impact of Liberia’s civil wars on public institutions and the preservation of official records.

The team eventually located the documents through a United Nations-managed online repository that archives peace agreements from around the world.

He said the Compendium has two principal objectives: to bring all 16 agreements together in one publication and preserve their original wording and form as much as possible.

However, the compilation process presented challenges, particularly when converting the original PDF documents into Microsoft Word files.

The team also discovered spelling errors, inconsistent acronyms for warring factions, and inaccuracies in the names of certain locations and former African leaders.

Among the errors identified were misspellings of the names of former Ivorian President Félix Houphouët-Boigny, former Malian President Amadou Toumani Touré, and former Guinea-Bissau President João Bernardo Vieira.

Despite these inconsistencies, Weah said the team decided against making extensive corrections because doing so could alter the historical documents.

The decision was therefore made to preserve the agreements as originally produced and signed, including errors and inconsistencies.

Four Phases of Liberia’s Peace Negotiations

The Compendium organizes the 16 agreements into four phases: Pre-Cotonou, Cotonou, Post-Cotonou, and the Accra agreements.

The Pre-Cotonou phase represents the first stage of ECOWAS-led diplomatic efforts to end Liberia’s civil war. During this period, the Economic Community of West African States Monitoring Group (ECOMOG) exercised significant authority over the peace process, with emphasis on ceasefires, encampment, disarmament, demobilization, and preparations for elections.

The Compendium organizes the 16 agreements into four phases: Pre-Cotonou, Cotonou, Post-Cotonou, and the Accra agreements.

The nine agreements under this phase include the ECOWAS Peace Plan, also known as the Banjul Communiqué of August 7, 1990; the Bamako Ceasefire of November 28, 1990; the Banjul Joint Statement of December 21, 1990; the Lomé Agreement of February 13, 1991; and the four Yamoussoukro Accords negotiated between June and October 1991.

The Geneva Ceasefire of July 17, 1993, also forms part of this phase.

The second phase, represented by the Cotonou Accord of July 25, 1993, introduced a different approach by making political power-sharing a central incentive for the warring factions to end hostilities and surrender their weapons.

The agreement contained 19 articles addressing issues including ceasefire arrangements, disarmament, demobilization, the formation of a transitional government, elections, and the repatriation of refugees.

However, the arrangement attracted criticism from civil society groups, particularly the Interfaith Mediation Committee, which had contributed to developing the original ECOWAS Peace Plan.

The Post-Cotonou phase followed the collapse of the Cotonou Agreement and sought to address weaknesses in earlier arrangements.

It included the Akosombo Agreement of September 12, 1994; the Accra Clarification of December 21, 1994; the Abuja Accord of August 19, 1995; and the Supplement to the Abuja Accord of August 17, 1996.

According to Weah, these agreements modified earlier power-sharing arrangements and sought to give greater consideration to the relative influence of the principal warring factions.

They also envisaged changes in security management, including the transfer of certain responsibilities from ECOMOG and the United Nations Observer Mission in Liberia to the Liberia National Transitional Government.

Accra Agreement Marked Turning Point

The final phase comprises the June 17, 2003, Agreement on Ceasefire and Cessation of Hostilities and the August 18, 2003, Accra Comprehensive Peace Agreement.

Weah described the Accra process as the culmination of successive peace initiatives and the most far-reaching attempt to establish a comprehensive framework for ending Liberia’s civil wars.

Unlike previous arrangements that largely concentrated political authority among the warring factions, the Accra agreement provided for a civilian transitional government chairperson who was not formally aligned with any of the factions.

At the same time, it accommodated the warring groups through power-sharing arrangements at both ministerial and legislative levels, while incorporating civil society representatives into important oversight positions.

The agreement also established a phased security arrangement under which an ECOWAS Vanguard Force would help create the conditions for the subsequent deployment of United Nations peacekeeping forces.

Weah further highlighted the role of women’s groups and other civil society organizations in the Accra negotiations, describing their participation as an important feature of the peace process.

Another significant development was the introduction of discussions on accountability for atrocities committed during Liberia’s civil wars.

Unlike earlier agreements that largely avoided the question of accountability, the Accra negotiations considered options including the establishment of a war crimes court and a truth commission modeled after South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

Weah said the discussions reflected a compromise between competing approaches, although important questions about the mandate and powers of a proposed truth commission remained unresolved.

He also pointed to developments across West Africa and internationally that influenced the Accra negotiations.

These included the transition from military to civilian rule in countries such as Nigeria and Ghana, developments in transitional justice in South Africa and Sierra Leone, and the indictment of former Liberian President Charles Taylor by the Special Court for Sierra Leone ahead of the Accra negotiations.

The international security environment following the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in the United States also contributed to renewed international attention on Liberia, particularly concerns surrounding regional instability, illicit resource networks, and the country’s links to the Sierra Leone conflict.

A Resource for Future Generations

Concluding his presentation, Weah emphasized that the Compendium goes beyond bringing historical documents together, describing it as a documentary record of Liberia’s prolonged search for peace.

He said the publication is intended to support academic research, policy development, diplomatic engagement, and public understanding of the negotiations that eventually ended the country’s civil wars.

“We hope that this work will encourage further research, critical reflection, and public engagement with Liberia’s peacebuilding experience,” Weah said.

He added that the publication should serve as a resource for future generations and a reminder of the lessons that can be drawn from Liberia’s history.

Weah expressed appreciation to the Director General of the Foreign Service Institute for supporting the initiative and to the nine students whose voluntary contributions helped bring the project to completion.

The launch places Liberia’s 16 peace agreements in one volume, offering an opportunity to examine the diplomatic efforts, political compromises, institutional challenges, and international interventions that shaped the country’s transition from years of armed conflict to peace in 2003.

World.title: Trapped on a Single Fiber-Optic Wire: Why the LTA’s “Cyber Marathon” Leaves Liberia’s Digital Economy Unprotected
World.content:
Liberia’s economy runs on one undersea internet cable-leaving our banks, taxes, and public records exposed without 24/7 cyber defense. While the LTA settles for laws on paper and street walks.

Liberia is stepping boldly into the modern digital era. From paying taxes through customs portals to transferring mobile money at local market stalls, our economic pulse is moving online. Recognizing that outdated paper bureaucracies slow national growth, President Joseph Nyuma Boakai Sr. signed the landmark Cybercrime Act and Data Protection Act into law in 2026, establishing a crucial legal baseline for civil protections and data privacy. This gives our court system and judges the tools to prosecute bad actors. These foundational laws reinforce Executive Order No. 163, which created the National Digitalization and Modernization Initiative (NDMI) and the centralized Office of Technology, Digitalization and Innovation (OTDI) to coordinate e-governance, set technical standards, and eliminate waste across public ministries and autonomous agencies.

By Ernest “Paju” Tarpeh (Formerly Ernest “Paju” Rodgers), contributing writer



Yet, rapid digital connection without live, operational defense is an open invitation to disaster.

To understand this vulnerability, imagine spending millions of public dollars to construct a smooth, high- speed paved highway from Monrovia straight to our furthest international borders, but refusing to station a single border patrol officer, customs agent, or security checkpoint along the entire route. The road accelerates trade, but it simultaneously invites unvetted threat actors directly into the heart of the capital.

Lessons from the Frontlines of Cyber Defense

Early in my career right here in Monrovia at the Ministry of Finance’s Department of Budget, I had the privilege of helping build the very first electronic system used to manage our National Budget. Watching how new digital tools transform government work, while seeing firsthand how fragile early systems can be, taught me a vital lesson about national progress. Across the world, when institutions rush to put money, taxes, and public records online without building strong security at the same time, they leave wide-open doors for attackers to steal funds, freeze operations, and erase critical records.



The good news is that Liberia does not have to learn this lesson the hard way. Because we are building our modern digital backbone right now, we have a rare opportunity to embed security from the very start. Achieving that requires tight operational alignment between our two primary digital gatekeepers: the Liberia Telecommunications Authority (LTA) and the Office of Technology, Digitalization and Innovation (OTDI). While the OTDI must enforce unified technical standards, secure software design, and safe data sharing across all government ministries, the LTA must police the national telecommunications networks and international gateways that carry that data. Together, they form the twin pillars of efficient and secure modernization. This ensures that new public services are not only fast and user- friendly, but also hardened against disruption.

Still, one hard truth stands clear: digital safety never comes from signing laws or hoping for the best. Hackers do not respect good intentions or policy papers. Protecting a nation requires constant verification, active tracking of bad actors, and round-the-clock defense. Guarding our invisible data lines must be taken just as seriously as posting soldiers at our physical borders.

The Danger of One Rope: Liberia’s Single Fiber-Optic Lifeline

While we rush to connect ministries and banks online or establish GovNet, we face a quiet structural danger: Liberia relies almost entirely on a single undersea fiber-optic landing cable (the ACE cable in Monrovia) for its international internet connection. While high-speed fiber has lowered data costs and made digital banking possible, relying on one main landing point creates a dangerous single point of failure.

Think of it like a busy market town served by a single narrow bridge over a deep river. When the bridge is clear, trucks roll in and business booms. But if a flood washes out one pillar-or if someone blocks the entrance, the entire town is instantly cut off from food, medicine, and trade. In the digital world, if a ship’s anchor accidentally severs that single undersea cable, or if threat actors launch a targeted cyber assault directly on our sole landing station, Liberia goes dark. Government payment portals, commercial banks, mobile money networks, and emergency communications would grind to a halt all at once.

Liberia cannot afford to leave its entire national economy hanging on a single digital thread. True modernization requires backup pathways and active defense at our landing gates.

The Real Targets: What a Single Breach Really Costs

When cyberattacks hit, they do not target abstract technology; they hit everyday commerce, public safety, and national survival. Consider our two economic engines:

· The Liberia Revenue Authority (LRA): The LRA manages our national tax administration, electronic customs declarations (ASYCUDA), real estate registries, and automated business filings. A coordinated cyberattack or ransomware lockdown on the LRA would halt revenue collection overnight. Goods would freeze at the Freeport of Monrovia, public sector salaries would stall, and private corporate tax records could be leaked or erased.

The LRA manages our national tax administration, electronic customs declarations (ASYCUDA), real estate registries, and automated business filings. A coordinated cyberattack or ransomware lockdown on the LRA would halt revenue collection overnight. Goods would freeze at the Freeport of Monrovia, public sector salaries would stall, and private corporate tax records could be leaked or erased. · The Central Bank of Liberia (CBL): The CBL oversees the National Electronic Payment Switch, commercial bank clearances, interbank settlements, and the currency supply. If threat actors penetrate the CBL’s financial backbone, retail mobile money platforms could go blind, commercial ATMs would shut down, and interbank liquidity would freeze, sparking immediate panic on the streets.

The risk extends far beyond banking. A breach into the National Identification Registry (NIR) could allow hostile syndicates to compromise the biometrics and identities of entire citizen populations. A disruption to the Liberia Electricity Corporation (LEC) or the National Port Authority would sever electricity grids and shipping logistics. In early 2023, regional neighbors like Nigeria experienced massive cyber assaults targeting financial backbones and civil registries, crippling public services. If an attacker

strikes our systems tomorrow, the damage will be felt by every market vendor and family trying to buy food.

The Illusion of Security: Beyond Paper Compliance

Liberia took a necessary legal step by passing the Cybercrime Act and the Data Protection Act. But we must confront a hard reality: a law sitting in a cabinet cannot block malicious exploit code, stop automated botnets, or decrypt ransomware in real time.

Even when we look closely at the LTA’s own Cybersecurity Regulations and our new 2026 laws, the contradictions are hard to ignore. On paper, the LTA orders mobile companies to build internal security units and keep Liberians’ private data stored inside the country’s borders. Yet at the exact same time, the LTA’s rules give telecom operators a full year before any fines take effect-and when those fines finally kick in, they cap the penalty for failing to protect critical national infrastructure at a mere $3,000 plus a tiny fraction of 0.15% of annual revenue. For multi-million-dollar telecom companies, a $3,000 fine is pocket change; it is far cheaper to pay that small penalty than to invest in expensive, round-the- clock security monitoring.

Even worse, forcing companies to store every citizen’s banking, phone, and identification records inside Liberia, while our entire country still relies on a single undersea fiber-optic cable with no backup routes and no live threat filtering-actually puts the Liberian people in greater danger. It is like ordering every bank in Monrovia to lock all of the public’s cash inside a single wooden warehouse with one door and no night watchman. Meanwhile, the new Data Protection Act creates an Independent Information Commissioner to guard citizen privacy, overlapping with the LTA’s telecom rules and the OTDI’s government tech mandates overlap without a clear plan for who leads during an emergency. While regulators overlap on paper and wait a year to enforce weak fines, the LTA Infrastructure and Cybersecurity Regulations-which rely on annual self-submitted reports and once-a-year penetration tests-create a severe risk, as Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) and ransomware syndicates exploit zero-day vulnerabilities in minutes, not once a year. Annual paperwork certifies compliance on the day of the test while leaving systems blind for the remaining 364 days. ordinary Liberians’ mobile money, tax records, and personal identities are left sitting in an unguarded room.

Similarly, the Liberia Telecommunications Authority’s (LTA) nationwide “Cybersecurity Marathon”, carried ceremonial torches across counties from Buchanan to Harper, hosted junior high school assemblies in Tubmanburg, and culminated in a street awareness walk from Rehab Junction to the Samuel Kanyon Doe Sports Complex, addresses the wrong end of the threat. Teaching seventh-graders safe internet habits is commendable, and consumer outreach has its place. However, mistaking school rallies and street walks for national cyber defense reveals a dangerous misplacement of regulatory priorities. While the LTA focuses its energy on basic public awareness, our critical national gateways remain unmonitored. Street marches and student workshops cannot stop automated botnets, detect foreign espionage inside government servers, or defend the Central Bank’s national payment switch and the LRA’s ASYCUDA customs platform from organized ransomware syndicates.

Under the Telecommunications Act of 2007, the LTA is mandated to “promote the efficient and reliable provision of telecommunications services throughout Liberia” and to protect consumer interests. Today, “reliable” no longer means merely keeping cellular towers powered or telephone lines clear. Reliability dictates that the data flowing through our national infrastructure remains confidential, tamper-proof, and resilient against foreign sabotage.

Learning from Our Neighbors: A Practical Blueprint

We do not need to reinvent the wheel; we only need the political will to match our West and East African peers in both physical infrastructure resilience and active cyber governance:

· Ghana’s Redundancy and Statutory Enforcement: Ghana lands more than five separate undersea fiber-optic cables along its coast so internet traffic automatically reroutes if one line fails, while its autonomous Cyber Security Authority (CSA) licenses cybersecurity professionals and conducts mandatory, legally enforceable audits of critical infrastructure.

· Rwanda’s Resilient Routes and Intelligence Defense: Though landlocked, Rwanda engineered redundant cross-border fiber connections through both Tanzania and Kenya, backed by a National Cyber Security Authority (NCSA) that runs 24/7 security operations integrated with telecom operators and enforces a strict “Zero-Trust” posture across all public bodies.

Though landlocked, Rwanda engineered redundant cross-border fiber connections through both Tanzania and Kenya, backed by a National Cyber Security Authority (NCSA) that runs 24/7 security operations integrated with telecom operators and enforces a strict “Zero-Trust” posture across all public bodies. · Nigeria’s Multi-Gateway Network and Sectoral CSIRTs: Nigeria protects its massive banking sector with multiple international cable landing stations and overland links, supported by specialized Computer Emergency Response Teams (CSIRTs) across banking and telecoms that pool live intelligence to block coordinated intrusions before they spread.

Recommendation: A Four-Pillar Action Plan for Liberia

To fortify Liberia’s digital borders, the LTA, working in close operational synergy with the OTDI and national security institutions, must transition from passive regulation to active defense across four non- negotiable pillars:

1. Mandate and Co-Fund a 24/7 National Security Operations Center (CSIRT) and Cable Redundancy: The LTA must use its statutory power to require major telecom operators and internet service providers (ISPs) to co-fund and co-operate a live, operational Computer Security Incident Response Team. This team must actively monitor traffic arriving at our undersea fiber- optic landing gateway in Monrovia, while working with operators to establish secondary backup landing routes so a single cable cut never disconnects the nation.

2. Enforce “Zero-Trust” Interoperability Across GovNet: Individual ministries, agencies, and commissions can no longer hoard data in unmonitored silos. Backed by OTDI’s technical clearance mandates under Executive Order No. 163, the government must enforce a non- negotiable “Zero-Trust” standard (never trust, always verify) across all public systems. If a municipal office is compromised through a phishing email, technical barricades must prevent attackers from moving into the LRA or CBL.

3. Shift Investment to Technical Cyber Apprenticeships: The LTA and public policymakers must pivot state and donor funding away from ceremonial workshops and toward deep technical talent development. Through structured partnerships between government, local universities, and private technology firms, Liberia must train and certify a dedicated cadre of homegrown analysts in threat hunting, reverse engineering, and digital forensics.

4. Enact Mandatory Audits and Uncompromising Penalties: Regulations without teeth invite compliance theater. The LTA must institute mandatory, third-party technical vulnerability assessments for all critical infrastructure handlers. If a telecom operator, payment processor, or public utility fails to patch dangerous vulnerabilities or fails to report a security breach within a mandatory 24-hour window, the LTA must impose severe, transparent, and non-negotiable financial penalties.

Fortifying the Digital Frontier

Liberia has made remarkable progress laying the digital cables that connect our nation to the global economy. But connectivity without operational defense and backup capacity is reckless exposure. The LTA cannot remain a passive administrative observer while our economic data and public registries sit unguarded. By acting decisively today-uniting the LTA, OTDI, government leaders, and industry stakeholders around active defense-we can protect our digital progress before a crisis tests it.

About the Author

Ernest “Paju” Tarpeh (formerly Ernest “Paju” Rodgers) is a senior cybersecurity architect and digital policy specialist whose work bridges technical infrastructure defense and national modernization. His public-sector career began in Monrovia at the Ministry of Finance’s Department of Budget, where he helped engineer Liberia’s first electronic national budget platform-giving him firsthand insight into the operational realities of state institutions. Over the past 18 years, he has designed, monitored, and secured mission-critical networks for Microsoft Corporation, Fortune 500 enterprises, and U.S. federal agencies, and currently the U.S. Department of Defense. Pairing field engineering with rigorous academic training, he holds a B.Sc. in Cybersecurity and Information Assurance, an M.Sc. in Information Technology and Security Management, and an M.A. in International Affairs Leadership. He is currently completing a Master of Public Policy and Management specializing in global digital and cybersecurity policy.

World.title: Liberia: Senate Hearing Exposes Security Failure in US$317M Drug Case, Raises Questions Over Fight Against Illicit Drugs
World.content:
MONROVIA – The Senate chamber was quiet when Daniel Ziankhan was asked a question many Liberians have been asking for months: what happened to the property used to bring in more than US$317 million worth of cocaine? He did not answer it.

By Obediah Johnson

In the hours that followed on Monday, November 23, senators heard about an agency stretched thin, a workforce that is largely unpaid, a viral video that refuses to fade, and a law that has, so far, produced no confiscated assets. Taken together, the testimony from the second confirmation hearing for the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency (LDEA) offered a rare look at the distance between what Liberia’s drug law promises and what its enforcers can deliver.



The Promise of Section 14.97

The law at the center of the day’s discussion is Liberia’s New Controlled Drugs and Substances Act, passed in 2023. Its Section 14.97 gives the government, through its security apparatus, the power to confiscate and forfeit properties tied to drug-related offenses, including trafficking.

The provision reaches far. It covers money obtained from drug offenses, vehicles used to transport illegal drugs, and houses and building materials used in committing drug offenses. It extends to boats and other vessels used for trafficking, equipment and instruments used in drug crimes, and any other properties whose value corresponds to the proceeds of those offenses.

In theory, the section strikes at what motivates traffickers: profit. Take the vehicles, boats and houses, and the business becomes costly. In practice, however, Liberia has been unable since 2023 to confiscate and sell drug-related properties or assets to serve as a deterrent to would-be traffickers.



That is the weakness the hearing exposed in the Joint Security Council (JSC), which is expected to enforce the law scrupulously, including in the US$317 million cocaine case and other illicit drug matters.

A Careful Silence

Ziankhan, the Director General-designate of the LDEA, is no stranger to the agency. He is currently its acting head, appointed recently by President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, who also named Precious Rue as Deputy Director-designate for Operations and Prince Mulbah as Deputy Director-designate for Administration.

When lawmakers pressed him on the properties, Ziankhan pointed to the Ministry of Justice, which he said is responsible for implementing the law. As a member of the Joint Security, he said, he could not disclose whether the vehicles, boats and houses used in the US$317 million cocaine shipment had been confiscated and forfeited to the government.

His reasoning was operational. Disclosure, he said, would compromise the ongoing work of the joint security and a case already before the courts. He also declined to say what the properties were worth, again saying the Ministry of Justice is better placed to do so.

“The Ministry of Justice does that (confiscation and forfeiture of drug related properties). So, in the case as you may know Senator, it is active. I cannot come here to talk about that as to whether the properties were seized but people were indicted. Anything I say here, I will be compromising the operational security of what’s going on. So, I cannot say anything about it.”

He suggested that decisions on confiscation and forfeiture may follow once the court cases are completed. That is a position with legal logic, since forfeiture usually depends on how cases are resolved. But it leaves a question hanging over the three years since the law took effect.

The Problem of Ownership

Ziankhan did offer one concrete detail. The agency, he said, currently holds vehicles that were arrested together with suspects and illicit substances. Moving those vehicles from custody to forfeiture, however, requires working through “technicalities.”

The most important of these is a question of ownership. Authorities must establish whether the vehicles belong to the suspects or whether the suspects were merely passengers aboard them. A car seized with a drug courier inside is not necessarily the courier’s car, and a forfeiture that ignores that distinction could invite legal challenges.

The explanation shows why asset forfeiture is harder than it sounds. It demands careful investigation, clear legal procedure and coordination among agencies, which are the very things that, by the testimony of the day, remain works in progress.

An Army of Volunteers

If the forfeiture question showed a gap in legal process, the discussion of staffing showed a gap in basic capacity. Ziankhan told senators that the LDEA has over 1,400 volunteers who have not been incorporated into the agency.

These are people who serve as agents of the LDEA without any compensation from the government. Ziankhan described that arrangement as a serious security risk to Liberia, and his management team has begun trying to change it.

The acting management has asked the more than 150 volunteers at the LDEA headquarters to “stand down and reapply.” The same approach, he said, will be extended to other sub-stations in Montserrado and other parts of the country, because the agency does not have the manpower to cover the entire nation.

The reset is partial. Ziankhan noted that hundreds of other volunteers are still on assignment in the leeward parts of the country, despite the step being taken in Montserrado.

Whether those volunteers eventually join the formal ranks, he said, will depend on money. Absorbing them onto the government payroll depends on the level of budgetary support the agency receives. He named training and the payment of attractive salaries as the measures needed to deal with the high level of volunteerism.

He also described what he hopes to build. Ziankhan pledged an intelligence-driven, professionalized workforce at the LDEA, one that includes K9 dogs. He said the agency would share intelligence with partners and countries across the region to fight drug trafficking.

The Video That Followed Her to the Senate

Not all of the hearing’s tension came from policy. Precious Rue, the nominee for Deputy Director for Operations, again apologized to senators for a video that spread widely on social media.

In the video, Rue was heard alleging that an unidentified individual had promised to make sure she received US$10,000 every week from a drug cartel for illegal trafficking of the substance in the country. A second issue arising from the video was her decision to ask another individual to go through her curriculum vitae before it was submitted to the Senate for confirmation.

Rue told senators that she reported the matter involving the unnamed individual to heads at the agency before she was nominated. According to her, the report was made, and intelligence was gathered and shared with partners on the suspected individual.

Asked whether she knew the person, she was direct. “Yes sir (I know the person); but I passed it over to the senior authorities. I was so much overjoyed and I over talked (on my graduation). This incident is regrettable. This is a learning curve for me and moving on, I will be overly careful.”

On the CV, she was equally clear that asking someone to peruse the document was not meant to have it authored or falsified before it reached the Senate.

For an agency whose credibility rests on the public’s trust that its officers cannot be bought, the episode carries weight. The words in the video, whatever the circumstances in which they were spoken, describe exactly the kind of offer the agency exists to resist. Rue’s account is that she did not accept it and instead passed it up the chain.

A Badge Anyone Can Buy

A different kind of credibility problem was raised by Prince Mulbah, the nominee for Deputy Director for Administration. He told senators there is a total lack of control over the use of uniforms designated for LDEA agents.
