Mulbah called on authorities of the Ministry of Justice to deal with the misuse and duplication of the uniform used by the LDEA and other state security bodies. Many volunteers and others, he said, continue to wear the uniform bearing the agency’s badge without having undergone proper training.

He traced the problem to the growing number of private security firms and stores that produce and sell their own uniforms without being regulated by the ministry. “There are lot of (uniform) stores around our country anybody can lay hands on LDEA badge. Anybody can wear the uniform of police, PSU- even the private security firms-there is no regulation or control on what kind of uniform they should wear from national security. There are lot we need to do when it comes to reform.”

The issue is not cosmetic. Mulbah said state security actors are unknowingly blamed for misconduct committed by officers from some private security firms. When a person in a lookalike uniform behaves badly, the public may not know the difference, and the agency whose badge was worn takes the blame.

The problem also connects to the volunteer question. Volunteers wearing the uniform without proper training blur the line between a trained, accountable officer and someone who simply looks like one.

A Senator’s Warning

The most forceful remarks came from Grand Cape Mount County Senator Dabah Varpilah. She told the nominees that the strength or success of a law lies in the way it is implemented by those responsible for doing so.

She encouraged them and other members of the joint security to implement the law scrupulously, without fear or favor, even as government budgetary support increases. “The LDEA and the entire security sector has to carry the drug law as your Bible or quoran, if you are a Muslim. The cartel or drug dealers are very strong because they control cash. I want to advice you, let’s take this as a responsibility for this country.”

Senator Varpilah observed that Liberia’s future and stability would be guaranteed by how seriously the war against illicit drugs is taken. She said those leading the LDEA should ensure the drug laws are thoroughly implemented to the fullest, no matter who is involved or connected.

She cautioned that poor implementation would come back to haunt the agency’s leaders if they failed to carry out their assigned tasks and responsibilities. Her view of the volunteer system was sharply negative. Varpilah described the increase in volunteers serving as agents at the LDEA as counter-productive to the fight against illicit drug trafficking and abuse in Liberia.

Yet she did not stop at criticism. She asked LDEA authorities to submit a realistic work plan that would attract more budgetary allocation, so that the fight against drugs can benefit the country and its citizens.

Cash Against the Law

Her remark that cartels are strong because they control cash points to the logic behind Section 14.97. If traffickers draw their power from money and the assets it buys, then the law’s forfeiture powers are among the most direct tools available to weaken them.

That makes the absence of seized and sold assets more consequential than a procedural delay. Each unused provision is an advantage left with the traffickers, and each month without a confiscation leaves intact the financial base that sustains the trade.

The hearing also showed how the pieces connect. Forfeiture requires investigators with training, a legal process that establishes ownership, and prosecutors and courts that move cases forward. An agency that depends on unpaid volunteers and cannot control its own uniforms will find it difficult to carry out any of that reliably.

The three nominees now await the Senate’s decision. Their testimony suggests they understand the scale of the task, even if some answers were deliberately withheld. Ziankhan has set out a plan built on training, better pay, intelligence-sharing, K9 units and a smaller, more professional force. Mulbah has put the uniform problem on the record and asked the Justice Ministry to act. Rue has apologized twice and said she will be more careful.

What the Senate asked of them, in the end, was less about promises than proof. Senator Varpilah’s message was that the law is only as strong as the people who carry it out. Her challenge was to treat it with the seriousness of a sacred text.

Whether the LDEA can meet that challenge depends partly on the nominees and partly on others: the Ministry of Justice, which Ziankhan says holds responsibility for forfeiture; the lawmakers who control the budget; and the courts where the biggest cocaine case is still being heard.

World.title: Iran War Prices Liberia’s Small Farmers Out of Fertilizer, Threatening Harvests
World.content:
Aaron Moore, a farmer in Miller Hill, Careysburg District, Montserrado County, points to the yellowing leaves of his pepper plants.

Summary:

Rising fertilizer prices and shortages caused by the US-Israeli war with Iran are putting pressure on Liberia’s small farmers.

Farmers reported struggling to afford supplies, raising concerns about smaller harvests, higher food prices and lower incomes.

Duty exemptions and government-backed distributions offer some support, but farmers outside those programs continue to face unaffordable prices.

By Nemenlah Cyrus Harmon, climate and environment reporter with New Narratives

MILLER HILL, Careysburg — Aaron Moore stopped among his pepper plants and pointed to the yellowing leaves. They should have been deep green by now. For a farmer whose harvest helps pay school fees and feed his six children, the pale leaves were alarming.



Moore, 49, has grown peppers and cucumbers on this plot for more than four years. He works there every morning and evening. But now he can no longer afford the fertilizer he needs to keep his crops growing.

“When the fertilizer is not there, the plant will not grow good,” he said. “The crops will die.”

Moore’s struggle reflects a widespread problem for Liberia’s small farmers. Agriculture specialists said the US-Israeli war with Iran, which began in February, has pushed fertilizer prices up and cut supplies. Iran has largely closed the Strait of Hormuz, a shipping route that carried nearly a third of the world’s traded fertilizer before the war. That threatened the vegetable harvests that support rural families and feed local markets. The stakes are high in a country where about one in five people do not have enough food year-round and a quarter of young children are stunted, according to the World Food Programme.

Francis Mulbah, the Ministry of Agriculture’s assistant minister for planning and development, said the government provided fertilizer to rice farmers through an emergency food production program funded by the African Development Bank, which ended in 2024. The amount each farmer received depended on the size of the land they farmed. Some government-supported projects also provide fertilizer to farmers growing rice, cassava and vegetables, but he could not say how many farmers had benefited.



Mulbah said the government is also in talks with OCP Africa, a fertilizer company based in Morocco, to supply fertilizer at lower prices. Under the plan, the government would buy fertilizer from the company for major importers in Liberia. The deal would also improve supply, provide soil testing and train farmers, but nothing has been signed. The ministry has also hired county-level agriculture staff to advise farmers on how to use fertilizer.

Mulbah said the crisis in the Middle East had added to fertilizer shortages and higher prices around the world, making it harder for Liberia to get supplies. He did not provide a current retail price for fertilizer.

Mulbah said fertilizer subsidies could make farm supplies more affordable.

“If we want to get the rightful yield as a country, it means that we have to invest into fertilizer usage,” he said. “It’s the only way to afford the maximum output.”

For Moore, the pressure is immediate. Fertilizer now costs about L$12,000 (about US$65) a bag, he said, compared with L$9,000 to L$11,000 a few years ago. Prices tend to dip during the rainy season and rise in the dry months. That offers little comfort when he does not have the money to buy a bag.

Experts said farmers across the country faced the same problem. Jonathan S. Stewart, chief executive of Agrotech Liberia, which supports farmers and food security projects, said just finding a bag can be a challenge. Some sellers have run out. Major suppliers are based in Monrovia, so farmers in other areas must also pay for transport.

“If you add the transportation, that’s a lot for people who are literally making less,” Stewart said.

The costs begin before fertilizer is even used. Stewart said a small pack of cucumber seeds costs US$20 to US$25. With fertilizer and other supplies, growing a cucumber crop can cost more than US$100, with no guarantee the harvest will earn that money back. A shovel that once cost US$7 now sells for about US$10.

The smallest buyers have little bargaining power. A customer ordering 100 or 200 bags can negotiate a discount, Stewart said. Someone buying one or two usually pays the full price.

Julius M. Bass, a cocoa farmer who previously led the Farmers Union Network, said those costs can overwhelm farmers working small plots. He has spent about 24 years in agriculture. The network brings farmers together to seek support from donors and aid programs, which has given Bass a close view of the problems growers face.

“Can you imagine a farmer using a hectare to grow cucumbers, and he needs fertilizer?” Bass said. “How does he get the money to buy it at that kind of astronomical cost?”

For Moore, money for these supplies must come from earnings spread across a long season. He said he makes about L$50,000 (about US$270) in some seasons and up to L$75,000 (about US$410) when the crop does well. His peppers take at least three months to begin producing. A full growing season lasts six to eight months.

Partial view of Aaron Moore’s pepper farm at Miller Hill, Careysburg District, Montserrado County

Without enough fertilizer, Bass said, a farmer expecting half a ton of peppers from a hectare might harvest only a quarter ton. “That’s a great slap in your face. But what do you have to do? You need food to eat, you need to send the children to school.”

The government has tried to ease import costs. In November 2024, President Joseph Boakai signed an executive order suspending import tariffs on farm supplies, including fertilizer. Government and donor projects also buy fertilizer in bulk and give it to farmers who take part in them.

But those programs are shrinking as foreign aid is cut, and growers outside them must buy at market prices. Importers set their own prices, and paperwork or delays at the port can add storage fees to their costs. There is no national fertilizer price. Each importer adds up its costs and decides what to charge.

For now, growers try to manage with what they have. Stewart said some have learned to mulch with leaves, which break down and add nutrients to the soil. But heavy rains can wash nutrients away. Moore loosens the soil around his plants to help them grow, but he said it does not work as well as fertilizer.

Wars far away squeeze Liberia’s farmers

Stewart blamed part of the squeeze on the Iran war and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Both have disrupted global supplies and shipping routes, raising costs for importers.

He said Liberia buys fertilizer from Turkey, China and Europe, while some local suppliers buy through neighboring Ivory Coast. Those supplies must reach Ivory Coast before they travel on to Liberia, which adds costs along the way.

Bass cautioned against treating overseas wars as the sole explanation, saying fertilizer was expensive before the latest disruptions. He urged Liberians with money to invest in agriculture and bring in cheaper fertilizer from other sources, so farmers are not stuck with costly supply routes even when global trade is running normally.

Food on the table

Experts warned that Liberia’s food supply, already strained by climate change and a lack of investment in farming, could be stretched further. Bass said small farmers grow much of Liberia’s everyday food, including peppers and other vegetables. When they cannot afford supplies, families feel it through less food and higher prices.

“These are the people putting food on our table,” Bass said.

Aaron Moore displays an empty fertilizer bag that he purchased several months ago.

Help that misses some farmers

Moore said he has received no government support.

“We don’t want to depend on the government,” he said. “But if they help us, you will see the progress of it. You will see the produce.”

Bass said farmers have long called for subsidies, where the government pays part of the cost of supplies. He welcomed the government’s push to bring in farm machinery but said fertilizer support must also reach growers with small plots. On Oct. 30 at Camp Ware in Careysburg, China handed over 304 pieces of farm machinery, including tractors and small harvesters, to the Liberian government.

Stewart proposed making fertilizer and certified seeds in Liberia to cut reliance on imports. Those ideas would take investment. For farmers facing costs now, the question is how to pay for the next bag.

He also pointed to gaps in national agricultural data, which make it difficult to establish how much harvests have fallen. His concern rests on what he sees in farmers’ fields.

On Miller Hill, Moore keeps tending his peppers and cucumbers. He said he will keep planting and try to bring another crop through to harvest.

“If there is no money, we will try,” he said.

This story was a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the Investigating Liberia Project.

World.title: Liberia: LRA Boss Tells Lawmakers Government Waived More Than It Collected On International Trade
World.content:
Capitol Building, Monrovia – The Committee on Ways, Means, Finance and Budget of the House of Representatives has kicked off hearings on the revenue component of the proposed US$1.539 billion Fiscal Year 2027 National Budget, a process that began with some startling revelations and staggering numbers that surprised the gathering.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

The main irony is that a government that waived US$442 million in customs duties in 10 months is now asking Liberians to pay 26% more in tax to fund a US$1.54 billion budget and that US$95 million of that budget is not even new money.



Exemptions, A Major Threat

Speaking at the opening day of the revenue hearings on Monday, November 23, 2026, the Commissioner General of the Liberia Revenue Authority (LRA), Dr. James Dorbor Jallah revealed how the country has lost massively in revenue due to tax exemptions.

Startlingly, he told the gathering of lawmakers and financial experts that between January and October 2026, customs exemptions amounted to US$442 million, compared with US$278 million actually collected on international trade.

In other words, he pointed out that more than 60 percent of potential trade revenue is being waived, citing it as one of the major challenges confronting revenue generations.



“Honorable Members, I must be candid. The greatest threat to our revenue base is the growth of tax exemptions.”

From 2023 to date, he intoned, exemptions have totaled US$1.3 billion, indicating that duty waivers on petroleum products alone rose to about US$10.7 million in 2025.

The Success Story – FY 2026 Performance

In what stands out to be a very encouraging statistic, CG Jallah disclosed that as of November 21, 2026, the LRA has collected US$1.260 billion in total revenue, which is 97 percent of the approved budget of US$1.302 billion.

He pointed out that domestic revenue stands at US$1.181 billion, which means LRA surpassed its full-year domestic target with about six weeks remaining.

Also, of these amazing numbers, he asserted that Customs collected 105 percent of its annual target; the Domestic Tax Department collected 99 percent, while Tax revenue alone reached 102 percent.

“The shortfall in total revenue is in external resources, mainly borrowings, which are not collected by the LRA. To put this in context, domestic revenue for the whole of 2025 was US$847 million. In about eleven months of 2026, we have already collected about 39 percent more than that, and domestic revenue has nearly doubled since 2023,” he furthered.

It is a projection by the LRA boss that total revenue will close the year at about US$1.380 billion, stating: “This is the result of the hard work of our staff, staff of other revenue-generating agencies, the cooperation of taxpayers, and the support of this Legislature.”

The FY 2027 Outlook

The draft budget projects total revenue of US$1.539 billion, of which US$1.392 billion is domestic revenue. For the first time, tax revenue is projected to exceed one billion United States dollars, at US$1.072 billion.

The envelope also includes US$92 million in external budget support, a US$55 million carry-forward from FY 2026, and US$40 million in contingent revenue from the APM Terminals and Marsa Maroc port agreements.

Accordingly, Dr. Jallah points out that, these projections rest on real GDP growth of 5.1 percent, with inflation easing to 6.8 percent, and four key policy measures.

One of these policy measures, he claims, is the replacement of Good Services Tax (GST) with a 15 percent Value Added Tax (VAT) from January 1, 2027. He noted that the result is expected to yield about US$225 million.

Also, CG Jallah cited a two (2) percent advance corporate income tax on the turnover of mining and agriculture companies as one of the policy measures, which is estimated at US$57.3 million.

Also, the LRA boss named the collection of petroleum taxes on import volumes rather than on gallons lifted and the provisions of the Tax Amendment Bill 2026, which will be submitted to the House of Representatives as some of the most critical policy measures taken.

The Reforms

To deliver these numbers, Jallah accentuated that the LRA will implement 24 reforms.

Key among them are the full rollout of ASYCUDA to all border posts and the National Single Window, VAT implementation and electronic invoicing; extending LITAS and real property tax administration to all 15 counties, the revenue assurance monitoring system in the gaming, telecommunications and mobile money sectors; integration with the Central Bank payment switch, and stronger integrity controls, including background verification and lifestyle audits for staff in sensitive positions.

Request For Five Percent

To bolster greater revenue generation, the LRA is proposing to the Legislature through the House of Representatives for the amendment of the LRA Act that will allocate five percent of the tax revenue it assesses and collects as its operational budget, excluding royalties, SOE and maritime contributions, fees, fines and external resources.

“We also ask this Body to work with us to review and rationalize exemptions. Fund the collector, and the collector will grow the collection,” he added.

Issues For Legislative Attention

Like Commissioner General Jallah, the Chairman of the House Committee on Ways, Means, Finance and Budget, Representative P. Mike Jurry, also identified revenue leakages, exemptions, concessions, weaknesses in revenue administration and statutory obligations of state-owned enterprises as key issues requiring legislative attention.

In his opening remarks, Chairman Jurry vowed that the Committee will work tirelessly to achieve its objectives for the hearing by identifying and finding remedies to revenue leakages, exemptions, concessions and weaknesses in revenue administration, among others.

“The Joint Committee will seek to achieve the following objectives: Examine the credibility and feasibility of the proposed FY2027 revenue projections; assess the assumptions and methodologies underpinning the revenue estimates; examine FY2026 revenue performance against approved targets; evaluate domestic revenue mobilization strategies and institutional collection capacities; identify and find remedies to revenue leakages, exemptions, concessions and weaknesses in revenue administration; examine statutory revenue obligations and contributions by state-owned enterprises; identify opportunities for expanding the domestic revenue base and provide evidence-based recommendations to inform legislative consideration and approval of the FY2027 National Budget,” he asserted.

A ‘Realistic’ Projection

At the same time, Deputy Minister for Fiscal Affairs at the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning, Anthony G. Myers, told the House Joint Committee on Ways, Means, Finance and Budget and the Public Accounts Committee that the proposed budget is expected to reach US$1,538,916,274 is nothing but realistic.

He explained that this projection represents an 11.5 percent increase over the FY2026 year-end revenue estimate of US$1.380 billion and 18.1 percent above the approved FY2026 budget of US$1.303 billion.

Myers noted that the FY2027 revenue projection is built primarily on recurring domestic revenue rather than one-off receipts, noting that tax revenue is expected to increase by 26.5 percent, from US$847.5 million to US$1.072 billion.

He explained that the FY2026 revenue performance benefited from exceptional mining receipts, including more than US$220 million in signature bonuses, but said the FY2027 forecast deliberately excludes similar windfalls from its baseline assumptions.

The Deputy Minister dismissed concerns that the proposed budget could face a significant shortfall without another major mining signature bonus, arguing that the country’s economic growth is increasingly driven by sectors beyond mining.

He stated that Liberia’s economic output was US$3.9 billion in 2025, with preliminary estimates placing it at US$4.1 billion in 2026 and projecting US$4.3 billion for 2027.

He said the services sector is expected to remain the largest contributor to economic activity, averaging US$1.5 billion annually over the medium term, followed by agriculture and fisheries at US$1.1 billion, while mining and quarrying are projected to average US$800 million.

Myers identified wholesale and retail trade as the largest projected revenue source, contributing US$466.2 million, including US$313.7 million from taxes on international trade. Services revenue is projected at US$378 million, while recurrent revenue from mining and quarrying, excluding signature bonuses, is estimated at US$323.3 million.

World.title: Liberia: House Opens Scrutiny of US$1.54B FY2027 Revenue Plan, Vows To Test Whether Revenue Targets Are Real
World.content:
Capitol Building – The Chairman of the House Committee on Ways, Means, Finance and Budget, Representative P. Mike Jurry, has assured Liberians that lawmakers would examine whether the proposed FY2027 revenue framework is realistic, equitable, administratively achievable and sufficient to support Liberia’s development priorities.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

As it goes on to do the business of the Liberian people, the Maryland County Electoral District #1 Representative insists that the committee will do due diligence to the process by properly cross examining the proposed financial instrument in the interest of Liberians and Liberia.



The declaration was contained in his opening remarks at the ongoing revenue hearing into the FY2027 National Budget. The hearing is intended to scrutinize the credibility of revenue projections, assess the assumptions and methodologies behind the estimates, review FY2026 collection performance and evaluate the capacity of revenue-generating institutions.

Issues For Legislative Attention

He also identified revenue leakages, exemptions, concessions, weaknesses in revenue administration and statutory obligations of state-owned enterprises as key issues requiring legislative attention.

“The Joint Committee will seek to achieve the following objectives: Examine the credibility and feasibility of the proposed FY2027 revenue projections; assess the assumptions and methodologies underpinning the revenue estimates; examine FY2026 revenue performance against approved targets; evaluate domestic revenue mobilization strategies and institutional collection capacities; identify and find remedies to revenue leakages, exemptions, concessions and weaknesses in revenue administration; examine statutory revenue obligations and contributions by state-owned enterprises; identify opportunities for expanding the domestic revenue base and provide evidence-based recommendations to inform legislative consideration and approval of the FY2027 National Budget,” he asserted.



The committee chairman stressed that domestic revenue mobilization is essential to Liberia’s fiscal sovereignty and long-term economic independence, adding that the country must strengthen tax compliance, broaden its revenue base, improve customs administration and use technology to reduce revenue losses.

Call For Fair Revenue Mobilization

He cautioned that revenue mobilization must be fair, arguing that compliant taxpayers and legitimate businesses should not bear an unreasonable burden while tax evasion, under-declaration, smuggling and other forms of non-compliance persist.

Rep. Jurry further emphasized that revenue collection must be matched by transparency and accountability in public spending, noting that citizens are more willing to meet their tax obligations when they see public resources being managed responsibly and used to deliver essential services.

The hearing is expected to provide lawmakers with an opportunity to question the Ministry of Finance, the LRA and other revenue-generating institutions on the assumptions, risks and policy measures underpinning the FY2027 revenue estimates.

MFDP Defends Budget

When given the time for remarks, Deputy Minister for Fiscal Affairs at the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning, Anthony G. Myers, defended the proposed US$1.54 billion Fiscal Year 2027 National Budget.

In so doing, he projected a significant increase in domestic revenue collection despite concerns over the feasibility of the estimates and the absence of major one-off mining signature bonuses.

The Projection That Matters

Deputy Minister Myers told the House Joint Committee on Ways, Means, Finance and Budget and the Public Accounts Committee that the proposed budget is expected to reach US$1,538,916,274, representing an 11.5 percent increase over the FY2026 year-end revenue estimate of US$1.380 billion and 18.1 percent above the approved FY2026 budget of US$1.303 billion.

Myers noted that the FY2027 revenue projection is built primarily on recurring domestic revenue rather than one-off receipts, noting that tax revenue is expected to increase by 26.5 percent, from US$847.5 million to US$1.072 billion.

He explained that the FY2026 revenue performance benefited from exceptional mining receipts, including more than US$220 million in signature bonuses, but said the FY2027 forecast deliberately excludes similar windfalls from its baseline assumptions.

The Deputy Minister dismissed concerns that the proposed budget could face a significant shortfall without another major mining signature bonus, arguing that the country’s economic growth is increasingly driven by sectors beyond mining.

He stated that Liberia’s economic output was US$3.9 billion in 2025, with preliminary estimates placing it at US$4.1 billion in 2026 and projecting US$4.3 billion for 2027.

He said the services sector is expected to remain the largest contributor to economic activity, averaging US$1.5 billion annually over the medium term, followed by agriculture and fisheries at US$1.1 billion, while mining and quarrying are projected to average US$800 million.

Myers identified wholesale and retail trade as the largest projected revenue source, contributing US$466.2 million, including US$313.7 million from taxes on international trade. Services revenue is projected at US$378 million, while recurrent revenue from mining and quarrying, excluding signature bonuses, is estimated at US$323.3 million.

He further disclosed that recurrent mining revenue is expected to remain strong, with tax revenue from the sector projected to increase from US$146.6 million to US$167.6 million, despite the absence of a major signature bonus.

VAT and Other Revenue Measures

The Deputy Minister outlined several policy measures expected to support the FY2027 revenue target, including the implementation of a 15 percent Value Added Tax (VAT), a two percent advance corporate income tax on mining and agriculture companies, and stronger tax compliance and administration.

He said VAT will replace the existing 13 percent Goods and Services Tax (GST) effective January 1, 2027, and is projected to generate US$224.8 million, comprising US$76.6 million in domestic VAT and US$148.2 million in VAT on imports.

Myers clarified that rice and petroleum products will remain outside the VAT regime, contrary to reports circulating in some sections of the public. He said the exclusion is intended to prevent disruptive price increases for consumers and producers.

He added that the two percent advance corporate income tax on the turnover of companies in the mining and agriculture sectors is expected to generate US$57.3 million in FY2027, compared with US$7.6 million in the FY2026 approved budget.

The measure, he explained, is intended to address risks associated with base erosion and profit shifting and will be reflected on a full-year basis in the 2027 budget following delays in its enforcement due to legal challenges by some concessionaires.

Other measures under the proposed Liberia Tax Amendment Bill of 2026 include electronic tax invoicing, stronger customs controls, authorization for the Liberia Revenue Authority (LRA) to match third-party information against tax returns, and excise taxes on fees charged for digital financial services.

World.title: Liberia’s Digital Economy Faces Cybersecurity Risks Amid Reliance on Single Undersea Cable, Expert Warns
World.content:
MONROVIA – As Liberia accelerates its transition toward a digitally connected economy, growing concerns are emerging over the country’s ability to protect critical national infrastructure, financial institutions, government databases, and citizens’ personal information from potential cyberattacks.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Cybersecurity architect and digital policy specialist Ernest “Paju” Tarpeh has warned that Liberia’s increasing dependence on digital services, combined with what he describes as inadequate cybersecurity infrastructure and limited operational preparedness, could expose the country to serious economic and national security risks.



In a commentary titled “Trapped on a Single Fiber-Optic Wire: Why the LTA’s ‘Cyber Marathon’ Leaves Liberia’s Digital Economy Unprotected,” Tarpeh argued that although Liberia has made progress in establishing laws and policies to regulate its digital space, the country has yet to develop the operational capacity required to defend its expanding digital economy against sophisticated cyber threats.

He particularly questioned the cybersecurity priorities of the Liberia Telecommunications Authority (LTA), arguing that public awareness campaigns, school outreach programs, and nationwide street activities must be accompanied by sustained investments in technical infrastructure, specialized personnel, and round-the-clock monitoring of critical digital systems.

According to Tarpeh, Liberia’s growing reliance on electronic banking, mobile money transactions, online tax administration, customs platforms, and government databases means that cybersecurity can no longer be treated as a secondary regulatory concern.

Instead, he maintained that protecting digital infrastructure must become a central component of national security, economic planning, and public service delivery.



His warning comes as government institutions increasingly embrace digital platforms to improve efficiency, facilitate financial transactions, expand access to public services, and strengthen revenue administration.

However, Tarpeh cautioned that the same digital transformation could create significant vulnerabilities if the infrastructure supporting it is not adequately protected.

Single Undersea Cable Raises National Security Concerns

At the center of Tarpeh’s concerns is Liberia’s dependence on the Africa Coast to Europe (ACE) submarine fiber-optic cable, whose landing infrastructure in Monrovia provides a major gateway for the country’s international internet connectivity.

He described the arrangement as a potential single point of failure, warning that physical damage to the cable or a major disruption at its landing infrastructure could affect several essential services that depend on uninterrupted international connectivity.

According to him, disruptions could have consequences for government payment platforms, commercial banking operations, mobile money services, customs administration, business transactions, and emergency communications.

He compared Liberia’s digital infrastructure to a busy commercial town connected to the outside world through a single bridge, warning that damage to that bridge could bring significant economic activities to a standstill.

“Liberia cannot afford to leave its entire national economy hanging on a single digital thread,” Tarpeh argued, calling for alternative connectivity routes and stronger protection of the country’s international telecommunications gateways.

He stressed that digital modernization should not be measured solely by the number of people connected to the internet or the expansion of online government services.

Rather, he said, the country must also consider whether its telecommunications infrastructure can withstand physical damage, cyberattacks, technical failures, and other emergencies.

For Liberia, he maintained, the absence of adequate backup connectivity could turn a technical failure into a broader economic disruption.

His concerns highlight the importance of developing alternative international internet routes, including additional submarine cable connections and cross-border terrestrial fiber-optic links that could provide backup connectivity if the primary route becomes unavailable.

LRA, Central Bank Among Critical Institutions at Risk

Tarpeh identified the Liberia Revenue Authority (LRA) and the Central Bank of Liberia (CBL) as two institutions requiring particular cybersecurity attention because of their central roles in the country’s financial and economic operations.

He warned that a successful cyberattack against the LRA could disrupt electronic customs declarations, tax administration, revenue collection, and other essential services.

Such an incident, he argued, could affect the processing of goods at the Freeport of Monrovia, delay government revenue collection, and expose confidential corporate and taxpayer information.

With customs and tax administration increasingly dependent on electronic systems, he said, a prolonged disruption could create difficulties for importers, exporters, businesses, and government agencies that rely on the Authority’s digital platforms.

The Central Bank, which oversees important components of Liberia’s financial and payment systems, is another institution he identified as potentially vulnerable.

Tarpeh cautioned that a breach affecting critical financial infrastructure could disrupt electronic payments, interbank settlements, and other banking services, with consequences for commercial activities and ordinary citizens.

He further identified the National Identification Registry, Liberia Electricity Corporation, and National Port Authority as institutions whose digital operations could have significant national consequences if compromised.

A breach involving national identification records, he warned, could expose sensitive personal and biometric information, potentially creating opportunities for identity theft, fraud, and other forms of exploitation.

Similarly, attacks against electricity and port infrastructure could affect essential public services, cargo movement, commercial operations, and the broader economy.

Tarpeh’s argument is that cybersecurity planning must extend beyond individual institutions to consider how interconnected government systems could be affected by a single successful attack.

He believes that protecting these institutions requires coordinated security standards, continuous monitoring, effective incident response procedures, and regular independent assessments of their digital infrastructure.

Questions LTA’s Cybersecurity Priorities

While acknowledging the importance of public cybersecurity education, Tarpeh questioned whether the LTA’s nationwide Cybersecurity Marathon adequately addresses Liberia’s most pressing technical vulnerabilities.

The campaign included activities such as carrying ceremonial torches across counties, engaging junior high school students in Tubmanburg, and conducting public awareness activities, including a street walk from Rehab Junction to the Samuel Kanyon Doe Sports Complex.

Tarpeh described public education as necessary but insufficient, arguing that awareness campaigns cannot substitute for specialized cybersecurity personnel, active threat detection, and continuous protection of critical national infrastructure.

He maintained that teaching students responsible internet practices and encouraging citizens to protect their personal information are important elements of cybersecurity preparedness.

However, he argued that these initiatives must be accompanied by the capacity to identify malicious network activities, detect unauthorized access to government systems, respond to ransomware attacks, and protect financial institutions against organized cybercriminal operations.

According to him, Liberia needs technical teams capable of identifying vulnerabilities before criminals exploit them and responding quickly when security breaches occur.

He questioned whether the country’s current approach places sufficient emphasis on these operational requirements.

His central criticism is that cybersecurity awareness must be matched by investments in the systems and personnel responsible for defending the country’s digital infrastructure.

Cybersecurity Laws Alone Cannot Stop Attacks

Tarpeh also examined Liberia’s emerging legal and regulatory framework, including the Cybercrime Act and Data Protection Act, which provide an important foundation for addressing cybercrime and protecting personal information.

However, he cautioned that legislation alone cannot prevent cyber intrusions or guarantee the security of government and private-sector information systems.

He questioned aspects of the LTA’s Infrastructure and Cybersecurity Regulations, particularly the enforcement timelines, financial penalties, and reliance on periodic compliance reporting.

According to his interpretation of the regulations, telecommunications operators are given a one-year period before certain financial penalties take effect, while penalties for some violations involving critical national infrastructure could be as low as US$3,000, alongside a percentage-based component.

He argued that such penalties may not provide sufficient financial deterrence for large telecommunications companies, particularly where violations could expose national infrastructure to significant risks.

Tarpeh also raised concerns about the reliance on annual self-submitted reports and periodic penetration testing, warning that cyber threats can emerge and exploit vulnerabilities between scheduled assessments.

“Hackers do not respect good intentions or policy papers,” he argued, emphasizing the need for continuous monitoring, active threat tracking, and rapid incident response.

He maintained that cybersecurity compliance should not be treated as an exercise conducted once or twice a year but as an ongoing responsibility requiring institutions to identify and address vulnerabilities continuously.

Beyond the regulatory requirements, Tarpeh questioned the coordination of responsibilities among the LTA, the Office of Technology, Digitalization and Innovation (OTDI), and the proposed independent data protection oversight framework.

In his view, unclear operational responsibilities during a major cyber incident could complicate the government’s response and delay efforts to contain an attack.

He therefore called for a clearly defined coordination structure establishing which institution leads during a cyber emergency, which agencies provide technical support, and who is ultimately responsible for protecting critical national information systems.

Calls for Stronger Institutional Coordination

Tarpeh identified the LTA and OTDI as two central institutions that must work together to strengthen Liberia’s digital security architecture.

While the OTDI is expected to coordinate government digitalization, establish technical standards, and promote secure information sharing across public institutions, he argued that the LTA must exercise stronger oversight of telecommunications networks and international connectivity infrastructure.

He said the two institutions should establish a coordinated framework to ensure that digital government services are not only accessible and efficient but also resilient against cyber threats.

One of his major recommendations is the adoption of a Zero-Trust security framework across government digital systems.

Under this approach, no user, device, or system is automatically trusted, even when accessing an internal government network. Every access request must be verified, with security controls designed to limit unauthorized access and prevent attackers from moving between connected systems.

Tarpeh believes such safeguards could reduce the risk of an intrusion into one government institution spreading to sensitive financial, identification, or national security databases.

He argued that government institutions should adopt stronger identity verification procedures, access restrictions, network segmentation, and continuous monitoring to ensure that sensitive information remains protected.

He also emphasized the importance of strengthening information-sharing arrangements among government agencies, telecommunications operators, and relevant national security institutions.

Lessons from Ghana, Rwanda and Nigeria

To demonstrate possible approaches, Tarpeh pointed to Ghana, Rwanda, and Nigeria as African countries whose cybersecurity and telecommunications arrangements offer lessons for Liberia.

He cited Ghana’s multiple submarine cable connections and the work of its Cyber Security Authority, which oversees cybersecurity regulation and the protection of critical information infrastructure.

He also referenced Rwanda’s cross-border fiber-optic connections through neighboring countries and the work of its National Cyber Security Authority.

Nigeria, meanwhile, was highlighted for its multiple international connectivity gateways and specialized Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTs) operating across important sectors.

According to Tarpeh, these examples demonstrate the importance of combining alternative connectivity infrastructure with specialized cybersecurity institutions and coordinated incident response systems.

He suggested that Liberia could draw from these experiences by investing in alternative internet routes, developing specialized technical teams, and strengthening collaboration between telecommunications companies and government security agencies.

He maintained that the country’s relatively small telecommunications market should not be an excuse for failing to establish adequate cybersecurity protections.

Rather, he argued, the government should prioritize investments based on the potential economic and national security consequences of a major digital disruption.

Four-Pillar Plan for Liberia

To address the vulnerabilities he identified, Tarpeh proposed a four-pillar action plan centered on strengthening national cybersecurity capacity, improving institutional accountability, and reducing Liberia’s dependence on a single international internet gateway.

First, he called for a 24-hour national cybersecurity response system.

He urged the LTA to work with major telecommunications operators and internet service providers to establish and co-finance a Computer Security Incident Response Team capable of monitoring threats, coordinating responses to cyber incidents, and working with network operators to protect Liberia’s international connectivity infrastructure.

The proposed team would provide continuous monitoring and help identify suspicious activities before they escalate into major security incidents.

He also called for the development of alternative submarine cable connections and other backup internet routes to reduce the country’s dependence on a single international gateway.

Second, he recommended enforcing Zero-Trust security standards across government institutions.

He said particular attention should be given to institutions operating sensitive financial, identification, and public service databases.

Under this approach, government systems would require continuous identity verification and controlled access, reducing the possibility of unauthorized users gaining access to sensitive information or moving across interconnected networks.

Third, he called for greater investment in technical cybersecurity training and local expertise.

Tarpeh argued that Liberia must develop a homegrown workforce capable of conducting threat analysis, digital forensics, reverse engineering, and advanced cyber defense operations.

He proposed partnerships involving government institutions, universities, and private technology companies to provide specialized training and build the technical capacity required to defend national infrastructure.

According to him, relying heavily on external expertise without developing local professionals could weaken the country’s ability to respond independently and effectively to cyber incidents.

Fourth, he advocated stronger regulatory enforcement and independent cybersecurity assessments.

He called for mandatory independent cybersecurity audits for telecommunications operators and institutions responsible for critical national infrastructure.

He also recommended stronger financial penalties for regulatory violations and a mandatory 24-hour window for reporting significant security breaches.

According to Tarpeh, these measures would move Liberia away from a system that relies heavily on periodic compliance documentation toward one built around continuous monitoring, accountability, and rapid response.

He believes the proposed reforms would strengthen public confidence in digital services while making it more difficult for cybercriminals to exploit weaknesses in critical systems.

A Digital Economy That Must Be Protected

Tarpeh maintained that Liberia’s digital transformation presents an important opportunity to improve public administration, expand financial inclusion, strengthen economic productivity, and make government services more accessible.

However, he warned that expanding digital services without corresponding investments in security and infrastructure resilience could expose the country to risks capable of disrupting essential economic activities.

He argued that cybersecurity must be treated as an essential national infrastructure priority rather than an administrative responsibility limited to regulatory compliance and public awareness campaigns.

“Connectivity without operational defense and backup capacity is reckless exposure,” he cautioned.

He is therefore calling for stronger cooperation among the LTA, OTDI, government institutions, telecommunications operators, and national security agencies to establish a coordinated defense system capable of protecting Liberia’s digital economy.

For Tarpeh, the central challenge is ensuring that as Liberia moves more of its economy and public services online, the systems supporting that transformation are sufficiently protected against disruption.

His warning also raises broader questions about the government’s digital development priorities, particularly whether investments in connectivity and online services are being matched by adequate investments in cybersecurity, infrastructure redundancy, and institutional preparedness.

As more government transactions, financial services, and commercial activities move online, the consequences of a major cyber incident could extend beyond individual institutions to affect public confidence, revenue collection, business operations, and national economic stability.

The challenge, therefore, is not simply to connect Liberia to the global digital economy but to ensure that the country has the technical capacity, regulatory safeguards, and backup infrastructure to remain connected and operational when disruptions occur.

About Ernest Tarpeh

Ernest “Paju” Tarpeh, formerly Ernest “Paju” Rodgers, is a senior cybersecurity architect and digital policy specialist with experience in technology infrastructure, network security, and public-sector modernization.

He began his public-sector career at the Ministry of Finance’s Department of Budget in Monrovia, where he participated in the development of Liberia’s first electronic national budget platform.

According to his professional profile, he has spent more than 18 years designing, monitoring, and securing critical networks for Microsoft Corporation, Fortune 500 companies, and United States federal agencies, including the U.S. Department of Defense.

He holds a Bachelor of Science degree in Cybersecurity and Information Assurance, a Master of Science degree in Information Technology and Security Management, and a Master of Arts degree in International Affairs Leadership. He is also completing a Master of Public Policy and Management, specializing in global digital and cybersecurity policy.

World.title: Liberia: ‘Move from Promises to Practice’ – Children’s Forum Speaker Urges Government
World.content:
Kakata, Margibi County—The Speaker of the Liberia National Children Representative Forum (LNCRF), Michael Wesseh, has called on the Liberian Government and development partners to place children at the center of national development, stressing the need for greater protection, meaningful participation, and investment in their future.

By Yawah Y. Jaivey

Wesseh made the call over the weekend during the celebration of World Children’s Day in Kakata City, Margibi County, under the global theme:, “My Day, My Rights, My Future,” and the national theme, “Every Child Matters: Our Rights, Our Voices, Our Future.”



The Speaker of the Liberia National Children Representative Forum, addressing scores of government officials, development partners, child protection advocates and children from across the country, emphasized that children should not be treated as an afterthought in Liberia’s national development agenda.

Wesseh, citing the preamble of the Children’s Law of Liberia, 2011, which recognizes children as the pillars and cornerstone of a greater Liberia, argued that government planning, budgeting, policymaking, and decision-making must prioritize children’s welfare and development.

He cautioned against using children as political tools or remembering them only during political campaigns and public ceremonies. “Children should not be used as political tools. We should not be remembered only during campaigns, ceremonies, or when our presence is needed to make an event successful,” Wesseh said.

He referenced Section 23 of the Children’s Law of Liberia, which provides a foundation for children’s participation and expression, urging authorities to ensure that the provision is respected and implemented in practice.



The LNCRF Speaker reflecting on discussions held during the World Children’s Day celebration, Wesseh said children demonstrated that they have ideas, solutions and a vision for a better Liberia.

He referenced an interactive session in which children were asked what they would do if given the opportunity to become President of Liberia for one day.

According to him, some children proposed strengthening healthcare services and improving the quality of education, while others called for stronger measures to protect children from violence in schools and communities.

Wesseh, however, advocated for the establishment of safe spaces across the country where children could freely express themselves, feel protected and participate in decisions affecting their lives.

He maintained that children are not short of ideas but need leaders and institutions willing to listen to their concerns and act on their recommendations.

The LNCRF Speaker also called for collective efforts to end violence against children, emphasizing that the responsibility should not rest solely with one institution or individual.

He urged the Government of Liberia, parents, schools, communities, civil society organizations and development partners to work together to protect children from violence, abuse, exploitation and neglect.

“Every child deserves to feel safe at home, in school, in the community and everywhere they go. We must move beyond speeches and act now,” he stressed.

He also called on the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection to ensure that workshops, training programs and policies translate into practical child-protection interventions and measurable improvements in children’s lives.

Wesseh clarified that the forum’s concerns were not intended to condemn the government but to highlight the realities children face and encourage collective responsibility in addressing them.

Wesseh further stressed that children should be recognized as partners in shaping Liberia’s future rather than merely beneficiaries of development programs.

He noted that children’s participation should extend beyond radio appearances, public ceremonies and other social engagements to include policy development, budget preparation and national decision-making processes.

“Our voices should not only be heard when you need us to appear on radio programs, attend ceremonies, or participate in public events. Our voices must be heard in the rooms where policies are developed, budgets are prepared and decisions are made,” he said.

He further called for the decentralization of children’s representation to ensure that those in all 15 counties have meaningful opportunities to participate in decisions affecting their welfare.

Wesseh appealed to the Ministry of Gender, the Government of Liberia, UNICEF, SOS Children’s Villages, the United Nations, and other development partners to strengthen children’s representation at county, district and community levels.

The children’s representative also urged government ministries, agencies, and development partners to follow through on commitments made during the celebration. He called for the documentation of children’s concerns and recommendations, identification of responsible institutions and establishment of clear mechanisms to monitor implementation.

According to him, commitments made to children must translate into tangible actions and improvements in their lives. He continued, “Children must be able to look back and see that the concerns they raised today resulted in meaningful changes. We must move from promises to practice, from paper to protection and from consultation to genuine inclusion.”

Meanwhile, Wesseh expressed appreciation to the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning for an announced allocation of US$50,000 to the Liberia National Children’s Representative Forum.

He described the support as an important contribution toward strengthening the institution’s work and advancing children’s representation and participation in national development. At the same time, Wesseh challenged national leaders to consider the future of children in their present-day decisions, particularly in education, healthcare, protection and resource allocation.

He noted that children who aspire to protect others from violence, improve healthcare and strengthen education could become future national leaders, including presidents and cabinet ministers.

However, he questioned whether enough was being done to prepare them for those responsibilities through quality education, protection, investment and opportunities for participation.

“The future of Liberia cannot be secured by excluding the very people who will inherit it,” he declared.

The LNCRF speaker reaffirmed the forum’s commitment to ensuring that every child, regardless of background, location, disability, or circumstances, has the opportunity to be heard, protected, educated, and empowered.

He, however, used the occasion to urge government officials and development partners to remember children in national planning, budgeting and decision-making.

“When you are planning, remember the children. When you are budgeting, remember the children. When you are making decisions, include the children. And when you are building Liberia, put the children at the center,” Wesseh said.

For her part, Gbeme Horace Kollie, Minister of Gender, Children and Social Protection, reminded the hundreds of children attending the celebration that the future ahead of them is not just about their individual aspirations but also about the future of Liberia.

Minister Kollie assured the leadership of the Liberia National Children’s Representative Forum (LNCRF) and children across the country of the government’s strong commitment to implementing the Liberia’s children’s laws.

She noted that, as part of its commitment to upholding children’s rights, the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection has supported the observance of national and international days dedicated to celebrating children and providing them with platforms to speak out on issues affecting their welfare.

The Gender Minister, however, cautioned members of the LNCRF against making themselves politically attractive, as she alleged some of their predecessors had done. Instead, she encouraged them to focus on advocating for their rights and ensuring that government officials fulfill their obligations to children.

“Don’t make yourself politically attractive; make yourself attractive to be able to meet your needs so your leaders can be challenged to know that they have obligations to you,” Minister Kollie said.

Continuing, she referenced President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s commitment to prioritizing future generations over electoral considerations.

“As President Boakai would always say, he is not concerned about the next elections, but concerned about the next generation, and that next generation is you!,” she stated.

She also urged the children’s representatives to remain polite and respectful in advocating for their rights and welfare, emphasizing that their advocacy should not be driven by self-centered interests but by the broader interests of the children they represent.

Meanwhile, Minister Kollie disclosed that, following consultations with the leadership of the Liberia National Children’s Representative Forum, the government is expected to purchase a bus for the organization to facilitate its activities.

She further revealed that the Ministry has allocated educational support funds to cover the schooling expenses of members of the forum’s leadership who have relocated from their respective counties to Monrovia.

In addition, the Gender Minister announced that funds have been allocated to the Children’s Forum to support community outreach activities aimed at raising awareness about violence against children in Liberia.

Also speaking at the occasion, Shairose Mawji, UNICEF Representative (Country Manager) to Liberia, reaffirmed UNICEF’s commitment to supporting the Liberian Government in ensuring that the rights of children across the country are protected and fulfilled.

Mawji disclosed that UNICEF has established several platforms to engage children and solicit their views, enabling the organization and its partners to better plan and implement programs that address their needs and promote their welfare.

She, however, encouraged the hundreds of children attending the celebration to speak out on issues affecting them, while ensuring that their advocacy is conducted respectfully.

World.title: Four MPs Lose Seats As High Courts Rewrite Disputed Parliamentary Results
World.content:
High Courts in Mansa, Livingstone and Kasama have removed four Members of Parliament from their seats in a run of election petition judgments. Over the same stretch, courts in Ndola, Lusaka, Chinsali and Mongu threw out challenges that losing United Party for National Development (UPND) candidates had brought against opposition and independent lawmakers.

The judgments came over roughly one week. The ruling party has lost two seats outright, and the courts handed both to the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP). Two more constituencies, one in Luapula and one in Western Province, now have no MP unless the rulings are reversed on appeal.

The heaviest blows landed in Luapula. Mansa High Court Judge Ruth Mbambi nullified the election of NRPUP Mambilima MP Ms Jean Chisenga after finding that malpractice, violence and intimidation had been proved to the required standard.

The petition came from UPND candidate Mr Nasir Kashiba, who polled 4,142 votes to Ms Chisenga’s 8,159. He told the court that the MP and her supporters threatened voters and electoral officials, and he cited an incident involving masked individuals at Mwense Town Council.

Ms Chisenga confirmed that she had lost the seat.

In the same court, Judge Mwaka Mikalile reversed the result in Bangweulu Constituency in Samfya District. She nullified the election of UPND candidate Happy Mampa on the grounds of multiple irregularities. She also declared NRPUP candidate Mr Anthony Kasandwe the duly elected Member of Parliament, which sends him straight to the House without a fresh vote.

A similar result came out of Northern Province. The Kasama High Court declared NRPUP candidate Mr Lazarous Chungu Bwalya the lawful winner in Lupososhi and set aside the declaration in favour of UPND’s Mr Shadreck Mwansa Katuta.

The Lupososhi dispute grew out of contradictory announcements by Returning Officer Mr Oscar Kafunda. His first declaration gave Mr Bwalya 9,533 votes against 6,890 for Mr Katuta. A later declaration reversed that outcome.

Mr Katuta accepted the judgment but did not rule out a fresh challenge.

“I respect the decision of the Court,” Mr Katuta said.

He said he would consult his lawyers and the UPND leadership before deciding on his next step.

In Western Province, Livingstone High Court Justice Kazimbe Chenda nullified the election of Mulobezi Independent MP Mr Hastings Sililo. The ruling upheld a petition by UPND candidate Mr Timothy Mwenda Zambwe.

The judge found that Mr Sililo had not been formally awarded the Grade 12 certificate that the Constitution requires of parliamentary candidates. He did hold a 2025 GCE statement of results, but the court ruled that this did not meet the requirement at the time of the election.

The Mambilima, Mulobezi and Lupososhi judgments were all delivered on Monday, 23 November. The Kasama High Court had earlier asked for extra police security for petition judgments set down between 20 and 26 November, which involved five judges.

On the Copperbelt, the UPND challenges failed. The Ndola High Court upheld the election of Chifubu Independent MP Mr Kondwani Winga and dismissed UPND candidate Mr Lloyd Lubosha’s petition on all grounds.

Mr Winga had won the seat with 15,552 votes against Mr Lubosha’s 8,322. After the judgment, he said it was time to put politics aside and focus on serving the people of Chifubu Constituency.

In Kabushi, Judge Chipola Bako ruled that NRPUP’s Mr Tillas Sichinga was duly elected. Mr Sichinga had taken the seat with 14,635 votes.

UPND candidate Ms Emelda Mpupuni accepted the outcome and said she would not appeal. She said she would keep working for the people of the constituency and focus on advancing the Grow Zambia Agenda.

In Lusaka, High Court Judge Derrick Mulenga dismissed UPND candidate Mr Lee Mukupa’s challenge to NRPUP’s Mr Kelvin Kaunda in Lima Constituency. Mr Kaunda had polled 22,760 votes to Mr Mukupa’s 8,041.

The judge found that the petitioner had not proved his allegations of malpractice, intimidation, violence and irregularities in the counting and announcement of results. He said the burden of proof rests with the person bringing the petition.

The pattern continued in Muchinga. Chinsali High Court Justice Catherine Lombe upheld the election of NRPUP’s Mr Francis Robert Kapyanga in Mpika North and dismissed a petition by UPND candidate Mr Mordecai Sichalwe. She found that the claims of bribery, intimidation and malpractice had not been sufficiently proved.

In Mongu, the High Court threw out UPND candidate Mr Sibeso Sefulo’s bid to overturn the victory of Mwandi Independent MP Ms Iris Kaingu, who had won the seat by 485 votes.

The UPND also lost a petition against Ms Margaret Miti, a defeat that governance group GEARS Initiative listed alongside the failed cases against Ms Kaingu and Mr Kapyanga.

GEARS Initiative urged losing aspirants not to take their cases further. It said appeals would waste both time and money.

The rulings are only part of a much larger caseload. A total of 67 parliamentary election petitions were filed in the High Court countrywide after the 14-day window for challenging the results of the 13 August general election closed.

The Lusaka High Court alone received 41 of them, and UPND candidates filed more than 35 of those. The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) was cited as a respondent in the petitions, and petitioners accused it of failing to comply with provisions of the Electoral Process Act.

NRPUP president Mr Ezra Tembo said early on that his party was concerned that almost all of its MPs had been taken to court.

The ECZ has pointed to Western Province as proof that its staff did their job. ECZ Commissioner Mr McDonald Chipenzi said only two of the province’s 26 constituencies produced parliamentary petitions, and that Sioma District recorded none at either parliamentary or local government level.

More judgments are on the way. The Chinsali High Court provisionally set today for judgment in the Mwenzo Constituency petition, in which UPND candidate Mr Nathan Musingwa Siame is asking the court to nullify the election of NRPUP’s Mr Lucas Simumba over alleged malpractice, corruption and violence.

World.title: Fire claims two in Masaiti
World.content:
Two people have died after a house they were occupying was gutted by fire in Kambono village, Tug-Argan area of Masaiti district.

Copperbelt Province Police Commissioner Edwin Kaluba has disclosed the incident in a statement to the media saying police received a report from Fridah Kalombe, sister to one of the deceased persons.

Mr Kaluba identified the deceased as 35-year-old Gertrude Kalombe and Gunduzani Banda, whose age is yet to be established.

He said the incident occurred on November 23, 2026, around 23:00 hours at Bowas Farm.

He said preliminary findings indicate that the fire may have started from a brazier found inside the house containing a pot of beans.

Mr Kaluba said neighbours attempted to rescue the occupants, who were trapped inside the burning house, by pulling down part of the brick wall.

He disclosed that the fire destroyed part of the house and household goods, while the bodies of the deceased were extensively burnt beyond recognition.

Mr Kaluba said the remains of the two victims have since been deposited at Ndola Teaching Hospital mortuary, awaiting postmortem examinations.

World.title: Chilanga authorities commence ECF vaccination campaign
World.content:
The Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock has commenced the vaccination campaign of cattle against East Coast Fever (ECF) in all the 12 wards of Chilanga district.

District Fisheries and Livestock Services Coordinator Alex Mupango has explained that the government has released one thousand doses of vaccine for the exercise, to be conducted for a period of ten days in all the wards.

Dr Mupango was speaking after monitoring the vaccination exercise in Chilongolo ward, where he explained that the exercise is targeting cattle aged between three months to two years.

He thanked the government through the Enhanced Smallholder Livestock Investment Programme (E-slip) for releasing the doses on time, to avoid an outbreak of the disease in the district.

And Chilanga District Assistant Veterinary Officer Twambo Munsanje explained that the disease can be quite severe on cattle once infected.

Mr Munsanje stated that ECF is among the most expensive diseases to treat as the drugs needed are very expensive and can cost as high as K1000 per bottle for parvexon, among other drugs, meant to treat the disease.

He said the government is conducting the vaccination campaign against East Coast Fever for only K55 per animal vaccinated and noted that the vaccination is done only once in the lifetime of the cattle.

Meanwhile, Buffalo Hill Investment Farm Manager Maureen Mulenga encouraged other farmers to take advantage of the vaccination campaign exercise going on to safeguard their animals.

Ms Mulenga thanked the government for the exercise being conducted in the area.

East Coast Fever (ECF) is a severe, often tick borne disease, which attacks cattle and is caused by the protozoan parasite theileria parva.

World.title: Mulyata hands over to Mwaliteta
World.content:
Immediate past Lusaka Province Minister Sheal Mulyata has advised her successor Obvious Mwaliteta to embrace teamwork as he takes up the helm at the provincial office.

Ms Mulyata who is now Minister of Community Development and Social Services says teamwork is required to achieve the Grow Zambia Agenda.

She was speaking during a ceremony to symbolise the official handing over of the office to the new Lusaka Province Minister.

Ms Mulyata who congratulated her successor expressed confidence that Mr Mwaliteta will deliver in his new role.

She said the Lusaka Province Administration has various developmental tasks which need attention, noting that Mr Mwaliteta is equal to the task.

Meanwhile Mr Mwaliteta thanked Ms Mulyata for laying the foundation, saying he will pick up from where she left.

The Lusaka Province Minister commended Ms Mulyata for her contributions to the office.

And Mr Mwaliteta reiterated that he will be guided by the Eighth National Development Plan and the Grow Zambia Agenda as he serves his role.

World.title: Prudent utilisation of public resources encouraged
World.content:
Northern Province Acting Permanent Secretary Beauty Undi-Phiri has called on Heads of Government Departments to ensure prudent utilisation of public resources.

Ms, Undi-Phiri says government resources should not be spent on unnecessary trips but that priority should be on investments that improve service delivery to the people.

The Acting Northern Province Permanent Secretary has reminded heads of government departments that government resources should not be spent on monitoring activities involving officers who have no direct role in the assignments, but should instead be channelled towards strengthening institutional capacity and improving operations.

She was speaking during a Provincial Heads of Government Departments management meeting in Kasama today.

The acting PS has urged departmental heads to consider investing in essential office equipment to enhance efficiency and ensure government offices remain operational even during power outages.

“It is unacceptable that on a trip for monitoring and officers whose work is not in line with monitoring can be included, invest in things that help you improve service delivery because they are the ones we serve,” she said.

Ms Undi-Phiri says the provincial administration will closely monitor expenditure and travel patterns among government officers to ensure accountability and that public funds are used for their intended purposes.

She has further called on Heads of Government Departments to embrace integrity and accountability, reminding them that government resources belong to the people and should be used to advance the country’s development agenda.

“Let us use government resources prudently, we should always uphold integrity, of knowing that the resources we use are for the people out there in communities,” she advised.

And Ms Undi-Phiri has also urged the department of gender in the province to broaden its focus to include the boy child, alongside efforts to protect girls from early marriage and other forms of abuse.

She said both boys and girls need guidance and support to become responsible citizens.

“All departments here are key in ensuring that the Grow Zambia Agenda is success, the Department of Gender, let us ensure we look at gender to include the boy child too, if we focus on women and girls alone we will be creating a gap, because we will have a population boys who are junkies,” she observed.

“Let us all move together, boys, and girls, women, and men, let each of our gender play their role and appreciate each other,” she added.

She says the development of the province requires collective responsibility and collaboration among government departments, traditional leaders and communities.

World.title: Solwezi Correctional facility undergoes expansion
World.content:
The Northwestern Provincial Administration has called for the expansion of the Solwezi Central Correctional facility to address congestion and deteriorating infrastructure.

Provincial Permanent Secretary Grandson Katambi says an assessment has already been conducted and plans to expand the existing infrastructure have been approved.

Colonel Katambi (Rtd) was speaking in Solwezi today when Zambia Correctional Service Commission Chairperson Evaristo Kalonga paid a courtesy call on him.

He has also urged the correctional facility to take advantage of the increased Constituency Development Funds (CDF) to mobilise resources for the expansion of the facility.

Col Katambi further calls for improved transport for correctional officers to enhance their mobility and enable them to effectively carry out their duties.

Meanwhile, Mr Kalonga says his entourage is in Northwestern Province for the implementation of the decentralisation programme.

He says the team will also facilitate the formulation of various committees to oversee the appointments, promotions, discipline, appeals and welfare of officers at provincial level.

Mr Kalonga says the team has taken note of the shortage of officers at the Solwezi Central Correctional and will consider the challenges affecting the facility.

He has also commended the correctional facility for positioning itself well to contribute to the Grow Zambia Agenda, particularly through agricultural activities.

World.title: Mundubile, Makebi plead not guilty
World.content:
-National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) leaders Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu have pleaded not guilty to two counts of seditious practices.

The two appeared before Lusaka Magistrate Webster Milumbe, where they denied the charges relating to social media posts allegedly published on August 14, 2026.

Mr Mundubile, 55 and Mr Zulu, 45, are alleged to have jointly engaged in seditious practices by publishing statements on Zulu’s facebook page intended to raise discontent and disaffection among the people of Zambia.

In the first count, the two are alleged to have published a statement indicating that Mr Mundubile would address the nation shortly.

The prosecution alleges that the publication was intended to cause discontent and disaffection among members of the public.

In the second count, the accused are alleged to have published a statement claiming that, based on information received from various polling stations and their tabulation, they had won the elections.

The statement further called for the immediate publication of election results in accordance with the law to fulfill the will of the Zambian people.

Both accused persons denied the allegations after the charges were read and explained to them, prompting the court to record pleas of not guilty.

Following the pleas, defence lawyers applied for bail pending trial under Section 123(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code, Chapter 88 of the Laws of Zambia.

The defence argued that the offences were bailable and that the two accused persons had fixed abodes and were willing to meet any conditions the court might impose.

Defence Lawyer Norman Siwila submitted that detention before conviction should be an exception rather than the rule, adding that the accused were presumed innocent until proven guilty.

He further argued that both had stable social and economic ties and no history of absconding court proceedings.

The court adjourned the matter to December 1, 2026, at 09:00 hours for hearing of the bail application.

Trial is scheduled to commence from December 14 to 18, 2026.

The State was represented by Deputy Chief State Advocate Samuel Simwaka, alongside other prosecutors.

World.title: DPP Seeks to arrest bail ruling in Mundubile case
World.content:
The Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) has applied to arrest the ruling in the constitutional bail application by Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and others, a move that has delayed the much awaited decision.

Mr Phiri, appearing for the State, asked the court to arrest the ruling when the matter came up for delivery of the ruling in the Lusaka High Court.

Speaking to journalists outside court after the proceedings, a defense lawyer Chifumu Banda said the application was taken up urgently, but argued that most of the defence law firms had not been served with the documents.

He said if service was done at all, it was done after the defence had already been informed of the proceedings.

Arguments were heard for and against the application by the State and the court is now expected to deliver its decision tomorrow.

The defence expressed hope that there would be no further application by the State.

The lawyer also welcomed the release of some of the accused who were not committed to the High Court for trial, saying the defence was looking forward to more releases.

This is in a matter in which Brian Mundubile and 13 others have applied for constitutional bail after the State applied to halt the ruling.
