World.title: PPC chief dismisses fears of cement oversupply as projects gather pace
World.content:
PPC chief executive Matias Cardarelli has dismissed concerns that a wave of proposed cement investments in Zimbabwe could result in market oversupply, arguing that most of the projects involve grinding stations reliant on imported clinker rather than fully integrated plants.

Responding to an analyst’s question about the risk of repeating the structural oversupply experienced in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) about a decade ago, Cardarelli said Zimbabwe’s current demand could accommodate the planned investments.

He said the company was assessing the market against its estimated annual demand of three million tonnes, including the proposed 1,5 million-tonne plant.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Government unveils US$400m drought buffer
World.content:
GOVERNMENT has unveiled a US$400 million war chest to mitigate the effects of a predicted strong El Niño-induced drought.

The plan is anchored on enhanced strategic grain reserves, accelerated climate-smart production, an integrated financing architecture, livestock drought mitigation, enhanced imports, and coordination, early warning systems and capacity-building.

In a post-Cabinet media briefing in Harare this Tuesday, Information minister Zhemu Soda said Treasury had set aside US$400 million for the El Niño-induced drought response.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Storm blows off roof at Chinhoyi clinic
World.content:
HEAVY storms on Tuesday afternoon blew off the roof of Shackleton Clinic in Chinhoyi’s ward 15, flooding the facility and rendering it unusable.

The clinic is the sole health facility serving the former mining community of 4,000 people as well as surrounding farming communities.

The damage might force patients to travel more than eight kilometres to the nearest health facility in Alaska.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Land barons invade Malbereign open space
World.content:
HARARE is fast descending into anarchy with land barons running riot and invading open spaces in the city.

After invading two council farms over the weekend, land barons reportedly descended on an open space along Warbury Road in Malbereign this Tuesday.

Ward 16 councillor Denford Ngadziore confirmed the fresh invasion in his ward today.

World.title: Senegal reclaim AFCON crown after CAS ruling
World.content:
SENEGAL have been reinstated as the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations champions after the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) overturned the Confederation of African Football’s (CAF) decision to strip them of the title and award it to Morocco.

In a landmark ruling delivered in Lausanne, Switzerland, today, CAS upheld an appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF), bringing an end to a lengthy dispute over the controversial January 18 final.

The ruling overturns CAF’s March 17 decision, which declared Senegal to have forfeited the final following their players’ walk-off protest and awarded Morocco a 3-0 victory.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Foreign delegates tour Serima Mission after regional modern art conference
World.content:
DELEGATES from more than 70 countries visited St Mary’s Serima Mission in Gutu, Masvingo province on Monday 23 November, after attending an International Committee for Museums and Collections of Modern Art (CIMAM) conference in Harare, the Ministry of Tourism and Hospitality Industry has said.

The visitors toured St Mary’s Church, known for its distinctive architecture and detailed artwork by Father John Groeber, who founded the mission in 1948. Work by his students is also on display at the site.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Senegal/Morocco: Senegal Reclaims AFCON Crown After Winning Appeal
World.content:
The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has reinstated Senegal as the official winner of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON), following a review of an appeal filed by the Senegalese Football Federation. The CAS verdict sets aside a previous decision by the CAF Appeal Board to strip Senegal of the trophy after an appeal from the Royal Moroccan Football Federation.

In its initial appeal, Morocco argued that the Senegalese side forfeited the January 18, 2026 AFCON final by walking off the pitch in protest of a late penalty.

In response, the Senegalese federation argued that the referee's decision to resume the match in the 109th minute and allow it to conclude with a "sporting result" could not be overturned.

In its ruling, CAS stated: "After having examined the arguments raised by the Parties, the Arbitral Panel considered that the referee's decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority. By blowing his whistle to restart play, the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met - both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume."

In the final on January 18 at the Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium in Rabat, Pape Gueye scored in extra time to give Senegal a 1-0 victory and their second Africa Cup of Nations title.

World.title: Africa: Malawi Agriculture Minister Champions Investment-Led Economic Transformation
World.content:
Roza Fatch Mbilizi calls for a shift from raw commodity exports to agro-industrial development, placing agriculture at the heart of Malawi’s economic transformation.

LILONGWE, Malawi, November 24, 2026 – Malawi’s Minister of Agriculture, Roza Fatch Mbilizi, has called for a fundamental transformation of the country’s agricultural sector, positioning it as a catalyst for industrialisation, export competitiveness and sustainable economic growth.

Presiding over the Malawi Investment Summit 2026 on Monday at the Bingu International Convention Centre in Lilongwe, Mbilizi outlined a vision that seeks to move Malawi beyond its traditional dependence on raw agricultural commodity exports towards a more diversified, productive and value-added economy.

The Minister emphasised the need to accelerate investment in agro-processing, irrigation, agricultural mechanisation and modern storage infrastructure to unlock the country’s productive potential, create employment opportunities and strengthen its position in regional and international markets.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Her leadership at the Summit underscored the central role of agriculture in advancing Malawi 2063, the country’s long-term development blueprint, and delivering on the economic transformation agenda of President Professor Arthur Peter Mutharika.

From dialogue to tangible investment

In a strong call for accountability and results, Mbilizi stressed that the success of the Summit should not be measured by the quality of discussions alone, but by the concrete investments, strategic partnerships and development projects that emerge from it.

Her message reflected a determination to translate policy ambitions into tangible economic outcomes, while positioning the agricultural sector as an attractive destination for domestic and international capital.

For Malawi, where agriculture remains a cornerstone of livelihoods and export earnings, greater investment in value addition presents an opportunity to increase farmers’ incomes, expand industrial capacity, generate foreign exchange and strengthen economic resilience.

Creating an enabling investment environment

The Summit, held under the theme “Transforming Malawi’s Investment Climate for Sustainable Industrial Growth and Export Competitiveness,” also highlighted ongoing government efforts to improve the business environment.

Minister of Industrialisation, Business, Trade and Tourism Simon Itaye reinforced the government’s commitment to attracting investment, acknowledging investor concerns over regulatory predictability, bureaucratic hurdles and the speed of administrative approvals.

He highlighted measures to strengthen the One Stop Service Centre at the Malawi Investment and Trade Centre (MITC) and operationalise the Special Economic Zones framework.

These initiatives complement broader legislative and policy reforms, including the Investment and Export Promotion Act 2024, the Special Economic Zones Act 2024 and the draft National Investment Policy.

According to a Financial Times briefing note prepared for the Summit, MITC projects foreign direct investment inflows of US$1.2 billion by the end of the current fiscal year, although infrastructure gaps and regulatory uncertainty remain challenges.

Agriculture as a gateway to regional and global markets

Malawi’s membership in the Southern African Development Community (SADC), the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) and the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) offers significant opportunities for agricultural producers and investors seeking access to larger markets.

Close 

By championing agro-industrial development, Mbilizi is placing agriculture at the intersection of food security, industrialisation, job creation and international trade.

Organised by the Financial Times and Philip Morris International, in collaboration with MITC and key government ministries, the Summit brought together policymakers, international investors, diplomatic missions, financial institutions, local producers, exporters and development partners.

The gathering provided a platform for Malawi to articulate its investment priorities and demonstrate its commitment to economic reform.

Under Mbilizi’s leadership, the agricultural sector is being positioned not simply as a source of raw commodities, but as a strategic engine of industrial development and long-term prosperity.

The challenge now will be to convert that vision into investments that deliver measurable benefits for farmers, businesses and the wider Malawian economy.

World.title: Mozambique: Mondlane Denies Being Responsible for Inciting Crowds to Destroy Public Infrastructure
World.content:
Maputo — Venâncio Mondlane, a former presidential candidate and leader of the National Alliance for a Free and Autonomous Mozambique (Anamola), who's standing a trial for allegedly committing five crimes related to 2024 post-election mass demonstrations, denies being responsible for inciting crowds to destroy toll booths, telecommunications towers, or other public and private infrastructure.

Mondlane - who was being questioned on Monday by the lawyer Rodrigo Rocha, who acts as an assistant to the Attorney General's Office (PGR) on behalf of the controversial state-owned company Revimo (Mozambique Road Network) - claims that his calls for demonstrations intended to protest against the alleged fraudulent results of the general elections.

The politician explained that he only called for peaceful demonstrations, which means that he is not responsible for the destruction of public or private infrastructures.

Mondlane challenged Rocha to present video evidence showing him ordering or instigating the burning of public or private facilities, when he was questioned about the real intention behind his statements. He added that his statements were politically motivated and were not intended to encourage acts of destruction or vandalism.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

When questioned about the alleged destruction of 59 telecommunications towers, Mondlane responded that was unaware of such destruction, calling for presentation of evidence. He also said that his calls for demonstrations were peaceful, citing the singing of national anthem as an irrefutable fact of his actions.

Mondlane is standing trial for allegedly committing five crimes related to 2024 post-election mass demonstrations, namely: public apology for a crime; incitement to collective disobedience; public instigation to crime; instigation and incitement to terrorism. The mass demonstration he called to protest started peacefully but then degenerated into rioting.

Revimo is basically a state-owned company. 70 percent of its shares are held by the government's Road Fund, 15 per cent by the Bank of Mozambique Pension Fund, and 15 per cent by the National Social Security Institute (INSS).

Among the roads operated by Revimo are the Maputo Ring Road (71.4 kilometers long), the Maputo-KaTembe bridge, and the connecting roads to the border with the South African province of Kwazulu-Natal (187 kilometres), and the Beira-Zimbabwe highway (287 kilometres).

Rioting and destruction halted the collection of tolls in December 2024. Rioters who infiltrated the demonstrations utterly destroyed some of the tollgates.

World.title: Americans don’t have to choose between our AI future and ripping off copyright owners
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

One of the biggest court battles over artificial intelligence (AI) is putting an age-old legal principle to the test — and raising important questions about the Trump administration's AI policy.

Several news organizations, including The New York Times, are suing OpenAI and Microsoft for using millions of newspaper articles to train AI systems. The newspapers argue that the tech firms violated basic copyright protections. The tech firms contend that training their models on those articles qualifies as "fair use," a longstanding principle that allows copyrighted material to be used in certain ways without permission from or compensation to the copyright owner.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has sided squarely with OpenAI's position — breaking with the administration's previously more balanced stance on the issue. The DOJ filed a statement of interest embracing an extreme vision of fair use that would grant AI companies virtually unfettered access to copyrighted material for commercial training, without obtaining permission from or compensating the creators whose works fuel these systems.

MIKE DAVIS: THE TRUMP DOJ SHOULD WITHDRAW ITS STATEMENT OF INTEREST IN THE OPENAI LAWSUIT

This expansive interpretation threatens to turn a narrow copyright exception into a blanket exemption for the world's most powerful and profitable industries.

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION

Those concerns deserve consideration. But the DOJ's aggressive arguments in the brief depart from more measured guidance elsewhere in the administration. The White House's official AI framework acknowledges valid arguments on both sides of the copyright debate.

Likewise, the Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies, adopted by G20 ministers at the Commerce Department's recent Innovation Ministerial, recognize that the intersection of AI and copyright poses "complex legal and policy questions." The principles note the "essential role" of copyright protections in supporting creators and call for respecting IP as a pillar of G20 AI policy.

MUSIC INDUSTRY FENDS OFF FLOOD OF AI MUSIC 'STEALING' THE CHARTS

The DOJ statement also overlooks how its stance could favor larger AI companies over smaller firms and startups. Several AI startups have argued that paying for the material they use provides more reliable access to training material, reduces legal uncertainty and improves models. Other companies have emerged to aggregate copyrights and make licensing easier.

It's particularly problematic for large AI companies to complain about paying for access to copyrighted materials. They are among the best positioned to pay for those materials, and doing so would help develop the kind of licensing markets they claim are lacking.

OBAMA CRITICIZES TRUMP ON APPROACH TO AI, ESCALATES WARNING FOR STRONGER REGULATION

And even if national security were a legitimate justification, the government could not simply disregard property rights. The Constitution and other laws require just compensation when private property is taken for public use, and intellectual property rights are still property rights. Letting AI firms appropriate creators' IP without permission or compensation would be akin to letting data center builders seize private land without paying fair value.

If courts adopt the DOJ's position that fair use protects AI developers in virtually all circumstances, it would reduce incentives to create new works. Copyrights encourage creative work by assuring writers, artists and other creators that their work can't be easily stolen or copied. Licensing those rights allows creators to earn a living and underpins over $1 trillion in U.S. economic activity.

Weaker copyrights could result in fewer human-created books, articles, research papers, films and songs. Ironically, that could eventually leave AI systems with fewer and lower-quality materials to train on – a scenario that serves no one's interests.

All of this is why the Trump administration would be wise to follow its own AI framework and let the court system evaluate AI copyright disputes case by case, rather than arguing for unfettered fair use exceptions.

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

Policymakers also have a role to play. One promising bill is the bipartisan CLEAR Act. Introduced in February by California Democrat Sen. Adam Schiff and Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis, the CLEAR Act would require AI developers to publicly disclose the copyrighted works used in each new generative-AI model's training dataset.

The proposal would not settle whether any particular training practice qualifies as fair use. But it would give creators more information about whether their work helped train an AI system, enabling them to pursue appropriate compensation or other remedies when they believe their rights have been violated.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That kind of targeted reform offers a useful model for copyright enforcement in the age of AI. Rather than treating licensing as an obstacle to innovation, policymakers should foster a market where AI developers can efficiently license copyrighted material while respecting creators' rights.

AI innovation is vital to America's future. But America's creative industries still depend on strong copyright protections. Policymakers need to promote both.

World.title: ‘Nobody Wants This’ star Tovah Feldshuh has ‘no animosity’ toward co-star despite Israel disagreement
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

"Nobody Wants This" star Tovah Feldshuh said in a new interview that co-star Adam Brody asked for a private meeting with her following criticism of his remarks accusing Israel of "genocide."

Speaking with Us Weekly ahead of a Paley Museum panel on Monday, Feldshuh said there is "no animosity" between her and Brody. She noted that she still considers him an "incredible friend," but that they remain in "profound disagreement" over the Middle East conflict.

"After he said his comments, he asked to see me. So, we’ve talked privately about it," Feldshuh said, adding that she hopes Brody will eventually reconsider his view "based on fact and history."

'NOBODY WANTS THIS' STAR ACCUSES ISRAEL OF 'GENOCIDE'

The disagreement began in September when Brody, who identifies as Jewish and plays a rabbi on the Netflix series, told GQ Magazine that he believes Israel is committing a "genocide" in Gaza. He added, "put me down as wanting a free Palestine."

Feldshuh, who plays Brody’s mother on "Nobody Wants This," pushed back against her co-star at the time, telling the New York Post that "to accuse the Jewish people of genocide is wild." She added that doing so is "right out of Hitler’s playbook. You take the victim, and you make the victim the perpetrator."

RABBI WHO WORKED ON ADAM BRODY'S NETFLIX SHOW SLAMS ACTOR OVER GAZA COMMENTS

Feldshuh told Us Weekly that she does not plan on publicly speaking out against Brody, saying that they are colleagues and can disagree with one another without "being disagreeable."

"However, I’m sure everybody is very clear about how I stand and this isn’t a political statement. This is a statement based on whether or not I have a right to live," she added.

ISRAELI ACTRESS CALLS OUT HOLLYWOOD STARS 'SILENCING ARTISTS' WHO SUPPORT JEWISH STATE

Feldshuh was not the only person behind the show to disagree with Brody. The series creator, Erin Foster, who converted to Judaism in 2019, previously said that she disagrees with Brody while praising the respectful dynamic among the cast.

Speaking on the "Not Skinny But Not Fat" podcast in October, Foster said, "I think our work environment, our set is very similar to dinner tables around the world where people are having debate and discussion and disagreeing."

MICHAEL RAPAPORT TELLS CRAIG CARTON THAT HIS SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL HAS COST HIM WORK IN HOLLYWOOD

She added, "While I love Adam, I also disagree with him. And that’s okay."

Feldshuh acknowledged Foster's support in her new interview, telling Us Weekly she feels "lucky" the showrunner shares her perspective, and reiterated that she "will not cross swords with Adam."

ROB LOWE CALLS OUT HOLLYWOOD DOUBLE STANDARD AFTER FESTIVALS REJECT BEN SHAPIRO-WRITTEN FILM

"He plays my son, and you know what else? He’s been an incredible friend to me. When they showed my documentary at the temple that hosted us, who came out of all the cast? Adam Brody. He sat next to me," she said.

Entertainment critic Christian Toto praised Feldshuh’s approach, telling Fox News Digital that the actress prioritized the show and its crew over personal politics.

"Kudos to Tovah for tackling this issue head on and not using the press to fight her battles. She's right, of course. We can all agree to disagree, and it shouldn't stop people from working together," Toto said.

He added that while Feldshuh has "more wisdom and insight into the matter than Brody," keeping the peace on set shows that she "put her show and the many people who work on it above any personal vendettas."

"Plus, ‘Nobody Wants This’ is a culture war weapon, in a way. The rom-com shows the Jewish community in a way that's flawed, funny and oh, so human. That's more important than her storming off the set or raging against her co-star," Toto said.

World.title: Al Gore buys hometown Tennessee newspaper, vows to preserve local outlet's 'independent voice'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Former Vice President Al Gore is buying his hometown newspaper in Carthage, Tennessee.

The Carthage Courier announced Monday that the family of Hershel and Geraldine Lake will be handing the paper's ownership to Gore, and that an agreement and ownership transfer will be finalized in the coming weeks.

Carthage is roughly 60 miles east of Nashville.

20 YEARS LATER, AL GORE AND HIS DIRECTOR DEFEND THEIR CONTROVERSIAL CLIMATE MOVIE 'AN INCONVENIENT TRUTH'

"I’m so grateful to the Lake family for their decades of leadership in supporting independent news here in Smith County," Gore said in a statement. "Having spent my early years as a military reporter in Vietnam and later at the Tennessean, I am a firm believer that a free, independent local press is irreplaceable for the enduring health of our community. When my hometown paper came up for sale, I saw an opportunity to help preserve the Courier as an independent voice for Carthage and Smith County."

"I look forward to supporting the Carthage Courier team, many of whom have served this community for decades, as they continue to provide vital information and serve this community for generations to come," he added.

AL GORE SAYS CLIMATE CHANGE SUPPORTERS ‘KEEP QUIET’ ABOUT THEIR BELIEFS FOR FEAR OF RETALIATION

The Lake family put the Courier up for sale this fall after 50 years of operating the 113-year-old paper. Geraldine Lake died on Nov. 1 at 84.

The Courier also announced that its longtime publisher, Scott Winfree, will transition into a part-time role, citing health issues, and that newspaper advertising director Roger Wells will step in as the Courier's new publisher going forward.

The paper assured readers that publication will continue during the ownership transition and that all current staff will be retained.

This isn't Gore's first foray into media. The former VP previously launched Current TV in 2005, which featured programs hosted by various media and political figures including Keith Olbermann, Joy Behar, Gavin Newsom, Jennifer Granholm and Eliot Spitzer.

The network was sold to Al Jazeera in 2013.

Before entering politics, Gore worked as a military journalist in the U.S. Army, serving during the Vietnam War, and later worked as an investigative reporter for The Tennessean.

World.title: Trump says pardon is always an option for Jensen Huang, and that invoking the Fifth isn’t necessary
World.content:
President Donald Trump said that while pardoning Jensen Huang for any potential criminal activity remains an option, he doesn’t think that will be needed for the newly reinstated Nvidia CEO.

“It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary,” Trump told the New York Post in an interview published Tuesday night.

Asked about Huang’s scheduled appearances next week on Capitol Hill, Trump said, “I don’t think he needs to take the Fifth. I think it’s an interesting story for people.”

“I think I want him to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100% aboveboard, and you know a very smart person,” the president said.

A representative for Huang declined to comment on Trump’s comments. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for further comment.

Speaking at a news conference Tuesday, Attorney General Todd Blanche indicated he would have told Trump if Huang had been involved in any criminal activity.

“To the extent that, that the department, that the Department of Justice had information that he was committing crimes or something like this, that is, that is, that’s just not, that’s something that I would have certainly told the president had it been true,” Blanche said.

In Congress, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are preparing to grill Huang over their national security concerns.

A spokesperson for the Republican-led House Intelligence Committee told NBC News that Huang’s reinstatement “changes nothing” and that there “are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers.”

Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter are expected to sit for transcribed interviews next Tuesday and Wednesday before the House Select Committee on China, the House Intelligence Committee and the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

Huang, who has not been charged with a crime, resigned from his post as CEO of the chip giant following reports that he had a relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies believed was a Chinese spy. In a Nov. 8 memo to Nvidia’s staff, he said, “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Trump worked behind the scenes over the weekend to get Nvidia’s board to bring Huang back. That move has been met with bipartisan backlash.

Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., on Monday raised concerns over Nvidia’s quick reversal to rehire Huang after indicating it wouldn’t.

“His own board described his behavior as lacking ‘candor.’ I’ve served on a public company board. His behavior does not support reinstatement,” Ricketts wrote in a post on X.

Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., wrote that with Nvidia’s rehiring of Huang, “the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens.”

Cramer and Ricketts are both members of the Senate Banking Committee, where Huang is scheduled to testify in public Dec. 3.

In celebrating Huang’s return, Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social post that the U.S. government “has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”

Similarly, Nvidia’s board said it reached the decision to reinstate Huang after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that his “reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

World.title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaves the U.S. for Spain a ‘free man’
World.content:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia has been ordered by a federal judge to leave the United States by Tuesday, a U.S. official confirmed to NBC News.

He was spotted Tuesday night boarding a commercial flight at Washington Dulles International Airport bound for Madrid, Spain, bringing to a close one of the most closely watched and controversial immigration cases.

In a statement Tuesday evening, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Maryland, said Abrego Garcia is “traveling to a country of his choice, a free man — unharmed and with dignity.”

Abrego Garcia, wearing a dark hooded jacket, was seen at the airport with his wife and brother, as well as lawyer Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, and representatives from immigrant rights group We Are CASA (Central American Solidarity and Assistance).

They declined to comment.

The Salvadoran national became a central figure in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown last year after he was mistakenly deported to his home country.

The Washington Post reported earlier in the day that Abrego Garcia voluntarily agreed to leave the United States under an agreement with U.S. authorities who had sought his removal. The agreement, it said, would end those proceedings.

Court records in Maryland have yet to reflect such an order. There has been a handful of sealed filings in his civil case against the administration over the past several weeks, however.

The 31-year-old man immigrated to the U.S. illegally as a teenager, but has been in the United States for years, is married to an American and has a child with her.

He had lived and worked in Maryland for years under the regular supervision of Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from gang members.

Guards lead a man identified by his wife as Kilmar Abrego Garcia through the Terrorism Confinement Center in Tecoluca, El Salvador, in 2025. U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland via AP

He was deported there anyway in 2025 and sent to the CECOT megaprison. Activists have decried alleged abuses there and described inmates being packed into cells with no time outdoors.

Prison officials allowed Abrego Garcia a brief outside meeting with Van Hollen, who told reporters that Abrego Garcia had “experienced trauma” after an “illegal abduction.”

He was returned to the U.S., where ICE officials admitted in court filings that his deportation there was an “administrative error.”

Not long after his return to U.S., Abrego Garcia was charged with human smuggling in a case stemming from a 2022 traffic stop for alleged speeding in Tennessee in which he was driving a van with multiple immigrant passengers.

Abrego Garcia told Tennessee Highway Patrol troopers he was taking the group of nine to a construction job. Authorities there did not pursue charges. A federal judge dismissed the 2025 Department of Justice case, saying the Trump administration failed to rebut the “presumption of vindictiveness.” The government appealed.

The administration continued to pursue Abrego’s removal, and he was fighting that in a lawsuit that was ongoing prior to today’s news.

Abrego Garcia has been fighting deportation to Liberia, as proposed by Department of Homeland Security officials. He wanted to go to Costa Rica, according to court records.

President Donald Trump and immigration officials alleged Abrego Garcia was an MS-13 gang member, something he denied.

In 2019 records from a loitering case in which he was picked up in a Home Depot parking lot, authorities in Prince George’s County said that Abrego appeared to be an MS-13 member.

They said they made that conclusion based on his clothing (including a Chicago Bulls hat) and tattoos, as well as a proven confidential informant. Abrego Garcia was not formally arrested that day, police said, and they did not have contact with him again. Abrego Garcia’s lawyers later called the evidence of his gang membership “hearsay.”

U.S. District Judge Waverly Crenshaw, who presided over the Tennessee smuggling case, warned top Trump administration officials to stop making statements about Abrego Garcia that were “exaggerated if not simply inaccurate” and could influence a potential jury.

World.title: Fort Hood mass shooter makes legal move to stop Pentagon’s firing squad execution
World.content:
The former Army officer whose scheduled military execution by firing squad provoked outrage over an initial proposal to livestream his death is planning to file a constitutional challenge that could halt his December execution, his lawyers said Tuesday.

Nidal Hasan, convicted in the 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, that claimed 13 lives, filed a motion for a stay of execution so he can submit what’s known as a habeas corpus petition, which requires the government to justify a person’s detainment.

“There is no question that the violence committed at Fort Hood caused unimaginable pain and loss,” Anna Arceneaux, deputy director of the ACLU’s Capital Punishment Project, said in a statement. “But the gravity of that loss does not change the government’s obligation to uphold the principles that define our justice system. Mr. Hasan, like every person facing an irreversible punishment, must have a chance to pursue federal review of his case.”

Hasan, 56, had officially exhausted his military justice appeals, opening the door to President Donald Trump in October approving his death sentence and the Army setting an execution date.

Hasan’s request was filed in civilian court, which is another process available to military prisoners. Military experts told NBC News the legal maneuver to file a habeas corpus petition would all but assure Hasan’s case will be tied up in a lengthy review process that could effectively stall his pending execution to well beyond the end of Trump’s term. At that point, they say, Trump’s successor may avoid setting another execution date.

The motion was filed on behalf of Hasan by the ACLU of Kansas. Pentagon and Army officials could not immediately be reached for comment.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth first raised the prospect of livestreaming Hasan’s execution, telling a conservative news outlet that he would ensure “people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”

But John Baker, the federal public defender for the Western District of North Carolina whose capital habeas unit is assisting Hasan, said the case deserves further review by a federal court.

“The President, the Secretary of Defense, and others have turned Mr. Hasan’s case into a political spectacle,” Baker said in a statement. “Our government cannot be permitted to execute Mr. Hasan until his death sentence has received full and fair review, which the Constitution safeguards through our federal courts.”

Mourners at a memorial service for the thirteen victims of the shooting rampage at Fort Hood in 2009. Joe Raedle / Getty

Few details were made available about how a firing squad execution could unfold, although Army officials said it would occur at 1 p.m. Dec. 3 at Fort Hood — around the time the attack occurred at the military base. During the shooting, Hasan was injured by responding officers and paralyzed and now requires a wheelchair.

Within days of Hegseth’s announcement, Trump said he would ultimately decide whether Hasan’s death could potentially be watched by millions of people online. He subsequently said in a Truth Social post that while livestreaming the execution “might have been a strong deterrent,” there are other people who “would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device.”

“He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad,” the president said, “but this event will not be streamed.”

Hegseth’s announcement had set off immediate backlash from a bipartisan group of lawmakers, human rights organizations and religious leaders, many of whom said a livestreamed execution would be “medieval” and “barbaric,” echoing public killings conducted by the most brutal totalitarian regimes and terror states and harkening back to the nation’s dark period of public lynchings and racism.

In the U.S., the last large-scale gathering for a lawfully public execution occurred in 1936 in Kentucky, where a Black man convicted of raping a white woman was hanged in front of thousands, according to news reports.

Opponents of livestreaming Hasan’s execution also warned it could be used as propaganda by jihadist militants, while playing into the desires of Hasan, an American-born Muslim who had become radicalized.

“I’m paraplegic and could be in jail for the rest of my life,” Hasan told a mental health panel following the shooting spree. “However, if I died by lethal injection, I would still be a martyr.”

The U.S. military has not put a service member to death by firing squad since 1945 and last executed a service member in 1961, by hanging. Both were conducted privately.

Currently, four people, including Hasan, are on the military’s death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.

World.title: Chinese tech giant Huawei convicted of federal charges, including fraud
World.content:
Chinese tech giant Huawei was convicted of multiple federal charges in New York on Tuesday after prosecutors accused the company of stealing technology from U.S. companies, abusing the American financial system and helping Iran spy on its citizens.

A jury in New York’s Eastern District found the company and three of its subsidiaries guilty of seven conspiracy counts that included bank fraud, wire fraud, money laundering, defrauding the United States and conspiracy to steal trade secrets.

In the roughly two-month trial, Huawei was also convicted of bank fraud and wire fraud. Huawei was acquitted of two counts, a racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice.

“For over two decades, Huawei built its global empire on a foundation of fraud, theft and deception,” Assistant Attorney General Tysen A. Duva said in a statement. “Huawei’s crimes threatened the U.S. financial system, took advantage of American companies that compete honestly in the global telecommunications market, and undermined our national security.”

In a statement, Huawei said the charges are “without legal or factual merit,” and it said it welcomes the racketeering verdict.

“We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests,” the company said.

Huawei attorney Brian Heberling said the company plans to appeal. At sentencing, which is scheduled for Sept. 14, Huawei could face fines, forfeiture and restitution.

Prosecutors accused the company, which makes smartphones and has telecom networks around the world, of encouraging its workforce of 200,000 in 170 countries to lie, cheat, and steal “for a competitive advantage to grow and protect its business.”

Huawei was accused of misappropriating intellectual property like source code, user manuals for internet routers, antenna technology and robot testing technology, prosecutors said. T-Mobile, Cisco, Quintel and CNEX were among the companies whose technology was stolen, federal prosecutors said in a news release Tuesday.

In Iran, the company assisted the regime with “turnkey” internet services and mobile networks, prosecutors said, and it provided surveillance cameras that allowed officials to monitor protests. Huawei also helped intelligence agents monitor and censor the internet, prosecutors said.

Huawei then lied to banks about the nature of its business in Iran, allowing the company to obtain billions of U.S. dollars and become what prosecutors described as “a sophisticated participant in a global marketplace for telecommunications services.”

In an interview Tuesday, Heberling rejected the government’s allegations, saying prosecutors presented a “caricature-like portrait” of Huawei of as a corrupt organization with company policies that condoned crime.

“That was just profoundly inconsistent with the company that I experienced in my work, but more importantly, [with] the evidence, which really showed a series of isolated events over a 20-year period,” he said. “No company can insure perfection over that period of time.”

Heberling argued that the racketeering acquittal — the most serious charge the company faced — showed a “profound rejection of the narrative the United States pursued in this case.”

Huawei was previously banned from selling equipment to U.S. carriers over fears that it poses a security risk, according to the Associated Press, and it was blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and Britain.

World.title: ‘Shocking’ decline seen in hep B vaccination against incurable virus, including babies with infected mothers
World.content:
Fewer newborns are being vaccinated against hepatitis B, an incurable infection that can lead to liver disease, including babies whose mothers are known to have the virus, a large new analysis has found.

As of June, just 66% of newborns got the hepatitis B vaccine within a day of their birth, down from 80% in 2022. The birth dose serves as a safety net especially for babies whose pregnant mothers are unaware they’re infected with the virus and unknowingly transmit it during childbirth.

Up to 90% of babies with the virus develop chronic infections, putting them at risk for liver failure and liver cancer later in life. Vaccinating them at birth dramatically lowers those odds.

The new study from Truveta, a health care and analytics company, included medical records from more than 1.3 million babies born in the United States from January 2018 through June this year.

During that time period, newborn vaccination rates increased from 76% in 2018 to 80% in 2022 before declining in mid-2023, falling to 66% by June this year.

“It’s shocking to see a nearly 15% decline in three years,” said Nina Masters, lead author and principal applied research scientist at Truveta. “Infants born to mothers with hepatitis B have a 90% chance of perinatal infection. That can mean a lifetime of chronic liver disease, cirrhosis and early death. This is a real preventable tragedy.”

The decline began before federal vaccine advisers voted in December to abandon a decades-old recommendation that all babies be vaccinated against hepatitis B at birth. (That decision was later halted by a federal judge in response to a lawsuit filed by the American Academy of Pediatrics. The block remains in effect.)

The findings mirror increasing trends in anti-vaccine behavior in general. A recent NBC News data investigation found three-quarters of U.S. counties that track kindergarten immunization rates no longer meet the minimum threshold to prevent measles outbreaks.

Now, measles outbreaks are popping up nationwide, with nearly 6,000 cases and at least 13 deaths, according to state health departments. The U.S. lost its measles elimination status Nov. 16, reversing one of the country’s greatest public health achievements this century.

“We talk about measles being the canary in the coal mine. We’re seeing those outbreaks,” said Dr. Richard Besser, a pediatrician and president of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. “This one — hepatitis B and the rise in unvaccinated newborns — these are the kinds of things that are silent, that you don’t see for years and years until these babies grow up and end up having liver disease.”

The study, published Tuesday in NEJM Evidence, also revealed that hepatitis B vaccination rates have fallen among babies born to mothers known to be infected with the virus. Up to 98% of those babies were vaccinated between 2018 through 2025. But between January and June, that rate dropped to 94%.

Cases of acute hepatitis B fell dramatically in children after the the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention began recommending a universal birth dose in 1991, falling 99% from 1990 to 2019. A CDC analysis of children born from 1994 to 2023 estimated that hepatitis B vaccination prevented more than 6 million infections and nearly 1 million hospitalizations.

Last year, the University of Minnesota’s Vaccine Integrity Project published a review of more than 400 studies, finding no evidence of short- or long-term health problems from the hepatitis B shot after birth.

“Reversing the successes of previous public health programs puts individuals’ lives at risk,”

Dr. James Conway, a pediatric infectious disease physician and medical director of the UW Health Immunization Program in Madison, Wisconsin, wrote in an email. “It’s sad, tragic and preventable.”

World.title: Maps show how far lead dust from Iowa detonation could travel
World.content:
New maps of the Army's planned lead azide detonation in southeast Iowa show a plume of toxic dust drifting southwest toward northeast Missouri between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. Wednesday.

The Army plans to detonate about 5 tons of degraded lead azide, in 68 barrels, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown at 9 a.m. Wednesday, the day before Thanksgiving, according to an emergency alert sent to cellphones Tuesday morning. The alert said some people within 5 miles southwest of the plant may be evacuated and told people up to 20 miles away to stay indoors with windows closed. Officials expect the wind to blow southwest, away from Burlington, a city of just under 25,000 people on the Mississippi River.

The last controlled detonation of lead azide happened in 1977.

The Army moved the detonation from Friday, citing more favorable wind and time to add safety measures, according to a government court filing. A federal appeals court cleared the way Monday for the detonation after it had been delayed several times amid lawsuits from environmental groups and concerns from elected officials in Illinois and Iowa.

The maps show the modeled lead dust from 9 a.m. until 5 p.m. Wednesday. At 9 a.m., a red circle is centered near the plant. By 9:45 a.m., the shaded area becomes a long oval running from near Burlington southwest toward the Missouri line.

By early afternoon, the shaded area stretches far into northeast Missouri, passing Knox City. By late afternoon, it narrows to a band running from the Burlington and Keokuk area toward Macon, Missouri, with Quincy, Illinois, just southeast of it.

Maps of the planned lead azide detonation in Middletown show the shaded area stretching from near Burlington toward Macon, Missouri, by noon Wednesday. The forecasts will change with the weather. CBS Chicago

Wind arrows on the maps point southwest. Illinois officials said Monday that NOAA's latest model showed no Illinois counties would be affected. The Illinois EPA had asked the Army for updated modeling but had not received it, officials said, and Gov. JB Pritzker has directed state agencies to remain on alert.

Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe said state agencies are setting up additional monitoring of air and water quality.

The maps are forecasts and will change with the weather. Under the EPA's permit, the Army must update its plume forecasts six hours before the detonation and hourly after that until it is finished. The Army's forecasts do not establish that harmful exposure will occur at every location inside a projected plume, and sampling will be needed to show where lead settles on farmland, playgrounds and other surfaces.

Officials recommend that people stay indoors during the detonation and rinse outdoor surfaces with water afterward.

The USDA estimates 250 farms could be impacted by the detonation.

"If we don't have a healthy herd, we don't have a healthy paycheck," said Steve Lucie, Iowa cattle farmer. "We're very concerned about what that's going to do to the health of our soil and our livestock."

Why the Army is detonating the lead azide, and the pushback

"Inaction is no longer an option," said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, who leads the operation.

The Army says the lead azide has been stored at the plant for more than 20 years in earthen-covered containers, in a bath of ethanol and water meant to keep it stable. A routine check this year found some of the water had evaporated, and the material has since recrystallized, making it increasingly sensitive to friction and shock. Army officials say moving the barrels now risks setting them off, and experts say the stockpile will become more volatile as temperatures cool, since less liquid in the barrels makes the solution more prone to freezing, which raises the risk of a chain reaction.

The Army has added blast barriers around the bunkers where the lead azide will be detonated, plans to apply ballistic gels and foams to absorb dust, and will douse the materials with thousands of gallons of water. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said the goal is to keep as much of the dust as possible on the plant's grounds. The Army considered "every viable solution," he said, and concluded a controlled detonation is safest. The EPA issued an emergency permit for the detonation Nov. 13.

The plan has drawn criticism from both parties. A bipartisan group of Illinois and Iowa elected officials asked the Army and EPA to delay it and look for safer alternatives, citing poor communication with the public. Sen. Tammy Duckworth, an Illinois Democrat, called the operation a "failure of leadership of epic proportions." Earthjustice sued on behalf of the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club's Iowa chapter, challenging the validity of the EPA's emergency permit. The 8th Circuit Court of Appeals temporarily blocked the detonation last week, then declined Monday to stop it, saying the groups had not shown they were likely to succeed and that the degraded explosives risk an uncontrolled blast without the permit's safety measures. The judges said the Army evaluated "a full range" of alternatives, including neutralizing the lead azide with other chemicals and thermal treatment.

President Trump said on social media that in addition to the court's go-ahead, he wanted Gov.-elect Rob Sand to approve the detonation. Sand, a Democrat who takes office in January, has said the decision is fully up to the administration. Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds said Tuesday she supports the plan after speaking with military leaders.

World.title: Army to detonate unstable explosives in Iowa Wednesday morning
World.content:
The Army is set to detonate 5 tons of explosives containing lead azide at a munitions plant in Iowa on Wednesday morning after a back-and-forth that has played out between politicians and in court.

The detonation will take place at 9 a.m. Central time, acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said Tuesday at a press conference. Telle said the unstable explosives become more dangerous as temperatures drop, and the weather forecast for Wednesday is "ideal to protect public health and safety across the region."

"Inaction is no longer an option," Army Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, the commander of the operation, said Tuesday. "It would be irresponsible for us to not take the determined, consensus-based course of action moving forward."

The government has argued the detonation — which is expected to send a plume of toxic lead particles into the surrounding area — is necessary because the lead azide could spontaneously explode.

"There is consensus across the experts, across the country, that a controlled mitigated detonation of the lead azide here at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is far preferable to an uncontrolled, spontaneous detonation of that substance," Telle said Tuesday.

A federal appeals court on Monday declined to block the Army from detonating the explosives. The court's ruling came after environmental groups challenged the validity of the emergency permit granted by the Environmental Protection Agency and argued the EPA hadn't given enough notice to residents.

Following the ruling, the Army noted Monday night that current Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds "has given her support to go forward."

"It is the unanimous judgement of our people — the Army, Navy, EPA, ATF, FBI, DARPA, DoE, CDC, HHS, FEMA and every other agency involved — that the Army should proceed with an extensively mitigated, carefully controlled detonation, which will occur this Wednesday morning, as previously scheduled, based on forecast wind conditions," Telle said on X.

The 8th Circuit Court of Appeals temporarily blocked the detonation last week to give itself time to issue a longer-lasting ruling. On Monday, the court said the environmental groups that challenged the plan had failed to show they are likely to succeed.

"We are mindful of the very real risks presented by the Army's planned detonation of the stores of degraded lead azide," the ruling said. "However, we must acknowledge the realities of the situation: the degraded explosives present a risk of an uncontrolled and unplanned explosion, which would occur without the benefit of the safety measures that the Permit puts in place."

President Trump said earlier Monday the government would not carry out the detonation until the appeals court ruled and unless Democratic Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand signed off. Mr. Trump added that government experts felt detonating the material was the best option.

"If [Sand] or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation," the president said on social media.

Sand, whose input was not required and who is not yet in office, said on social media the Trump administration "should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks."

"Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation, and learn why the administration believes this is the best path forward," Sand said.

The government has argued that even if the appeals court had stayed its EPA permit, the Army has the legal right to move forward without a permit to "respond to the immediate threat of an uncontrolled explosion."

The Army has stored the lead azide in earthen-covered containers for decades at its ammunition plant in Middletown, a small town located near the Mississippi River in southeastern Iowa. The EPA has said the government discovered earlier this year that the material deteriorated over time, risking explosion if it is moved or disturbed.

The Pentagon asked the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Lincoln Laboratory to study the detonation plan, officials told CBS News.

In a statement posted to Facebook Tuesday night, the laboratory agreed that the detonation plan is better than the possibility of a sudden, unexpected explosion.

"Lincoln Laboratory has performed a review of the Army's planned lead azide detonation at the request of the DoW," the laboratory said. "Based on the Army's documentation, we concurred that conducting the detonation under the planned controlled conditions is preferable to accepting the risks associated with a potential unplanned detonation."

As part of an earlier detonation plan that had been previously slated for Friday, the Army asked some Middletown residents to temporarily evacuate their homes for six hours, and said people could expect loud noises, vibrations and a dust plume.

Environmental groups and Iowa and Illinois politicians from both parties criticized the plan, arguing the detonation could lead to widespread lead contamination in both states and pressing the EPA and Army to consider other options.

The Sierra Club and the Iowa Environmental Council asked the federal appeals court to step in and review the EPA's permit last week. The environmental groups said the EPA failed to fully assess the risks of the detonation or consider alternatives, and argued the Army was operating on an "extraordinarily rushed timeline" that prevented residents from getting enough notice.

On Monday, a panel of three appellate judges sided with the federal government. The court found that the EPA "adequately incorporated safeguards" to mitigate the risks, including barriers and plans for environmental monitoring, and the Army considered a range of alternatives.

World.title: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will petition to delay his execution
World.content:
Nidal Hasan, the Army soldier who fatally shot 13 people in the attack at the Texas Army post in 2009, told a federal court Tuesday that he plans to file a petition to delay his execution by firing squad.

In the filing, which was signed by Hasan himself, he says that he "intends to demonstrate that the military court's judgment and his resulting sentence of death were obtained and are maintained in violation of his federal constitutional and statutory rights."

According to the court document obtained by CBS News, Hasan, a former military psychiatrist, said his constitutional rights were violated "due to unlawful command influence" of President Trump and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, "who are driven by unlawful racial and religious animus."

Hasan, who is Muslim and of Palestinian descent, was found guilty of multiple counts of murder and attempted murder related to those killed and the more than 30 who were wounded by gunfire in the attack. Hasan acknowledged at trial that he was responsible for the shooting, claiming he opened fire on fellow members of the Army in an attempt to protect Islamic insurgents from U.S. military forces. He was an outspoken opponent of the U.S. war on terror and called it a "war against Islam."

Trump-appointed judge to hear the case

Court records show that Hasan's case has been assigned to Judge Tony Mattivi in U.S. District Court in Kansas. It was filed there because Hasan is being held at the military prison at Fort Leavenworth in the state.

A hearing has been set for Wednesday morning, according to court records.

Mattivi was nominated by Mr. Trump to serve as a federal judge and was just confirmed by the Senate on June 9.

According to his judicial biography, from 2009 to 2013, Mattivi was the lead prosecutor in the capital military commission at Naval Station Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, against the al-Qaida operative who masterminded the bombing of the USS Cole.

Asking for a broader definition of victims

Hasan's filing comes as military officials said Tuesday that three survivors of the shooting at Fort Hood will not be allowed to witness Hasan's execution.

On Nov. 10, the Army said the three cannot attend the execution scheduled for Dec. 3 because none of them was the direct victim of those charges, citing regulations governing military executions. An email sent Tuesday and shared with The Associated Press by recipients said military officials rejected their request for reconsideration, citing security and space issues.

The three argued that the Army should apply a broader definition of "victim" from the Uniform Code of Military Justice that says a victim can be someone who suffered "direct physical, emotional or pecuniary harm." They argued that the military's refusal to allow them to attend was saying they had not been victims because they were not struck by bullets.

Retired Colonel Kathy Platoni, who would have been Hasan's supervisor during a planned deployment to Afghanistan, said the denial felt like a betrayal.

"I would desperately like to attend," Platoni said from her home in Ohio. "To look Hasan in the eye and say, 'You didn't get me.'"

The letter signed by the commandant of Fort Leavenworth said the three cannot appeal again. "Please understand that this is not meant as a judgment on any emotional injury you or others suffered as a result of CP Hasan's crimes," it said.

A previous plan to livestream the military execution, the first since 1961 and the first by firing squad since World War II, was rescinded by Mr. Trump last month after bipartisan backlash.

"I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social.

The Army noted in a statement Tuesday that regulations specify who can witness a military execution, and reiterated the size and space restrictions.

"Efforts have been made over the years, from the trial to notifications to memorials and now to the execution, to recognize the impacts and support the victims," the Army statement said.

Former Army Sgt. Alonzo Lunsford, who was among the 32 injured in the attack, said he will attend the execution but opposed the public livestream. "I want to be in the room where I can see him, and he can see me," he told CBS News last month in an interview.

"This will not be closure for me," Lunsford said, adding that his closure comes from helping others. He said he carries the bullet that was pulled from his body with him every day as a reminder of what he survived.

A blood-stained uniform and memories of the attack remain

Those targeted were unarmed soldiers who were at the readiness center as they were preparing to deploy. Hasan fired 146 times.

Platoni said the survivors from her unit deployed to Afghanistan 29 days after the attack because, "we still served our country, and if we didn't, (Hasan) would have won."

She said the building where Hasan initially opened fire had been crowded with returning soldiers and those preparing to deploy. She had been moved to another building when the attack began.

"The looks on the faces of my friends and colleagues as they carried in the dying and wounded that day … it will haunt me for the rest of my life," she said.

She said they carried in the badly wounded captain who had rushed Hasan with a chair to try to stop the shooting.

"I was throwing computers to the ground trying to get the tablecloths because we needed blankets. We didn't have medical supplies or even water," she said. "I still have that blood-stained uniform, from kneeling down next to that young man, trying to get him to stay with us. That will be with me forever."

Julia Wilson, who was nine months pregnant when Hasan opened fire, said her request to witness was also denied. She said the way the military has handled the case has caused her anguish.

"We have faced institutional betrayal after institutional betrayal," Wilson said. "We remain on that battlefield because of that … if they don't fix it, we're never going to leave that battlefield. We'll never heal."

Platoni had been on the list of victims and survivors kept by the military's victim liaison since Hasan's 2013 court-martial trial. Everyone on that list received notification in March that there had been movement in scheduling the execution, Platoni said.

Platoni said she did not think space was really the issue. The military told victims and survivors that about 160 witnesses would be allowed to attend the execution, and through her work with survivors and families of victims she believed about 90 people had decided to go. Platoni conceded that those details may have changed.

An Army official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive plans, said that the military is not planning to release any details about the firing squad or protocols, including the number of service members involved.

Feeling a duty to attend the execution

Retired Major C. Alan Hopewell testified at Hasan's trial. He confirmed Hasan's identity after he was shot by two service members attempting to halt his rampage. One of those officers had asked Hopewell to accompany her to the execution.

He said Tuesday that he would accept the denial but with mixed feelings.

"I'm disappointed that our status as victims is not recognized," Hopewell said. "A bullet missed me and hit my car. I guess if the bullet had hit me … they would consider me a victim and let me attend."

Hopewell, Platoni and Wilson said that even after the execution, they will continue to push for the Fort Hood shooting to be redefined as an act of domestic terrorism instead of workplace violence.

Hopewell recently underwent surgery unrelated to the shooting and said he's not certain his doctors would have cleared him to witness the execution. Nonetheless, he had hoped the Army would grant him the right.

"I guess it feels more like a duty, like a fulfillment of my responsibility to those soldiers who were killed and injured, who were threatened," Hopewell said.

World.title: China launches first foreign astronaut to its space station
World.content:
China on Wednesday launched the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft with three astronauts — two Chinese and a Pakistani — sending the first foreign crew member to its space station.

Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, is flying alongside Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39, after the craft blasted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China on Wednesday morning. It successfully separated from a rocket and entered its predetermined orbit.

The launch marked the first joint flight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program.

Hours earlier, crowds of people attended a send-off ceremony, with many holding up their phones to capture the moment.

Astronauts Muhammad Zeeshan Ali of Pakistan and China's Wu Yi and Tang Hongbo wave at a send-off ceremony on Nov. 25, 2026. Andy Wong/AP Photo

The crew will conduct more than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests during their mission, official Chinese news agency Xinhua earlier reported. Ali will conduct a photosynthetic cyanobacteria experiment in orbit during his short-term mission before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou 23 spacecraft, it said.

Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif offered his best wishes to the astronauts ahead of their mission.

"Pakistan-China friendship is surpassing the heights of the Himalayas in its journey to outer space," he said on X on Tuesday.

The joint flight is part of an agreement signed by China and Pakistan in February 2025.

While this was the first spaceflight for Ali and Wu, Tang has flown on two previous missions and is set to become the first astronaut to board the Tiangong space station three times, national broadcaster CCTV said.

At a news conference on Tuesday, Tang said that differences in language, culture and psychology had made learning to work together more challenging on this mission, but that both sides' efforts were paying off.

In front of reporters, those efforts were reflected in Ali's Mandarin proficiency. He cited a line of Chinese poetry about climbing one story higher to see farther.

"It's like my daily training. Day after day, reaching new heights," he said in Mandarin.

Speaking in English, he said he hoped the next chapter of space cooperation between the two countries would go from one astronaut in one flight to multiple joint flights and to the moon, Mars and beyond.

In May, China launched Shenzhou 23, which carried three astronauts, including one crew member who was set to remain in space for about a year.

China is preparing for its first crewed lunar landing by 2030. The U.S. is widely seen as China's main space rival, with NASA aiming to land astronauts on the lunar surface in 2028.

World.title: How tariffs, fuel and fertilizer costs are squeezing the U.S.'s biggest apple region
World.content:
How tariffs, fuel and fertilizer costs are squeezing the U.S.'s biggest apple region

Loading...

As Sean Gilbert stepped out of his white GMC pickup, he breathed in the scent of applewood and Columbia Basin dust. Here, just south of Wapato, Wash., one of his 50-acre Gala and Red Delicious apple orchards is ground into huge piles of mulch chips. The wood chipper is the size of a semi-truck and belts out a screeching racket.

He said this ground will lay fallow. It will cost this fifth-generation apple farmer less to leave it unplanted and weedy than to plant another orchard or crop. He scooped up a handful of applewood mulch. "It's a bit of a relief that we're not going to continue to be hemorrhaging dollars on orchards that the market doesn't want," he said. "It hasn't been making sense for a while."

Washington's $9 billion industry grows nearly 70% of the nation's fresh apples, according to Jon DeVaney, president of the Washington State Tree Fruit Association.

DeVaney said farmers are being pressed by the costs of labor, fuel, fertilizer, equipment, as well as weak exports from international tariffs and a strong dollar that diminishes foreign purchasing power.

He estimated thousands of acres of apple orchards across the Northwest are being rapidly torn out, or are not being actively cared for, because many farmers aren't making money growing the fruit. And after several years of similar economic conditions, many farms have gone deep into debt – with even some large, well-established operations filing for bankruptcy.

Sponsor Message

Loading...

Andrea Starr

Andrea Starr

toggle caption i Andrea Starr

In the late summer and fall, unpicked apples have been left to rot in branches and on the ground. Over the past few years, an estimated thousands of acres have only been partially picked or not picked at all, according to Kate Tynan, senior vice president of the Northwest Horticultural Council, a trade association that advocates for the Northwest tree fruit industry on federal policy issues and international trade.

Recent federal regulatory changes would effectively lower wages for some immigrant workers and take housing costs out of their paychecks. Tynan said with updates to the way wages are calculated, farm owners are hoping they'll be able to break even – but the farm workers union has pushed back on these changes and an upcoming federal judicial decision could put operators on the hook for backpay for the 2026 season.

U.S. farmers have also been especially hard hit by tariffs and high input costs. The Trump administration announced $12 billion in payments to farmers at the end of 2025 that primarily targeted farmers who grow crops such as soybeans and corn. Tynan said much of that relief has not reached farmers that grow specialty crops like fruit and vegetables.

"The Pacific Northwest has lost an unprecedented number of tree fruit farms in recent years," Tynan said. "Economic conditions have worsened drastically since then, so we know that number is far higher today."

Sponsor Message

She points to a USDA census conducted every five years that recorded a 15% drop in Washington tree fruit farms between 2017 and 2022. In neighboring Oregon, more than a quarter of apple, pear and cherry farms were lost in that same time period. By the numbers, apple acreage in Washington increased slightly during this period. But small, family-run farms face another threat: large, well-funded corporations are buying out orchard owners, reducing competition when profits are already tight.

"Some of that was new investment from [private equity] coming in during that time. That acreage trend has since reversed," said Jon DeVaney, emphasizing that the industry is losing growers.

"From 2023, 2024 and 2025 have been the really hard years," said Sean Gilbert, who co-owns Gilbert Orchards, a family-run company founded in 1898 that manages 4,000 acres of fruit in Washington state.

While Gilbert Orchards has worked to navigate these broad economic shifts, visual journalists with Northwest Public Broadcasting chronicled a full year of the business of growing apples.

World.title: The U.S. government is investigating Iranian ties to as many as 50 hacked commercial vessels
World.content:
The U.S. government is investigating Iranian ties to as many as 50 hacked commercial vessels

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

The U.S. government has intelligence suggesting that up to 50 commercial shipping vessels were recently compromised by cyberattacks, activity federal officials are investigating as potentially linked to Iran.

That's according to a U.S. official familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak on the record, a former military cyber operator and an industry executive briefed on the attacks. The series of breaches was first reported by the The Wall Street Journal.

The attacks against the maritime sector, if officials' suspicions are correct, may be the latest example of Iranian cyberattacks against global critical infrastructure during the ongoing war with the United States.

Sponsor Message

NPR has reported that cybersecurity experts and U.S. officials believe Iranian hackers were responsible for a series of digital attacks against U.S. water treatment systems across the country in August as well as a pattern of attacks targeting refrigeration cooling systems that led to spoiled food at grocery stores on U.S. military bases and all across Europe as recently as early November.

The Coast Guard and the FBI first partnered in August to send a "highly specialized team" to board two different foreign commercial vessels "in the Gulf of America" heading to U.S. ports, according to a statement provided by the FBI and the Coast Guard. "The captain, crew, and shore-side corporate staff were critical partners in helping to ensure the threats were mitigated," according to the statement.

The FBI and Coast Guard press offices also told NPR that there are no current "reports of operational disruptions, vessel instability, physical danger to crews, or environmental impacts."

However, there are dozens more ships in international waters that the U.S. government believes have been compromised by hackers and many others who might be vulnerable to similar attacks.

According to the U.S. official familiar with the investigation, bad actors took advantage of known vulnerabilities in Fortinet FortiGate devices, which are frequently used in the maritime industry. The Coast Guard and FBI released a cyber bulletin in September warning the industry that bad actors were breaking into these devices, which help manage firewalls and virtual private networks. "Threat actors routinely scan for specific, unpatched vulnerabilities to gain a foothold," the bulletin read.

According to the U.S. official, in some cases, employees aboard the ships suspected something nefarious was going on when they noticed email disruptions or couldn't log in to their accounts, or, in at least one case, an extended communications blackout. The U.S. official declined to comment on how the U.S. government knows about the extent of breaches across the sector.

Sponsor Message

However, according to the U.S. official, hackers were able to break in using the Fortinet vulnerability and then pivot from the ships' IT systems over to their network of devices controlling physical processes on the ships, what's called operational technology.

The U.S. official said the bad actors "could have impacted the systems on board that control propulsion, steering, navigation, and cargo management," though they did not share any examples of that kind of activity occurring. In at least one case, one of the ships affected was an LNG tanker designed to transport liquified natural gas. It's important to keep systems at a certain temperature to prevent dangerous accidents if a ship's cargo includes explosive materials –from chemicals to fuel.

While commercial vessels are accustomed to physical security reviews entering the United States following the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, digital threats are becoming all the more important to track as adversaries can break in and cause damage from afar. "It's a totally new paradigm that these tankers are networked in this way," the U.S. official said.

Even so, national security officials have feared something like this might happen for years. A former Navy official who requested anonymity to discuss internal operations tells NPR that "we had been tracking the possibility to exploit and take control of [operational technology] systems on Navy ships and Merchant [Marine] ships for a long time, and now this is coming to fruition."

While the U.S. government is wary of advertising Iranian hacking efforts during the war, officials also want to spread awareness of the vulnerability of internet connected devices, particularly those that are linked to the technology that controls critical processes. "These are not sophisticated attacks," the official said. "This is a known vulnerability that could be mitigated with some pretty basic cyber hygiene."

Sponsor Message

"Modern ships are highly integrated systems. A cyberattack presents significant risks, including the potential for a collision, grounding, oil spill, or even an explosion. The Coast Guard regularly publishes bulletins on cyber vulnerabilities and actions vessel owners and operators can take to secure their networks," according to a statement from the Coast Guard.

Ahead of the winter and a busy holiday season for commercial shipping, officials are bracing themselves to investigate any ship entering U.S. ports that could be compromised.

"People never think about what a modern blessing electricity is until it goes out. People take the marine transportation system for granted until there's a problem and their stuff doesn't get there by Christmas," the U.S. official said. "I wish more Americans knew how complex this system is."

World.title: Who really owns the Albanian land Jared Kushner wants to turn into a 5-star resort?
World.content:
Who really owns the Albanian land Jared Kushner wants to turn into a 5-star resort?

toggle caption i Rob Schmitz/NPR

ZVERNEC, Albania — In the summer of 2021, Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump boarded a yacht owned by Nat Rothschild, an heir to the European banking family. On the way from Montenegro to Greece, the yacht anchored off the coast of Albania.

And, as Kushner told an investment conference last year, that's when Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama arrived at the boat to tell them about his plan for the country.

"I was very impressed by what he wanted to do with the country," said Kushner. "I really didn't know anything about the country and I didn't understand the history, and the darkness of the history with the communism and terrible leadership led to it being fully undeveloped as a nation."

Sponsor Message

A year later, Kushner was looking for development opportunities in the Balkans. He returned to the Albanian coast — to the city of Vlore, which was finishing the construction of an airport atop a wetland near an undeveloped coastline. "And obviously, a country's going to build an airport by the coast in a place they think is most beautiful," Kushner told the conference, "so we went there and we were looking for opportunities, and we found some incredible opportunities."

Kushner found those opportunities at Hidrovor Beach, an expanse of caramel-colored sand along the southern Albanian coast, with the gentle waves of the Adriatic lapping its perimeter and a view of an uninhabited island.
