World.title: 22 injured after car bomb strikes central Colombia governor’s office
World.content:
Twenty-two people were reportedly injured and more than 80 buildings were damaged in a car bomb attack on the Governor’s Office of Meta in Villavicencio, central Colombia.

According to Meta’s Security Secretary, Franklin Olivos, the car that exploded carried approximately 100 kilograms of explosives and caused damage to buildings that were located more than 100 meters away from the blast.

Among the injured are five private security guards. One of them needed surgery, according to his employer.

Olivos blamed the attack on the 39th Front, a unit of the FARC dissident group EMC, which has opposed the peace process that started 10 years ago on Tuesday and controls large swathes of jungle territory in the south of Colombia.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said that “narcoterrorism is desperate because we are confronting it head-on. It seeks to intimidate us and force us to back down so we seek another sham peace process.”

De la Espriella, an opponent of the peace process, has been advertising an “iron fist” policy against organized crime and illegal armed groups.

The president’s alleged offensive has failed to produce any results and guerrilla groups have continued to attack State security forces and infrastructure.

World.title: Colombia strips key critics of security details
World.content:
Colombia’s National Protection Unit (UNP) has withdrawn the security details of journalist Daniel Coronell, a major critic of President Abelardo de la Espriella, after vowing to protect the freedom of the press.

Coronell’s local security detail was removed because he lives in the United States, which would make it impossible for the UNP to reassess his protection plan.

The Miami-based journalist frequently travels to Colombia for his work and was in Bogota to receive a lifetime achievement award from the national journalism prize.

While receiving the prize, Coronell sharply criticized De la Espriella for promoting self-promotion over governance. using state resources to censor critics, restricting public information to “friendly media,” and leveraging a history of aggressive lawsuits against reporters.

The journalist’s criticism triggered a clash with Interior Minister Alejandro Ordoñez, who accused Coronell of being angry for having State subsidies pulled.

After press freedom foundation FLIP responded to defend Coronell, Ordoñez claimed that “the freedom of the press enjoys full protection and guarantees from the government.”

We value and defend freedom of the press as a cornerstone of democracy. The press is free, but it is also responsible. It is not a license to abuse, slander, defame, fabricate stories, spread misinformation, or engage in politics. Nor is it a license to destroy democracy or its institutions with lies. Interior Minister Alejandro Ordoñez

Coronell played a key role in Colombian journalism since the late 1980’s and was forced to flee Colombia in 2005 after reports on the ties of former President Alvaro Uribe and paramilitary groups escalated death threats.

The journalist currently works with Noticias Uno and Caracol Radio, and has more than 700,000 subscribers on YouTube.

The UNP previously stripped former President Gustavo Petro and former presidential candidate Claudia Lopez of their security details.

World.title: Illegal armed group carries out first urban drone attack: three injured in northeast Colombia
World.content:
A couple and their 18-month-old baby were injured in a drone attack on a police station in Cucuta, the first major city to be struck from the sky by guerrilla explosives.

The attack damaged more than 60 homes near the Norte de Santander Police Department in the Tasajero neighborhood in the north of the regional capital, the province’s security secretary, George Quintero, told press.

As of now, the situation is as follows: more than 60 damaged homes located just 20 meters from the police headquarters, and three people injured. Security secretary George Quintero

The homes were hit because the police department’s signal-jamming systems reportedly caused the drones to miss their target.

An unknown number of drones were able to reach the interior of the Police Department’s compound, leaving only minor damage.

Guerrilla group ELN has been carrying out multiple drone attacks in Catatumbo, a nearby region with major coca cultivations, and exercises control in the peripheral slums of Cucuta.

The group was accused of attacking the same police department with home-made mortars in August. This attack injured seven policemen.

In a response to the guerrilla attack, President Abelardo de la Espriella in October ordered the militarization of the border city, which has been struggling with security issues for years.

De la Espriella vowed that he “will not allow narco-terrorism to continue sowing fear and threatening families” in Cucuta and the surrounding Norte de Santander province.

According to the authorities, the militarization of the city sought to “strengthen territorial control, protect citizens, and confront” the illegal armed groups that operate in and around Cucuta.

The president’s offensive against illegal armed groups and organized crime has been hampered by an increase in the use of drones that are equipped with explosives.

All kinds of illegal armed groups use the relatively new technology to push back the authorities from areas under their control.

World.title: Colombia asks X to suspend Petro’s social media account
World.content:
Colombia’s communications ministry said Sunday that it had requested social media platform X to suspend former President Gustavo Petro for “possible incitement to violence.”

In a statement that was published of X, the ministry said it reported Petro’s account to X’s Public Affairs, Safety, and Rules Enforcement Team.

According to the statement, the request to suspend the leftist former president, who has more than 9 million followers, was due to a November 21 post in which Petro asked “the people of Colombia to demand Abelardo’s resignation now.”

Petro has been trying to promote popular opposition against De la Espriella, who he has called an illegitimate president.

According to the ministry, Petro’s call to “take action in the streets” could constitute a call for violence against the government.

In a response, the former president said the De la Espriella administration sought to impose censorship on him, which is “expressly prohibited by the Constitution.”

The ministry’s request “demonstrates the extent of the current government’s illegitimacy,” added Petro.

The former president is now the leader of the Historic Pact (PH) opposition party and has actively been promoting a general strike in response to his successor’s controversial policy decisions.

Petro is a member of the PH’s more radical wing and can still count on a significant following among Colombia’s population.

World.title: De la Espriella calls on US to prosecute Petro in response to call to “resign now”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the US Justice Department to “investigate, prosecute and hopefully jail former President Gustavo Petro after the latter called on the people to “rise up” and “restore real democracy.”

De la Espriella addressed the nation at the end of a day of anti-government marches that mobilized tens of thousands of people throughout Colombia.

Petro led the march in Cali and called on his supporters to “rise up,” call a general strike and force the president to “leave now,” less than four months after De la Espriella took office.

Reiterating fraud accusations and the president’s business ties to paramilitary warlords and drug traffickers, the former president told the crowd that “it is not about waiting until 2030; an illegitimate government must leave now.”

A government whose policy goes against the people must leave now. A government whose policy builds hunger and death for the people of Colombia must leave now. Life must be restored, democracy must be restored, and the slogan “Abelardo, resign now!” must become the slogan of the majority of the Colombian people. An agreement will eventually be made to transition back so that the Constitution of Colombia and the laws in favor of the Colombian people prevail. But from here on out—and that is why we must move to a national strike, that is why we must move to a general strike—within the people’s right of expression and decision, an illegitimate government that goes against the interests of the Colombian population must leave now. Gustavo Petro

De la Espriella told Petro that he would never accept they “attack democracy, promote a coup d’état or attempt to destroy Colombia, just as he did when he was a guerrilla fighter.”

The president claimed that the former President and congressional opposition leader Ivan Cepeda “have no moral authority whatsoever. However, as I tell you, I will not accept them attacking democracy, attacking institutionality, or promoting a coup d’état in an attempt to destroy Colombia.”

De la Espriella repeated his threat to extradite his predecessor if requested to do so by the administration of his ally, US President Donald Trump.

I make a direct call to the judicial authorities of the United States so that investigations related to acts of corruption, drug trafficking, or any other criminal conduct move forward with full rigor and the independence of the judicial system in the United States. Petro’s government was a criminal enterprise, and international laws and provisions were violated. The United States has jurisdiction to investigate him, prosecute him, and hopefully imprison him. Let the North American justice system act, let the whole truth be known, let the evidence be examined, and let those found responsible answer before the law without regard for anything other than the application of the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president has tried to criminalize the opposition and the former government ever since taking office in August without much success.

World.title: Colombia rejects US proposal to conduct joint strikes against drug trafficking: NYT
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rejected a US plan to conduct joint military operations, anonymous US officials told the New York Times (NYT).

According to the NYT, De la Espriella told the US government he supported working with the US military, but lacked congressional support invite US soldiers on Colombian soil.

The conversation would have taken place in the week ahead of US defense secretary Pete Hegseth’s visit to Colombia on Wednesday.

In a response, the president and the defense secretary said that the alleged US plan was “fake news.”

“I have not rejected any proposal of the Government of President Donald Trump,” De la Espriella said on social media platform X.

Colombia and the United States maintain strong and increasingly close cooperation in the areas of security, intelligence, and the fight against drug cartels and narco-terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president confirmed that congressional approval would be required for him to invite foreign troops into Colombia.

Between visits to Venezuela and Ecuador, Hegseth briefly stopped in Colombia, and met with Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora and Foreign Minister Omar Bulla.

The defense secretary expressed his support for the government’s plans to combat drug trafficking.

“You, sir, are never going to have a stronger partner than President Trump, Secretary Hegseth an the War Department,” Hegseth told Bula.

Both the US and the Colombian governments have assumed a militaristic approach to drug trafficking, contrary to their predecessors.

World.title: “Basic food stuffs exempt from sales tax:” De la Espriella on tax reform bill
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rolled back his government’s plan to impose sales tax on basic food stuffs in an attempt to seek approval for his tax reform in Congress.

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella said that “basic household goods will be exempt from VAT. I made that clear from the very beginning.”

Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo and Finance Minister Miguel Gomez last month announced the introduction of a 19% sales tax on basic food stuffs and the creation of a mechanism that would allow the poor to recover this money.

The radical proposal was necessary to prevent Colombia from defaulting on debt, said Gomez.

However, “after several analyses, they adjusted the proposal to protect the basic food basket, which required a greater effort on the part of the government,” the president said Sunday.

De la Espriella’s tax reform, which will have to pass before December 16, got stuck in Congress after the coalition Liberal Party said they wouldn’t support taxing the basic food basket.

Also the far-right Democratic Center party opposed the measure, which almost immediately triggered calls for a national strike.

The president suggested that he would cut expenses he blamed on the leftist “criminal organizations” that won the 2022 elections with former President Gustavo Petro.

My true tax reform is the fight against corruption, against the criminal organizations that squandered the state’s resources for so many years. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“There is still a lot to do, but you can’t fix that disaster in three months,” said De la Espriella.

Contrary to campaign promises to reduce the State apparatus, De la Espriella proposed a 2027 budget that increased state spending.

On top of that, the government has been talking to the International Monetary Fund about a credit line that would support his increased spending.

World.title: An Excursion 30 Years in the Making
World.content:
Photo Feature by Fabiana del Valle

HAVANA TIMES – In the late 1990s, my school organized trips to the Jardín de Aspiro campground. These outings were supervised by teachers and a few parents who joined in the adventure. However, my mother wouldn’t let me go. For her, anything beyond familiar boundaries entailed a lurking danger.

It’s true that on one occasion, after much begging and pleading, she gave me permission. But since bad luck has followed me since childhood, the bus that was supposed to pick us up broke down along the way, and the trip was postponed until the following weekend. My mother saw this as a divine sign or some kind of omen and withdrew her permission.

I remember the innocent envy I felt toward my best friends, who never missed a single excursion. Every Monday, the classroom was filled with stories of swimming in the river and nights under the stars. My teenage imagination placed that spot on a par with London, a city I dreamed of visiting someday.

That little corner in the foothills of the Sierra del Rosario, in the municipality of San Cristobal, retained for me the allure of the forbidden and the unattainable. But I grew up and never had another opportunity to go, nor did I seek one. My life changed, and adulthood took me toward other horizons.

Still, that unfulfilled longing remained buried deep inside me, and my husband, knowing my story, was determined to make the trip happen. He made some inquiries, and a friend told him we could get there on our electric motorcycle without any problems. Although the campground remains closed to the public, we could go to the river or enjoy the natural pool.

The idea of fulfilling a wish nearly three decades in the making excited me. Since walking the damp streets of London remains a dream with no foreseeable prospect of coming true, at least I could immerse myself for a few hours in the natural surroundings Aspiro promised. We prepared some sandwiches, a bottle of soda, and some water to quench our thirst, and set off early that morning. What we hadn’t anticipated was the condition of the route. The steep hills and the road, deteriorated from a lack of maintenance, proved quite a challenge for our motorcycle.

Since the heat is less intense at this time of year, we hoped to find some privacy. But Cubans aren’t afraid of the cold, and as the morning wore on, other people began arriving at the pool, seeking to wash away their everyday troubles in the refreshing water.

We had been looking for some privacy in a place where we could breathe fresh air and disconnect for a while. Our dream refuge ended up crowded with people, their speakers blasting reparto music through the vegetation, disrupting the natural harmony and the haven of peace we had both envisioned for our getaway.

Despite everything, it was worth immersing ourselves in those crystal-clear, cold waters, so cold that our skin felt as though it were burning the moment we touched the water. Those natural surroundings brought us a revitalizing sense of relief. And we were only there for a few hours!

Before returning home, we stopped at the entrance to the Jardín de Aspiro campground, and I asked the guards for permission to take some pictures. I couldn’t leave without seeing the inside of the place I had so longed to visit as a teenager.

I did a little research and discovered that the campground opened in 1982. The site was chosen to take advantage of the river, the natural pool, its proximity to the waterfall, and the mountain trails with their numerous caves.

The name Aspiro is associated with the Spanish merchant Don Jose de Aspiro, who was one of the owners of those lands. The grounds of this enclave once formed part of several estates where agricultural activities were combined with botanical experimentation. I have read that in the early 19th century, a garden featuring exotic species and a wide variety of flora was established there, where the naturalist and botanist Jose Blaín Cervantes conducted his studies.

The facility was repaired and refurbished last year so that it could be operational this summer. But on this island, after 1959, objectivity was lost. A video room, a restaurant, a game room, and remodeled cabins with air conditioning, kitchens, and bathrooms.

All of this without water, since the blackouts prevent water from being pumped to the facility. The services the center was supposed to offer have been reduced to zero, and there is no hope of recovering the investment. The place possesses an undeniable beauty, and it is a shame that it cannot be enjoyed.

Although we returned home satisfied — once again managing to escape the suffocating reality we live in with very few resources — I cannot shake the sad conviction that there is no future for an island that sinks deeper into misery, neglect, and darkness with each passing day.

See more photo features here on Havana Times.

World.title: A Week of “Normality” Ended
World.content:
By Veronica Vega

HAVANA TIMES – Since everything that begins must come to an end, this morning the spell was broken and Cinderella’s carriage turned back into a pumpkin.

What I mean is that the seven days of DAF (Automatic Frequency Tripping) on the circuit to which our building was assigned have come to an end.

These circuits ration access to electricity in this new, nameless phase we are living through in Cuba. (There is an urgent need to give it a name to make historians’ work easier.)

I have no idea what DAF actually means, but in practice, it entails a week of uninterrupted electricity and a return to our lost normality.

A functioning refrigerator, food that you are not forced to pack into small containers crammed into the freezer among jars of ice. Because you have to make as much ice as possible to withstand the long hours of blackouts, maintaining a temperature that allows you to preserve your food.

That food, with its heart-stopping prices, robs you of your peace of mind three times: when you buy it, when you cook it — if you have no gas available and depend on an electric burner and whatever brief spell of electricity you get — and finally, when you rack your brain trying to fit whatever is left for the next day into a freezer that is no longer running.

That blessed week also means cooking in the electric cooker without fear that the process will be interrupted and the beans will remain hard. Or the rice half-cooked.

Feeling a strange peace that gradually begins to rock you like the waves, transporting you back to almost idyllic times, when the word “crisis” was still the subject of jokes rather than this constant tightness in your stomach, this bitter feeling of stagnation and of having lost your way.

Night falls, and the lights around you reassure you that there is life outside: televisions switched on, fans and air conditioners providing that minimum level of comfort and restoring the home to its status as a sacred refuge.

Some people play dance music, and the lights of small private businesses twinkle like costly harbors of hope, of other people’s prosperity.

When I go out to walk my dogs, I sense a kind of tranquility in the air, a feeling of shared goodwill throughout the area where DAF reigns, or a sense of relief that rekindles the memory of what a country can be, even amid shortages, if at least a basic level of functionality prevails.

But the full bliss of DAF is only achieved if you are lucky enough for that week to coincide with water flowing into the communal cistern.

Then there is no need to rush to fill tanks, buckets, and all kinds of containers in an agonizing race against the ever-uncertain hours of electricity.

You can do everything at the pace of nature, at the pace of life. Relax. Remember a way of living in which everyone can enjoy a glass of cold water, a hot meal, and a warm bath, even if they don’t have a solar panel, EcoFlow power stations, or gas paid for by a relative abroad.

You can feel that your time belongs to you again, face life’s other minor setbacks without experiencing them as anonymous and unexpected assaults.

“We used to live like this…” you tell yourself and immediately wonder how long ago that was and what we did (or failed to do) to lose the little we had.

Who marked us on the map of the world with an ominous sign? And why? After surviving the promises, the lies, and the disintegration of a fledgling society that never became prosperous, just, or equitable.

A disintegration all the more terrible because it is so inconspicuous. There are no bombs or explosions. No wounded people shedding that blood which assaults the eyes and which Facebook mercifully covers up as soon as it detects it, to protect its users’ visual sensibilities.

No, nobody sees us. Nobody hears us. The entire island could disappear, just as even the sharpest outlines are swallowed up by darkness.

As though we were being engulfed by the waters that separate us from the most powerful country in the world.

If an unspoken joy awakens with the arrival of DAF, a heavy sadness settles over everything when the day comes when the blessing shifts to another circuit that you will see glowing at night, while we return to the darkness and the wretched feeling of abandonment.

Then you console yourself by counting the weeks it takes for DAF to rotate through each of the circuits, like the hands of a clock, like the rotation of the Earth, until it is our turn once again to experience that fleeting season of normality.

Read more from the diary of Veronica Vega here on Havana Times.

World.title: AI Data Centers: Local Damage, World Threat
World.content:
Demonstrators protest against a planned data center in Decatur, Georgia. ‘Concerns over AI, rising energy costs and the environment are intermeshing.’ Photo: Erik S Lesser/EPA

By Jomo Kwame Sundaram and Rachel Gong (IPS)

HAVANA TIMES – Mass local opposition to AI data centers influenced the US mid-term elections. Perverse incentives have driven speculative investments to build more despite poor returns so far. Worse, financing investments using loans risks causing a major financial crisis.



The massive computing demands of AI (artificial intelligence) requiring hyperscale data centers have grown rapidly over the last decade, greatly exceeding traditional storage cloud providers for general web hosting or standard information technology.



The number of such data centers worldwide has nearly tripled, with most in the US, but local opposition has slowed plans to build more. It is unclear how many data centers are being built, as details are often withheld, even from governments.



AI data centers in the US have been very unpopular with local communities. They are noisy and ugly, draining energy and water resources, with most profits going to the mainly US companies building them.



They use much electricity, straining electricity grids and driving up electricity prices. Data centers largely run on fossil fuels, exacerbating greenhouse gas emissions and planetary heating.



Data centers need a huge amount of freshwater to prevent overheating. Yet, more are being built despite spreading droughts and water stress.



There are also other significant health and environmental concerns that promoters hide, claiming modern data centers use ‘closed-loop systems’ reducing their adverse impacts.

Rachel Gong

Governments claim they create employment, although only a small fraction of promised jobs have materialised. Unsurprisingly, there is growing local opposition to AI data centers worldwide.



After meeting with China’s leader Xi Jinping following the midterms, Trump threatened tough measures against building data centers abroad, deeming their US presence necessary to maintain US dominance.



AI expects AI bubble to collapse



Dean Baker asked various AI chatbots whether pension and hedge fund investment managers face perverse incentives when investing in AI-related companies.



If they did not invest in companies which have far outperformed others in recent times, their performance would fall behind their peers, costing them bonuses and even their jobs.



And if all AI stocks fell, they would not be penalised as other fund managers had done likewise. AI agreed that asset managers would keep investing in AI even though their market performance did not make sense.



They would continue such investments as keeping their jobs required following the herd and ‘riding the wave’.



Such perverse incentives may also induce similar behavior among top executives at Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle.



All of them have “committed hundreds of billions of their companies’ capital to building data centres to support the AI producers, primarily OpenAI and Anthropic”.



And what if AI companies have ‘over-invested’ trillions in data centers with limited prospects of profitability? If this view of AI’s future is widely shared, it would make sense to stop building and cut losses.



But what if AI top executives still believe it is better to continue investing? Perhaps AI will eventually pay off. And if they stopped investing to cut their losses, they could also lose trillions, probably ending their careers.



Hence, they keep building data centers even if they suspect they are pouring in good money after bad. AI generally agrees that top executives are likely to continue investing.

Jomo Kwame Sundaram

After the AI bubble bursts, it is likely there will be some obligatory investigations into how and why the AI boom became a dangerously unsustainable bubble until ‘business as usual’ resumes.



When the bubble bursts



William H. Janeway notes the notion of an ‘AI speculative investment bubble’ has recently been widely accepted. Since bubbles inevitably burst, fears are now rising that time is running out.



Janeway warns that the AI industry’s heavy and still growing reliance on borrowed money risks triggering a major financial crisis. AI hyperscalers have to keep increasing profits to justify the still rising investments and borrowings.



If generative AI delivers productivity gains across a wide range of applications, the current frenzy may be remembered as a productive bubble.



But it is unlikely these gains will be large and soon enough to justify the huge investments in AI infrastructure to date.



Growing reliance on private credit to fund current data center building, with lenders themselves borrowing from banks, implies the AI bubble is enmeshed with the financial system.



The AI bubble can still deflate gradually rather than burst abruptly. Hence, slowing AI growth and data center construction delays may actually be better for the economy.



However, the risk of sudden collapse remains. The second Trump administration’s record so far generates broader concerns about how it is likely to handle an AI bust.



Thankfully, however, history reminds us that speculative bubbles may leave behind some valuable infrastructure in their wake despite bankrupting those financing them.



Rachel Gong is Associate Director of Research at the Khazanah Research Institute studying the intersections of digital technologies, society and policy.
