Vale's New York shares fell 4.39% to US$9.37, the lowest close in 12 months, on 24 November 2026 as weak Chinese steel demand weighed on iron ore.

Iron Ore — the daily wrap.

Key Facts Vale’s New York shares fell 4.39% to US$9.37, the lowest close in 12 months.

the lowest close in 12 months. China’s October steel output fell 1.6% to 70.83 million tons.

to 70.83 million tons. Vale is down 10.08% in five sessions and 20.86% in 20 sessions.

and 20.86% in 20 sessions. Rio Tinto, the mining group, fell 2.56% to US$73.19; CSN Mineração slipped 1.59%.

CSN Mineração slipped 1.59%. The dollar index eased 0.45%, yet miners still fell.

Today’s Focus Vale, the Brazilian miner that ranks among the world’s two biggest iron ore exporters, closed Tuesday, November 24, 2026 at its lowest in at least a year. Its New York shares have lost 37.9% in 60 sessions, a fall that tracks the price of iron ore, the red rock that is melted into steel. The reason is China, which makes more than half the world’s steel. Mills there are cutting output, earning thin profits and buying less ore, just as new supply from Guinea’s Simandou mine arrives. Falling bond yields and a softer dollar normally help miners. This time they did not, which tells you the problem is the ore market itself, not the wider financial mood. 03 Why it moved

First and heaviest: Chinese steel is shrinking. October output fell 1.6% to 70.83 million tons, according to China’s statistics bureau. Mills earn thin margins, so they will not stock up on ore.

Second: supply keeps arriving. Guinea’s Simandou mine is adding tons to the market.

Third, Vale’s own news. Its third-quarter core profit (EBITDA, earnings before interest, tax and depreciation) fell 20%, it said output would land at the low end of its 335 to 345 million ton guidance.

The usual helpers disagreed with the move. The dollar index eased 0.45% to 103.85 and the 10-year Treasury yield slipped to 4.93%, which normally supports commodities, while the S&P 500 lost 0.50% and the VIX fear gauge sits at 26.36. Gold’s fund fell 2.27%, which suggests investors were selling metals broadly. We rate the China-demand explanation as medium confidence.

04 The trend behind it

This is a continuation, not a fresh shock. Vale is down 20.86% in 20 sessions and 10.08% in five, and Tuesday’s close set the low of the past 12 months.

Rio Tinto is 14.64% lower over 20 sessions but still 3.9% above its November 2025 low of 70.47, so it has not yet broken that floor.

In our own price history since 2007, Vale’s shares fell 20.9% in 20 sessions in 23 earlier independent cases. They were higher 20 sessions later in 12 of those, or 52%, with a median change of +0.4% and a worst case of -43.4%. History is not a forecast, but it says a steep fall alone does not guarantee a rebound.

05 What it means for Latin America

Brazil feels this most. Iron ore is among its largest exports, and Vale pays taxes, royalties and dividends that reach pension funds and the federal budget. The real is also exposed, because lower ore revenue means fewer dollars flowing into the country.

Local investors in Sao Paulo hold Vale and CSN Mineração, both pressured. Peru and Chile, which mine copper rather than iron, are less directly hit, though broad metals selling drags their miners too.

06 The names to watch

Vale is the main proxy. Its production guidance and dividend policy are the company-specific swing factors.

CSN Mineração has a 12-month low of 4.08 from 19 May and Rio Tinto has 70.47 as support. Their trading near those marks will show whether the selling is broadening.

07 What would end it

Vale’s close is its own 12-month low, so the chart offers no floor beyond the round US$9 mark. The first sign of a turn would be a rise in Chinese steel output.

The next dated catalyst is China’s November steel output report in December. A stimulus push for property or infrastructure would also help. Without it, the slide can continue, and the honest answer is that it stops only when Chinese mills start buying again.

08 What to watch

China steel output: Monthly readings from China’s statistics bureau show whether mills are buying more ore.

Monthly readings from China’s statistics bureau show whether mills are buying more ore. Vale guidance: Output at the low end of 335 to 345 million tons and any dividend change drive the shares.

Output at the low end of 335 to 345 million tons and any dividend change drive the shares. Rio Tinto at 70.47: A close below its November 2025 low would signal broader miner stress.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Vale shares fall on Tuesday, November 24, 2026?

Weak Chinese steel demand pushed iron ore lower, and Vale’s New York shares fell 4.39%.

Is Vale’s share price the iron ore price?

No. It is a proxy, since Vale earns most of its money from iron ore, but its shares also reflect costs, output and dividends.

How does this affect Brazil?

Iron ore is a major export, so lower prices reduce Vale’s taxes and dividends and the dollars entering Brazil.

Will iron ore rebound?

Our history shows 12 of 23 similar falls were followed by gains 20 sessions later, so it is close to a coin toss, and China’s steel output is the deciding factor.

World.title: US Oil Fund Gains 1.55% as Oil Stocks Sink | Oil Wrap, Nov 24

The USO oil fund gained 1.55% on 24 November 2026, yet YPF fell 4.43%, Ecopetrol 3.15% and Petrobras 0.89% as investors priced in a supply surplus.

Oil went up while the shares of oil companies went down, which is unusual and revealing. It tells us investors are looking past the day’s price to the months ahead.

Crude at the moment is being driven by supply returning, not by demand falling.

Key Facts Brazil’s Petrobras and Colombia’s Ecopetrol posted six-month closing lows on Tuesday, 24 November 2026.

on Tuesday, 24 November 2026. The USO oil fund rose 1.55% to US$135.43, yet sits 20.1% below its 23 October high.

Oil — the daily wrap.

Today’s Focus Oil rose on Tuesday, but the companies that pump it in Latin America kept sinking. The fund that tracks American crude, USO, gained +1.55% to US$135.43, a pause after a punishing month. Petrobras, Brazil’s state-controlled giant, closed at US$15.67, its lowest in at least six months and 40.1% below its 23 October high of 26.16. Ecopetrol, Colombia’s state oil company, closed at US$12.93, also a six-month low, while Argentina’s YPF ended at US$31.71. The reason is a feared glut. Gulf exports are returning, and forecasters now expect more oil than the world can burn. 01 The session in one read

02 The board

Across the board, only the oil fund rose. Petrobras slipped -0.89%, Ecopetrol lost -3.15% and YPF fell -4.43%.

YPF’s drop was the sharpest, which fits a company whose growth story rests on expensive shale drilling that needs firm prices.

03 Why it moved

First and heaviest: the surplus. The International Energy Agency (IEA), the rich countries’ energy watchdog, expects a supply surplus to return in the fourth quarter, with a larger build in 2027, as Gulf exports recover.

Second, US stocks rose. The US Energy Information Administration (EIA), the government’s energy statistics agency, reported commercial crude stocks of 417.8 million barrels in the week to 13 November, up 3.4 million.

Third, the usual drivers did not explain much. The dollar index eased 0.45% to 103.85 and the 10-year Treasury yield slipped to 4.93%, which normally helps oil, while the S&P 500 lost 0.50% and the VIX fear gauge stood at 26.36.

Our best reading, with medium confidence, is that crude bounced on technical buying after its slide while equity investors sold producers on the surplus outlook. Reporting on the individual stock moves is thin, so treat the explanation for YPF’s size of fall as low confidence.

04 The trend behind it

This is a continuation, not a new phase. The oil fund is 20.1% below its 23 October high and has fallen 3.43% in five sessions, though it remains 104.7% above its 12-month low of 66.17 from 16 December 2025.

Petrobras tells the harsher story: five straight down sessions and 29.73% lost in 20 sessions. Ecopetrol is 29.2% below its 15 September high of 18.26.

RT’s own history since 2007 adds perspective. The oil fund fell 17.4% in 20 sessions; in the 29 earlier cases of a move that large, it was higher 20 sessions later in 15, or 52%, with a median of +0.1% and a worst case of -32.4%. For Petrobras, only 5 of 12 earlier cases (42%) were higher, and for Ecopetrol just 1 of 6. History is not a forecast.

05 What it means for Latin America

Brazil and Colombia feel it most in their state-linked companies, whose dividends help fund government budgets. Petrobras and Ecopetrol, both partly state-owned, have lost value that matters to pension funds and public finances.

Argentina’s bet is Vaca Muerta, the giant shale formation YPF is developing; lower crude makes each new well harder to justify. Guyana, Mexico’s Pemex and Venezuela all depend on oil revenue as well, though we have no fresh figures for them this week.

For consumers in importing countries, cheaper crude is a welcome relief at the pump.

06 The names to watch

Petrobras is the bellwether: a close below its 12-month low of 11.54 from 7 January would signal deep distress, though it is still 35.8% above that level. Ecopetrol, 40.4% above its 9.21 low from 19 December 2025, has the longest losing streak.

07 What would end it

The next dated event is the OPEC+ meeting on Sunday 29 November, where Iraq is seeking a higher production quota. A deal that curbs output would help prices; a quarrel would add to the surplus fear.

On the chart, resistance for the oil fund sits at the 169.53 October high and support at the 12-month low of 66.17. Watch weekly US stock data too: sustained builds would extend the slide, while drawdowns would signal that the glut is not arriving.

08 What to watch

OPEC+ meeting: Sunday 29 November: 2027 production targets and Iraq’s capacity dispute.

Sunday 29 November: 2027 production targets and Iraq’s capacity dispute. US crude stocks: Weekly inventory reports after Thanksgiving; builds feed the surplus story.

Weekly inventory reports after Thanksgiving; builds feed the surplus story. Middle East exports: Further recovery would deepen the supply glut that the IEA projects.

Further recovery would deepen the supply glut that the IEA projects. Petrobras and Ecopetrol: Whether they hold above their 12-month lows after six-month-low closes.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did oil stocks fall when oil rose?

Investors price the future, and they expect a surplus of oil. Tuesday’s gain looked like a bounce after a steep decline.

Is the oil fund the oil price?

No. USO is a fund that tracks US crude, so its level differs from the price of a barrel.

What happened after similar falls before?

In RT’s history, the oil fund was higher 20 sessions later in 15 of 29 cases. That is not a forecast.

What is the key date?

The OPEC+ meeting on Sunday 29 November, which sets production targets for 2027.

World.title: Lithium Fund Falls 1.85% as SQM Drops 3.78% | Lithium Wrap, Nov 24
World.content:
Lithium miners fell on 24 November 2026: the LIT fund lost 1.85% to US$53.69 and Chile's SQM dropped 3.78% to US$46.88, its lowest close in six months.

Lithium brine evaporation ponds at the Salar de Atacama, seen from the International Space Station, March 2016 (Photo: NASA, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

Think of lithium miners as farmers whose crop price has just been cut. On Tuesday, 24 November 2026, the lithium fund LIT fell -1.85%, Albemarle -2.36% and SQM -3.78%.

SQM’s drop was the sharpest, and it matters most because it closed at the lowest level in at least six months. The fund fell for a second reason too: investors are reducing risk across metals, not only lithium.

Key Facts SQM, Chile’s lithium producer, closed at US$46.88 (-3.78%), its lowest close in six months.

its lowest close in six months. The LIT fund, which holds lithium miners, fell 1.85% to US$53.69.

fell 1.85% to US$53.69. Albemarle, the US lithium producer, fell 2.36% to US$80.63, near its 12-month low.

near its 12-month low. The dollar index eased 0.45% and the 10-year yield fell, yet miners still fell.

yet miners still fell. After earlier falls this large, LIT was higher 20 sessions later in 14 of 19 cases.

The LatAm Brief One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life. Yesterday’s subject line: “Petrobras plans US$122 billion of investment” Get the brief

Today’s Focus Lithium shares fell again on Tuesday, 24 November 2026, and Chile’s SQM, one of the world’s largest producers, closed at its lowest level in at least six months. Over 60 sessions (trading days) its shares have lost 40.7%, and Albemarle’s have lost 40.3%. The trigger is price, not demand. On 17 November SQM told investors that what it earns per tonne of lithium in the fourth quarter could be substantially lower than in the third, and the market has been repricing every miner since. The fall also arrived on a day when metals as a group were sold: a gold-tracking fund lost 2.27% and the S&P 500 slipped 0.50%. Lithium miners are caught in two squeezes at once, a weak product price and a nervous market. Lithium is the key ingredient in electric-car batteries, and the companies that dig it up are being valued as if the boom of early 2026 is over. What matters today. SQM’s price warning, not a lack of electric-car demand, is dragging the whole lithium sector to fresh lows.

01 The session in one read

Assessment — A price slump, not a demand collapse MEDIUM The best-supported reading is that lithium is going through a painful price reset after a surge, and the shares are discounting further falls in what producers can charge. SQM’s own warning is the strongest evidence, and the 20-session losses of 22.26% for SQM and 18.52% for Albemarle show how fast the repricing has been. The variable to watch is whether the next price signals from producers show the fourth-quarter drop is a one-off or the start of a longer slide.

Lithium — the daily wrap.

02 The board

The price board shows the whole sector in red, with SQM weakest. Remember that the LIT fund is a basket of mining company shares, not the price of lithium itself, so it can move more sharply than the metal.

Albemarle, at US$80.63, is hovering just above its 12-month low of 79.70 from 20 November. SQM has already broken through to a new low, which leaves no recent price to act as a floor.

03 Why it moved

First and heaviest is the producers’ own warning. On 17 November SQM said fourth-quarter lithium prices could be substantially lower than in the third quarter. Its New York shares fell sharply the next day and Chile’s main stock index, the IPSA, dropped with them. Confidence: high.

Second is a risk-off day for metals. Gold-tracking fund GLD fell 2.27% on the session and 7.67% over five sessions, while the VIX fear gauge, which measures expected stock-market swings, rose 3.53% over five sessions. Lithium miners were sold alongside everything cyclical. Confidence: medium.

The conflicting signals are real. A softer dollar and a lower 10-year yield usually help commodity shares, yet they did not here. The best explanation is that company-specific news about prices outweighed the macro relief, and I could find no fresh figures on electric-car battery demand to say otherwise. Overall confidence: medium.

04 The trend behind it

This is a continuation, not a new phase. The LIT fund has fallen 4.84% over five sessions and 29.7% over 60, and it is 3.3% above its 12-month low of 51.98 set on 20 November.

Albemarle is 62.6% below its 12-month high of 215.62 on 16 April, and SQM is 50.8% below its 95.31 peak the same day. A boom that lifted both shares to those peaks has now been unwinding for more than seven months.

Our own price history since 2010 offers a calming but limited fact. After 19 earlier falls as large as the fund’s 14.27% drop in 20 sessions, it was higher 20 sessions later in 14 cases, a median gain of 4.3% and a worst result of a further 14.9% loss. For SQM, after 20 earlier falls this deep, it was higher in 15, with a median gain of 10.9% and a worst case of a 34.2% loss; for Albemarle it was higher in only 17 of 32. History is not a forecast.

05 What it means for Latin America

Chile feels it first. SQM is the country’s flagship lithium company, and its fall dragged the IPSA index lower after the 17 November warning, which touches pension funds that hold Chilean shares as well as the state’s royalty income from the Atacama salt flat.

Argentina and Bolivia sit in the same Lithium Triangle, the salt-flat region where most of the region’s lithium lies. I found no fresh news from either country this week, but lower prices make new Argentine projects harder to finance and give Bolivia, which has struggled to develop its reserves, even less urgency from foreign investors.

For travellers and savers outside the region, the effect is indirect: a weaker mining sector tends to soften Chile’s peso, which can make Chilean trips cheaper but hurts local mining-town budgets.

06 The names to watch

SQM is the barometer. It is the shares that closed at a 12-month low, and the company’s own price warning is the main pressure.

Albemarle, the US rival, sits only 1.2% above its recent low. A close below 79.70 would put it in uncharted ground for the year.

07 What would end it

The nearest floors are the LIT fund’s low of 51.98 from 20 November and Albemarle’s 79.70 low the same day; SQM has no floor to point to because it is at its low now. The ceilings are far away: 91.62 for the fund, 215.62 for Albemarle and 95.31 for SQM.

The thing that would change the picture is evidence that lithium prices have stopped falling, whether in producers’ next price update, SQM’s fourth-quarter results or the Federal Reserve’s next policy meeting, which will shape risk appetite. Until then, the honest answer to whether this stops is: not yet, but the bounce odds from history are better than the mood suggests.

08 What to watch

SQM price disclosures: Any figure for fourth-quarter lithium prices will show how deep the cut really is.

Any figure for fourth-quarter lithium prices will show how deep the cut really is. Albemarle’s 79.70 low: A close below it would confirm the slide is still running.

A close below it would confirm the slide is still running. Metals risk appetite: Gold and copper selling has spilled into lithium; a calmer market would help.

Gold and copper selling has spilled into lithium; a calmer market would help. Chile’s IPSA index: SQM’s weight in the index makes it a gauge of Chilean market stress.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are lithium shares falling?

SQM said on 17 November that its fourth-quarter lithium prices could be substantially lower than in the third quarter. That hit the whole sector, as lower prices mean lower profits.

Is the LIT fund the price of lithium?

No. LIT holds shares in lithium mining companies, so it reflects investor mood and company earnings as well as the metal’s price.

Is this a good time to buy lithium shares?

Our history shows the LIT fund was higher 20 sessions later in 14 of 19 earlier cases like this, but the worst case was a further 14.9% loss. That is not a forecast and not advice.

How does this affect Chile?

SQM is a leading Chilean company and a major lithium producer, so its fall weighs on the IPSA stock index and on mining royalties.

Copper — the daily wrap.

Key Facts The copper fund CPER fell 3.87% to US$32.50, a six-month closing low.

The cause is a double blow. Investors doubt that the AI data-centre boom will keep demanding vast amounts of copper wire, and they expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates in December and January. For Chile and Peru, which supply a large share of the world’s copper, the slide matters to budgets, currencies and mining shares. 03 Why it moved

First and heaviest was the AI trade. Investors had bought copper as a way to bet on data centres, and a short-lived rally in AI shares faded on Tuesday, taking copper with it. Our confidence in this cause is medium to high.

Second came the Federal Reserve. Markets now expect rate rises in December and January, and higher rates make it costlier to hold commodities that pay no income. Confidence here is medium.

The usual signals did not fully agree. The dollar index eased 0.45% to 103.85 and the US 10-year yield slipped 3 basis points to 4.92%, which normally helps metals, yet copper still fell. The S&P 500 lost 0.50% and the gold fund fell 2.27%, which suggests investors were selling whatever they could, not choosing carefully.

04 The trend behind it

This is a continuation, not a fresh shock. The copper fund is down 9.70% over five sessions and 21.6% below its 12-month high of 41.43, reached on 22 September 2026.

Southern Copper is 37.1% below its 25 August peak of 217.40, and Freeport-McMoRan is 40.3% below its own high of 79.91 set that day. The miners peaked weeks before the metal, a classic warning that investors were already leaving.

One cushion remains. The copper fund is still 4.5% above its 12-month low of 31.11, set a year to the day earlier on 24 November 2025.

05 What it means for Latin America

Chile is the world’s largest copper producer and Peru the second, so both feel this directly. Lower prices cut export earnings and tax receipts, and they tend to weigh on the Chilean peso and the Peruvian sol, which lean on mining dollars.

For Mexico, Southern Copper’s New York shares show the pain, at 33.8% lower over 60 sessions. For a traveller or importer in these countries, a softer local currency makes imports and foreign trips dearer.

The picture is not all bad. Brazil, Colombia and Argentina sell little copper, and cheaper metal reduces costs for manufacturers who import it.

06 The names to watch

Southern Copper is the cleanest Latin American proxy, since its mines sit in Peru and Mexico. It is down 28.87% over 20 sessions yet still 12.4% above its 12-month low of 121.72.

Freeport-McMoRan has fallen 27.63% in 20 sessions. Our own price history since 2007 holds 14 earlier cases of a fall this large, and it was higher 20 sessions later in 7 of them, or 50%, with a median move of minus 2.1% and a worst case of minus 61.0%. History is not a forecast, but it says a deep fall does not guarantee a rebound.

07 What would end it

The nearest floor is 31.11, the 12-month low of the copper fund, just 4.5% below Tuesday’s close. A break under it would open a new phase of selling, while a recovery toward the 41.43 September high looks distant.

The decisive events are the Federal Reserve’s December meeting and the January meeting, plus any new Chinese industrial data. A signal that the Fed will hold off, or a firm Chinese factory number, would likely stop the slide.

Does it stop? Not on its own: the AI doubt and the rate fear both need to ease first. Until then, rallies are likely to be short.

08 What to watch

Federal Reserve: The December and January meetings decide whether rate-rise bets are confirmed, which is the main pressure on metals now.

The December and January meetings decide whether rate-rise bets are confirmed, which is the main pressure on metals now. AI spending: Any new data-centre investment news will move copper, because investors treat it as an AI proxy.

Any new data-centre investment news will move copper, because investors treat it as an AI proxy. The 31.11 floor: The copper fund’s 12-month low is only 4.5% below the close, so a break would signal fresh selling.

The copper fund’s 12-month low is only 4.5% below the close, so a break would signal fresh selling. China: Chinese factory data show whether demand supports the metal.

World.title: Gold Funds Fall 2.27% as Silver Slides 5.32% | Gold & Silver, Nov 24
World.content:
Gold and silver funds fell sharply in New York on 24 November 2026, with GLD down 2.27% and SLV down 5.32%, while spot gold held near US$3,636 an ounce.

One-ounce silver bullion bars. Photo: Gage Skidmore / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

Spot gold edged up 0.13% on Tuesday, 24 November 2026, while spot silver dropped 1.03%. In New York the gold fund GLD fell 2.27% and the silver fund SLV 5.32%, so the calm in spot gold hid a hard US session.

Gold bounced from its 12-month low of 3,533, struck on 20 November, and now sits 2.9% above it. Silver sits 3.9% above its own low, so neither has escaped the danger zone.

Key Facts The GLD gold fund fell 2.27% to US$325.45 in New York on Tuesday, 24 November 2026.

on Tuesday, 24 November 2026. The SLV silver fund fell 5.32% to US$36.84; spot silver ended 1.03% lower at US$42.73.

Today’s Focus Spot gold held near US$3,636 on Tuesday, 24 November 2026 (+0.13%), but New York trading was harsher: the GLD gold fund fell 2.27% and the SLV silver fund 5.32%. Spot silver fell 1.03%. Silver is the bigger story. It is 62.7% below its highest close of the past 12 months, 114.59 on 28 January, and 3.9% above its 12-month low of 41.13 from 20 November. The cause is a mix of a strong dollar and fears that the US Federal Reserve, the American central bank, may raise interest rates again. Higher rates make metals that pay no interest less attractive. That points to forced selling by funds as stock markets wobble. What matters today. Gold has stopped falling for now, but silver is still under pressure, and the Fed’s next move on interest rates decides whether the lows hold.

01 The session in one read

Assessment — A bruised bounce, not a recovery MEDIUM Spot gold has edged up for two sessions, yet the GLD fund fell 2.27% in New York and gold remains 10.48% lower over 20 sessions, so this looks like a pause inside a downtrend rather than a turn. Silver, down 1.03% on the day, has not even managed a pause. Our best-supported reading is that rate fears and fund selling drive both metals, with safe-haven buying too weak to offset them. The variable to watch is the 10-year US yield, now 4.92%: a sustained fall would let gold recover first.

Gold & Silver — the daily wrap.

02 The board

Gold’s two-session winning streak is modest next to its losses of 5.52% over five sessions and 10.48% over 20 sessions. Silver’s one-day slide extends a much steeper fall of 9.99% over five sessions.

Silver usually swings harder than gold, because its market is smaller and more tied to factories. That is why it has lost 33.4% over 60 sessions against gold’s 16.0%.

03 Why it moved

First and heaviest is the Federal Reserve. Specialist reports from mid-November said gold and silver fell on rising Treasury yields, a firm dollar and expectations of more US rate rises, after hot inflation data on 10 November.

Second is US data. The Conference Board’s consumer confidence index jumped to 103.3 in November against 92.5 expected and 91.9 before, while ADP Employment Change (weekly) showed 21,000 against 23,000 the week before (RT economic calendar). Strong confidence supports the case for higher US rates, which weighs on gold.

Third is forced selling. The S&P 500 fell 0.50% on Tuesday and is down 1.90% over five sessions, while the VIX fear gauge stands at 26.36. When funds lose money on shares, they often sell metals to raise cash, even in a nervous market where gold would normally attract buyers.

That explains the awkward fact that the dollar eased 0.45% and the 10-year yield fell 3 basis points, yet silver still dropped. Gold’s small gain shows some safe-haven buying, but not enough to lift silver.

Fourth is silver’s factory side. Oil rose 1.55% in the USO fund and investors have been steering clear of industrial metals, which hurts silver more than gold. We hold the Fed and forced-selling reading with medium confidence, and the factory link with low-to-medium.

04 The trend behind it

Gold is 32.7% below its highest close of the past 12 months, 5,400 on 28 January, and has lost 16.0% over 60 sessions. Silver has had the harder year, falling 62.7% from its own January high.

This looks like a continuation of a long downtrend rather than a new phase. The new element is speed, with silver down 21.56% in just 20 sessions.

Our price history since 2007 gives a rare guide. Gold has fallen as far as it did in 20 sessions on 8 earlier occasions, and 20 sessions later it was higher in 6 of them, or 75%, with a median gain of 5.0% and a worst case of a 7.5% loss.

Silver has had 9 comparable falls, and it was higher 20 sessions later in 7 of them, or 78%, with a median gain of 2.2%. The worst case was a 22.3% further loss, so history is a guide to odds and not a forecast.

05 What it means for Latin America

Mexico is the world’s biggest silver producer, with roughly a fifth of global output, according to the World Silver Survey, the annual report of the Silver Institute, an industry body. Its output fell 5% in 2025, the third annual decline in a row, so lower prices land on an industry already shrinking.

Peru is second and its output rose 7%, which means more ounces now sell at far lower prices. Mining taxes and royalties feed both governments’ budgets, and miners’ share prices follow the metal.

For savers in the region, gold priced in dollars is cheaper, but a weak local currency softens the fall. A strong dollar is the common thread, because it also pressures the Mexican peso and the Peruvian sol.

06 The names to watch

Watch the dollar index, now 103.85, because the metals have fallen as it has climbed. Watch the 10-year US Treasury yield at 4.92%, since a retreat there is the clearest relief for gold.

Watch the VIX at 26.36 and the S&P 500 at 7,201 too. If stock markets steady, fund selling of metals should ease.

07 What would end it

The nearest support is the 20 November low of 3,533 for gold and 41.13 for silver. A close below either would show that sellers are still in charge.

On the upside, gold needs to climb back toward the round figure of 3,700 before the damage of recent weeks looks repaired. The long-range ceilings remain the January highs of 5,400 and 114.59.

The next dated catalysts are the Fed’s December meeting and the next US inflation report. Softer inflation or a pause in rate-rise talk would end the slide, while another hot reading would extend it.

08 What to watch

US yields: The 10-year Treasury yield at 4.92% is the main brake on gold; a steady fall would help.

The 10-year Treasury yield at 4.92% is the main brake on gold; a steady fall would help. The dollar: The dollar index at 103.85 has driven metals lower; a reversal would lift both.

The dollar index at 103.85 has driven metals lower; a reversal would lift both. Support levels: The 20 November lows of 3,533 for gold and 41.13 for silver are the lines to defend.

The 20 November lows of 3,533 for gold and 41.13 for silver are the lines to defend. Mexico and Peru: Silver output and mining revenue in both countries track the metal’s slide.

Why did silver fall on Tuesday, 24 November 2026?

Silver fell 1.03% as fears of more US rate rises and fund selling outweighed a softer dollar.

Is gold in a downtrend?

Yes. Gold is 32.7% below its 28 January peak and down 16.0% over 60 sessions.

Which Latin American countries matter most for silver?

Mexico is the top producer and Peru is second, according to the World Silver Survey, the annual report of the Silver Institute, an industry body.

Does a big fall mean a rebound is coming?

Often, but not always. After earlier falls this large, gold was higher 20 sessions later in 6 of 8 cases, and history is not a forecast.

The S&P/BMV IPC, the benchmark index of the largest companies listed in Mexico City, rose 0.83% to 69,933, while the peso fell to 19.41 per US dollar — the weakest close in at least 12 months. A weaker peso is a bit like a sale on Mexican goods: companies that earn dollars and pay costs in pesos look better. That is why exporters and airports climbed even as the currency sagged. World.title: Guanacaste Now Builds More Large Homes Than San José
World.content:
Guanacaste registered 882 new homes of 200 square meters (2,150 square feet) or more in 2025, compared with 542 in San José, according to preliminary construction statistics from the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC). The Guanacaste homes carried a declared value of 102,000 million colones (about $229 million), against 61,100 million colones (about $137 million) for those in San José. Nationwide, 2,507 homes of that size were recorded, which places just over a third of them in Guanacaste.

San José still leads in the total value of residential construction, with 194,500 million colones (about $437 million) to Guanacaste’s 181,600 million (about $408 million). Two cantons account for most of the province’s figure. Santa Cruz registered 557 large homes worth about 62,300 million colones (about $140 million), more than the 542 recorded in San José. Carrillo registered 219, worth about 27,700 million colones (about $62 million). Together they represent roughly 88% of Guanacaste’s large homes.

Santa Cruz also ranked first in the declared value of residential building permits, at 99,774 million colones (about $224 million). In Carrillo, 73.7% of the 37,540 million colones in new-home permits went to houses of more than 200 square meters. Santa Cruz includes Tamarindo, Flamingo and Playa Grande. Carrillo includes Playas del Coco, Playa Hermosa and Ocotal.

The tourism observatory at the National University (OBTUR-UNA) attributes the growth to tourism, second homes and capital that arrived after the pandemic. It reported price increases of up to 400% for some coastal properties between 2020 and 2023. At the top of the market, three of the five most expensive properties listed in Costa Rica in June were on the Papagayo peninsula, the costliest of them at $30 million.

The INEC figures are preliminary, and a home of 200 square meters or more is not necessarily a luxury property. The construction is concentrated in a province where water supply is under strain. The national water utility, AyA, estimated this month that more than 306,000 people, most of them in Guanacaste, could be affected by shortages linked to El Niño.

World.content:
Hollywood actor and director Mel Gibson is in Costa Rica, immigration authorities confirmed today. The General Directorate of Migration and Immigration said Gibson entered the country on Sunday, November 22, and that as of Tuesday, November 24, there was no record of him leaving. Officials gave no details about the purpose of the trip, how long he plans to stay or where he is staying, and Gibson has made no public statement about the visit.

Gibson has owned a large private estate for nearly two decades at Playa Barrigona, a remote stretch of coast on the Nicoya Peninsula in Guanacaste. He came across the land in 2006 while scouting locations for Apocalypto, his film about the decline of the Maya civilization. The production was eventually shot in Veracruz, Mexico, but Gibson bought the property in 2007 for a reported $26 million (about 11.6 billion colones at the current exchange rate).

The estate covers some 162 hectares (400 acres) of jungle and includes three hilltop villas, a dining pavilion and more than 3.2 kilometers (two miles) of shoreline. The beach below, about half an hour north of Sámara, shows no visible development and is regularly described by travel writers as one of the most secluded on the Pacific coast.

Gibson has tried for years to sell and the property first went on the market in 2010 at $35 million (about 15.6 billion colones) and was later relisted more than once at $29.75 million (about 13.2 billion colones). No sale has been reported, and it has not been confirmed whether he still owns all of it or is staying there on this trip.

His relationship with the area has not always been smooth. In 2016 a national television report accused the estate’s administrators of blocking public access to the beach and of building in violation of the Maritime Terrestrial Zone Law, which guarantees public use of the first 50 meters (164 feet) inland from the high tide line. A representative for the property called the report inaccurate and sensationalist. At the time, Gibson had not visited the country in nearly a year.

His ties to Costa Rica run deeper than real estate. In 2007 he met with then President Óscar Arias at the president’s home in San José to discuss a donation to support the Indigenous communities and he has spent the New Year holiday and his birthday here on more than one occasion.

Speculation about a longer stay grew in January 2025, after Gibson lost his Malibu home in the wildfires that tore through Los Angeles. Asked on Joe Rogan’s podcast whether the disaster might drive him out of California, he said it might and pointed to Costa Rica. He said he has a place here that he loves, and that it sits away from the tourist crowds.

The current visit comes at a relatively quiet point in his schedule. Gibson has wrapped filming on The Resurrection of the Christ, his long awaited follow up to The Passion of the Christ, which Lionsgate will release in two parts. Part One is set for May 6, 2027, and Part Two for May 25, 2028, with Finnish actor Jaakko Ohtonen in the role of Jesus. Gibson also serves as one of President Donald Trump’s special ambassadors to Hollywood.

Born in Peekskill, New York, in 1956 and raised in Australia, Gibson rose to fame in the Mad Max and Lethal Weapon franchises. He directed and starred in Braveheart, which won five Academy Awards, two of them for Gibson as director and producer. His other directing credits include The Passion of the Christ and Hacksaw Ridge.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Critically Endangered Sawfish Is So Rare Even Scientists Struggle to Find It
World.content:
Costa Rica’s rivers and coastal waters are home to a fish that can grow to nearly 6.5 meters (21 feet), yet it is so elusive that some researchers have written entire theses on it without ever seeing one alive. The sawfish, recognizable by its long, flattened snout lined with teeth, is among the world’s most threatened marine animals.

Its populations have fallen by about 70% over the past six decades, according to Mario Espinoza, a biologist at the University of Costa Rica (UCR), and researchers are still working out where the remaining animals live and how to protect them. Sawfish are rays, closely related to sharks, Espinoza said. Five species exist worldwide and two have been recorded in Costa Rica, the largetooth sawfish (Pristis pristis) and the smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata).

Unlike most marine species, sawfish move between freshwater and saltwater. In Costa Rica, most reported sightings come from the San Juan River along the border with Nicaragua, with others from the Térraba-Sierpe National Wetland on the southern Pacific coast. Finding one is another matter. Espinoza has studied the species for about a decade, and for much of that time his team has relied less on direct observation than on local fishermen and riverside communities. Through interviews, the researchers reconstructed past sightings and identified the areas where sawfish were most likely to survive.

Those accounts pointed the team to the Térraba-Sierpe wetlands and the San Juan River system, including waters connected to Barra del Colorado on the northern Caribbean coast. The researchers also turned to environmental DNA, or eDNA, a technique that detects the genetic traces animals leave behind in water. By sampling sites where residents reported sightings, the team could look for sawfish without having to catch or see one.

The method worked. In 2019 and 2020, the team detected sawfish DNA at several sites, mainly in rivers of the northern zone and the northern Caribbean, and the findings were published in 2025 in the journal Endangered Species Research. In 2022, UCR researchers also caught and released a largetooth sawfish near the San Juan River.

All five sawfish species are classified as critically endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Red List. One of the greatest threats comes from the very feature that makes them so distinctive. The saw-shaped snout tangles easily in nets and other fishing gear. Espinoza said many fishermen do not know how to release the animals safely, so accidental captures often end in death.

In northern Costa Rica, spearfishing for tarpon poses another risk. Some fishermen have killed sawfish by mistake after confusing their silhouette underwater with that of the fish they were hunting, according to Espinoza. Sawfish have been protected by law in Costa Rica since 2022, when a reform Espinoza worked on with legislators was signed. Before that, neither species had any legal protection in the country.

World.title: Ten Years After Hurricane Otto, Remembering the Storm That Changed Costa Rica
World.content:
On November 24, 2016, Costa Rica lived through one of the most devastating natural disasters in its recent history. Hurricane Otto swept across the country’s northern region, claiming 10 lives, forcing thousands of residents from their homes and leaving entire communities struggling to recover.

A decade later, the tragedy remains a powerful reminder of Costa Rica’s vulnerability to extreme weather, and of the solidarity that emerged in the aftermath. For generations, Costa Rica’s geographical location had largely spared it from direct hurricane strikes. Storms passing to the north often brought indirect effects, but Otto shattered the perception that the country was protected. It became the first hurricane on record to cross Costa Rican territory.

Otto came ashore on the afternoon of November 24 in southern Nicaragua, just north of the border. The U.S. National Hurricane Center later concluded that it made landfall as a Category 3 hurricane with winds of about 185 kilometers per hour (115 mph), stronger than the Category 2 reported at the time.

From there its unusual track carried it southwest across northern Costa Rica and out to the Pacific through the Gulf of Papagayo late that night, bringing torrential rain, destructive winds and widespread flooding. In the hardest-hit areas, about 200 millimeters (7.9 inches) of rain fell in six hours, roughly what normally falls in an entire month, according to figures the government released at the time.

Upala, Bagaces and Bijagua were among the hardest-hit areas. Rivers overflowed, roads became impassable and landslides tore through communities on the slopes of the Miravalles Volcano. Six of the victims died in Upala and four in Bagaces, and three of the 10 were children. One of the most heartbreaking losses came near Guayabo de Bagaces, where four members of the same family were killed.

Official figures put the number of people directly affected at 10,831. About 1,600 homes were damaged or destroyed, 2,778 kilometers (1,726 miles) of roads were damaged, thousands of residents sought refuge in emergency shelters and numerous communities were cut off.

Yet amid the destruction, Costa Ricans showed extraordinary solidarity. Emergency responders, volunteers, community organizations and ordinary citizens mobilized to deliver food, clothing, shelter and essential supplies. Aircraft sent by Panama and the United States helped carry aid to communities isolated by the storm.

The recovery required extensive reconstruction, including repairs to homes, schools, roads, bridges and other essential infrastructure. Beyond the material losses, Otto pushed Costa Rica to rethink its emergency preparedness and the risks that come with extreme weather.

For the families who lost loved ones, the anniversary carries a meaning that goes far beyond statistics or reconstruction. November 24 remains a day to honor the victims, recognize the resilience of the affected communities and remember the nationwide solidarity that emerged during one of Costa Rica’s toughest moments.

World.title: Your Uber Ride in Costa Rica Could Cost Twice as Much Under a New Bill
World.content:
A ride-hailing trip that costs about 5,000 colones ($11.21) in Costa Rica today could cost 10,000 colones ($22.41) if a bill awaiting a vote in the Legislative Assembly becomes law in its current form, according to Uber. The company says the same bill would also end app pickups and drop-offs at Juan Santamaría International Airport, which it describes as the single busiest place for Uber requests in the country.

Laura Santillán, Uber’s general manager for Costa Rica, Panama and the Caribbean, presented the estimates at a press conference on Monday. She said the figures come from the company’s internal simulations of how the proposed rules would affect pricing and demand. They have not been independently verified.

The bill, titled the Law to Regulate Digital Transportation Platforms, is waiting in the queue for a first debate in the full Assembly. It would treat drivers as independent contractors and require them to register with the Costa Rican Social Security Fund (CCSS) and the Finance Ministry, carry civil liability and occupational risk insurance, complete training, present a clean criminal record and stay current on traffic fines.

Uber’s objections center on two pricing provisions. The first would have the Economy Ministry (MEIC) and the Public Works and Transport Ministry (MOPT) set a minimum profit per kilometer that drivers must earn before platform commissions, calculated from fuel, maintenance, average trip distance, insurance, social security contributions and driver earnings. The second would require the driver and passenger to agree on a price before each trip, and agree again if the route or destination changes.

Santillán said those rules together would double fares and cut demand for trips by up to 40 percent. She said the company also expects the new requirements to raise drivers’ operating costs by 10 to 20 percent. Uber said a minimum earnings floor could backfire on drivers, who would receive fewer requests and wait longer between trips.

The figures on drivers at risk differ in how they were reported. Uber said around 110,000 people have earned income through its app and similar platforms over the past 12 months, and that roughly 45,000 of them could lose earning opportunities if the bill passes unchanged. Uber also said more than two million people used its service in Costa Rica in the last year, and that about 1.6 million tourists have used the app in the country.

The provision with the most direct impact on visitors is Article 5. It would bar platform drivers from picking up or dropping off passengers at airports, ports, docks, international maritime terminals and other transport terminals run under concessions. Drivers who break the rule could face fines of up to 2 million colones ($4,483), although the text allows exceptions with authorization from the competent authority. Uber says the restriction would also cover bus terminals.

The airport question has been contentious for months. Licensed tourism transport operators protested in September against any move to open airport access to ride-hailing apps, and the airport’s orange taxis hold the concession for pickups at Juan Santamaría. The airport recently consolidated taxis, shuttles and rental cars into a single ground transport area.

When a legislative committee approved the airport restriction in July, Uber had not commented publicly on the text. The company has since watched the bill move toward a floor vote with its main requests still left out, Santillán said. She said Uber supports a legal framework for the sector but not the bill as written.

Santillán said the company has raised its concerns with the Minister of the Presidency, Rodrigo Chaves, with the vice minister and with lawmakers from several parties. The Presidency had not publicly responded to Uber’s estimates as of Tuesday morning.

Uber said it held a meeting in August with other platforms, drivers, taxi representatives and the tourism sector. Santillán did not announce layoffs or any withdrawal of investment, and noted that the company’s technology center in a Heredia free zone employs more than 400 people.

The debate pits app drivers and their passengers against a licensed taxi fleet that has shrunk by nearly half since Uber arrived, and which wants platforms held to comparable rules. Even within apps, prices already vary widely, with red taxis booked through Uber costing up to 2.5 times more than a standard ride.

Whatever the final text, the vote will shape how millions of people get around Costa Rica, from daily commutes in the Central Valley to the first ride out of the airport. Lawmakers can still amend the bill on the floor before a first vote.

World.title: Costa Rica Prosecutor’s Office Employee Detained in Border Drug Case
World.content:
Costa Rican judicial police detained 12 people today in an operation against a group suspected of moving cocaine to Nicaragua, among them an employee of a prosecutor’s office who investigators allege leaked confidential case information to the organization. The Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) made 24 raids on homes and businesses in Los Chiles, Cartago and the Southern Zone. Agents moved in at 3:00 a.m. alongside the Public Prosecutor’s Office, backed by the agency’s tactical response unit.

Eleven men and one woman were detained in what authorities call the Caso Norte and the woman is a judicial technician at the Los Chiles prosecutor’s office, identified by the surnames Flores Parrales. OIJ acting deputy director Vladimir Muñoz said she is suspected of using her administrative access to case files to pass along details of proceedings against the suspects and to warn them of internal movements.

Two officers of the Fuerza Pública, one posted in Los Chiles and the other in the Southern Zone, were also identified as suspected collaborators, accused of relaying police movements and vehicle database checks. Both officers are under investigation. Muñoz said the group had contacts inside several institutions and relied on that information to anticipate the authorities’ actions.

The investigation dates to 2021 and centers on a structure based in the Los Chiles border area. By the OIJ’s estimate, it moved up to 100 kilograms (220 pounds) of suspected cocaine a month. Investigators allege the drugs arrived in the south, traveled north by road and crossed into Nicaragua along the border track in the hands of couriers carrying about 8 to 10 kilograms (18 to 22 pounds) each. Proceeds were allegedly laundered through commercial premises, real estate and vehicle businesses and pawn shops.

The OIJ named two alleged leaders, a Nicaraguan national living in Costa Rica and a second man linked to operations in the south and Cartago. The agency said the group, known as Los Topos, has operated in Los Chiles for years. Seizures over the course of the investigation total about 200 million colones (roughly $449,000) plus significant sums in US dollars, and agents took high-value vehicles on Tuesday.

The detainees are to go before the Public Prosecutor’s Office. No charges have been announced and all are presumed innocent unless convicted. The case follows operations in early September in which two judges, a judicial investigator and a police officer were detained in a separate organized crime investigation.

World.title: American Woman Found Dead in Costa Rica Condo as US Man Is Detained
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) is investigating the death of a 24-year-old American woman whose body was found Monday inside a house in a condominium in La Guácima, Alajuela. A man who is also a United States citizen has been detained in connection with the case.

The OIJ has preliminarily identified the woman only with the last name of López and its account is that a security officer at the condominium discovered her at about midday. She lived in the complex, according to the judicial information released so far. Red Cross records put the emergency call at about 11:14 a.m. Paramedics who arrived at the house determined that she no longer had vital signs.

Judicial agents who carried out the first examination reported burns and blows on the body however those observations are preliminary. The Judicial Morgue will conduct the autopsy, which is expected to establish the cause of death and assess the injuries. Agents detained a man who is a US national and he is to go before the Public Prosecutor’s Office who will define his legal status. No charges had been announced as of this morning.

Authorities have also not officially determined the relationship between the two and the man’s age has not been released. The OIJ has not determined the cause of death and it remains undetermined pending the forensic results. La Guácima is just west of San José, a short drive from the San Jose Airport and has a number of gated residential developments.

The investigation remains open, and the autopsy findings and any request by prosecutors for precautionary measures are the next steps in the case.

World.title: UNESCO Condemns Killing of Costa Rica Journalist as DEA Offers Help
World.content:
The head of UNESCO has condemned the killing of Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodríguez Chaverri and called on authorities to find those responsible, one week after he was shot on Route 32. Director-General Khaled El-Enany asked for a thorough investigation that brings the perpetrators to justice and said impunity for crimes against journalists must never be tolerated. He warned that unpunished attacks can intimidate the profession as a whole.

Rodríguez was driving from his home in Guápiles toward San José on Nov. 16 when two people on a motorcycle pulled alongside and fired several times. He was 50. Reuters described the case as the first killing of a journalist in Costa Rica in 25 years.

The statement adds to a week of pressure from outside Costa Rica. Attorney General Carlo Díaz, on a working visit to Washington, reported that the US Drug Enforcement Administration is willing to assist the investigation, describing the offer as part of existing cooperation between the two institutions.

Díaz has placed the case under a special team of prosecutors. Prosecutors say several lines of inquiry remain open, including possible links to drug trafficking and to politics, the two areas Rodríguez most often wrote about. The Public Ministry has not asked for the case to be handled under the country’s organized crime jurisdiction. Its press office said the investigation is at an early stage and no such request exists for now. Only the attorney general can make it.

No arrests have been announced and how the justice system responded before the killing is now a separate question. Vladimir Muñoz of the Judicial Investigation Agency has said Rodríguez filed about 10 complaints over threats in the past two years. According to Díaz, he was referred to the victim and witness protection program and chose not to enter it.

The Legislative Assembly’s Security and Drug Trafficking Committee voted unanimously, with nine deputies present, to examine whether prosecutors and the judicial police handled those complaints properly. Díaz, deputy prosecutor Mauricio Boraschi and acting agency director Michael Soto are to be called.

The committee has said its review covers institutional conduct before the killing and will not interfere with the criminal case. One deputy, Abril Gordienko, cautioned that the inquiry could be premature and risked political contamination. The journalists’ association Colper held a vigil in defense of press freedom. Investigators have not said when they expect to identify suspects.

World.title: Man’s Best Friend, Brother’s Worst Enemy: Brothers reconcile in court after drunken fight and threats of death over ‘smelly’ dog named Snow
World.content:
Man’s Best Friend, Brother’s Worst Enemy: Brothers reconcile in court after drunken fight and threats of death over ‘smelly’ dog named Snow

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A drunken dispute between two brothers over a black dog named Snow that allegedly escalated into a death threat involving a machete ended peacefully in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court after the younger sibling chose forgiveness over prosecution.

Walter Sheran, 65, walked free after charges of aggravated assault with a machete and threat of death against his younger brother, Kert Sheran, were withdrawn before the Chief Magistrate.

Also present at court was none other than Snow, the four-legged subject of the entire controversy, who accompanied his owner but was not permitted inside the courtroom to give his side of the story.

The incident occurred during the early morning hours of September 23, 2026, at the brothers’ family home following a night of drinking.

According to Kert, the argument started when Walter questioned why Snow was inside the house and called Snow “stinky” and “smelly.”

Kert took offense to his brother’s remarks, and the confrontation allegedly escalated when Walter grabbed a machete and threatened to chop off his younger brother’s head.

Police were called to intervene, and both brothers were initially detained. Walter was subsequently charged.

In court on Tuesday, Kert admitted that both brothers were heavily intoxicated at the time and told the Chief Magistrate that he had forgiven his older brother and wanted no further court action.

Meanwhile, Snow, who reportedly accompanies Kert wherever he goes, waited patiently outside the courthouse. Kert had initially attached the dog’s leash to his belt buckle but secured it to a bench under a tent and asked a security guard to watch over his beloved companion while he went inside to testify.

Kert spent less than five minutes in court.

The charges were subsequently withdrawn, and the brothers were seen leaving the courthouse together, having put their differences aside.

Speaking to Breaking Belize News outside the courtroom, Kert referenced the biblical story of Cain and Abel, explaining that he did not want their family dispute to end in tragedy.

“No time to fight and war against your family. It’s time for peace and make love,” Kert said.

Snow was also present during the interview but declined to comment on the allegations concerning his personal hygiene.

World.title: International News: Decades of gains against AIDS at risk as global HIV funding dries up
World.content:
International News: Decades of gains against AIDS at risk as global HIV funding dries up

By Zoila Palma: Decades of progress in the fight against HIV and AIDS could be reversed as funding shortages threaten access to life-saving treatment, prevention programmes and community health services, the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) has warned.

Although advances in medicine have transformed HIV from what was once considered a death sentence into a manageable health condition, the agency says a US$4.3 billion funding gap in low- and middle-income countries is putting those achievements at risk. Currently, approximately 32.1 million of the 40 million people living with HIV worldwide are receiving treatment.

HIV prevention programmes have been among the hardest hit by funding cuts. UNAIDS reported that approximately 446,000 fewer people accessed pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) in 2025 compared to the previous year. PrEP use also declined among key populations, including sex workers, people who inject drugs, transgender people, and gay men and other men who have sex with men. Global condom distribution fell from three billion to 2.7 billion between 2024 and 2025, while voluntary medical male circumcision procedures declined by 53 percent across priority countries.

UNAIDS Executive Director Winnie Byanyima warned that weakening prevention services could lead to more infections, increased treatment costs and preventable deaths. She also highlighted the impact of funding cuts on community organizations, many of which provide essential support to vulnerable populations. One study found that more than three-quarters of surveyed civil society organizations experienced service disruptions, while over 80 percent were operating at less than half their capacity by the end of 2025. Byanyima stressed that these organizations are often the only trusted connection between healthcare systems and people most at risk of HIV.

The funding crisis is particularly challenging for countries heavily dependent on international assistance to finance their HIV programmes.

According to UNAIDS, external resources account for as much as 98 percent of HIV funding in Nigeria, 94 percent in Mozambique and 80 percent in Uganda.

International donors also finance all reported HIV prevention spending in Eritrea and Zambia. Meanwhile, mounting national debt and limited government health budgets are making it increasingly difficult for these countries to compensate for reductions in international support.

UNAIDS warned that the full consequences of the 2025 funding cuts may not yet be visible, but disruptions to testing, prevention and treatment services could eventually result in rising infections and AIDS-related deaths.

Warning signs include fewer people being tested or starting treatment, weakening laboratory services and reduced support for patients. Testing for advanced HIV disease declined by 35 percent across six countries between 2024 and 2025. Advanced HIV disease affected approximately 3.4 million people worldwide in 2025, with about one in eight dying within a year, highlighting the importance of early diagnosis and access to specialized care.

Despite the challenges, UNAIDS maintains that ending AIDS as a public health threat by 2030 remains achievable.

World.title: International News: Shein to pay US$100 million settlement over misleading consumer practices
World.content:
International News: Shein to pay US$100 million settlement over misleading consumer practices

By Zoila Palma: Chinese fast-fashion retailer Shein has agreed to pay US$100 million to settle allegations by the United States Federal Trade Commission (FTC) that it misled consumers about shipping times, product reviews and the origin of cotton used in some of its products.

The settlement was outlined in court documents filed on Tuesday and will also require the company to make changes to its consumer protection and business practices, Reuters report.

According to the FTC, Shein advertised fast shipping despite knowing that some customers received their orders days or even months late, while others never received their packages. The agency also accused the retailer of filtering out negative product reviews, including complaints about defective items and products that caused skin staining. Under the settlement, Shein must stop misrepresenting shipping times and preventing customers from posting negative reviews. The settlement funds will be used to reimburse affected consumers.

The FTC also raised concerns about the company’s sustainability and supply chain claims. Shein had marketed certain products under its “evoluSHEIN” label, suggesting they came from suppliers with above-average social responsibility audit scores. However, the agency said the company could not provide independent audits to support those claims.

Regulators also questioned Shein’s statements about the origin of cotton used in products sold in the United States, citing testing that was often inaccurate or inconclusive.

Shein said it had not admitted liability and disagreed with some of the FTC’s allegations, but agreed to strengthen its consumer practices and compliance efforts.

World.title: Ministry of Agriculture and Food and Agriculture Organization provide coconut pest management training to farmers and students
World.content:
Ministry of Agriculture and Food and Agriculture Organization provide coconut pest management training to farmers and students

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Agriculture, Food Security and New Growth Industries (MAFSNGI), in partnership with the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), has conducted a series of specialized training sessions aimed at strengthening Belize’s coconut industry through improved pest and disease management.

The workshops were held across northern and central Belize to help protect coconut production from major phytosanitary threats and promote sustainable agricultural practices.

The training sessions form part of FAO’s global initiative, One Country One Priority Product (OCOP), which is being spearheaded in Belize by the Ministry of Agriculture. In the Corozal District, 27 coconut farmers benefited from a two-day workshop held on October 27 and 28.

The initiative was also extended to academic institutions, reaching more than 50 students at the University of Belize on November 5 and Centro Escolar México Junior College on November 17 and 18.

Participants received practical training on identifying major pests and diseases affecting coconut production, as well as sustainable methods for controlling and managing them. Students also participated in hands-on field and laboratory exercises, allowing them to identify different coconut pests and pathogens while developing a better understanding of plant health and agricultural sciences.

The initiative aims to strengthen the technical capacity of both farmers and future agricultural professionals to protect Belize’s coconut resources.

World.title: Corozal Agriculture Department hosts training on thrips management and pest control
World.content:
Corozal Agriculture Department hosts training on thrips management and pest control

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Corozal Agriculture Department conducted a one-day training workshop focused on integrated thrips management and pest control, as part of efforts to strengthen sustainable agricultural practices and protect local crop production.

The training was held in collaboration with FORAGRO Guatemala representative Ingeniero Hector Mejicanos and BELAGRO representative Carlos Medrano, with coordination support from CRESAP officer Uziel Vasquez.

A total of 20 participants, including agriculture extension officers, attended the workshop to strengthen their technical knowledge and understanding of effective thrips management. The training focused on helping participants identify different thrips species, understand their life cycles, and recognize early signs of pest damage in locally grown vegetable crops.

Among the crops discussed were sweet pepper, watermelon and cucumber, which can be affected by thrips infestations. Participants also received guidance on monitoring techniques, cultural practices, resistance management and broader Integrated Pest Management (IPM) strategies aimed at controlling pests while promoting more sustainable farming methods.

The workshop also featured a presentation on FORAGRO’s thrips control program, including the use of the insecticide Seiken, its mode of action, proper application timing and the importance of rotating insecticides to prevent resistance. Participants also explored an interactive display of agricultural products offered by FORAGRO and BELAGRO.

The Corozal Agriculture Department said the initiative aims to equip extension officers and farmers with the knowledge and practical skills needed to accurately identify pest damage, improve pest control practices and protect crop yields.

World.title: International News: Armed men seize supermarket and take at least 25 hostages in Colombia
World.content:
International News: Armed men seize supermarket and take at least 25 hostages in Colombia

By Zoila Palma: At least 25 people were taken hostage after a group of armed men with their faces covered seized a supermarket in Cartagena, Colombia, today triggering a tense standoff with police.

Colombian officials said the incident began when the suspects fled into the supermarket following an unsuccessful attempt to rob an armored truck, AP reports.

President Abelardo de la Espriella described the suspects as common criminals and said they initially held approximately 30 people hostage before releasing at least five elderly women.

Footage circulating on social media showed dozens of people fleeing the Éxito supermarket in the city’s La Castellana neighborhood, while local media reported seeing police snipers positioned on nearby buildings.

The incident also disrupted operations at Cartagena’s airport, which temporarily suspended services before announcing that operations were gradually returning to normal.

World.title: International News: Huawei found guilty in US criminal case involving Iran business and trade secrets
World.content:
International News: Huawei found guilty in US criminal case involving Iran business and trade secrets

By Zoila Palma: Today, Chinese telecommunications giant Huawei was found guilty of multiple criminal charges in a major United States case involving allegations that it deceived international banks about its business dealings in Iran and stole trade secrets from American technology companies.

A federal jury in Brooklyn convicted the company on 10 of the 12 counts it faced, while finding it not guilty of racketeering conspiracy, which alleged that it operated as a criminal enterprise, Reuters report.

The case, which began in 2018, involved allegations of bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations, and conspiracy to steal trade secrets and obstruct justice. Prosecutors argued that Huawei misled banks, including HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas, about its operations in Iran to continue conducting business despite US sanctions. The company also faced accusations of stealing proprietary technology from several American firms over a period of approximately 20 years.

During the more than two-month trial, prosecutors presented testimony from more than 60 witnesses and introduced evidence involving alleged theft of technology from Cisco Systems, wireless telecommunications company Quintel, and semiconductor firm CNEX. Jurors also heard allegations involving a Huawei employee who reportedly took part of a T-Mobile testing robot and an engineer accused of secretly photographing equipment at a trade show.

Huawei rejected the latest convictions, maintaining that the charges lack legal merit and pledging to take all necessary legal action to defend its rights and interests.

World.title: 22 Agro-processing startups receive seed grants following entrepreneurship training
World.content:
22 Agro-processing startups receive seed grants following entrepreneurship training

By Zoila Palma: A total of 22 agro-processing startups have successfully completed a three-day Entrepreneurship and Technical Training Workshop aimed at strengthening local businesses and improving their capacity to compete in Belize’s growing agro-processing industry.

The training was conducted under the Agricultural Product Processing Innovation and Incubation Project, which seeks to equip emerging entrepreneurs with the technical knowledge and business skills needed to develop sustainable enterprises.

The workshop forms part of the Startup Acceleration Program, funded by Taiwan through its International Cooperation and Development Fund (ICDF).

Participants received practical training in Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP), food safety requirements, processing standards, business management, product costing and pricing, financial literacy, and marketing strategies. The sessions focused on improving production practices while helping entrepreneurs better manage and expand their businesses.

Representatives from several institutions also facilitated specialized sessions to provide participants with information on available business development resources.

The Development Finance Corporation (DFC) addressed business financing opportunities and requirements, while the Belize Companies and Corporate Affairs Registry (BCCAR) provided guidance on business registration and formalization. BELTRAIDE covered marketing, investment planning, and business model development, alongside presentations from the Taiwan Technical Mission on its agro-processing startup acceleration program.

Following the completion of the workshop, all 22 participating startups were officially inducted into the program’s incubation cohort. Each startup received a seed grant of US$500 to assist with operational improvements, the purchase of raw materials, and strengthening production activities.

The financial assistance is intended to help entrepreneurs put the knowledge gained during the training into practice and improve the overall quality and market readiness of their products.

The program will also provide continued support beyond the initial training and seed grants.

The initiative reflects the collaboration between the Government of Belize, the Government of Taiwan through Taiwan ICDF, and the Taiwan Technical Mission to strengthen local productive capacity and promote entrepreneurship.

World.title: Fi Wi Land: The fight to save Jamaica’s dying lignum vitae
World.content:
A symbol of Jamaica’s natural beauty and national identity, the lignum vitae holds a special place in the island’s heritage. But despite its significance as Jamaica’s national flower, this treasured species is facing growing threats to its survival, raising concerns about the future of one of the country’s national symbols.

Renowned for its exceptionally hard and durable wood, the lignum vitae has faced years of overexploitation, habitat loss and land degradation, contributing to a decline in its population.

With the species subject to international trade restrictions under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), protecting and restoring its population is an important conservation priority.

In this week’s episode of Fi Wi Land, Environmental Officer for Flora at the National Environment and Planning Agency (NEPA), Ashleigh Sanderson, sheds light on the threats facing Jamaica’s national flower and the efforts being made to safeguard its future.

From population surveys revealing concerns about its decline to conservation action plans and environmental protection measures, discover how NEPA is working to preserve the lignum vitae and other threatened plant species across the island.

Catch the latest episode on the Jamaica Observer’s YouTube channel and other digital platforms.

World.title: From ‘Bulbie’ to ‘Blackman’, the evolution of the Klansman gang
World.content:
The United States has designated the St Catherine-based Klansman gang as a transnational criminal organisation (TCO), a move that will bar purported members of the criminal group from entering the country.

Prime Minister Andrew Holness disclosed the development following a recent meeting with US Assistant Secretary of State for Western Hemisphere Affairs Juan Pablo Segura and members of his delegation, who were visiting Jamaica.

The TCO designation is a formal US government label placed on criminal groups that operate across international borders, and includes major criminal outfits and terrorist organisations such as the Sinaloa Cartel and Hezbollah.

During the 2000s and 2010s, the Klansman gang’s violent turf wars in Spanish Town, resulted in police crackdowns like Operation Kingfish, and the arrests and deaths of reputed figures such as Donovan “Bulbie” Bennett and Tesha Miller.

READ: US designates Jamaica’s Klansman Gang as transnational criminal organisation

ORIGINS OF KLANSMAN

Based in the southeastern parish of St Catherine, west of the capital Kingston, despite the name, the Jamaican gang has no connection to the Ku Klux Klan, an American white supremacist group whose members are called “Klansmen”. Anecdotal tales say the local gang was formed when young men met in a house in Dela Vega City and decided to become one ‘clan’, and set up an extortion racket in the Old Capital of Spanish Town.

The history of the Klansman gang is like a top ten Netflix movie: rival factions, secret burial sites, homicidal bosses.

The recent trials of dozens of members of the gang in Jamaica is shedding light on how criminal groups function on the island. At one time, police said the gang was raking in J$1.8 million weekly from extorting mainly business owners and transport operators. The gang also reportedly made money through targeted killings and weapons trafficking.

The gang’s status and organisation also helped rake in the cash. Its primary means of revenue, according to prosecutors, is extortion. One witness said that extortion payments from a section of the bus park in Spanish Town ranged from $80,000 to $100,000 a day.

One popular loan company, Torpedo, also paid up to $150,000 a month to a splinter faction of the gang, claimed one witness. The witness revealed that another organisation, which he refused to name due to security concerns as it includes “powerful individuals”, paid $200,000 a month.

Fifteen members of the One Don splinter faction of the gang, including leader Andre “Blackman” Bryan, were in March 2023 convicted under Jamaica’s anti-gang legislation. Meanwhile, 25 alleged members of the reputed Tesha Miller faction are now before the Supreme Court answering to 16 offences – including murder and robbery – allegedly committed over the span of five years between August 2017 and November 2022.

According to prosecutors and witnesses in the Klansman trial, the criminal outfit is now firmly a third-generation gang. The testimony of two former gang members stated that the Klansman reportedly had some 400 members within its different factions. The gang also had clearly defined roles, corrupt links with the police, international criminal connections and even allegedly carried out hits ordered by a celebrity musician.

Here are some of the generational figures that have defined the history of the Klansman, a firmly established third generation gang with tentacles in St Catherine, Clarendon and even Manchester.

BEFORE ‘BULBIE’: THE ‘PUPPY STRING’ CHAPTER

Derrick “Puppy String” Eccleston was an early leader of the Klansman, before Donovan “Bulbie” Bennett assumed control.

Eccleston was killed on May 12, 1993. His death marked a change in the gang’s leadership, with Bennett subsequently taking over.

Although some accounts alleged Bennett’s involvement in Eccleston’s killing, that allegation was never proven in court.

BALLAD OF ‘BULBIE’

Donovan “Bulbie” Bennett, the leader of the Klansman gang and Jamaica’s most-wanted man for over a decade, was fatally shot on October 30, 2005, during a joint police-military raid in Clarendon.

Bennett gradually built up a criminal empire through murder and extortion whose assets included 80 motor vehicles and heavy equipment used in construction and hauling industries throughout Jamaica.

Authorities believe he gained leadership through the murder of then leader Eccleston in 1993.

During the early 1990s, Bennett led the gang against their rivals, the One Order Gang, resulting in numerous gangland shootings and other violence in Spanish Town.

READ: From ‘Bubba’ to ‘Thickman’: The ill-fated leadership of the One Order Gang

He later established an elaborate extortion operation targeting local business, particularly taximen, in both the central and south central regions of St Catherine. He would later be connected to criminal activities in Old Harbour and Portmore, St Catherine and May Pen.

He was thought to have briefly fled from authorities in Kingston to Great Britain under a false identity in 2001.

In 2005, security forces under Operation Kingfish cornered the 43-year-old Bennett at a lavish, seven-bedroom hideout he had built in the secluded hillside district of Tanaky (near Rock River), Clarendon.
