According to police reports, security forces came under gunfire as they approached the compound in the pre-dawn hours. In the ensuing gun battle, Bennett and his driver, identified only as Nathan, were killed.

Police recovered a .50-caliber Desert Eagle pistol from Bennett, a Ruger pistol from his driver, and a large cache of cash and jewelry. At the time of his death, his wealth—amassed through extortion, construction equipment, and heavy haulage—was estimated at over J$100 million.

News of Bennett’s death triggered immediate violent reprisal across Spanish Town. Gang members mounted roadblocks, burned effigies of then-National Security Minister Dr Peter Phillips, and launched a gun attack on the Spanish Town Police Station, injuring two officers.

Following his elaborate funeral in De La Vega City and burial in Goshen, Clarendon, leadership of the Klansman gang allegedly passed to Tesha Miller, a welder by profession.

THE RISE OF TESHA

Tesha Miller, who grew up in Spanish Town after being born in De la Vega City, gained national attention in 2005 when he was charged with four counts of murder and three counts of shooting, for which he received bail.

Miller however, allegedly absconded to the United States.

He is also known on the streets by the nickname “Rat” (sometimes spelled “Ratt”). He has allegedly also used the alias Marlon Andre Williams (or Marlon Williams) on travel documents during past immigration incidents in The Bahamas and Jamaica.

Authorities linked the organisation under his alleged leadership to widespread extortion networks targeting transport operators, bus terminals, and businesses across Spanish Town and St Catherine.

He became even more notorious, attracting national attention over the June 2008 killing of JUTC chairman Douglas Chambers outside the company’s Spanish Town depot. Sentenced in January 2020 to more than 38 years for being an accessory before and after the fact, Miller had those convictions overturned in March 2026 because of jury-selection errors. The Court of Appeal ordered a retrial.

His history also includes capture and deportation from The Bahamas, where he reportedly travelled under a false identity. He is separately standing trial alongside 24 co-accused on an anti-gang indictment concerning alleged offences across several parishes between 2017 and 2022. Miller maintains his innocence and denies leading a gang.

MILLER HAS A LONG RAP SHEET

On May 3, 2007, after being caught by US officials, he was deported to Jamaica and was slapped with a nine-month prison term for absconding bail.

On March 5, 2008, Miller was fined $100,000 for breaching his curfew order.

On July 7, 2008, a cell phone was allegedly found in Miller’s rectum during a search of his cell at Horizon Remand Centre after the device reportedly rang. Miller strongly refuted the claim.

On November 21, 2008, Director of Public Prosecutions Paula Llewellyn took the decision not to proceed with a triple-murder case against Miller, as the police were having difficulty locating the sole eyewitness in the matter. He had been charged with the murder of Orane Jackson, Jeffrey Johnson and Nicole Allen who were shot in Braeton, St Catherine, on January 14, 2005.

On March 25, 2009, Miller was back before the court, and was denied bail, as he awaited trial for the murder of Rohan Haughton, who was fatally shot on St John’s Road, Spanish Town in April 2004. The eyewitness in the case was reportedly shot dead in St Elizabeth in August 2008.

After being in custody for almost a year, Miller was found not guilty for the murder of Haughton on June 10, 2009 as the Crown offered no further evidence against him as there was nothing to link him to the offence.

On December 26, 2009, Miller was arrested while at the Boxing Day show, Sting, after he allegedly breached a curfew order imposed by the court.

On May 2010, Miller turned himself in to the police after being listed among 25 men wanted for allegedly being gang members and area leaders.

On June 2010, Miller was detained under a State of Emergency. October 15, 2010, Miller was taken into custody for questioning in relation to an upsurge of shootings and other crimes in the St Catherine North Police Division.

On December 21, 2010, Miller was charged with robbery with aggravation involving a motor car and illegal possession of a firearm. Not long after, his 23-year-old sister Renase James was shot and killed while she was a passenger in a taxi in Spanish Town, St Catherine, in December 2011.

On April 15, 2011, Miller was sentenced to 15 years’ imprisonment for robbery with aggravation. He was also sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment for illegal possession of firearm with the sentences to run concurrently.

Miller’s conviction for illegal possession of a firearm and robbery with aggravation was quashed and his sentence set aside on March 22, 2013 by the Court of Appeal.

He left Jamaica for the United States of America in April 2013.

Five months later, he was arrested there and charged with illegal re-entry, having previously been deported, and for having an identification card in another person’s name. Miller was convicted of the offences and sentenced to two years and eight months in prison. He was subsequently deported in March 2016. While Miller was in custody in the US, two of his brothers were shot and killed in 2015.

On August 7, 2016, Miller was listed by the police as a person of interest with claims being he could assist with investigations into several murders recorded in Spanish Town and Portmore, St Catherine.

On April 4, 2017, Miller was deported from The Bahamas after illegally entering the country. Fifteen days later, Miller was fined the $100 maximum fine under the law after he pleaded guilty to making a false declaration to Jamaican immigration officials.

THE RISE OF ‘BLACKMAN’

The One Don gang, led by Andre “Blackman” Bryan, emerged as a breakaway faction of the Klansman following a power struggle with reputed leader Tesha Miller around 2017.

Prosecutors alleged that the faction carried out murders, extortion, arson and firearms offences across St Catherine between 2015 and 2019, particularly in Spanish Town and Jones Avenue.

In March 2023, Chief Justice Bryan Sykes convicted Bryan of leading a criminal organisation and facilitating serious offences in a landmark anti-gang trial. Fifteen of the 33 defendants were convicted. Bryan was subsequently sentenced in October 2023 to 39 years and six months in prison.

Bryan was allegedly once the top hitman for reputed Klansman boss, Tesha Miller. The split dates back to at least 2017, when Bryan appears to have rebelled against Miller and began killing his associates.

Bryan’s ability to operate freely was significantly enhanced in 2016 when both men were on trial for the 2008 murder of senior transport official Douglas Chambers. While prosecutors said Miller ordered the hit and Bryan was the gunman, Miller was sentenced to over 38 years in jail for being an accessory before and after the fact, and Bryan was exonerated. Miller’s conviction was subsequently overturned due to jury selection errors.

Witness testimony has painted Bryan as an incredibly violent individual who laughed upon learning targets had been killed. State witnesses said they were forced to join the gang out of fear for their lives.

During sentencing hearings in late September and early October 2023, Bryan addressed the court and openly acknowledged his leadership role, showing his sense of fearlessness and growing hubris.

World.title: ‘Beaver’ supermoon to illuminate skies on Tuesday
World.content:
The Beaver Supermoon captured by James M from Rainham, Kent, UK, 23 November 2026 at 22:19 local time. (Photo: BBC Sky at Night Magazine)

The first of four supermoons expected between the end of 2026 and the beginning of 2027 will light up the night sky on Tuesday.

A supermoon occurs when a full moon coincides with the moon’s closest approach to Earth, making it appear larger and brighter than usual.

November’s full moon is traditionally known as the Beaver Moon, as it coincides with the period when beavers are typically busy preparing for winter. It is also known by several other names, including the Digging Moon, Deer Rutting Moon, Whitefish Moon, Frost Moon and Freezing Moon.

Tuesday’s full moon is expected to reach peak illumination at 9:53 am, with the best viewing opportunity anticipated shortly after sunset as it rises in the eastern sky.

Sunset in Jamaica is expected at 5:29 pm.

Skywatchers will also have the opportunity to see the moon alongside a cluster of stars known as the Pleiades, or the Seven Sisters.

The remaining three supermoons are expected on December 24, 2026, and January 22 and February 20, 2027.

World.title: Killer strikes again!
World.content:
A 70-year-old Portland man who was out on parole after serving 24 years for killing, dismembering ,and burning a woman with whom he had a relationship in 1989, has been sent back to prison after he again chopped and killed another woman with whom he claimed to be in a relationship in 2021.

The man, Jasper Jemison, otherwise called Sojie, a farmer of Hopefield District in the parish, had been sentenced to life in prison for the first murder.

On November 17 this year Jemison, who has been before the courts since 2022, pleaded guilty to the July 2021 murder of Cynthia Hinds, also called Tiney, in St Margaret’s Bay.

Supreme Court judge Justice Judith Pusey, who presided over the trial, slapped Jemison with a 25-year sentence at hard labour. He will be eligible for parole after serving 20 years.

The case was prosecuted by Acting Deputy Director of Public Prosecutions Malike Kellier and Crown Counsel Nyron Wright.

The court heard that Hinds left her home on the morning of July 22, 2021 for her farm, which was neighbouring Jemison’s, on lands located across from Ken Jones Aerodrome in St Margaret’s Bay. Her partner, after calling her several times on her cellular phone with no success, later that morning went to her farm and found her hut ablaze, but saw no sign of her.

After summoning help, the partner, along with Hinds’ daughter and a police corporal, who was seen along the way, returned to the farm and attempted to put out the blaze. Hinds’ charred body was then found face down with the lower part of the right leg missing.

Investigations led to Jemison being taken into custody after it was discovered that he was the last person to see her alive. Three days later he told cops in a caution statement that he and Hinds were in a quarrel when he chopped her, using her own machete, after she attacked him. He claimed she then fell into a fire in her hut where she had been cooking and was burnt.

Jemison later led the lawmen to his farm where he dug up the machete that he had buried. A day later, in the presence of his attorney, Jemison was charged with murder and arson. When cautioned he said, “Officer, mi neva mean fi kill Tiney, and when mi tell yuh seh mi slap her wid mi cutlass, mi mean fi seh chop.”

When cautioned for the offence of arson, Jemison made no comment.

He later claimed during an interview before sentencing that he had been “experiencing remorse since the incident”, claiming he had shared an intimate relationship with Hinds and described her as a good person who was well regarded by himself and the community.

Vaginal swabs of Hinds’ body revealed semen which matched buccal swabs taken from Jemison, according to the evidence unveiled in the matter.

An assessment of the farmer, who claims to be a Muslim, by the Portland Probation Office said Jemison’s behaviour was of “significant concern, particularly given that he was previously convicted of murder and was afforded the opportunity of clemency through parole”.

In noting concern that the crime was committed while he was on parole for another crime, the parole office said it suggested that his previous experience with the justice system did not “sufficiently deter him from further offending”.

Additional concern was voiced over the fact that Jemison appeared to have withheld information from investigators about his behaviour, as community and family members said before the murder Jemison began “consuming alcohol and displaying behaviours they considered uncharacteristic of him”.

Probation officers further lamented the fact that his age had not acted as a deterrent noting, “Research on recidivism identifies age as an important consideration in understanding patterns of offending… studies have generally establish that offending tends to peak during adolescence and early adulthood before declining as individuals advance in age. However, at the age of 70, Mr Jemison has found himself once again before the court.”

The probation officers also said, “The offender’s actions suggest not only a lack of appreciation for the value of the lives of others but also a resistance to societal norms and values. In addition, his violation of the conditions of his parole order further indicates that community supervision has been ineffective and a custodial sentence is therefore the most appropriate disposition of this matter before this Honourable Court.”

In the murder of then 19-year-old Dorothy Williams for which Jemison was first tried and convicted, he had, for days, told individuals, including the man he accused her of cheating on him with, that she had gone to Kingston and would return shortly.

Ironically, that man was among the people who discovered the body of Jemison’s second victim.

When Jemison confessed to the first murder in February 1989, he told police who had taken him into custody as a person of interest that on January 31 he was going down a steep hill with his cutlass in hand and Williams was behind him. He said she held onto his shoulders and both of them slid down the gully bank at which point she fell onto the cutlass and started to bleed from her neck.

He claimed that he covered her up with a bag and decided not to tell anyone. He told the court at the time that when he returned another day “something had eaten her hands and feet and so he put trash on the body and burnt it”.

He was found guilty in the Port Antonio Circuit Court and sentenced to life. Jemison lost a subsequent appeal in which the court ruled that the burnt body was enough for the jury to infer that he was responsible for Williams’ death and that there was sufficient evidence to rebut the defence of an accident.

World.title: ‘Go back to the JDF’
World.content:
Opposition Leader Mark Golding speaking at a news conference at the Office of the Opposition Leader in St Andrew on Monday. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

INSISTING that someone must be held accountable for the less than desirable state of affairs at the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM), Opposition Leader Mark Golding has called for the resignation of the agency’s head, Commander Alvin Gayle.

The call comes following last Tuesday’s release of an Auditor General’s report that uncovered a litany of problems at the disaster management agency in relation to its handling of relief supplies meant for victims of Hurricane Melissa which devastated south- and north-western parishes in October 2025.

According to Auditor General Pamela Monroe-Ellis, only 31 of 200 container houses donated by the Chinese Government have been accounted for and hundreds of bags of rice, crackers, and other food items meant for victims of the hurricane were spoiled after they became infested with insects.

Questions have also been asked about how hurricane relief money was spent.

Gayle was seconded from the Jamaica Defence Force (JDF) in November 2025 to serve as director general of ODPEM, but Golding is unimpressed with his performance to date, in light of the unflattering auditor general report.

Golding made the call for his head on Monday during a press conference at the Office of the Opposition Leader in St Andrew.

“In terms of what Commander Gayle has said, as far as I’m concerned, Commander Gayle should really step down as the head of ODPEM and return to the JDF,” said Golding.

“What has happened under his watch is totally unacceptable, and if the prime minister is going to deny accountability for it, Commander Gayle, as the de facto CEO of the agency over this period, cannot,” he added.

Golding noted that after Melissa struck on October 28 last year, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness took a decision to relocate ODPEM to the Office of the Prime Minister (OPM) in November 2025, “promising in doing so, that it would manage the situation to the highest standards of transparency and accountability”.

“The various Auditor General’s reports to come out in 2026, including this most recent one, show the abject failure of the prime minister as the accountable minister for the Office of the Prime Minister, in executing on that commitment,” Golding said.

He argued that Jamaica must hold Holness and the Government fully accountable for what has happened on his watch.

Asserting that the prime minister has failed to deliver on his promise, Golding spoke to what he said was delivered instead.

“Money that was donated for the benefit of victims of the hurricane, trust funds, diverted and paid to clear goods for third parties,” said Golding. He suggested that it was obvious that Jamaica Customs “received a lot of those funds so no doubt the Government was paying itself with money that was entrusted for the benefit of the people who needed it”.

Golding charged that there has also been a total failure to account for the supply of goods that has come into the country through ODPEM, with only 15 per cent of donated container homes accounted for. He also emphasised that 15 donated containers remained unopened.

“It is a litany of woes for which the Government must be fully accountable,” Golding insisted. He also took a swipe at the prime minister, remarking that “good leaders take the blame for their failures and give their teams credit for their successes. Weak leaders take the credit for successes and publicly blame the team when things go wrong”.

Golding asserted that the prime minister cannot take control of ODPEM and then disown the results of ODPEM’s work under his watch.

“Prime Minister, you cannot promise the highest standards and then try to wash your hands of those standards when you fail to execute and maintain the very standards that you’ve promised to keep; accountability is not a convenience,” the Opposition leader said.

He demanded that the prime minister make a full statement to Parliament accepting responsibility for ODPEM’s non-performance under his office. He also demanded that the report of the Disaster Risk Management Review Committee be published with an indication of which recommendations have already been implemented. Additionally, he called for the publication of every cash and in-kind donation received showing where it went and who received it.

“And the Government needs to urgently put in place an appropriate legal mechanism for receiving donations from outside of Government that are intended for disaster victims and for distributing those donations in a timely, transparent and accountable manner,” Golding said.

He also called for the $45.1-million that was wrongly diverted from the donations account to be clawed back and instead be spent for roof repairs or other direct support for Melissa victims.

“And we would like to see a list of who received the 200 prefabricated houses that were donated,” he added.

According to Golding, “Jamaica deserves a Government that treats every dollar, and every item of every donation as if it belongs to the people for whom it was given.”

He said a future PNP Government would remove ODPEM from under the OPM and pushed back on claims that the decline of ODPEM started under the previous PNP Administration.

“That’s more than 10 years ago. If that were so, and it isn’t, the Government has had over 10 years to address the issue and has deep responsibility to do so in the context of what’s happening globally with climate change,” Golding argued.

World.title: MECA isn’t closed!
World.content:
International rapper Offset enjoying himself at MECA during a past visit to Jamaica.

Michael Dawson, owner of MECA nightclub, is dispelling rumours that the Kingston hot spot is shutting its doors.

Adamant that the entertainment establishment isn’t going anywhere, Dawson said plans are underway to catapult the club into a new era.

Speaking with the Jamaica Observer, Dawson said the club’s parent company, MECA-Whirlwind Group, is preparing for a busy period, centred on international theatre productions and an even bigger announcement still to come.

“We have been legally handling some social media posts about us being closed and out of business, so we want to take care of that before dropping the biggest news in our nightclub’s history,” he said, highlighting that expansions are underway at MECA.

“There is so much happening right now that I am not at liberty to say just yet. I just want persons to know that the club that reignited Kingston’s nightlife and reimagined nightly entertainment will raise the bar even higher,” he said. “We remain the celebrity hot spot of choice. I know people’s memory can be short, but I don’t want you to forget where the likes of Cardi B, Offset, Chris Brown, and Kartel chose to party when they craved an unforgettable experience.”

“We are still very much in business and when you see what we have in store, there will be no doubt about which entertainment spot continues to give quality experiences,” he added.

In the meantime, Dawson shared that the group’s Whirlwind Live Performances division, continues to carry the entertainment baton through its US theatre tour over the weekend.

The tour will take Jamaican theatre to nine American cities for 10 performances over 14 days.

Billed under the banner ‘Jamaican Theatre Is Back’, the tour features two productions led by veteran comedians Oliver Samuels and Glen “Titus” Campbell.

Samuels will headline Where Dere’s A Will, Dere’s A Criminal, while Campbell takes centre stage in Patrick Brown’s Boopsie’s Homecoming.

The productions will travel through Florida, Connecticut, New York, and Georgia, bringing Jamaican theatrical comedy to audiences across the Caribbean Diaspora. The schedule includes stops in Tampa, Orlando, Hartford, Brooklyn, Atlanta, Queens, Coral Springs, Bridgeport, and the Bronx, with the two productions running concurrently in different markets.

World.title: Lack of preparation letting down U-17 W-Cup Boyz, say coaches
World.content:
HALLIMAN... this is the World Cup, the highest level we can get to, and yet the team was not properly prepared — and this is unfair to the players (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

VETERAN football coaches Lebert Halliman and Patrick “Jackie” Walters have blamed a lack of international practice games for the below-par performance of Jamaica’s young Reggae Boyz footballers at the FIFA Under-17 World Cup in Doha, Qatar.

The Jamaicans have given up 12 goals in two games in losses to Italy and Uzbekistan in Group E, and the odds of them advancing to the knockout round is all but over.

After going down 0-6 to Italy in their opening game on Friday, Jamaica led Uzbekistan twice on Monday, with goals from Kelvin D Brown, before collapsing to a 2-6 defeat.

Italy, who beat Ivory Coast 2-1 on Monday, lead the group with six points, followed by Uzbekistan and Ivory Coast with three each. The Jamaicans are without a point.

Only two teams have conceded more goals than Jamaica so far, Fiji with 21 and Concacaf neighbours Cuba with 14.

Both Walters and Halliman, who have coached at the national junior team level, said not having friendly games against international teams left the young Boyz short on preparation.

“Look how long the team qualified for the World Cup and the team got no exposure after the Concacaf qualification [ended in March],” Halliman noted.

“This is the World Cup, the highest level we can get to, and yet the team was not properly prepared — and this is unfair to the players,” added Halliman, who won Manning Cup schoolboy football titles as coach of Excelsior High and St Andrew Technical.

Walters, one of the most respected youth coaches in the country, said while Brown caught his eye with two “excellent goals” overall, he was less than impressed with what he saw.

“What can we really expect?” Walters asked. “The team did not get the right kind of preparation, they did not get proper exposure,” he said, pointing out that Uzbekistan played 21 games, and Italy almost the same number, leading up to the World Cup.

He noted that the team appeared to lack pace in both games.

“The players were slow to react, and this could be a mental thing. They had little spatial awareness, in that they did not seem to be scanning wide areas of the field and were only focused on small areas.”

Additionally, Walters slammed the selection of the team, saying more scouting should have been done.

“There seemed to be a focus on players in Kingston, and that is disgraceful,” he said.

Dwight Jeremiah, head coach at Trelawny-based William Knibb Memorial High and broadcast analyst, agreed with Walters. He the federation’s technical development plan had not spread far enough across the island.

“It appears the programme is only in Kingston, and as such, players outside that geographical area are not fully included and so we don’t always have the best players for representation.”

On Monday, Uzbekistan scored five unanswered goals after Jamaica took a 2-1 lead. The Uzbekistan team dominated the game, earning 18 corners and accruing 40 attempts at goal, with 14 on target.

Sukhrob Sadirdjanov scored a hat-trick to lead Uzbekistan, who had lost 1-2 in their opening game to Ivory Coast.

Brown gave Jamaica the lead with a fine finish in the eighth minute, beating goalkeeper Olimjon Shamuratov to his right.

But Uzbekistan responded almost immediately, with Laziz Abduraimov pouncing on a ball that was only partially blocked by goalkeeper Omario White, firing into the unprotected goal.

Brown restored Jamaica’s lead in the 25th minute when he received a pass from the left wing and muscled his way past two defenders to fire into the corner of the goal.

Sadirdjanov got his first in the 31st minute when he brought Uzbekistan level at 2-2, and then scored in the 47th and 58th minutes to kill off the game as a contest.

Amikhon Erkinov scored Uzbekistan’s fifth in the 79th minute before substitute Akhrorbek Ravshanbekov added a sixth in second-half stoppage time.

World.title: SMALL ISLAND, BIG DREAMS
World.content:
Jamaica’s Allyson Swaby (right) and teammates (from left) Drew Spence, Deneisha Blackwood, and Atlanta Primus celebrate scoring the team’s first goal during the Women’s World Cup Group F football match versus Panama at Perth Rectangular Stadium in Australia on July 29, 2023. (Photo: AFP)

WHEN Michael Ricketts became Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) president in 2017, hosting a FIFA World Cup was far from being a reality. Now nearly a decade late, the island’s confirmation as a co-host of the 2031 FIFA Women’s World Cup has given him reason to celebrate a milestone he believes will transform the country’s sporting landscape.



Following the Jamaica Observer’s report last Friday, FIFA President Gianni Infantino officially announced Jamaica as a co-host alongside the USA, Mexico, and Costa Rica at Monday’s FIFA Extraordinary Congress in Zurich, Switzerland.

It’s a significant moment for the island which will not only become the first Caribbean country to host a senior World Cup but also secure automatic qualification for the Reggae Girlz, who could make their fourth-consecutive appearance at the tournament.

Although joining the bid in October 2025, Jamaica wasn’t initially part of the plan. However, that changed following a game-changing conversation between Ricketts and Montagliani during the Reggae Girlz’s second World Cup appearance in Australia and New Zealand in 2023.

“The thought came up about how Jamaica could be rewarded for being so consistent with our women’s programmes and the suggestion came up that maybe we should try and bid for a World Cup tournament,” Ricketts told the Observer. “The truth is that we were focused initially on a youth world cup tournament but as it turned out Victor and myself had some discussions and then he introduced me to Cindy Cone [US Soccer president] and then Cindy and myself started having some intense discussions and then it became real.

“We then invited Victor to Jamaica maybe two or three years ago and we sat with Minister Grange and we posed the questions — how would Jamaica handle this? Would the stadium be ready? Would you really be interested? And she was super-excited and then we got further word from her that the Prime Minister [Andrew Holness] was as excited as she was so the preparations really got into high gear and, like I said, the rest is history.”

Ricketts admits turning discussions to tangible results wasn’t easy but believes divine intervention and the support of a strong team helped made it possible.

“It looked then an impossible task but you know, there’s the scripture that says, if Christ is in the vessel, you can smile at the storm,” he said. “We would have had some tumultuous times in my tenure, but we would have had some good times, some good moments, some great achievements, some historic achievements.”

“God has been good to me, he has given me some good people to work with, my directors have stood by my side and we have put a lot of work into this. Now we have crossed the line, and we must now bask in the glory of an achievement that seemed impossible some years ago.”

Ricketts was on hand in Zurich to witness Jamaica’s confirmation as co-host alongside former JFF Operations Manager Omar McFarlane, Concacaf President Victor Montagliani and the respective presidents of USA Soccer, Mexico Football Federation and Costa Rican Football Federation.

The JFF boss knew the announcement was coming days in advance, but nothing could prepare him for the moment it became official.

“It’s no longer a dream, it’s no longer a plan, it’s no longer a proposal. It is now real, it is now formal, it is now official,” said Ricketts. “[Monday’s] exercise was indeed one for the history books and we are just absolutely delighted, we are happy, we are excited. It is for real and the whole world will descend on Kingston in 2031 so we are just excited.”

All eyes will now be on Jamaica’s readiness for the tournament in less than five years’ time with the construction of the National Stadium central to the country’s plans.

However, Sports Minister Olivia Grange remains confident that all deadlines will be met.

“The Government of Jamaica, through the Ministry of Sport remains fully committed to fulfilling every obligation and to delivering an outstanding tournament experience,” she said. “Preparations are already underway [and] we will continue to work closely with the JFF, the Local Organising Committee, and all stakeholders to ensure Jamaica is ready to host the world in 2031.”

It’s being estimated that the expanded 48-team World Cup will see nearly five million fans in attendance and generate over US$4 billion ($633.8 billion) in revenue.

Ricketts says Brand Jamaica will be one of the tournament’s biggest selling points.

“People want to come to Jamaica not just to watch a game of football but to see what Jamaica is — to see our beaches, to participate in fun activities, to have Jamaican food, to listen to reggae music,” he said.

“We do not just want it to be a footballing event, but we want it to be an event that is going to socially impact the well-being of every single Jamaican from a commercial standpoint to a footballing standpoint, to providing a kind of catalyst so that people want to see what football brings and, of course, this will bring a number of tourists to our shores, which must have an impact from a commercial standpoint.”

World.title: Alberto Núñez Feijóo: One step away from running Spain
World.content:
“He’s part of a generation that studied and came of age during the democratic transition” that followed the dictatorship, Puy said. “He was instilled with the values of the constitution, of democracy and, above all, how that democracy was achieved, through consensus and agreement.”

Feijóo became president of Galicia in 2009, winning the first of four consecutive terms, each with a full parliamentary majority — an unusual accomplishment in Spain’s fragmented politics.

“He achieved it by doing two things,” said Puy, who pointed out that the early years of Feijóo’s tenure were accompanied by the eurozone financial crisis. “Firstly, through good administration, using funds that were increasingly thin on the ground; secondly, through explanations. He made difficult decisions, but he always explained them, explained the context.”

However, key context is also required when explaining Feijóo’s multiple election victories, given Galicia’s status as a conservative heartland where the right has governed for 37 of the last 45 years. Such was the PP’s strength there that a doddery, 82-year-old Fraga won the 2005 election, although he was unable to form a government.

“The Galician electorate is conservative, in the sense of keeping things as they are,” said Pilar Mera, a political scientist from the UNED national distance learning university, who is from the region. She says the voter profile there was a good fit for the young Feijóo.

“In Galicia, the PP has traditionally been more moderate, positioning itself closer to regional nationalist ideology, with more emphasis on social policy,” she added. “It was relatively easy for Feijóo to cultivate that [centrist] image which probably comes to him more naturally than a more aggressive profile.”

World.title: ‘Everything that concerns Libya concerns Italy’: Why Ukraine’s Med strike is a problem for Meloni
World.content:
The Italian foreign ministry said Tajani spoke with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Sybiha on Tuesday.

"The Minister reiterated to his Ukrainian counterpart how vital it is for Italy to continue working to prevent the conflict with Russia from spreading to the Mediterranean as well," the ministry said in a statement. For Italy, "it is essential to respect Libya’s sovereignty and to continue working towards the country’s stability, unity and sovereignty."

Matteo Salvini, the leader of the far-right League, a pro-Kremlin junior partner in Meloni’s governing coalition, that opposes further military aid to Ukraine said that “it wouldn't make sense” if military support provided to Ukraine “ends up making wars and sinking ships around the world.”

Kyiv defended its right to strike Russian vessels — even those docked in Benghazi, thousands of kilometers away from the battlefield.

The issue threatens to become a headache for Meloni.

Rome is especially concerned about destabilizing Libya, a former Italian colony, fearing that if the politically fragile country collapses into disorder again, it could spark a migration wave across the Mediterranean.

World.title: James Cleverly is ready to run for London mayor. Labour is still waiting on Sadiq Khan.
World.content:
Current Labour mayor Sadiq Khan is holding his cards close to his chest over whether or not he wants to run again — and some frustrated Labour colleagues think it’s a risky move.

Make up your mind

As Khan keeps quiet on whether he wants to seek a fourth term, Labour MPs are warning that he is giving Cleverly a head start.

“There’s going to be a James Cleverly sized vacuum where he can spend months talking down about London with no one to challenge him,” said one London Labour MP, granted anonymity, like others in this piece, to discuss internal party calculations. That MP said there is a reluctance among potential candidates to enter full campaign mode “out of respect” for Khan.

The timeline for Khan to announce his intentions should be brought forward from spring 2027, as he has currently set out, two more MPs agree.

“I think it would be in everyone’s interests if he made a decision either way,” said one.

The feeling extends to some Labour colleagues in City Hall, who think the next election will be a much harder fight for the party after last year’s locals saw Labour hemorrhage votes and council seats to the Greens and Reform UK.

World.title: Efforts to free caged rabbits, calves wait on top EU court ruling
World.content:
Besides being a fateful day for Europe’s farmed animals, the verdict will also test the strengths of a key tool for citizens to weigh in on European Union rules. The previous Commission promised action in 2021 following a European Citizens’ Initiative that gained almost 1.4 million signatures to “End the Cage Age.”

“What is the purpose of the European Citizens’ Initiative as a democratic tool, if the Commission fails to act following a successful ECI with the support of 1.4 million citizens?” Tripley said.

The Commission said back then that it it “intends to propose to phase out and finally prohibit the use of such cage systems” for a range of animals, following a sweeping but nonbinding vote in the Parliament. Their deadlines was to put out a propsal by the end of 2023 that would be in effect by 2027.

But no proposal saw the light of day before the 2024 European election brought a new Parliament and Commission to power.

The current Commission promised to phase out cages for chickens and pigs in its Livestock Strategy in July 2026. The proposal for chickens is expected on Dec. 9, and a similar proposal for pigs is expected in 2027.

The Commission declined to comment before the ruling, but European Commissioner for Health and Animal Welfare Olivér Várhelyi told a group of MEPs Tuesday that “the Commission will study the judgment, and we will comply with it in the best possible way.”

The commissioner was questioned on a range of topics at a meeting with the informal Animal Welfare Intergroup in Strasbourg. He did not answer when asked if proposals for any other animal species are coming. Várhelyi stressed that the same standards should apply to imports so that European farmers don’t face unfair competition.

World.title: The good, the bad and the French: EU countries get fiscal report cards
World.content:
Sofia is the only capital facing a cash fine for failing to rein in its spending. But there are plenty of other countries that have broken the fiscal rules, which are designed to keep the gap between government spending and what they collect in revenue to 3% of economic output. They also aim to keep public debt-to-GDP ratios below 60%.

Brussels currently has red flags pinned in 10 countries, including France, Belgium and Italy, to signal to investors which governments have fallen foul of the EU rules. Countries shed the undesirable labels once they convince Brussels that their spending is under control. But the Commission has allowed for extra budgetary leeway for 19 countries to build up their militaries in an effort to deter further Russian aggression.

These are POLITICO’s grades, weighing countries’ fiscal outlooks alongside Brussels’ findings.

Bulgaria and Hungary: F

Budapest and Sofia have strayed so far from their spending commitments that Brussels is prepared to punish them. Both governments could lose access to some EU funds, while Bulgaria faces a fine of up to €23 million.

Even after allowing extra leeway for defense spending, Hungary’s spending overshoot is estimated at 3.1% of GDP this year, and Bulgaria’s at 2.3%. Only eurozone countries can be fined, sparing Hungary that particular punishment.

Belgium and France: E

Passing on paper is one thing. Delivering is another. France has produced a draft budget for next year, but its government is struggling to get it through the National Assembly. Belgium’s five-party coalition, meanwhile, can’t agree on its spending plans.

World.title: 5 reasons why everyone should care about Jensen Huang’s market-moving return ​
World.content:
The negative news alongside the seemingly relentless rise of AI stocks meant the U.S. tech industry saw its worst week since the Covid-19 crisis last week, plunging into a bear market and reviving warnings that the AI bubble has well and truly popped.

Huang's reinstatement saw the value of Nvidia, seen as a bellwether for the wider tech market, soar $1 trillion in a single day on Monday — but, after dropping 8.5% on Tuesday, it's down 37% since its peak in early October.

Even for finance types, markets are particularly erratic right now, but prices going up and down don’t tend to worry political obsessives. So why should they care now?

POLITICO runs through five reasons why it's a good time to panic, maybe just a little bit.

1. Their own pensions

Britain's pensions watchdog warned holders of retirement funds last month that they should try to minimize overexposure to AI stocks, urging them to consider how a market downturn could hit portfolios through “hidden exposure.” Politicians should care about the possibility of their constituents’ pensions crashing, but they'd be forgiven for worrying even more about their own.

More than half of British parliamentarians' pensions are held in overseas equities, which are overwhelmingly U.S. stocks interlinked with the AI boom story. According to the pension fund’s annual review last year, the largest stocks in the portfolio were Apple, Microsoft, and Alphabet.

World.title: Quantum may be a bigger security risk than AI. Europe’s got a plan.
World.content:
Even as AI has helped to disrupt services from supermarket fridges to the European Commission’s own platforms over the past month, computer scientists contend that another, potentially more perilous moment for cybersecurity is on the horizon: Q-Day.

The fear is that quantum computers, which can process more than the classic 0s and 1s used by today’s machines, will eclipse current security vulnerabilities by breaking the standard methods of encryption that scramble information in order to lock it down — rendering everything from secure government systems to hospitals digitally defenseless.

Brussels’ new law should “further strengthen the preparedness ... for the timely and coordinated transition” to a world where quantum technology has outpaced current encryption methods, the draft says.

Europe’s plan to deal with this next generation of computers is not so different from the one it has to deal with AI-powered cyberattacks. It contends that the technology needs to more quickly and better serve defenders rather than attackers who want to exploit it.

“With quantum, we know it’s coming with risks … because it’s able to break the current safety measures we have in our data,” Henna Virkkunen, the EU’s executive vice president for tech sovereignty said at tech conference Slush last week. “But at the same time, quantum is also giving good opportunities … to have safer quantum communication.”

The other objective of the new law is to support Europe’s nascent quantum technology industry by favoring European companies in public services — in part because quantum computing is seen as too critical to rely on non-European suppliers.

World.title: Dispute over bird nests threatens to derail centrist peace talks in EU Parliament
World.content:
The disruption reflects a growing chasm between the political forces that got Ursula von der Leyen reelected as European Commission president over the bloc’s environmental rulebook.

Members of European Parliament spent weeks carefully crafting a political agreement between the centrist forces on the legislation. That agreement fell apart after the right-wing European Conservatives and Reformists group proposed a change to the law asking to reopen the EU’s nature laws.

According to internal meeting notes seen by POLITICO, EPP group head Manfred Weber at a group meeting on Tuesday said the group had to support the amendment because it reflects the party’s position. During the same meeting, Radan Kanev, the EPP’s lead negotiator on this file, recommended that the EPP abstain on the change to protect the deal, the notes show. Kanev declined to comment.

In the end, the S&D said it would only support the overall deal if the ECR's amendment was rejected — a demand that brought negotiations to a halt. Annalisa Corrado, the Socialist MEP negotiating this file, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Negotiations are now set to resume until another vote on the file takes place Wednesday.

“Manfred Weber has made it up a political decision to hijack the file and that is obviously then breaking down the platform deal that we had,” said Emma Ytterell, the Renew MEP leading negotiations on the file, adding that “overall trust within the platform is deeply damaged.”

World.title: Tech giant Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
World.content:
Chinese tech giant Huawei has been found guilty of stealing trade secrets and bank fraud by a US jury but was acquitted of a more serious charge of racketeering, according to multiple reports.

 

The verdict, delivered on Tuesday, followed an 11-week trial at the US District Court for the Eastern District of New York.

Huawei has strenuously denied any wrongdoing.

In a statement, the company said the acquittal on the racketeering charge "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years."

"We believe the government’s remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit," it added.

The US first announced the charges against Huawei in January 2019. The allegations were later expanded.

“The tone was set at the top by Huawei leaders and executives who themselves engaged in criminal conduct, like lying to Congress, lying to banks, violating US sanctions and trying to interfere with the very criminal investigation that led to this case,” prosecutor Meredith Arfa told the jury at the trial, the Associated Press reported.

Brian Heberlig, a lawyer for Huawei, said in his closing argument that prosecutors had leaned on "innuendo and facts ripped out of context" as well as testimony from ex-employees "with a bone to pick"

“Huawei didn’t steal its way to success,” Heberlig said, adding that much of the material the US alleges was stolen was already publicly available.

Heberlig said Huawei would appeal the convictions.

This is a developing story. Check back here for further details.

World.title: Europe Tonight debriefs: can the EU budget compete with China and the US?
World.content:
A major showdown is underway over the European Union’s next seven-year budget, pitting the European Parliament against EU member states while deeply dividing national capitals over proposed spending cuts, digital levies, and agricultural subsidies. As negotiations intensify, governments remain locked in a tug-of-war over how to balance traditional farm aid with new strategic priorities.

 

Euronews' daily evening show Europe Tonight welcomed Lukas Gutenberg, director of Bertelsmann Stiftung, to discuss issues such as how the EU plans to do more with less, as well as the latest proposal put forward by Antonio Costa, which foresees another round of big cuts. The Germans say it's a step in the right direction, but not enough, while the French even say it's unacceptable. How can the EU compromise?

World.title: 'It's simply cheaper to fund Ukraine': Ukrainian economist warns Europe against cutting aid to Kyiv
World.content:
Europe risks facing higher defence costs and further security threats if it withdraws financial support for Ukraine, the president of the Kyiv School of Economics Tymofiy Mylovanov told Euronews.

 

His comments come as financing for Kyiv emerges as a major sticking point in negotiations over the European Union's next long-term budget, with leaders set to discuss both issues at a summit in Brussels this week.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has linked an agreement on the EU budget to continued financial assistance for Ukraine, while Slovakia, Hungary, Czechia and Bulgaria have signalled their reluctance to provide further funding.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has urged EU leaders to accelerate the delivery of financial assistance after the European Commission last week proposed an additional loan of up to €45 billion for 2027, aimed at covering roughly two-thirds of Ukraine's estimated €70 billion financing shortfall.

Mylovanov said Ukraine's mounting defence costs reflected both the increasing scale of Russian attacks and the growing sophistication of battlefield technology.

"Russia is putting more money to the war, to the tech, so we are forced to respond also with more tech," he told Euronews.

"In practical terms, there's more drones, more missiles. We need more interceptors."

Drones equipped with advanced sensors, software and artificial intelligence are becoming increasingly expensive, he added.

Meanwhile, Russian attacks on energy and transport infrastructure are disrupting logistics, public transport and access to education, placing additional strain on the Ukrainian economy as winter approaches.

Ukraine's resistance is buying Europe time, Mylovanov says

Mylovanov argued that continued assistance to Kyiv should be seen as an investment in Europe's own security.

Weakening Ukraine, he said, would risk triggering a political or military crisis that could give Moscow greater capacity to threaten other European countries.

"As long as Ukraine is containing Russia, Europe gets a breathing space to build up its capabilities and defence," he said.

"It's simply cheaper to fund Ukraine and support Ukraine."

Mylovanov pointed to the Baltic states, Poland and southern Europe as areas that could face the consequences of a withdrawal of Western assistance.

"Russia will divert resources immediately to operations in the broader European area," he warned.

He also rejected the argument that withholding financial assistance could hasten an end to the war by forcing Kyiv to make greater concessions at the negotiating table, citing Russia's record of violating previous agreements with Ukraine.

"So, forcing Ukraine to compromise simply means speeding up issues for Europe. Speeding up further aggression," he said.

'Talk is cheap, actions are costly'

Mylovanov also expressed scepticism about the renewed US-mediated diplomatic process, arguing that Moscow had yet to demonstrate any genuine willingness to end the war.

Rather than relying on assurances from the Kremlin, he said, Ukraine's partners should create the conditions under which Russia would have no alternative but to engage in substantive negotiations.

Asked whether Moscow could agree to a ceasefire before broader political negotiations, as advocated by Kyiv and its European partners, Mylovanov drew on his background in economics.

"I'm an economist by training and we have the entire field of strategy which is called cheap talk, which means talk is cheap, actions are costly," he said.

He suggested starting with limited, tangible agreements, including prisoner exchanges, a temporary halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, a Black Sea ceasefire or geographically limited truces.

"So we need to demonstrate something real in addition to words," he added.

While welcoming the involvement of European negotiators in the peace process, Mylovanov questioned how a future agreement would be enforced, raising the possibility of troop deployments, joint security budgets, military training and technology sharing.

What would make a deal last?

With diplomatic pressure on Kyiv mounting, Mylovanov cautioned against judging a prospective settlement solely by the concessions it would entail.

"In the end, we'll have a bad deal for everyone," he said.

"What is the right question is not whether the deal should be good or bad, but how do we ensure that this deal is the final deal and there is no continuation of the war two or three years from now, five years from now."

Achieving that, he argued, would require a clearly demarcated contact line backed by credible security arrangements, including observers and troops separating the two sides.

World.title: Miro G cargo vessel refloated after running aground off southwest France
World.content:
A cargo ship that became stranded off the coast of southwestern France was towed back out to sea on Tuesday after running aground overnight into Friday.

 

The Maltese-flagged Miro G had been heading to the port of Rouen in Normandy when it came into difficulty amid heavy swells off Lit-et-Mixe in the Landes department.

Nineteen crew members were winched to safety and taken to the town of Saint-Julien-en-Born after the ship ran aground.

The vessel was reportedly not carrying any cargo when the incident occurred.

France's Atlantic Maritime Prefecture confirmed on Tuesday that the operation to refloat the vessel had been successfully carried out.

"Following the operation, the French Navy deployed a Falcon 50 aircraft to conduct a maritime surveillance flight and assess the environmental situation," the prefecture said in a statement. "No marine pollution was detected in the area where the ship ran aground or along its transit route."

"We're getting off very, very lightly, and it's truly remarkable... We're heading toward the most favourable scenario," Landes Prefect Gilles Clavreul told reporters, per the AFP news agency.

The Miro G is now set to be helped on to Le Verdon-sur-Mer, where it is due to undergo a technical inspection.

World.title: EU won't return to Russian energy regardless of US-led peace talks, Jørgensen tells Euronews
World.content:
The EU will never return to Russian energy, regardless of the outcome of talks between Washington and Moscow, EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen has told Euronews.

 

Speaking to On the Record with Maria Tadeo, Jørgensen described Russia as an enemy of Europe and vowed to press ahead with plans to end Russian energy imports.

"We will never again, if it's up to me, import as much as one molecule from Russia. We do not trust Russia," he said.

His comments underline a growing divergence between Brussels and Washington.

Donald Trump's administration eased restrictions on Russian diesel last month ahead of the November midterms and has indicated it could support Moscow's return as a global energy player if a peace deal is reached in Ukraine.

Washington has even floated the prospect of Russian energy returning to Europe, according to media reports earlier this month.

But Jørgensen insisted that no deal between Washington and Moscow could override EU legislation.

“No matter what happens in these negotiations, European legislation is made in Brussels, proposed by the Commission, made by the Parliament and the Council co-legislators,” he said. "The EU wants to make sure it never has to rely on Russian gas again."

Rather than relying on sanctions, which could be lifted once the war ends, the EU has adopted legislation to permanently phase out Russian gas imports.

"We've actually banned [it], which is stronger than sanctions because sanctions have to be renewed every six months," he said, suggesting that " if there's a peace, then probably the sanctions will fall away" but the legislation will remain in place.

The bloc has already cut its dependence on Russian gas from 45% to around 10% and expects to end imports altogether next year.

“Even if there's peace, we will not trust them, and we do not want to repeat the mistakes of the past,” Jørgensen said.

Difficult winter ahead

Jørgensen also warned consumers to brace for higher fuel and gas prices this winter, despite the recent fall in oil prices.

"We are looking into a winter that will be quite difficult at the pump because gasoline, diesel and gas will be more expensive," he said.

Average gas prices in Europe rose by 163% year on year in October, according to figures cited in the report, with colder weather potentially driving bills even higher.

As governments come under mounting pressure to shield households from rising prices, Jørgensen pushed back against calls for an EU-wide windfall tax on energy companies, arguing that national governments should decide.

"In some member states it probably will be a good idea. I do not think it is a good idea to have an overall European one size does not fit all," he said.

Six EU countries – Austria, Germany, Italy, Poland, Portugal and Spain – have called on Brussels to consider a bloc-wide levy on energy companies' excess profits.

The Commission instead wants governments to cut electricity taxes, arguing that high levies discourage consumers from switching away from fossil fuels. Jørgensen said taxes account for around 29% of the average household electricity bill.

Asked about the prospect of a prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz, Jørgensen said Europe should prepare for the worst rather than bank on political promises of an imminent end to conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.

"We do prepare for a world where the uncertainties are so big. We don't know what will happen," Jørgensen said, adding that the EU should prepare for the worst rather than rely on political promises that conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East will soon end.

World.title: At least 24 injured after car bomb detonates in central Colombia
World.content:
At least 24 people were injured after a car bomb exploded in Villavicencio in central Colombia on Monday, authorities said.

 

The blast damaged a regional government headquarters as well as neighbouring buildings.

Video footage circulating on social media shows piles of rubble alongside wrecked vehicles and a large crater in the road.

The attack, which has so far not been claimed by any group, comes amid a wave of violence in the South American nation.

Alexander Baquero, the mayor of Villavicencio, has since imposed a temporary ban on motorcycle traffic along several key roads in the city, which is the capital of the Meta Department.

The Colombian army's Seventh Brigade has also been deployed to the area.

Both the mayor's office and the regional government are offering up to 150 million Colombian pesos (around €38,000) for information leading to those responsible.

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella arrived in Villavicencio at around 9 am local time on Tuesday as he prepared to hold a security meeting and visit the scene of the blast.

"Narcoterrorism is desperate because we are confronting it resolutely," de la Espriella wrote in a post on social media. "It seeks to intimidate us and force us to back down in order to pursue another false peace process."

In a later update, he added that he would "not back down or negotiate with criminals."

"I will confront them with absolute determination and use every tool granted to me by the Constitution and the law to restore security," he wrote on X.

World.title: Matryoshka: What is the Russian disinformation campaign targeting Spain's election?
World.content:
Pro-Russian actors are spreading fake news reports and misleading videos ahead of Spain's 29 November snap election, impersonating media outlets to undermine support for Ukraine and European sanctions against Russia.

 

What is the Matryoshka campaign?

Today's episode of Euronews Verify takes a look at the disinformation campaign known as Matryoshka, which takes its name from the traditional hollow, wooden Russian dolls that decrease in size and are stacked one inside the other.

It's been in action since at least 2023, according to France's foreign digital interference watchdog, VIGINUM, and primarily focuses on spreading anti-Ukraine narratives to try and weaken support for it in the West, although it pushes out fake claims about other European countries too.

One of its main strategies is to mimic legitimate sources, such as news outlets and research organisations, by stealing their visual identity to spread disinformation through a veneer of credibility.

It's also sometimes known as Operation Overload, a name used to refer to the campaign's other tactic of bombarding journalists, fact-checkers and researchers with fake claims to literally overload their resources.

Why is Matryoshka going after Spain?

Spain's government has recently been hit by railway disasters, corruption scandals, and a migrant crisis, meaning the conservative People's Party is now topping most polls.

The anti-immigration and Eurosceptic Vox party could also pose a threat, as it is consistently polling in third place and pinching votes from the Socialists.

Amid all this political instability, Matryoshka and other similar disinformation campaigns aim to capitalise on the uncertainty, interfering in the democratic process to try and destabilise Spain further, weaken Europe, and shake support for Ukraine and sanctions on Russia.

In a similar vein, they also try to spread narratives that benefit politicians more sympathetic to Moscow, or those who outwardly state they will reduce aid for Kyiv.

What's Matryoshka's prime target?

The economy appears to be the weak point that Matryoshka is trying to score hits on, in order to damage citizens' trust in democracy.

"It's one of the topics that are behind the defeat of [US President] Donald Trump in the mid-term elections," Andreu Casero-Ripollés, professor of journalism and political communication at Universitat Jaume I, told Euronews Verify.

"And this type of disinformation tries to generate the sensation that the economy is going very badly and has a lot of problems that can only be solved with radical measures," he added.

Is Europe prepared for a wave of political deepfakes?

Also in today's episode, from a fake video targeting the Spanish prime minister's wife to an AI-generated campaign video featuring Greece's prime minister, AI seems to be increasingly targeting political communication, with growing concern about deepfakes.

One reason for the rising use of AI is that it is cost- and time-effective, Kuhu Badgi, from the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Euronews Verify.

"In the past, to create a political ad, whether it be an  on TV or even a social media campaign, it would require resources like time. It would require many millions of dollars in terms of funding these initiatives."

What are the risks and how can voters spot deepfakes?

Experts claim that the use of AI-generated content is being spread and created across political lines.

In Europe, some parties using this tool are labelling their content as such, even if the font and colour are arguably too small, while others are not.

Under the EU's AI Act, manipulated video content that resembles existing persons, places or entities needs to be clearly disclosed.

These videos are also subject to national laws. For example, a former Socialist Party member in Spain has reportedly accused the People's Party of defamation and digital identity theft.

This is after a video used her likeness to hint at accusations that she worked to undermine the judiciary and law enforcement to help the Socialists.

While politicians discuss how ethically and politically correct this new wave of videos is, almost nine in 10 EU citizens agree that online manipulation, including AI-generated content and deepfakes, poses a threat to democratic processes.

In just under 11 minutes, our new format goes beyond the headlines to make sense of what's happening, fact-checking and untangling the day's most pressing issues to explain why they matter to you.

World.title: From the track to the gallery: Dakar's autumn in the spotlight
World.content:
This November, Dakar hosted two exceptional events: the Youth Olympic Games, which ran until 13 November, and Dak'Art, the Dakar Biennale of contemporary African art, which runs from 19 November to 19 December. The Games were the first Olympic event ever held on the African continent, and the Biennale now brings together artists from across Africa and its diaspora. In this episode, we hear from participants in both events.

Advertising

Dakar, Senegal, hosted the Youth Olympic Games from 31 October to 13 November, a landmark event widely celebrated across the country..

It was the fourth edition of the Games for young athletes, but the first Olympic event ever held on the African continent.

Dancers form the word "Dakar" during the opening ceremony of the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games at the Abdoulaye Wade Stadium in Diamniadio on 31 October, 2026. © AFP - SEYLLOU

In this episode, you'll hear from Kirsty Coventry, President of the International Olympic Committee (IOC), and from RFI English's sports journalist, Paul Myers. Both agree that it was a unique event, and they look ahead to the future of the Games in Africa.

As Senegal sets Youth Games medal record, Olympic hero calls for more investment

After sport, there's art

Then, just a few days after the Games closed, Dakar launched Dak'Art on 19 November. The Biennale runs until Saturday 19 December 2026 and features artists from across the continent and its diaspora.

The theme of this edition is "(Anti)fragility", which, according to the curator and organisers, refers to "the capacity to turn fragile situations into a space for invention and expressive power".

The main venue is the former Law Courts building, now the National Art Gallery.

Cultural exchanges beyond borders as African art gains global interest

"The project emphasises social and community bonds, co-creation, acts of care, and responses that allow the experience of shocks to be transformed into new possibilities," the curator said.

This year's artists include Nu Barreto from Guinea-Bissau, who won one of the main prizes; Ibrahima Cissé and Eva Diallo, both from Senegal; Chemu Ng'ok from Kenya; and Souad Abdelrasoul from Cairo, among many others.

Billboards advertising the Dakar Biennale 2026, the 16th Dakar Biennale of Contemporary African Art, the most important event of its kind on the continent, which showcases the best of African art and its diasporas through hundreds of cultural events combining painting, sculpture, and performance. © Patrick Meinhardt / AFP

Alpha Thiam, Senegal's Minister of Culture, Crafts and Tourism, said these events were "drawing on the philosophy of Senghor" and embracing "modernity without ever forsaking our authenticity".

In his view, the participants show that "contemporary African creation is not merely a superficial construct, but a genuine assertion of sovereignty", allowing Africans to build their future on their own terms.

In this episode, Souad Abdelrasoul, who had just arrived in Dakar for the opening, and her gallery manager, Menna Genedy, of the Misr Gallery in Cairo talked to RFI.

You'll also hear from the Senegalese storyteller, or griot, Bocar Niang, and his associate, the artist and philanthropist Amélie Mourgue d'Algue, of the French charity the Bureau of Invisible Hours (Bureau des heures invisibles).

Dak'Art is also an opportunity for other artists from the region to share their work. Among them is Bocar Niang, a griot, poet and performer, who has set up his own museum in his hometown of Tambacounda. The museum is dedicated to the culture of griots, the travelling musicians and storytellers who keep the tradition of oral history alive in parts of West Africa.

Beyond Senegal

Dakar is also a meeting point for artists from all over Africa, especially in the 'off 'programme.

The book, Made in Sierra Leone — Edition 02, will be unveiled during the fair for instance; it is the expanded second edition of the limited edition book by multidisciplinary artist Sahr Martin Kabba known as Sabanoh, from Freetown, Sierra Leone.

Made in Sierra Leone, Edition 02: by artist Sabanoh © Unx-art

The publication extends his exploration of Sierra Leone’s contemporary visual language through image, design, and cultural memory, as the artist and the curator, Sarah Hachi-Duchene of Unx-art, tell us.

This episode was mixed by Nicolas Doreau.
