World.title: Higher Prices, Fuller Hotels: Prague Is Becoming a Luxury City Break
World.content:
Prague is strengthening its position as a high-end tourist destination, attracting visitors willing to spend more on accommodation and services.

The Czech capital has ranked ahead of Vienna and Berlin in an international tourism index, while demand for luxury hotels continues to rise.

More than 2.3 million tourists visited Prague between July and September 2026, representing a three percent increase compared with the same period last year.



The city received a score of 92.7 out of 100 in the Global Tourist Perception Index, compiled by Data Appeal and Mabrian Intelligence. Vienna scored 85.6, while Berlin received 78.4.

The ranking assessed several aspects of the visitor experience, including satisfaction with accommodation, safety and the variety of tourist attractions.

According to František Cipro, chairman of the board of Prague City Tourism, the results reflect a shift in the city’s tourism profile.

“Prague clearly demonstrates that it is no longer a budget tourist destination, nor does it wish to be one,” he said.

The trend is also reflected in visitor spending. During the first half of 2026, Prague welcomed more than 3.8 million tourists, a one percent increase year-on-year. However, Mastercard payment data showed that spending by visitors from selected foreign markets rose by 18 percent.

Tourists from China and South Korea recorded the most significant increases in spending.

Accommodation figures point in the same direction. Almost two-thirds of guests staying in Prague hotels choose four- or five-star properties.

In 2025, the average price of a hotel room in the capital stood at around CZK 3,000 per night. In central Prague, the average rose to approximately CZK 4,100, while luxury hotels charged around CZK 5,800.

Demand for higher-end accommodation has remained strong despite rising prices. In September 2026, luxury hotels recorded an occupancy rate of 83 percent, their highest September result in seven years.

Germany Remains the Largest Source Market

Tourism continued to grow during the first nine months of 2026, with Prague recording more than 6.1 million visitors, a two percent increase compared with the same period in 2025.

Germany remained the largest source market for international visitors during the third quarter.

Some other markets also recorded notable growth. Visitor numbers from Taiwan increased by 27 percent, followed by Israel at 26 percent and Ireland at 23 percent.

World.title: How to Choose a High School in the Czech Republic: Open Days and School Fairs
World.content:
Choosing a high school is an important decision for students and their families.

School websites and brochures can provide useful information, but visiting schools in person offers a much better idea of what studying there is actually like.

Open days and high school fairs are two ways to explore the available options, meet teachers and students, and find out which school might be the right fit.



This is the first article in our series on choosing a high school in the Czech Republic.

Visit Schools During Open Days

Open days give prospective students and their parents the opportunity to look around a school before applying.

High schools open their doors to visitors, allowing them to explore classrooms, workshops and laboratories, meet teachers and current students, and ask questions about studying there.

An open day can help families find out more about:

Study programmes: What courses and specialisations does the school offer?

Admission requirements: What are the conditions for applying, and how does the entrance examination work?

Future opportunities: What options are available after graduation, including further education and employment?

School environment: What is the atmosphere like, and would the school be a good fit for the student?

Open days take place throughout the school year, with many schools organising them ahead of the application period.

Dates vary from one institution to another, so check individual school websites or use the online overview of high school open days to find upcoming events.

Compare Schools at High School Fairs

High school fairs offer another opportunity to explore different institutions without having to visit each one separately.

In Prague, one of the main events is SCHOLA PRAGENSIS, where visitors can meet representatives of secondary schools from different regions.

Students and parents can compare study programmes, ask questions about admission procedures and learn more about individual schools directly from their representatives.

These events are particularly useful for students who have not yet decided what they want to study or are still considering several different options. Meeting representatives from multiple schools in one place can help narrow down the choices.

If you live outside Prague, you can also find a high school fair in your region.

Use Worksheets to Help Make Your Decision

Comparing schools, admission requirements and study programmes can quickly become confusing, especially when several institutions are under consideration.

Free worksheets are available to help students organise information, compare their options and think about what they want from their future school.

You can download the worksheets here.

World.title: EF English Proficiency Index: Brno Speaks Better English Than Prague
World.content:
Prague has improved its English proficiency score, but it still trails Brno, according to the latest EF English Proficiency Index (EF EPI).

The Czech capital gained nine points over the past year, while Brno recorded a slight decline. Despite the contrasting trends, the South Moravian city remains ahead.



The Czech Republic ranked 24th out of 117 countries and regions in this year’s global index, published by education company EF Education First. Its score of 569 points represents a drop of 13 points and one place compared with the previous year.

The country remains in the high-proficiency category, although several neighboring states performed better. Austria ranked second worldwide with 613 points, followed by Germany in fourth place with 611. Slovakia came 11th with 594 points, while Poland ranked 15th with 587.

Slovakia’s performance is particularly notable. The country has gained 49 points since 2016, making it one of Europe’s most improved performers over the past decade. Although its score fell slightly compared with last year, it still leads the Czech Republic by 25 points.

Brno Maintains Its Lead Over Prague

Brno scored 613 points in this year’s assessment, placing it 28 points ahead of Prague, which recorded 585.

The gap between the two cities has narrowed, however. Prague improved from 576 points last year, while Brno fell from 620.

Brno’s result is particularly strong in an international comparison. Its score matches Austria’s, which ranked second among the countries included in the global index.

The regional figures also support Brno’s position. The South Moravian Region recorded 606 points, the highest score among Czech regions.

Sweden Takes First Place in Global Rankings

The Netherlands has lost its position at the top of the global English proficiency rankings, with Sweden taking first place this year with 615 points.

The Dutch finished fifth with 609 points. Austria, Denmark and Germany occupied the places between them, scoring 613, 612 and 611 points, respectively.

The survey was conducted through the Ipsos Instant Research application and focused on respondents’ self-assessments of their language abilities.

World.title: Massive Attack to Headline Colours of Ostrava in 2027
World.content:
British trip-hop pioneers Massive Attack will perform at Colours of Ostrava on July 22, 2027, organisers have confirmed.

The band will take the main stage at the four-day festival, which runs from July 21 to 24 at the former Dolní Vítkovice industrial complex in Ostrava.

The announcement marks Massive Attack’s return to the Czech Republic after a nine-year absence.

The Bristol-born group, formed in 1988, is regarded as one of the most influential acts in the development of trip-hop.

The band is best known for songs including Teardrop, Angel and Unfinished Sympathy. Its music combines electronic sounds with elements of hip-hop, soul and dub, creating a distinctive style that helped shape British music in the 1990s.

Massive Attack’s live performances also feature large-scale visual projections, often incorporating political and social commentary.

They join an already announced line-up for Colours of Ostrava 2027 that includes Robbie Williams, Ellie Goulding, Martin Garrix, 5 Seconds of Summer and David Kushner.

World.title: Leo Express Opens Prague–Munich Train Tickets From 49 CZK
World.content:
Leo Express has started selling tickets for its new Prague–Munich express service, which will replace České dráhy on the route from December 13.

The cheapest domestic fares currently available start at just 49 CZK for journeys between Prague and Plzeň.

The new service, known as Ex36, will be operated by Leo Express for five years after the company won a public tender. It will take over the route currently served by České dráhy’s Bavarian Express trains.



International tickets are not yet available. Although German stations already appear in the booking system, passengers can currently only book journeys within the Czech Republic. Leo Express says bookings for the full Prague–Munich route will open in the coming days.

The lowest advertised fare between Prague and Plzeň is 49 CZK. The same starting price applies to journeys as far as Domažlice. Business class tickets start at 199 CZK.

Prices will vary depending on demand and availability, so not all seats will be offered at the lowest fares. A second-class ticket between Prague and Plzeň will cost up to 236 CZK, equivalent to the standard OneTicket fare.

For comparison, České dráhy currently charges between 155 CZK and 235 CZK for the same journey, depending on the time of travel. Passengers can also use the cheaper Berounka express service by combining tickets from the Prague Integrated Transport (PID) and Plzeň Region Integrated Transport (IDPK) systems.

According to the booking system, most trains will have six carriages, including two business-class carriages. The operator will use former Deutsche Bahn carriages purchased by Spanish railway company Renfe and leased to Leo Express.

The trains will include both open-plan seating and traditional compartments. Eight services will run in each direction every day, matching the current timetable of České dráhy’s Bavarian Express.

World.title: Prague’s Abandoned Vyšehrad Station Begins Its Transformation Into Apartments
World.content:
Work has begun on the redevelopment of Prague’s historic Vyšehrad railway station, set to become part of a residential complex with 138 micro-apartments, shops and two new buildings.

Developer Karlin Port Real Estate, led by Milorad Mišković and his business partner Miki Goldshtein, began preparatory work at the end of October.

The company plans to start the main renovation and construction works in March 2027.



The developer acquired the station and surrounding land in early 2024 from Cyprus-based company Miquelira Limited, which has been linked to businessman František Savov. The deal followed months of negotiations and extensive checks, as the listed historic building was in a serious state of disrepair.

The plans include the restoration of the original station building and construction of two additional buildings. The development will offer 138 micro-apartments, around 50 underground parking spaces and up to 13 retail units on the ground floor.

The apartments will be sold rather than operated as rental accommodation. According to Mišković, they could appeal to students, young professionals, investors and families looking for temporary accommodation for children studying in Prague.

The developer also wants to improve the wider neighbourhood, including the streets connecting the station with Albertov and the Vltava riverfront.

More projects planned across Prague

Karlin Port Real Estate is also preparing other residential developments in the capital. In Hostivař, the company plans to start construction of the Výhledy Košík project in 2027. It will include 228 apartments and approximately 1,500 square metres of retail space.

The company is also exploring opportunities involving former railway properties and preparing to enter Prague 9, where it plans to focus on the redevelopment of former industrial sites.

Mišković said brownfield regeneration remains his main interest, although the company is now considering projects across Prague rather than concentrating exclusively on the city centre.

World.title: 9 Czech Castles and Chateaux to Visit During Advent 2026
World.content:
Christmas markets are not the only way to enjoy the festive season in Czechia.

Across the country, castles and chateaux are preparing special Advent programmes, with decorated interiors, traditional markets, candlelit tours and activities for families.

Here are nine places worth visiting in the weeks leading up to Christmas and during the holiday season.



1. Loučeň Chateau

Located in Central Bohemia, Loučeň Chateau is hosting a Christmas exhibition titled The Story of the Christmas Tree until January 17, 2027.

Visitors can also explore the illuminated Labyrinths of Light in the castle park. One of the main highlights will take place on November 28, when the country’s largest Advent wreath will be blessed in the courtyard.

Special Advent tours and children’s programmes will run throughout December.

2. Karlštejn Castle

One of Czechia’s most famous castles will also welcome visitors with Christmas decorations.

From November 27, 2026, to January 3, 2027, selected tours of the Imperial Palace will include festive decorations and an introduction to Christmas traditions associated with the court of Charles IV.

The castle will be closed from December 21 to 25.

3. Sychrov Chateau

Sychrov Chateau in the Liberec Region will host its traditional Advent Market on November 28 and 29.

The market will feature Christmas decorations, seasonal products and food stalls in the castle courtyard.

Visitors planning a trip during the Christmas holidays can also explore the decorated interiors through self-guided tours from December 27 to January 3, 2027.

4. Křivoklát Castle

Křivoklát Castle, one of the most important medieval castles in Central Bohemia, will host its traditional Royal Advent event on December 5–6 and 12–13.

The programme includes an Old Bohemian Christmas Market, with artisan stalls selling traditional products, dried fruit, Christmas biscuits, sausages and mulled wine.

Visitors will also be able to explore the castle interiors at their own pace.

5. Hrádek u Nechanic

Built in the Windsor Gothic style, Hrádek u Nechanic will open its doors for Advent visits on selected weekends between November 28 and December 13.

The decorated interiors will feature Christmas trees, traditional ornaments, nutcrackers and nativity scenes. Guided tours will also explain how Christmas was celebrated in the past.

Special candlelit evening tours are scheduled for November 28, December 4 and December 11, while Advent concerts will take place on December 5 and 12.

The castle kitchen will also serve traditional English punch.

6. Dětenice Castle

Dětenice Castle in the Jičín area will offer a festive programme throughout December.

On December 5, children can take part in a St. Nicholas celebration in the medieval tavern. Visitors can also see Krampus performances on December 4, 5 and 12.

The castle’s medieval entertainment programme runs daily from 7 p.m. to 10 p.m.

More Advent Destinations Across Czechia

Other places organising seasonal events include Třeboň Chateau, which will host Advent markets on December 5 and 6, and Jindřichův Hradec Castle, where a weekend programme of theatre, music, dance and traditional crafts is planned for the same dates.

In South Moravia, Valtice Chateau is displaying 30 Christmas trees decorated with more than 2,500 handmade glass ornaments. The exhibition runs until December 23.

Villa Stiassni in Brno is also offering special Christmas tours, featuring period decorations and an exhibition of historical toys.

World.title: Looking for a Team Challenge in Prague? This Venue Has 25 Different Tests
World.content:
Looking for something to do in Prague beyond the usual sightseeing?

TEPfactor offers an indoor adventure combining physical challenges, puzzles and teamwork, just a short walk from Wenceslas Square.

Located at Vodičkova street, the 1,500-square-metre venue takes inspiration from the TV show Fort Boyard.



Its main attraction features 25 challenges testing participants’ strength, logic, dexterity, patience and ability to work together.

Visitors compete in teams of two to six people, tackling a series of tasks that require both physical effort and problem-solving skills. The main game takes approximately three hours, making it an option for groups of friends, families and visitors looking for an alternative to traditional tourist activities.

For those seeking something more intense, TEPfactor also operates Fear House, a horror-themed attraction with several levels of difficulty. Options range from group experiences to more demanding individual challenges.

The most intense version, Hardcore + Kidnapping, includes a staged kidnapping scenario and must be arranged in advance.

The venue also caters to organised groups. Schools can book activities designed to encourage communication and cooperation, while companies can use the challenges for team-building events. Birthday celebrations, stag and hen parties and private gatherings are also among the available options.

Beyond the adventure games, TEPfactor offers event space for larger gatherings. Facilities include a theatre-style room with a stage, sound equipment and the option to arrange a DJ and catering.

Additional entertainment can include pub quizzes, stand-up comedy, mobile casino activities and theatre performances.

Reservations can also be made through its online booking system.

World.title: Magyar and Zelensky discuss energy, trade and EU membership as Hungary and Ukraine seek closer ties
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky held what the Ukrainian leader described as a “friendly conversation” in Berehove on Tuesday, discussing energy cooperation, railway development, agricultural trade and Ukraine’s EU ambitions.

The meeting, held at the Ferenc Rákóczi II Transcarpathian Hungarian University, followed the two leaders’ joint wreath-laying ceremony in Uzhhorod earlier in the day. It marked an important step in efforts to improve relations between the neighbouring countries.

Zelensky thanked Hungary for condemning Russia’s aggression and supporting an end to the war. He also expressed appreciation for the joint tribute to Ukrainian soldiers killed in the conflict.

Energy supplies and railway links among key topics

According to 444.hu’s report, energy was one of the main issues discussed, with Ukraine needing diesel and looking to Hungary for support. Magyar said Hungary had also brought generators and other energy equipment as part of a HUF 1 billion (approximately EUR 2.7 million) humanitarian aid package, which includes medicines, patient monitoring equipment and vehicles.

The leaders also discussed modernising existing railway infrastructure, building new border crossing points and developing healthcare and social projects in Transcarpathia.

Agricultural trade was another topic. Zelensky offered to supply maize to drought-hit Hungary, while Magyar highlighted a shortfall of around two million tonnes in this year’s Hungarian maize harvest, which has caused difficulties for livestock farmers. He said the two countries should explore purchases of Ukrainian maize under state supervision and with appropriate checks. Food security was also discussed.

Magyar calls for faster implementation of minority rights deal

Magyar said Ukraine’s parliament had approved the ten-point programme agreed by the two countries to improve the situation of ethnic Hungarians in Transcarpathia, including their language, education and minority rights. He called for its implementation to be accelerated.

The Hungarian prime minister said the two countries had a long way to go and that trust would have to be built continuously. He also raised the issue of the Turul statue, which was removed from Mukachevo Castle in 2022, saying he would like to see it restored.

Hungary maintains reservations about Ukraine’s EU funding

The leaders also discussed Ukraine’s European Union membership prospects. Magyar reiterated that Hungary would continue providing humanitarian assistance but could not support linking Ukraine’s financing directly to the EU budget in a way that would oblige member states to participate in joint borrowing. He argued that each country should retain the freedom to decide how it supports Ukraine.

On EU accession talks, he stressed that membership must be based on merit and that there would be no fast-track process. He pointed to Hungary’s own 13-year path towards membership and Serbia’s lengthy accession process, adding that resolving minority rights issues was a prerequisite for Hungary to support opening the relevant negotiating cluster.

Magyar also said the visit had helped halt political escalation and put the relationship on a path towards good-neighbourly cooperation. The two leaders even joined students for a game of volleyball during their visit to the university.

The meeting follows two earlier discussions between Magyar and Zelensky: one on the sidelines of the European Council meeting in Brussels on 16 October and another at the European Political Community summit on 12 November. Magyar had said the two leaders wanted to meet in November, with Transcarpathia chosen as the location.

World.title: Young Hungarian talent Martin Molnár to race in Formula 3 from 2027
World.content:
Hungarian racing driver Martin Molnár will step up to the FIA Formula 3 Championship in 2027, joining the renowned Italian team Prema Racing and becoming a regular competitor at Formula 1 grand prix weekends.

Hungarian driver in Formula 3

The 18-year-old’s move marks a significant milestone in a career that has progressed through the British junior single-seater championships. Formula 3 is an important stage on the development path towards Formula 1, bringing together some of the most promising young drivers in international motorsport.

Molnár has already worked with his new team, completing 256 laps across two official post-season tests in Jerez and Barcelona. The sessions gave him an opportunity to get acquainted with Prema’s engineers and the demands of the category ahead of his first full campaign.

“I made a very good impression on them during the tests, and I am happy that we will be working together,” said Molnár at the announcement. He added that the reality of reaching this level became clear when he began testing and simulator preparation.

What are Formula 3 cars capable of?

According to the official website of the FIA Formula 3 championship, the cars are the same for every driver. They are capable of reaching 100km/h in around 3 seconds, and have a top speed of 300km/h, depending on their settings. This is comparable to modern day supercars, but thanks to the leightweight chassis and the downforce the cars create, they can turn far more quickly than any roadgoing car.

A prestigious team and a demanding step up

Founded in 1983, Prema is one of the best-known teams in junior motorsport. It has won five FIA Formula 3 teams’ championships since 2019 and has helped develop several drivers who went on to reach Formula 1, including Charles Leclerc, Oscar Piastri, Oliver Bearman and now world champion Andrea Kimi Antonelli.

Prema chief executive Stephen Mitas said Molnár had made a strong impression during the Jerez and Barcelona tests. He said the team was looking forward to helping the Hungarian make the most of his first season in the championship.

Molnár’s move follows three seasons of progress in British single-seater racing. He began competing in British Formula 4 in 2024 with Virtuosi, finishing eighth overall in his debut year and becoming the leading rookie. He improved to third in the standings in his second season before moving to the GB3 Championship, commonly referred to as British Formula 3.

Racing for Rodin, he finished fourth overall after claiming seven podiums during the season. He was also the team’s highest-placed driver. The 2027 FIA Formula 3 championship is scheduled to begin in March, with ten rounds on the calendar. The opening event is due to take place in Bahrain, and all rounds are held as part of Formula 1 race weekends.

Read also: Budapest faces new rival in race to host the 2036 Olympic Games

Hungarian backing and a new ownership structure

Molnár will continue to receive backing from 4iG Group and One Hungary, which have supported his career since 2024 and are set to act as his main sponsors in 2027. The announcement also included a change in the business structure behind the driver. Through its investment subsidiary, 4iG intends to acquire full ownership of MOTAM Kft., the company managing Molnár’s career. The transaction remains subject to domestic and international competition approvals.

MOTAM’s management is expected to remain unchanged, with Tamás Őry continuing as managing director and former professional racing driver Pál Tamás Kiss leading its sporting programme.

Kiss said the tests showed that Molnár was technically ready for Formula 3, although adapting to the car and tyres will be a major challenge. With limited track time, drivers must learn quickly and extract maximum performance from each session. Physical and mental preparation will therefore become increasingly important.

Molnár will be the second Hungarian to contest the FIA Formula 3 championship after László Tóth, who competed in 2021 and 2022. Kiss previously raced in the series’ predecessor, GP3, where he won a race.

What is the best online casino in the US judged on?

How often do new casino sites launch?

Types of Casino Bonuses in the UK

Most offers at the best online casinos fall into a few families. Each is credited differently, and each has one term that decides whether it’s worth claiming.

Free Spins and Wager-Free Cash Spins

Free spins are the most common welcome deal. They go on one or a few named slots at a fixed value per spin, often 10p. Winnings either carry wagering or are paid as cash. Check the spin value, the eligible games and the expiry, which can be as short as 48 hours.

Wager-free spins pay winnings straight to your cash balance. They’re the cleanest deal available, though many still cap what you can withdraw.

Matched Deposits and No Deposit Offers

A matched deposit adds a percentage of your deposit as bonus money, such as 100% up to a set amount. The money sits in a separate balance until you meet the wagering. Check the multiple, and whether it covers the bonus alone or the deposit plus bonus.

No deposit bonuses give you spins or a small credit just for registering. They’re rarer at licensed sites. Expect strict win caps and short expiry.

Existing players get reload bonuses on later deposits, daily free games and reward wheels that hand out spins or small prizes. Many of the top UK casino sites run these every day. Check whether the prizes carry wagering and how long they last.

Loyalty and VIP schemes award points for play, which turn into bonuses or cash. Look at how points are earned and whether they expire.

The best online casino bonuses also follow one firm rule: offers that require you to play across different products, such as casino and sports betting, to claim them are banned.

How Wagering Requirements Work at UK Casino Sites

Wagering requirements tell you how many times you must bet bonus money (or bonus winnings) before you can withdraw it. A 10x requirement on a £10 bonus means £100 in bets. From January 2026, UKGC rules cap casino bonus wagering at 10x.

Here’s an example with round numbers. You deposit £20 and get a £20 bonus with 10x wagering on the deposit plus bonus. That’s £40 x 10, so you place £400 in bets before the bonus money becomes withdrawable cash.

Before you claim at any of the best online casinos, check these terms:

You may get 30 days, 7 days or as little as 24 hours. Win caps: Some offers limit how much you can withdraw from bonus winnings.

Offers with 1x to 5x wagering are far easier to clear. Fewer bets mean less of the house edge eats into your balance. That’s why the best UK casino sites increasingly lead with low-wager or wager-free deals, and why top platforms make all of these terms easy to find.

Both rules lower the house edge further. French tables are worth seeking out if you mostly bet on red, black, odd or even.

Other formats include Lightning Roulette, which adds random multipliers, and auto roulette, where the wheel spins mechanically without a host. Auto tables are faster, so you stake more per hour. Pace yourself.

UK Gambling Laws: What Players Need to Know

UK gambling laws are among the strictest anywhere, and they protect you as much as they control the sites. These are the rules that affect your play.

Best Online Casinos UK FAQ

Are UK online casinos safe to play at?

Yes, if they hold a UKGC licence. Licensed UK online casinos must use tested games, protect your funds and data, and offer safer gambling tools. To check, find the operator’s name and licence number in the site footer. Then search for it on the UK Gambling Commission’s public register. Make sure the web address listed matches the one in your browser. If you can’t find a match, don’t deposit.

How are casino sites rated?

Licence status comes first, then safer gambling tools. After that, sites are compared on bonus value and fairness, games, mobile performance, banking and support. Everything is judged from what a player can see: published terms, the cashier, game information screens, help pages and the public register. A big offer with harsh terms scores lower than a modest one with fair terms.

Do I pay tax on casino winnings?

No. Gambling winnings are tax-free for players in the UK, whether you win a few pounds on a slot or a large jackpot. You don’t need to declare them as income. The operators pay the tax, not you. Keep your account history anyway, because it’s a useful record of what you’ve spent and won.

What documents do I need to verify my account?

Usually two things: photo ID and proof of address. A passport or driving licence covers ID. A recent utility bill or bank statement showing your name and address covers proof of address. Some sites may also ask for proof of your payment method, such as a photo of your debit card with the middle digits hidden. Upload clear, uncropped images so the checks pass first time.

Which payment method pays out fastest?

E-wallets such as PayPal and open banking services such as Trustly are usually quickest, often within hours. Some sites offer fast card payouts too. Standard debit card withdrawals and bank transfers can take several working days. Many welcome offers exclude e-wallet deposits, so weigh payout speed against bonus eligibility.

What should I check in a welcome bonus?

Start with the wagering multiple, which can’t be higher than 10x under the current rules. Then check whether it applies to the bonus alone or to the deposit plus bonus. Look at the expiry date, the maximum bet while wagering, any cap on winnings and which games count. Finally, check which payment methods qualify. Using the wrong one can mean missing the offer entirely.

What can I do if I have a complaint?

Raise it with the casino first through its official complaints process, usually found in the terms or help pages. Keep screenshots and dates. If the site doesn’t resolve it in its stated timeframe, you can take it to an independent dispute service such as IBAS, the Independent Betting Adjudication Service. The casino’s terms should name which service it uses. Using one is free for you.

What Makes an Online Casino in the UK New?

A site counts as new for one of three reasons. Which one applies tells you how much history sits behind it.

Are New Casino Sites Safe in the UK?

A licence settles the safety question. The age of the site matters far less.

The Same Rulebook as Older Brands

UKGC-licensed new casinos follow exactly the same rules as long-running ones. Games must be fair and tested. Your data must be protected, and the site must tell you how your money is held. Safer gambling tools and a complaints process are compulsory too.

If a complaint isn’t fixed, you can take it to ADR (alternative dispute resolution), an independent service such as IBAS, at no cost. What’s different is a shorter track record. Even the top new online casinos have less player feedback to judge them by. If years of proven payouts matter more to you, see our list of the best online casinos in the UK.

Unlicensed Lookalikes

Plenty of new online casinos that look polished are actually offshore. Sites without a UKGC licence that target UK players are illegal here. They offer no ADR, no GamStop link and no protection if they refuse to pay.

The House Edge Doesn’t Change

Every casino game has a built-in house edge, so over time the casino comes out ahead. A new lobby or a big bonus doesn’t alter that. Only spend what you can afford to lose. If gambling stops feeling like fun, GamCare offers free, confidential support.

Reasons to Try New Casino Sites

These benefits are typical rather than guaranteed. Each site handles them differently.

Fresher Games and Simpler Offers

Newer sites often launch with recent releases and studios you won’t see everywhere. Their welcome offers frequently include free spins with no wagering, so what you win from them is yours to withdraw.

Support teams tend to be keen too. A brand still building a reputation usually answers chat quickly and doesn’t want early complaints.

Tools and Tech Built in From the Start

Safer gambling tools are part of the design from day one rather than bolted on later. Limits, time-outs and reality checks usually sit a tap or two from the main menu.

Sites and apps are generally easier to use, with cleaner menus and quicker search. Payments lean modern as well: open banking for instant bank transfers and mobile wallets for one-tap deposits are common on a new casino site.

Rewards With a Game Feel

Gamified rewards are popular at launch. Think daily prize wheels, missions that pay out for trying certain games, and progress bars. The best new online casinos tie these to small, clear prizes rather than endless grinding.

Community features add another layer. Slot tournaments and leaderboards let you compete with other players for extra prizes, usually without any added cost to enter.

A deposit match adds bonus money to your first payment, and some packages spread it over several deposits. Check the maximum bet allowed while wagering, the expiry date and which games count. At a new UK casino, a package split across deposits can take weeks to collect in full.

Free Spins, Cash Spins and No Deposit Offers

Free spins either carry wagering on winnings or come with none. Cash spins pay winnings straight into your real balance. No deposit bonuses are rare, smaller and usually come with tight win caps. For all three, look at the win cap, the eligible games and how long the spins last.

Reloads, Cashback and Everyday Rewards

Reload offers top up later deposits. Cashback returns part of your losses, ideally as cash rather than bonus funds. Loyalty points, daily wheels and free games keep regulars engaged. Fresh launches tend to open with recent releases rather than old favourites. Here’s what usually fills the lobby, with example titles and the studios behind them.

Crash games show a multiplier climbing until it suddenly stops, and you must cash out before the crash. Aviator is the best-known example. Mines and Plinko are instant-win formats from the same studio, Spribe. Both types are fast, so rounds add up quickly. Session reminders are worth switching on.

Look for a separate section for new releases, which makes finding fresh games easier than scrolling the full library. A search bar with filters for features, such as bonus buys or hold-and-win, saves even more time.

Modern payment options are one of the clearest gains at the latest UK online casino sites. Speed depends on the method, though, and so does whether your deposit qualifies for the welcome offer.

Mobile-First Design at New Casino Sites

Most new casinos are designed for phones first and desktops second. Menus, game tiles and the cashier are laid out for a thumb, not a mouse.

You’ll usually get a choice between a native app and browser play. Apps can feel quicker and send notifications. Browser play needs no download and saves storage. At a new UK casino, the bonuses, games and cashier should be the same on both, so check before assuming an offer is app-only.

Many of the latest UK online casinos add features that only make sense on a phone:

Face or fingerprint login instead of typing a password

Apple Pay or Google Pay deposits in a single tap

Push alerts for limits, offers and withdrawals

Quick access to your account history

One check matters more than design. Make sure deposit limits, time-outs and self-exclusion are easy to find on a small screen. If they’re buried three menus deep, that’s a poor sign for how the site treats safer gambling.

How to Join a New Online Casino Step by Step

Signing up takes a few minutes if you have your details ready.

Confirm the licence. Find the UKGC licence number in the footer and look it up on the public register. Read the bonus terms. Check wagering, expiry, eligible games and which payment methods qualify. Register with accurate details. Use your real name, address and date of birth exactly as they appear on your documents. Set deposit and loss limits. Choose amounts you’re comfortable with while you’re still thinking clearly. Complete verification early. Upload any ID or proof of address the site asks for straight away. Pick a payment method in your own name. Cards or accounts belonging to someone else will block withdrawals. Make a small first deposit. Start low until you know how the site works. Test support and withdrawals. Ask chat a question, then withdraw a small amount to see how the process runs.

Most withdrawal delays, even on fresh platforms, come from details that don’t match or checks left unfinished at sign-up. Getting those right at a new online casino saves days later.

Trends of New UK Casino Sites

The market for new launches is changing quickly. These shifts shape which sites appear and what they offer.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are new online casinos in the UK legit?

Yes, provided they hold a UKGC licence. New online casinos in the UK with a licence must meet the same standards as older brands on fair games, protecting your money and handling complaints. If you can’t find a licence number you can verify on the public register, don’t sign up.

Which new UK casino pays out fastest?

That depends on the method rather than the brand. Look for instant bank transfer or instant card payouts, clearly listed withdrawal times and low minimum withdrawals. Then verify your account straight away, because unfinished checks slow every method down.

I’m signed up to GamStop. Can I join a newly launched site?

No. Every UKGC-licensed casino is connected to GamStop from launch, so your self-exclusion applies to new sites too. Any site that lets you in while you’re excluded isn’t licensed for the UK. Free support is available from GamCare if you need it.

I already play at one casino. Can I claim a welcome bonus at its sister site?

Often you can’t. Many operator groups allow one welcome offer per customer across all their brands. Ask support before depositing, and expect the answer to depend on who holds the licence rather than on the brand’s name.

How often do new casinos launch in the UK?

There’s no fixed schedule. Launches arrive throughout the year as brand-new names, international arrivals or relaunches. Most comparison sites treat a casino as new for 12 to 24 months after launch, so check the launch date on any listing.

The main difference between offshore and locally licensed casinos is the rules they follow. Independent Game Testing at International Casinos

A licence and a testing certificate cover different things. Here’s what each one tells you and how provably fair games add a third check.

What the labs check

Independent testing labs such as eCOGRA, iTech Labs, Gaming Laboratories International (GLI) and BMM Testlabs examine the random number generator, the software that decides each spin or card. They also check the game maths, so the stated RTP matches how the game actually pays over time.

Why a certificate isn’t a licence

A lab certificate says the game behaves as described. It says nothing about how the operator handles your money, your complaints or your identity documents. Many internationally licensed casinos display both a licence badge and a testing seal, and you should click through each one. A badge that links nowhere proves nothing.

Provably fair results

Some crypto-friendly sites offer provably fair games. These publish data that lets you check each result yourself after the round, using a published code. Even the best international online casino sites only offer this on certain titles, mostly crash, dice, Mines and Plinko games.

Slots and jackpots

Slots fill most of any library, often from dozens of studios. Many titles come in several RTP versions: Play’n GO’s Book of Dead, for example, ranges from 96.21% down to 84.20%, so check the info panel. Bonus buy slots such as Gates of Olympus let you pay to enter the feature round directly, usually at around 100x your stake.

Progressive jackpots grow with every bet until someone wins. Network versions such as Mega Moolah and WowPot pool stakes from many sites, so the prize can climb into millions, while local jackpots stay within one casino and pay smaller sums more often.

Roulette, cards and live dealers

European roulette has a single zero and a house edge of 2.70%. French roulette adds La Partage, which hands back half an even-money stake when zero lands and cuts the edge on those bets to 1.35%. American roulette’s double zero raises the edge to 5.26%.

Blackjack and baccarat come in standard and side-bet forms. A blackjack that pays 6:5 instead of 3:2 on a natural adds roughly 1.4% to the house edge, so read the help screen first. Live tables stream real dealers, and game shows such as Crazy Time and Monopoly Live add a presenter and bonus rounds. The best international casinos often run tables in several languages around the clock.

In a crash game such as Aviator or JetX, a multiplier climbs until it stops without warning. Cash out in time or lose the stake. Aviator, for example, runs at a stated RTP of 97%. Instant games such as Mines and Plinko settle in a single click.

How to Register at an International Casino: Step by Step

Signing up properly from the start saves delays when you want to withdraw.

Check the licence on the regulator’s register and read the restricted-country list. If your country is excluded, stop there. Open the registration form from the site’s own domain, not from a pop-up or a copy site. Enter your real name, date of birth and address exactly as they appear on your ID. Mismatches are a common reason withdrawals get held. Choose an account in your own currency if one is offered. If not, read how currency conversion is charged before you deposit. Complete verification early by uploading your ID and proof of address straight away, rather than waiting until you’ve won. Set deposit limits in your account before your first payment. Some sites also offer loss and session limits. Read the payment and bonus terms, including which methods count towards a bonus and the maximum bet while one is active. You can decline a bonus if the terms don’t suit you. Make a small first deposit, then request a small test withdrawal. A smooth payout tells you more than any review.

FAQ

Can I sign up to offshore casinos from my country?

Yes, if your country isn’t on the site’s restricted-country list and local law allows it. You give up the protections your home regulator brings, such as national self-exclusion, capped bonus wagering and a local complaints process. You rely instead on whatever the foreign licence requires, which can be far less.

How do I know if a site is safe?

Start with the licence. Look the licence number up on the regulator’s register and check that the operator and domain match. Then look for testing certificates that link to a lab such as eCOGRA or iTech Labs, clear withdrawal terms and a sensible complaint history. Missing or broken links are a warning sign.

Which licences do these sites usually hold?

Common ones come from the Curacao Gaming Authority, the Malta Gaming Authority, Anjouan and the Kahnawake Gaming Commission. Tobique and Panama appear less often. Malta and Kahnawake publish the most about complaints, while Anjouan and Tobique offer little public information.

Will I be able to play in my own currency?

Often, yes. Many sites offer USD, EUR, GBP, CAD and AUD accounts alongside crypto. If yours isn’t offered, every deposit and withdrawal may be converted, and the rate can eat into your balance. Check the currency options before registering, because some sites won’t change them later.

How long do payouts take?

It depends on the method and the site’s own processing time. Crypto and e-wallets are usually quickest once approved, while bank transfers can take several days. Expect a delay on your first withdrawal while verification is checked, and watch for pending periods.

Do I still need to prove my identity?

Usually, yes. Some sites let you deposit and play with minimal checks, but most still ask for ID and proof of address before paying out. Uploading documents early avoids a long wait when you want to withdraw.

Does national self-exclusion stop me using these sites?

No. National schemes only cover sites licensed in that country. That’s exactly why offshore sites are no substitute if you’ve excluded yourself. Blocking software and support from Gamblers Anonymous or a national helpline are the better options in that case.

World.title: Belgrade Court Convicts Bosnian Serb Woman of Wartime Killings
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

The Higher Court in Belgrade has convicted Visnja Acimovic of participating in the killings of at least 30 Bosniak civilians at the Mracni dol site near Vlasenica in June 1992, according to a statement issued on Tuesday by the Humanitarian Law Centre NGO, which monitors war crimes trials.

The court sentenced Acimovic to 13 years in prison under the first-instance verdict, which can be appealed.

“The court did not give credence to statements from defence witnesses, the so-called ‘alibi’ witnesses, who claimed that Visnja Acimovic had been in Backa Topola [a town in Serbia] at the time of the crime, assessing that their statements were given with the aim of absolving her of guilt. The objectivity of these witnesses was also called into question due to the fact that they were members of her family,” the Humanitarian Law Centre said.

Acimovic did not attend the reading of the verdict. Her defence cited her poor health as the reason for her absence.

When deciding on the 13-year sentence, the Humanitarian Law Centre said the court took into account the fact that the defendant was a young adult at the time the crime was committed as a mitigating circumstance, while the number of civilians killed was taken into account as an aggravating circumstance.

Other members of the Bosnian Serb Army, some who have yet to be identified, also participated in the killing of the civilians at the Mracni Dol site.

The Bosnian state court has previously sentenced Predrag Bastah to 20 years in prison for his involvement in the killings.

According to the original indictment, Acimovic, together with several Bosnian Serb Army members, participated in the shooting of 37 Bosniak men committed in early June 1992 at the Mracni dol site near the Susica detention camp in the municipality of Vlasenica.

In 2020, the Bosnian state court asked the Serbian Ministry of Justice to take over the prosecution of Acimovic, for whom an Interpol warrant had been issued as she was no longer in Bosnia. Her trial began in Belgrade in November 2020.

World.title: Former Srebrenica Commander Oric Arrested in Attempted Murder Probe
World.content:
Naser Oric, a former commander of Bosniak forces in Srebrenica during the 1992-5 war in Bosnia, was arrested on Tuesday as part of an investigation into an attempted in East Sarajevo in August.

Jelena Miovcic, from the State Investigation and Protection Agency, SIPA, confirmed that Oric was arrested in the Olovo area in the country’s Federation entity.

Miovcic also confirmed that Nikolina Sljivic, a former member of the national assembly in Bosnia’s Republika Srpska entity, had also been arrested, adding that police are investigating the attempted murder of the man, named as Kosta Pandurovic, in East Sarajevo. Another man, Djordje Zdrale, currently on the run, is suspected of the attempted murder.

In another, related development, the Republika Srpska Interior Ministry, MUP RS, said it was carrying out an operation codenamed “Emisar” targeting an organised criminal group, with five people arrested so far.

“Searches are being conducted at several locations across Republika Srpska and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including properties owned by Djordje Zdrale, who is being actively sought by MUP RS,” the ministry said.

Bosnia’s top court, the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, previously sentenced Zdrale to 20 years in prison for the murder of Ljubisa Savic Mauzer, former head of the Republika Srpska Police Administration, in June 2000. He was released from prison in February 2022 after the Court of consolidated his sentences and determined he had served the combined sentence.

Oric earlier faced trial for war crimes but was acquitted.

In 2008, the Appeals Chamber of the UN International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, ICTY, acquitted Oric of failing to prevent the murder and cruel treatment of Serb prisoners. This ruling overturned a first-instance conviction.

In 2018, the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina acquitted him of murdering three Serb prisoners in the Bratunac and Srebrenica areas during the war in Bosnia.

World.title: Croatian Border Police ‘Doing Europe’s Dirty Work’ with Migrants: Report
World.content:
“The EU needs to act to ensure that Croatia respects EU law and protects the rights of those at its borders,” he added.

HRW interviewed more than 80 people for the report, including seven unaccompanied children, four children travelling with family members, and six parents travelling with their children. It also interviewed 15 aid workers and others who provide information and support to asylum seekers and migrants.

Those interviewed said Croatian police beat or kicked them, took their money, and confiscated or destroyed their phones. In some cases, they said, border police seized their documents, took their shoes or even forced them to strip to their underwear before pushing them back across the border.

“We told them that we are a family, but [the Croatian police] still took my husband away in one van and me and my daughters in another,” a woman from Ghana said.

“We were separated for two days from my husband. They pushed me and my daughters to Bosnia through the woods. No phone, no food, no water. We were walking all day. We were lost and scared for many hours,” she added.

“There were maybe 12 underage boys with us, about 16 or 17 years old. The [Croatian] police hit all these underage boys, same as the adult men,” Rasul, 31, from Pakistan, told HRW.

“When the police caught me, they beat me severely and we went back to the Croatian border in a police van … We had to run to the river and swim through the cold water, and the water was sometimes over our heads. I was scared,” Jamal A., a 17-year-old boy from Morocco, said in his testimony.

“There are mechanisms that the European Union should be using to try to insist on improvements, but I think above all what it shouldn’t be doing is continuing to turn a blind eye to consistent reports of abuse, very serious reports that this situation is ongoing,” Michael Garcia Bochenek told BIRN.

The Croatian government has not prosecuted any police officers for participating in pushbacks, even when people suffered serious injuries or extreme forms of humiliation. Seven officers received disciplinary sanctions for mistreating migrants between 2020 and 2025, the Croatian Interior Ministry told HRW.

BIRN sought a response from the ministry on the HRW report but had not received a response by the time of publication.

The Croatian government has, however, strengthened the mandate of a border monitoring mechanism established in 2021 with EU funding to prevent and address pushbacks and other abuses at the border. But the programme has had little impact on police pushbacks, HRW said.

EU failing to react

World.title: After ‘Propaganda’ Ban, Bulgarian LGBT Pupils Report Greater Insecurity
World.content:
After Bulgaria prohibited LGBTQ+ “propaganda” in schools in August 2024, teachers began approaching Vasil Lozanov with a question: can we still talk about it?

Thirty-three-year-old Lozanov teaches philosophy and civic education at Sofia’s Spanish High School. He also has a background in law.

“Experienced teachers, with years of experience both as people and as teachers, were in the dark about what they should do,” Lozanov told BIRN.

Lozanov did not change the way he taught. In lessons about tolerance, pupils write questions and comments on slips of paper anonymously; the papers are shuffled, selected and discussed. Sexual orientation is one of the subjects that usually comes up.

“I have never censored them and I have no intention of censoring them,” said Lozanov.

A familiar controversy

The issue of the billionaire’s conflicts of interest have been a recurring feature of Czech political life, dominating public debate ever since Babis entered politics and founded his populist ANO movement some 15 years ago.

The basis of one of the country’s biggest fortunes, Agrofert was founded by Babis in 1993, a sprawling conglomerate comprising about 200 companies active in agriculture, chemicals, transport, logistics, forestry and, until recently, the media sector.

With annual revenues of over 210 billion crowns (more than 8.5 billion euros) and employing nearly 30,000 people, Agrofert is the eighth most valuable Czech company, according to the latest Czech Elite ranking.

Babis’s ownership of such a ubiquitous company – and crucially, one of Czechia’s largest recipients of state subsidies – became a focus of public debate in 2014 when the Slovak-born businessman became deputy-prime minister and finance minister. Soon he was facing calls, including from his prime minister at the time, Bohuslav Sobotka, to give up his 100 per cent stake in Agrofert.

The ANO leader has consistently described accusations of a conflict of interest between his business activities and public involvement as a targeted defamation campaign designed to undermine his political ambitions – an argument he still employs to this day.

Passed in 2017, an amendment to the Conflict-of-Interest Act – dubbed “Lex Babis” – introduced guardrails against government members’ business activities, and barred them from accessing public procurement contracts or from running media companies.

Babis, who would go on to become prime minister later that year after a landslide election victory, initially transferred his shares in Agrofert and the SynBiol holding (a separate entity for Babis’s business interests in healthcare and real estate) into two trust funds.

From the start, however, this solution was deemed insufficient by legal experts like Transparency International, who pointed out that while no longer its direct owner, Babis nevertheless remained the conglomerate’s founder and ultimate beneficiary. A 2020 European Commission audit would eventually concur with this assessment.

Compared with the much broader EU rules on conflicts of interest, “the Czech regulation is much more specific, which allows some public authorities to navigate through it, saying that in some regards Mr Babis is in a conflict of interest, while in others he is not,” explains Krystof Dolezal, a lawyer for the Czech chapter of Transparency International.

“However, when it comes to the ban on public subsidies and public procurement, the Czech regulation is actually very severe,” he tells BIRN.

From European Parliament resolutions to Czech court rulings and a so-called “Lex Babis II”, rarely a month has gone by without the issue of Babis’s potential conflicts of interests making headlines.

History, it seems, was soon to repeat itself. Having resumed direct ownership of the holding after dissolving the trust funds in 2024 and 2025 when he was out of office, Babis’s ANO party once again claimed victory in last year’s parliamentary elections.

Now facing the obstacle of President Petr Pavel, who insisted he would not appoint him to form a government until an appropriate solution was found to alleviate any conflict-of-interest concerns, Babis was eventually sworn in after promising to distance himself from his businesses.

In February, he eventually transferred his Agrofert shares into a fund called RSVP Trust, which stands for Rodinna sprava a vlastnictvi (“Family Management and Ownership”).

World.title: Serbia’s New Leadership Won’t Transform Old Policy on Kosovo
World.content:
The spectacular victory of the Student List has reignited policy debates in Serbia that have grown dormant in recent years, given the grasp on power exerted by Aleksandar Vucic and the Serbian Progressive Party. Chief among them is the question of Kosovo and the process of normalisation.

Whilst the incoming government’s policy is unlikely to be fundamentally different, particularly when it comes to the question of Kosovo’s status, a change in approach will create distinct possibilities – and complications.

The Student List, as with other opposition parties in Serbia, has reiterated that it considers Kosovo to be an “inalienable and integral part of the Republic of Serbia”. This should not come as a surprise, given the centrality of the constitution to their platform.

While some voices within the Student List are more open to discussion about Kosovo, not least for the sake of Serbia’s European path, they will remain marginal for the foreseeable future. A criticism of consensus-driven approaches is that they tend to favour the lowest common denominator, with polarising issues approached with a degree of conservatism.

In the current context, this is understandable. The dilution of the EU perspective in the Serbian political space has undermined one of the key drivers of compromise over Kosovo. Should the government promote a more positive posture on EU membership – and on the reforms required to achieve it – then debates on Kosovo will be framed very differently.

In the meantime, Belgrade should keep its options open. Boxing itself into a corner, by suggesting that past agreements be reviewed and revised, risks further gridlocking the normalisation process.

World.title: Serbia’s Student Movement Criticises European Parliament’s Vukovar Resolution
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Serbia’s student movement, which under the name Student List won the country’s recent parliamentary elections, has criticised a European Parliament’s draft resolution marking the 35th anniversary of the fall of Vukovar in eastern Croatia, calling for adequate recognition of war crimes committed against Serb civilians during the Croatian conflict.

In a statement on the Student List – Students Win website on Monday, it said the resolution does not contribute to an “objective understanding of historical events” or to reconciliation. It argued that the draft resolution overlooks some of the suffering of Serb civilians in Croatia, including killings, persecution and mass displacement, particularly during the Croatian military operations Flash and Storm in 1995.

“Responsibility for war crimes must be individual and established on the basis of evidence and final court judgments, rather than attributed to entire nations,” the students said.

“Serbia has an obligation to cooperate in clarifying the fate of missing persons and establishing responsibility for crimes committed, but the same approach must also apply to Serb victims and crimes committed against them,” the student movement said.

The eastern border town of Vukovar fell to the Yugoslav People’s Army and Serb paramilitaries on November 18, 1991, during the war in Croatia, after which the remaining population was expelled. Two days after the town fell, Croatian prisoners and civilians were taken from Vukovar Hospital to a nearby farm where at least 200 people were executed.

The student movement warned that remembrance of the past should not deepen existing divisions in the region.

“True reconciliation cannot be achieved by imposing one-sided interpretations of the past, but through an honest reckoning with all crimes, regardless of who committed them or against whom,” they added.

The European Parliament was set to debate the resolution on Monday, with a vote scheduled for Thursday. The debate in Strasbourg follows the submission of two motions for a resolution on November 20, commemorating the victims of the siege of Vukovar and the atrocities that followed.

One of the motions, submitted by members of the European People’s Party, EPP, the Socialists and Democrats, S&D, the European Conservatives and Reformists, ECR, and the Greens/EFA, notes that 1,725 cases of missing persons from the war remain unresolved, including 1,341 people whose fate remains unknown and 384 whose deaths have been confirmed but whose burial sites have yet to be located.

It also calls on Serbia to grant access to relevant wartime archives, disclose information about the locations of individual and mass graves, fight against impunity for war crimes and facilitate the identification and return of victims’ remains to their families. The proposal further urges Serbia to adopt its long-announced law on missing persons.

The motion condemns the denial and glorification of war crimes, specifically referring to the public honours paid in Serbia to the convicted war criminal and former Bosnian Serb commander Ratko Mladic at his funeral in Belgrade in September 2026.

It further calls for educational, cultural and commemorative programmes that promote a “fact-based understanding of the Croatian Homeland War and the 1990s”, while encouraging reconciliation and respect for all victims.

The proposal acknowledges the work of the International Criminal Tribunal, ITCY, for the former Yugoslavia in prosecuting crimes committed in Vukovar, but adds that not all those responsible have been brought to justice.

The motion also highlights the peaceful reintegration of Serb-held eastern Croatian into Croatia in 1998 as an example of successful post-war reintegration and the importance of rebuilding trust between communities.

World.title: Bosnia’s Dodik Gathers Votes, Seeking Veto Over State Policy
World.content:
On November 9, Milorad Dodik, leader of Republika Srpska's governing Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD), handed Nebojsa Vukanovic, leader of the opposition For Justice and Order movement, a slip of paper containing the names of people who might join the governing bloc in Bosnia's Serb-majority entity.

Vukanovic had asked whose votes Dodik was counting on for his promised two-thirds majority in the new entity National Assembly.

Vukanovic read parts of the note to reporters. Three days later, Dodik said Vukanovic had skipped the name of Djordje Vucinic, a deputy elected on Vukanovic’s list. Vucinic denied that he was joining the governing parties.

By November 16, two deputies had switched sides to join Dodik's camp in the Republika Srpska assembly. Vladimir Copic, elected on the Serbian Democratic Party, SDS, list, joined United Srpska, a partner of Dodik’s SNSD.

Meanwhile Snjezana Gvozden left the Safe Srpska Movement, PSS, for the SNSD – and was elected an Republika Srpska assembly deputy speaker.

Bosnian law allows deputies who change parties to keep their seats, and Gvozden defended her move, saying that voters had given her the mandate. Whatever the outcome of complaints, people who voted for the two opposition lists have seen a seat won with their votes go to Dodik's bloc.

The governing bloc thereby grew from 54 to 56 seats in the 83-member Republika Srpska assembly. Dodik’s candidate for speaker, Nenad Stevandic, received only 52 votes, however. While his coalition in theory controlled two-thirds of the seats, it still had to show that it could deliver all 56 votes on the same decision.

World.title: Bulgaria issues warning of dangerous weather for November 23 over forecast strong winds
World.content:
Bulgaria’s national meteorological bureau has issued the Code Orange warning of dangerous weather for numerous districts for November 23 because of forecast strong winds.

The districts subject to the Code Orange warning are Vidin, Montana, Vratsa, Pleven, Veliko Turnovo, Sliven, Yambol, Haskovo, Plovdiv, Pazardzhik, Kurdzhali, Sofia city, Sofia district, Pernik and Lovech.

All other districts are subject to the lesser Code Yellow warning of potentially dangerous weather, also because of strong winds.

The meteorological bureau said that on the morning of November 23, a moderate and strong southerly wind will blow. It will be cloudy with rain in many places.

It will be relatively warm for the season, with minimum temperatures between 5° and 10° Celsius and maximums between 14° and 19°.

In the afternoon, cold air will flow in a temperatures will drop quickly and significantly.

In a separate announcement, the Road Infrastructure Agency said that from November 23, a serious cold snap with rain is expected, and in the morning hours, negative temperatures and icing conditions are expected.

“The Road Infrastructure Agency appeals to drivers to prepare their vehicles for winter conditions, to set off on the road only with suitable tyres, to drive at a reasonable speed and to keep a distance so as not to block traffic and the work of snow removal equipment,” the agency said.

The national road network has been in winter maintenance mode since November 16. The regional road departments and the involved companies are monitoring weather forecasts for timely treatment of the pavements, especially in the passes and high-mountainous regions, it said.

World.title: Gavriil, Bulgarian Orthodox Church Metropolitan of Lovech, dies at 76
World.content:
Bulgarian Orthodox Church Metropolitan of Lovech Gavriil died on November 22 after a short illness, the church’s governing body the Holy Synod said in a statement.

Gavriil, who had been Metropolitan of Lovech since January 28 2001, was 76.

“His Eminence will remain in the history of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church – Bulgarian Patriarchate as a proper hierarch, a zealous monk, a fervent prayer leader, a clergyman with deep and sincere faith, and a true follower of Christ, who not only with his words, but also with his entire life and deeds proclaimed the gospel truth,” the Holy Synod said.

The statement said that the Holy Synod would meet in special session to decide on the date and time of the funeral of Gavriil, and to appoint a temporary head of the diocese.

Gavriil was born on July 16 1950 in Sofia with the secular name Tsvetan Metodiev Dinev. He took monastic vows in 1979 at the Klisura Monastery St. Petka near Bankya.

He held various clerical posts, including as head of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church in Moscow, before being elected Metropolitan of Lovech.

In 2012, a check into the Holy Synod of the time by the Dossier Commission found that Gavriil was one of only four members of the church’s 15-member governing body for which there was no evidence that he had worked for communist-era secret service State Security.

More recently, Gavriil opposed the decision of the Ecumenical Patriarchate to grant autocephaly (church independence) to the Orthodox Church of Ukraine. Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew signed the decree in January 2019.

Metropolitan Gavriil was among the three candidates for Bulgarian Patriarch both in 2013, when Neofit was elected, and in 2024, when Daniil was elected.

Gavriil’s death creates a vacancy in the church’s governing body, for which an election will be held in the coming months.

In Bulgaria’s 2021 national census, close to 63 per cent of Bulgarians said that they identified as Eastern Orthodox Christians.

(Photo via the website of the Bulgarian Patriarchate)

World.title: EC approves Bulgaria’s final payment request under NextGenerationEU
World.content:
The European Commission said on November 20 that it has partially greenlighted Bulgaria’s fifth and final payment request for 1.82 billion euro under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) of the bloc’s NextGenerationEU post-pandemic economic recovery plan.

Bulgaria submitted the payment request on September 30, the deadline set by the European Commission, which aims to wind down the NextGenerationEU programme at the end of this year.

The Commission said that its assessment found that Bulgaria “has satisfactorily completed 53 out of 59 milestones and targets set out in the Council Implementing Decision.”

As such, the EC said that it would withhold part of the funds requested, but did not give an exact figure, noting only that it would be “proportional.”

Speaking to reporters in Sofia after the announcement, Deputy PM Atanas Pekanov, the Cabinet’s senior official tasked with securing RRF funds, said that Bulgaria was slated to receive more than 1.7 billion euro under the fifth payment request.

The policy areas in which Bulgaria pursued reforms and investments tied to this payment request include decarbonising the energy sector, strengthening the anti-corruption framework, enhancing the sustainability of transport and improving social inclusion and healthcare, the EC said.

The disbursement of the payment can be made after the Economic and Financial Committee, a body composed of senior officials from national administrations and central banks, the ECB and the EC, has issued an opinion on the Commission’s preliminary approval. It has four weeks to do so.

This is the second large RRF payment request received by Bulgaria this year, following 1.1 billion euro granted by the EC in June.

Due to years of political instability and short-lived governments, the country has lagged behind other EU member states in making the requests, raising the prospect that it could miss out on a significant amount of the 6.17 billion euro allocated to it under the RRF.

Pekanov said that this year’s two payment requests would take the amount received by Bulgaria under the RRF to between 98.7 per cent and 99 per cent of the allocated funding.

World.title: Bulgarian Parliament elects 11 members of Supreme Judicial Council
World.content:
Bulgaria’s National Assembly voted on November 20 to appoint 11 members of the country’s Supreme Judicial Council (SJC), the body tasked with the appointment of senior magistrates in Bulgaria’s judiciary.

Parliament held individual appointment votes for all 21 nominees. Vote tallies showed that the candidates that secured appointment were uniformly backed by the governing Progressive Bulgaria, alongside the opposition We Continue the Change (WCC) and Democratic Bulgaria.

The three parliamentary groups have a combined 168 MPs, enough to meet the qualified two-thirds majority of 160 MPs in the 240-seat National Assembly, required for the appointment of SJC members.

Most successful candidates, save three, were also backed by the opposition GERB and Movement for Rights and Freedoms (MRF) parties. Only pro-Kremlin party Vuzrazhdane, whose sole nominated candidate was not elected, voted against all successful appointments.

Of the 11 members of the SJC appointed by MPs on November 20, seven were nominated by Progressive Bulgaria and two apiece by WCC and Democratic Bulgaria.

The council has 25 members and is presided over by the Justice Minister, who is not, however, a member of the SJC. Of the 25 members, 11 are elected by Parliament, 11 by magistrates and three are members ex officio – the country’s prosecutor-general and the heads of the two high courts, the Supreme Court of Cassation and the Supreme Administrative Court.

The 11 members elected by magistrates are voted by their respective branches – six by judges, four by prosecutors and one by investigators. This last one is part of the prosecutors college of the SJC, as the National Investigative Service is subordinated to the prosecutor’s office in Bulgaria’s judiciary.

MPs similarly elect six members of the SJC to the judges college and five to the prosecutors college.

The current SJC line-up, often criticised as being unduly under the influence of MRF leader Delyan Peevski – who is subject to US sanctions under the Magnitsky Act – has been in office nearly five years past the expiration of its five-year term.

That is because Bulgaria’s pollical instability since 2021, which saw eight parliamentary elections in five years, resulted in fragmented parliaments, some of them very short-lived, that had little appetite for tackling the issue of electing SJC members.
