World.title: Thailand asks China to help halt Myanmar mines over toxic rivers
World.content:
Thailand is asking China to help shut mines in northeastern Myanmar for at least six months as it tries to stop arsenic pollution from flowing across the border into rivers used by communities and farmers.

The request came during talks Tuesday involving Thailand, China and Myanmar, according to Thai officials. Bangkok is seeking Beijing’s involvement because Chinese companies operate some mines in Myanmar’s Shan State, and much of the mineral output is shipped to China, according to Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow and Science and Research Minister Yodchanan Wongsawat.

China hasn’t issued its own readout of Tuesday’s talks. Its Foreign Ministry and embassy in Bangkok didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment on the Thai officials’ accounts or the proposed six-month shutdown. Beijing said earlier this month it wasn’t familiar with specific allegations involving Chinese companies but that it requires its firms to protect the environment and is willing to cooperate with Thailand on water pollution.

World.title: U.S. criticizes Australia social media law as harming free speech
World.content:
The U.S. ambassador to Australia said the country’s proposed legislation governing major technology firms will limit free speech and unfairly burden U.S. companies, laying the groundwork for a dispute over the measure.

Australia’s Digital Duty of Care bill is due to pass parliament this week. The legislation aims to reduce online harm by requiring digital service providers, including social media platforms and AI chatbots, to build safety into their products.

To secure enough votes for passage through parliament, Communications Minister Anika Wells agreed to give individuals the right to sue companies and raise maximum fines for breaches to as much as 5% of global revenue.

The U.S. quickly responded, with Ambassador David Brat saying in a social media post that the legislation and its fines will “push platforms to censor lawful speech.” The U.S. is concerned about “regulations that impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors,” Brat said, hours after meeting Wells to discuss the bill.

Wells described their first meeting as useful, saying both sides understood each other’s positions and were working through their differences.

“We won’t take a backward step from protecting Australian kids and helping Australian parents, and they won’t take a backward step from their position. And that’s always been the case on this,” she said.

World.title: Data on clients’ assets also leaked in recent Rakuten Securities breach
World.content:
Rakuten Securities, which was hit by a massive data breach earlier this month, has disclosed that the leaked information included the asset balance data of approximately 1.68 million client accounts.

The firm also said Tuesday some 14,000 sets of clients’ self-reported annual income and roughly 2.71 million entries of self-reported assets were compromised. These consisted solely of figures selected by clients from a list of options in questionnaires; it did not contain specific monetary amounts.

The company said it has so far found no evidence of unauthorized access to client accounts or fraudulent transactions related to the incident.

It said that about 4.41 million sets of personal information, including branch and customer codes, login IDs, names, dates of birth, addresses and telephone numbers, had been leaked. The firm initially reported on Nov. 17 that up to 4.47 million data sets were affected by the breach.

Of these, roughly 3.22 million data sets belong to account holders while some 1.19 million were of individuals who have given their information but have not opened accounts.

In addition to the items disclosed in its initial report, the company on Tuesday confirmed seven other categories of information affected by the breach: gender; nationality; fax numbers; information on accounts held with the company; account openings, application processing and cancellation statuses; account application questionnaire responses; and account registration statuses.

The company has also determined that login credentials and branch codes for approximately 11.98 million accounts were leaked during the breach.

It has found no evidence of compromised passwords, PINs or other information required to log in to Rakuten Securities or conduct transactions.

More than 60,000 people had registered their interest in pursuing a class-action lawsuit against Rakuten Securities as of Monday.

Makino Law Office in Tokyo, the firm that is organizing the potential legal action, said that the breach is more serious than other incidents, as it can provide bad actors with a list of people along with their assets and addresses, and can also be used to facilitate scams.

World.title: Industrial labor group to seek ¥17,000 pay scale hike
World.content:
The Japanese Association of Metal, Machinery and Manufacturing Workers (JAM) has decided to call for a pay scale increase of at least ¥17,000 ($107) per month in the 2027 shuntō (spring wage negotiations), sources said Tuesday.

JAM, the fifth-largest industrial labor group in trade union confederation Rengo, has about 1,900 member unions, mainly from small- and medium-sized manufacturers, with a total of some 390,000 workers.

The 2027 pay scale hike demand matches the record-high figure from the last round of negotiations, reflecting the association’s goal of reducing the pay gap between large and small companies.

Including the pay scale increase, JAM will call for total monthly pay increases of ¥21,500 or more. This compares with Rengo’s call for small unions to seek total pay hikes of at least ¥20,000.

JAM is set formally adopt its pay increase demands in January.

The association also plans to stress the need to secure funds for pay increases by appropriately raising the prices clients pay, as the business environment for small firms has become increasingly severe in part due to rising raw material and energy costs stemming from conflict in the Middle East.

World.title: NPB stars Sato and Taira agree to major MLB deals
World.content:
Two of Japanese baseball’s top players have found new homes in MLB.

Reigning Central League MVP Teruaki Sato has agreed to terms with the Chicago Cubs, while right-hander Kaima Taira has landed a contract with the Toronto Blue Jays, according to multiple media reports in the U.S.

Sato’s deal is worth $120 million across six years, according to ESPN reporter Jeff Passan, who also reported that Taira agreed to a five-year, $80 million contract that includes an opt-out after the third year and a $5 million signing bonus.

World.title: In landmine-ravaged Myanmar, a rebel with an artificial leg vows to fight on
World.content:
Late one January night, platoon commander Pee Litt led a group of Myanmar resistance fighters into a village in the country’s central Bago region, where eight of their comrades had been killed and their bodies left behind.

As he cleared a path across an area strewn with landmines, two blasts wounded his comrades before Pee Litt, himself, stepped on a mine.

“I had always known that if I stepped on one of these mines, I would lose my foot,” the 28-year-old said, recalling the explosion that tore off his right leg below the knee.

World.title: COVID-era tech heads to Antarctica to help track climate change
World.content:
Scientists will deploy technology in Antarctica that was used to detect the coronavirus in Singapore at the height of the pandemic, as they seek to better understand the effects of a changing climate.

Researchers will use portable canisters to capture airborne microbes, which can act as natural tracers and biological indicators of environmental change. Sampling will be conducted in parts of western Antarctica for the first time, helping to fill data gaps and provide a more detailed picture of global warming.

“It’s all about using these microbes to better understand wind or humidity patterns or weather conditions,” said Benjamin Horton, dean of the School of Energy and Environment at the City University of Hong Kong, who will lead the researchers on the trip. “We know that what happens in Antarctica has a significant influence on many people in the Southern Hemisphere.”

Changing weather in Antarctica has been linked to extreme temperatures and droughts in the Southern Hemisphere, and understanding shifts in polar regions is vital because the poles are crucial regulators of the world’s climate and serve as early-warning indicators. The 75-person expedition kicks off on Wednesday and is being led by famed British explorer Robert Swan.

Swan has championed the continent’s preservation for the past four decades and was the first person to walk both the North and South Poles. After 27 trips in nearly as many years, Swan said this would be the final Antarctica expedition he leads, his “swan song,” but he plans to keep raising awareness. “Antarctica is trying to tell us something, and people aren’t listening,” he said.

Antarctica is vital for understanding global warming because its huge ice sheets and surrounding oceans drive and track global climate shifts. The planet’s most remote frontier is losing ice mass at an average rate of about 135 billion tons per year, contributing to sea-level rise, while the continent has been lashed by unexpected weather events such as extreme rainfall.

Scientists also see the first-ever documented cases of bird flu on Antarctica’s mainland more than two years ago as part of a broader climate-driven shift in the spread of wildlife diseases. For Horton, who will be joined by high school students and undergraduates from Hong Kong and Singapore on the expedition, this trip will offer a new look at the continent. He was last there in 2023, documenting pollution and plastics in the ice sheets.

On this expedition, researchers will seek to capture microbes in parts of western Antarctica using SASS 3100 dry air samplers, equipment used to detect Covid-19 in Singapore including a hospital during the pandemic. They work like handheld vacuum cleaners and are considered more effective in freezing conditions, where liquid samplers can become less efficient.

Samples will be sent to a lab in Singapore for DNA analysis after the expedition ends on Dec. 2 to help understand which regions the microbes may have been carried from via winds and moisture. The findings will contribute to a global study of environmental health by Stephan Schuster, a professor at the School of Biological Sciences at Nanyang Technological University in the city-state.

“We increasingly know how important microbes are for environmental stability,” Horton said. “Can we identify any new microbes?”

World.title: China’s Shenzhou-24 space flight launches with first Pakistani national on board
World.content:
China’s Shenzhou-24 space flight launched successfully on Wednesday morning with its three-man crew including a Pakistani national, who will be the first foreign astronaut to board the Tiangong space station.

Using a Long March-2F rocket, the spacecraft took off at 8:18 a.m. from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in northwest China.

Zeeshan Ali, a 40-year-old pilot who will become the first Pakistani in orbit, will work as a payload specialist and is set to stay at the station for 5 to 10 days, conducting experiments.

He is accompanied by Chinese commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi.

China is promoting Tiangong as a hub for international cooperation while the NASA-led International Space Station faces possible retirement by 2030.

To prepare for the flight, Ali trained for seven months in Beijing, during which he underwent intensive Chinese-language classes, learning Chinese songs and reading Chinese poetry. He also practiced calligraphy and played table tennis.

“I’m not flying for myself. I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder,” Ali told reporters on Tuesday.

World.title: After Tai Po fire, will Hong Kong’s renovation industry overhaul crush triad activity?
World.content:
Promised reforms to wipe out bid-rigging and prevent another Tai Po fire tragedy are in the works for the building maintenance and renovation industry. On the anniversary of the deadly blaze, Edith Lin and Vivian Au talk to industry players about what needs to change.

Alfred Tang Yu-chi, director of Sun On Engineering, is steeling himself to re-enter Hong Kong’s embattled building maintenance and renovation industry after a sweeping overhaul following the devastating Wang Fuk Court fire.

World.title: Home advantage: can Hong Kong turn sports bodies’ arrival into global influence?
World.content:
The growing number of global and regional governing bodies making Hong Kong their home, coupled with the imminent arrival of a major legal organisation, will strengthen the city’s sporting influence worldwide, leading figures have told the South China Morning Post.

While Switzerland, where the International Olympic Committee, Fifa and the Court of Arbitration for Sport are headquartered, remains the undisputed seat of administrative power, officials believe Asia can challenge the European country’s standing.

Aside from being a gateway to mainland China, at the heart of the claim lies a slow but steady flow of groups relocating to Hong Kong, with the Asia Lacrosse Association (ALA) becoming the sixth to establish a regional headquarters in the city.

World.title: Bloom KKCA Academy prepares future-ready learners through project-based education
World.content:
Therefore, it is essential to develop talents and qualities in each individual which will allow them to thrive in that future environment, in both personal and career terms, and to have a positive impact on those around them.

One tenet guiding the teaching philosophy at Bloom KKCA Academy is that tomorrow’s leaders will need an entrepreneurial mindset to find their place in a world sure to be defined by constant change and new challenges.

“As we see it, entrepreneurship is not just about starting companies,” says Renée Boey, Bloom’s founder and head of school. “It is about showing initiative, possessing resilience, and demonstrating creativity and leadership. Looking ahead, we believe success will belong to those who can identify opportunities, collaborate well, communicate effectively, and come up with new solutions.”

To that end, the school combines standard curriculum subjects with units of project-based learning at both primary and secondary levels to encourage ideas, experimentation and an interdisciplinary approach.

It also makes a point of giving pupils real-world experience outside the classroom, whether through sustainability investigations, industry visits and community-based projects in Hong Kong, or through immersive programmes such as archaeological fieldwork in England and project-based learning at Tian Zhen Yuan in China, where students engage in interdisciplinary studies that combine culture, wellbeing, science and environmental learning.“Everything we are doing began with a question: what if we designed a school for the world children would grow up in, not the one we already know?” says Boey, who has more than 20 years’ diverse experience as an educator and teacher. “Our education model is based on the concept of ‘care, think, act’ and the holistic development of students, which includes well-being, a positive mindset, the right values, and engagement with the community.”

The school opened in 2021 with bilingual primary classes, providing learning experiences in both English and Putonghua, which now run from Grades 1 to 6. A secondary section, Smart Too Bloom Academy, followed in 2024 and an extra grade is being added each year as the original joiners move up to more senior levels.

Lower secondary students follow the Key Stage 3 (UK) curriculum with the full range of subjects from languages and humanities to mathematics, science and computer science, but there are then options to continue to International A-Levels, take the local DSE curriculum in Putonghua, or follow a US-accredited pathway. The school emphasises that project-based learning complements rather than replaces academic rigour, with students building strong foundations in languages, mathematics, science and the humanities.During a typical school day, mornings are for core subjects, with afternoons then dedicated to co-curricular project-based assignments with an emphasis on STEM themes, investigating problems, and becoming familiar with AI.

“The projects all involve learning by doing and real-life experiences,” Boey says. “Students don’t just create something by the end of a unit, but also have to show a deeper understanding by explaining what they learned and how it can be applied beyond the classroom.”

Outside experts are invited in to offer advice and suggestions, and Fridays are often reserved for field-based learning experiences, perhaps at a sustainable farm, a game design studio, a social enterprise, or local business connected to students’ project work.

To back that up, the school has its own science labs and makerspace workshop to encourage children to keep trying new things and to feel no constraints when doing so.

“The aim is to open doors, not close them, by helping young people notice what matters and want to do something about it,” says Boey, adding that the school currently has a total of around 330 students and room to grow. “We are now in the fourth year of our project-based programme and are confident in both its impact on students and our ability to deliver it effectively."As a sign of that, an upcoming trip is being organised for senior pupils to Malaysia and Singapore, with a focus on the commercial practicalities of game design, as well as sustainability initiatives.

Those who join the China study tour will have the chance to learn more about everything from Taoism, calligraphy and Chinese literature to agriculture, biodiversity and traditional Chinese medicine.

“There will be a lot packed into each trip and a lot for students to unpack afterwards,” Boey says. “We trust our teachers to develop follow-on programmes which will build on the main themes and weave them into other elements of the curriculum. This gets the juices flowing and helps to inspire the next generation.”

Recognising that the world of work will look substantially different even a few years from now as AI, robotics and nanotechnologies reshape industries and professions, the school is preparing students to solve problems and make decisions, rather than see the future in terms of specific jobs.“Knowledge, though, remains essential; you can’t think critically about something you don’t understand,” Boey says. “Therefore, we are cultivating the qualities we think will be most important – intellectual curiosity, sound judgement, courage to take the initiative, and the ability to adapt.

“Looking ahead, the world will need the type of people who can also show empathy and compassion and are comfortable dealing with uncertainty.”

Two examples of secondary entrepreneurship education:

Sustainable fashion

Bloom students integrate digital tools and foundational design principles into their creative projects. From research and field visits to business pitches and direct engagement with buyers, they conclude by running a Sales day event to introduce their T-shirt designed with sustainable fashion embedded at a local fashion chain, ‘Determinant’.

Food innovation

The CEO of Gingko House, Mr. Kenneth Choi, joined Bloom students for a dialogue during their field visit, inspiring them to link their classroom learning of the “Triple P” model (Profit, People, Planet) directly to real-world business practice. Combined with a baking workshop led by Gingko House’s elderly staff, this experience was a prelude to Bloom students’ design of their own enterprise proposals for the elderly community.

World.title: Ex-husband named his father as Abby Choi’s killer to avoid charges, court hears
World.content:
The former husband of the late Abby Choi Tin-fung has complained that police misled him into giving an inaccurate statement about who murdered the Hong Kong socialite, saying he thought he could avoid prosecution by naming his father as the killer.

Alex Kwong Kong-chi told the High Court on Tuesday that he had previously volunteered to testify against his father, Kwong Kau, in exchange for prosecutors dropping a murder charge against him.

Testifying under cross-examination, the defendant said police misled him into giving a three-page statement in February this year as he was under the impression it would not be used to incriminate himself.

World.title: Gleneagles Hospital Hong Kong’s eHealth access suspended after leak of patients’ data
World.content:
Hong Kong health authorities have suspended the eHealth registration of Gleneagles Hospital following a suspected leak of patients’ data through the private hospital’s mobile app.

On Tuesday, just hours after Gleneagles Hospital Hong Kong disclosed unauthorised access to its mobile app for patients, the Health Bureau said it had paused the hospital’s registration with eHealth, the electronic records platform developed by the government, and disconnected its link to the platform.

“During this period, Gleneagles Hospital Hong Kong will not be able to obtain or provide the electronic health records of registered healthcare recipients through eHealth, so as to ensure the system security and integrity of eHealth,” the bureau said in a statement.

World.title: Beijing warns against exploiting Tai Po fire to destabilise Hong Kong
World.content:
Beijing has urged Hong Kong to remain vigilant against attempts to “exploit disasters” to destabilise the city ahead of the first anniversary of the deadly Tai Po fire, warning that any efforts to provoke social division and undermine the government will not succeed.

Commentaries published on Tuesday by the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office (HKMAO) and Beijing’s liaison office in the city praised Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s administration for its post-disaster relief efforts and work on reforms.

World.title: Nobel laureate leads University of Hong Kong study to spot diseases early
World.content:
The University of Hong Kong (HKU) has launched a 20-year study tracking blood samples from 15,000 locals to build an affordable screening tool that spots cancer, diabetes, cardiovascular diseases and chronic respiratory illnesses before symptoms appear.

The “Protecting.Health Hong Kong” study, launched by HKU’s Institute for Precision Prevention on Tuesday, is led by its director Professor Ferenc Krausz, a 2023 Nobel laureate in physics who was recently recruited by the university.

The long-term study will enrol 15,000 people aged 40 to 70 in Hong Kong. It comprises a 10-year active follow-up period involving repeated clinical assessments and blood sample collection, followed by another 10 years of health data collection.

World.title: Have the 7 construction players linked to Tai Po fire been dealt with?
World.content:
The role of unscrupulous private sector players was exposed by the deadly Tai Po fire and even as authorities have vowed reforms and made arrests, some can still operate, as Lam Ka-sing finds out in this series marking the anniversary of the blaze.

Former Wang Fuk Court resident Betty Ho Pui-shan cannot understand why professionals and contractors blamed in a report on the deadly blaze can still keep working and hold on to their licences a year after the tragedy in Tai Po.

“The report named them but they can just keep doing what they do. I don’t think the authorities are listening at all,” the 61-year-old retiree said.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019309/A Simple Question About Leftovers Divides China’s Internet
World.title: A Simple Question About Leftovers Divides China’s Internet
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019309/A Simple Question About Leftovers Divides China’s Internet
World.content:
“Xiao Ming and his mom and dad are eating out at a restaurant. After they finish eating, his mom wants to take home the leftovers, but his dad thinks it’s unbecoming. What would you do and say if you were Xiao Ming?” poses a Chinese exam question.

“If I were Xiao Ming, I would tell my mom not to pack the leftovers because we have plenty of money, and it would be embarrassing if people saw us doing so,” one student responds.

This answer to a primary school Chinese language exam question has sparked online debate over how schools should balance encouraging children to express their opinions with promoting moral values, with a related hashtag attracting over 46 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Tuesday.

The controversy began when the parent of a third-grader in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province, shared a photo of the assignment alongside their child’s answer in a WeChat parent group, which was later leaked, according to domestic media. The child’s teacher marked the answer incorrect, deducting all four potential points. Above, a large red check mark adorns a revised answer written by the student that states: “1) I would pack the leftovers with my family. 2) I would tell my dad that all food is grown through the hard work of farmers, and we shouldn’t waste it just because we’re afraid of losing face.”

Many social media users pointed out the apparent conflict between nurturing critical thinking and penalizing it. “It’s unreasonable to punish students for such answers in a Chinese language exam,” one user wrote. “While it may appear to promote ‘the right values,’ deducting scores as a means of enforcement only teaches children to lie to get what they want.”

Others agreed with the teacher, saying that schools also have a responsibility to help children develop sound values and moral judgment. “(Children) should be encouraged to think outside the box, but their ideas must be grounded in the correct values,” wrote another user.

In recent years, China has sought to curb food waste, enacting the Anti-Food Waste Law in 2021 to cut waste across the food supply chain. In 2020, the Ministry of Education also urged schools to teach frugality and the importance of reducing leftovers. Authorities have also cracked down in recent years on banquets, discouraging excessive food ordering as a display of wealth and generosity.

Zhao Tongwei, a senior teacher and principal of Shanghai-based Shengqiao Central Primary School, told local media that the student’s response reflected a tension between attitudes absorbed from everyday life and the values schools seek to promote.

“Chinese language education is about more than teaching practical skills; it also has a humanistic and educational role. Upholding sound values is a principle that must not be compromised,” he said.

The aim, Zhao said, should be to help students think for themselves. Simply deducting marks could discourage children from expressing what they genuinely believe, he warned, and instead advocate reflection through writing exercises, one-on-one conversations, or whole-class discussions on the topic.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019315/Singled Out: What’s Behind the Mismatch on China’s Marriage Market?
World.title: Singled Out: What’s Behind the Mismatch on China’s Marriage Market?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019315/Singled Out: What’s Behind the Mismatch on China’s Marriage Market?
World.content:
Almost 30 years ago, Carrie Bradshaw opened the TV phenomenon “Sex and the City” with a question: “Why are there so many great unmarried women, and no great unmarried men?” Later, she backs up her assertion with data, declaring that “there are 1.3 million single men in New York, (and) 1.8 million single women.”

Carrie was speaking about turn-of-the-millennium New York, but women in major Chinese cities such as Beijing and Shanghai will have little problem understanding her plight. Marriage rates have declined across the board in recent years, but the drop has been felt most keenly by two very different groups: urban women and rural men.

To get an idea of the problem, take a map of China and color each prefecture-level city red if men there are more likely to be single than women, and blue if the reverse is true. The result is striking. Less developed inland provinces such as Yunnan, Guizhou, and Gansu turn deep red. The country’s richest urban clusters — the Yangtze River Delta, the Pearl River Delta, and the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region — turn deep blue. The line between them follows, almost exactly, the line between China’s poorer and wealthier regions.

In other words, China’s cities are full of highly educated single women. In less developed areas, singles are disproportionately men with little education.

China’s skewed sex ratio can explain why there are more single men than single women overall. Yet it cannot fully explain the geographic distribution of single men and women. For its part, media coverage tends to oversimplify the phenomenon as a problem of willingness, with young Chinese rejecting the concept of marriage altogether.

But is that true? Our research, based on two decades of data from national population censuses and the comprehensive China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) surveys, paints a more complete — and complex — picture of how demographic transformation in educational attainment, regional imbalances in skills and industries, and cultural norms have contributed to China’s unbalanced marriage market.

Let’s start with education. Over the past several decades, Chinese women have quietly but quickly caught up with men in educational attainment. Among Chinese born between 1960 and 1995, the education gap between men and women steadily narrowed. For the cohort born around 1985, women college graduates outnumber their male counterparts. And for Chinese born in the mid-1990s or later, the gap in women’s favor is large and continues to widen, especially at the postgraduate level.

This shift coincided with a decisive transformation in China’s economic structure. The services sector, which is disproportionately concentrated in major cities, has grown, drawing women, especially those with degrees, out of agriculture and manufacturing. In 2000, college-educated women were 17 percentage points less likely than college-educated men to work in the services sector; by 2015, they were 21 points more likely to hold such positions.

Service jobs — whether in finance, professional services, education, health care, or technology — cluster in big, wealthy cities, and so do the women who hold them. But while China’s educational and employment landscape has transformed dramatically, marriage norms haven’t. Census data show a strong and remarkably stable pattern of hypergamy, in which women marry men with higher socioeconomic status. This norm spans regions and educational backgrounds, meaning that urban women with higher degrees also tend to marry those who are more educationally and professionally advanced than they are.

This norm made sense in a world in which men were usually more educated than women. In a new reality where urban women are more likely to attend college and have a decent job, it becomes counterproductive for matchmaking.

Together, these three factors have contributed to a mechanical mismatch. But how can we quantify it? After all, no one can run a real-world experiment on national marriage rates.

To find the answer, we built a model of a counterfactual parallel world — one in which gender differences in education, occupation, and migration patterns in 2015 were the same as they were in the year 2000.

In that counterfactual world, the national singles rate, defined as the proportion of individuals who stay single from the earliest legal marriage age to the time they turn 45, falls by roughly 30% for women and 12% for men. In developed cities, the female singles rate drops by nearly 40%, and among highly educated women there, by more than half.

About one-third of this drop comes from the narrowing education gap; the other two-thirds comes from the reduction of service jobs in large cities available to women in this hypothetical world.

What does that mean for the future? While we do not have access to perfect projections, if the gender gap in educational attainment and service sector employment in developed cities merely widens at the same speed from 2015 to 2030 as it did between 2000 and 2015, our model suggests that by 2030, the singles rate among highly educated women in developed cities will rise to 15.2% — roughly one in seven. Meanwhile, among low-skilled men in less developed regions, it will rise from 8.7% to 12%, or about one in eight.

Of course, history is rarely linear. The Chinese government has made marriage rates and fertility rates a top priority, with local officials experimenting with all kinds of interventions and welfare policies to prevent marriage rates from entering a free fall. Some regions have even introduced cash rewards for newlyweds.

But our findings raise questions about the effectiveness of such policies, showing that financial incentives alone are not enough to reverse the trend. Using our model, we expect a subsidy as high as 10% of household income to lower the national female singles rate from 3.46% to 3.17% and the male singles rate from 8.17% to 7.89%.

This is because no amount of money can conjure up a partner who fits traditional expectations. Other interventions, such as encouraging more educated men to move to big cities or encouraging more educated women to move back to smaller cities, might work on paper, but they would raise serious gender fairness questions by effectively punishing educated women.

What is urgently needed is a rethink of hypergamic norms. Educated women should be celebrated as proof of the transformative power of education, migration, and hard work. They are no longer passive participants in a marriage market, but active planners of their own lives who can and should choose partners regardless of educational and financial status.

Men must also adjust their expectations to accommodate partners who may not meet hypergamic norms. And the gatekeepers of those norms — families and relationship gurus among them — must catch up with contemporary society, realizing that no single mode of relationship is the key to a fulfilling life.

It is likely that the red and blue on China’s marriage map will grow darker in the coming years. Yet nothing is set in stone. After all, even Carrie Bradshaw eventually found love.

Huang Zibin of Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Wang Yushi of Hainan University, and Yang Yu of Peking University made equal contributions to this research.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019305/Chinese Archaeologists Announce Findings From Four Key Sites
World.title: Chinese Archaeologists Announce Findings From Four Key Sites
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019305/Chinese Archaeologists Announce Findings From Four Key Sites
World.content:
Chinese archaeologists have announced discoveries from four sites across the country, including Paleolithic campsite ruins and greater details of an aristocratic cemetery of the Neolithic Liangzhu culture.

The findings, announced at a Wednesday conference held by China’s National Cultural Heritage Administration, come from four years of work at four sites along the Yangtze River. They include Taohuahe in the southwestern Sichuan province; Fanshan in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province; Lingtoushang in the eastern Jiangxi province; and Laohudun in the central Hubei province.

The discoveries were presented by Archaeology China, a government program launched in 2018 to fund long-term excavations investigating the origins of farming and civilization.

Taohuahe, discovered in 2022, has yielded over 13,000 Paleolithic-age stone artifacts, including large stone choppers, and 179 animal fossils dating from 300,000 to 50,000 years ago, researchers at the conference announced. Excavations have also revealed stone-working and storage areas, cobblestone surfaces, and a semicircular refuse pit.

Wang Youping, an archaeologist at Peking University, told domestic media that, unlike in other archaeological digs in southern China, numerous animal bones have been recovered at Taohuahe.

“Southern China’s acidic soil usually destroys bone,” Wang said. “Researchers had assumed that people in the lush south relied mainly on plants. The (presence of animal) bones suggests that meat was equally important to their work, daily lives, and evolution.”

The second site discussed at the meeting, Fanshan, was discovered 40 years ago and is the highest-ranking aristocratic cemetery of the Neolithic Liangzhu culture ever found, researchers said. The Liangzhu culture, located in northern present-day Hangzhou, flourished about 5,000 years ago. UNESCO added the ruins of its walled city and system of dams and reservoirs to its World Heritage List in 2019.

Excavations that began in 2024 indicate that a walled compound enclosed the site’s cemetery mound. At least three buildings stood at its center, including a large oval structure raised on stilts, likely used for ceremonies. The compound lies on a ridge that formed part of the surrounding area’s water system, leading researchers to hypothesize that the tombs, ritual spaces, and dams were planned as a single complex.

After last year’s discovery of a courtyard wall at the Fanshan site, archaeologists uncovered a group of three related buildings this year. Wang said the wall may have formed the cemetery’s outer boundary, while the buildings may have served as sacrificial halls. He added that the culture may already have had a mausoleum system.

Researchers also announced at the conference that they have discovered Neolithic and Shang dynasty (c.1600–1046 BC) settlements at a third site, Lingtoushang. The settlements contained evidence of smelting and large quantities of copper, shedding light on close cultural exchange and how the societies exploited and controlled metal resources.

Excavation of the fourth site, Laohudun cemetery in Hubei, began this year. According to researchers, the area contains the highest concentration of Qin dynasty (221–206 BC) tombs in southern China.

At the site, archaeologists unearthed bamboo and wooden slips — writing materials used before the invention of paper — along with numerous inscribed lacquerware and wooden artifacts. The inscriptions cover a wide range of topics, including politics, military affairs, literature, medicine, folklore, and art, offering greater insight into society at the time.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Stone artifacts found at the Taohuahe site in Sichuan province. From the National Cultural Heritage Administration)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019307/Lost Ground: China’s Coffee Brands Break Starbucks and Nestlé’s Grip on Yunnan
World.title: Lost Ground: China’s Coffee Brands Break Starbucks and Nestlé’s Grip on Yunnan
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019307/Lost Ground: China’s Coffee Brands Break Starbucks and Nestlé’s Grip on Yunnan
World.content:
For coffee growers in China’s southwestern Yunnan province, Starbucks and Nestlé used to be the only buyers in town. Every harvest season, their purchasing stations would have lines of loaded trucks stretching for days.

Plantation owner Zou Qingquan recalls once waiting a whole week to sell her beans to Nestlé. Back then, she says, the company revised its purchase price twice a week based on changes in the international commodity market, “so your beans were making or losing money as they sat there in the truck.”

Over the past five years, however, these two global giants have been losing their grip on the Yunnan coffee market. Rapid growth among domestic brands such as Seesaw, Manner, Luckin, and the Mixue Group, along with a shift toward specialty coffee, has opened new sales channels for farmers and pushed up prices.

According to the agricultural industry analysis platform Beedata, Nestlé and Starbucks paid an average of 48.09 yuan ($7.20) and 48.18 yuan per kilogram, respectively, for commercial-grade Yunnan green beans in the first quarter of 2026. For Luckin, it was 50.37 yuan.

But while growers’ incomes have risen, some warn that an increasingly indiscriminate buying frenzy, which in some cases is leading to the sale of unripe beans, risks disrupting established trade relationships and negatively affecting the quality and image of Yunnan coffee.

Light roast

Ma Xiaojin, who manages two coffee-growing cooperatives in Yunnan’s Menglian Dai, Lahu and Va Autonomous County, used to regularly drive the 10 hours from his farm to the Starbucks Farmer Support Center, a training and purchasing facility in central Pu’er, a city arguably best known for its eponymous tea. There, he’d join the line of trucks and wait four or five days to have his beans graded, costing him at least 2,000 yuan in truck rental costs.

Starbucks has exacting quality standards and purchases beans only from growers certified under its Coffee and Farmer Equity (CAFE) Practices program, which in January included 3,400 farms in Yunnan. The American company is also known for paying more for high-quality beans than its Swiss competitor, Nestlé.

“You can’t just show up and expect Starbucks to take your beans,” says Hao Yi, who used to work for Starbucks in coffee production. “They don’t just check each batch; they monitor your quality over several consecutive years. That’s why, in the early days, getting your beans into Starbucks was a source of pride. It also brought your subsequent harvests to the attention of specialty coffee roasters.”

In 2017, Starbucks began selling selected Yunnan beans as part of its high-end Reserve line. For growers, making the cut was no easy feat. If their products passed a preliminary check, they had to provide three large samples from each sack for testing and agree to follow-up screenings.

Specialty beans from Zou’s estate were selected in 2021, with Starbucks offering 48 yuan per kilogram. At the time, her farm was selling to the open market for more than 60 yuan per kilogram. “We earned less, but working with a big brand was good publicity for us, so it was still a net gain,” she says. The following year, many new buyers approached Zou to purchase the same beans.

Nestlé and Starbucks’ strong bargaining power stemmed not only from their steady and large purchasing orders but also from their role in establishing industry rules and standards in the region. In 1989, Nestlé introduced the province to catimor, an arabica coffee cultivar popular for its high yields and resistance to coffee leaf rust, while Starbucks has helped standardize commercial production here since the late 2000s.

Both companies also set up local agricultural support centers, dispatching agronomists to train farmers and promote good practices. Ma, whose beans were selected for the Starbucks Reserve line in 2025, remembers training sessions taking place every month or two in the early days.

“The older generation of coffee growers is very grateful to Nestlé,” says Zhang Yong, founder of Pushan Coffee, a local bean trading company. He notes that while visiting Yunnan’s coffee-growing regions last year, he found multiple farmers who were still willing to sell to the Swiss company even though its prices were lower than other brands.

However, not everyone has remained loyal to the two biggest players. On a recent trip to Pu’er, Hao talked with coffee growers and traders who said they had sold very little to Starbucks in 2025. One farmer whose beans had previously been selected for the Reserve line revealed he was now targeting other specialty coffee brands that pay more.

Ma’s two cooperatives produce 120 to 130 tons of beans a year. More than half of this output used to go to Starbucks, but over the past two years this has fallen to just over 10 tons of Reserve-grade coffee.

“It’s hard enough to buy beans in Pu’er, but it’s even more competitive in Baoshan,” Hao says. Baoshan, Yunnan’s other main coffee-growing area, is almost 10 hours by road from the Starbucks Farmer Support Center in Pu’er. With the demand for beans soaring, few are now willing to make the trip.

Working with Starbucks and Nestlé once brought huge pride and prestige, but Ma believes that the global titans’ stringent standards are increasingly seen as “too demanding,” particularly by younger farmers. It’s just easier to sell directly to smaller companies, he adds.

Taste test

Seesaw and Manner, both founded in the eastern metropolis of Shanghai, were among the first domestic coffee brands to establish a presence in Yunnan.

After launching a 10-year plan in 2014, Seesaw sent buyers to teach growers in Pu’er and Baoshan refined harvesting and processing techniques, and introduce them to specialty coffee.

Hua Runmei, a third-generation coffee grower from Pu’er, took over the family farm in 2015 after graduating from university. That year, international coffee futures — the global benchmark for pricing — were depressed, and Yunnan beans were typically sold cheap.

She agreed to transition toward growing specialty coffee in collaboration with Seesaw, which assigned a technician to guide her and assist with processing. “They tell us what they’re looking for, coffee with a clean taste and certain flavor notes, and we need to figure out how to achieve that,” Hua explains.

Her farm delivered its first 3 tons of specialty coffee beans to Seesaw in 2016. The following year, the company placed an order for 40 more.

Manner, which operates about 2,000 outlets nationwide, entered the Yunnan market in 2018, opening purchasing stations in Menglian and Baoshan. “It’s not just about a commitment to buying local. Yunnan beans are genuinely high-quality,” Wang Xu, an executive assistant to Manner CEO Jin Binbin, told the domestic media outlet Kankan News in March 2025.

The shift toward specialty coffee brought greater financial returns for growers. Hua recalls that many brands offered favorable prices and advance payments. “I think the brands that came to Yunnan in the early days were genuinely driven by a passion for locally grown coffee,” she says.

Brands generally set prices for premium beans based on production costs, allowing farms a profit margin of about 20%. They would pay up to 40% above the international futures price, sometimes more depending on the beans’ flavor profile. This not only secured beans that met their specific requirements but also encouraged growers to continue investing in cultivation and processing.

However, as domestic brands expanded, specialty coffee prices began to align with those for bulk-bought commodity coffee. “Starting around 2019 or 2020, companies changed the way they purchased beans,” Hua says. “Everyone started to want coffee that was both good and cheap.”

What emerged was a new category of bean between commodity-grade and specialty: premium commercial beans. These beans don’t have distinct flavor notes, but they do have cleaner flavor profiles and lower defect rates than standard commercial-grade beans, and typically sell for 1 to 3 yuan per kilogram more than the international futures price.

Specialty coffee brands bought relatively limited quantities of these beans. The real force reshaping supply and demand in Yunnan was companies with larger needs, such as Mixue Group and Luckin.

Mixue, a food and beverage giant based in Zhengzhou, capital of the central Henan province, acquired the budget coffee chain Lucky Cup in 2020 and expanded it as a franchise, requiring vast quantities of beans. After visiting dozens of farms, the company decided to offer freshly brewed Yunnan coffee in all of its 20,000 outlets nationwide and signed agreements with several growers for their green beans.

Chen Junxian, whose trading company Senyu Coffee was among Mixue’s first suppliers in Yunnan, recalls that local farmers and processing plants were initially lukewarm toward the Zhengzhou company, best known at the time for its ice cream and tea products.

“People didn’t really know the brand,” he explains. “They thought it was purely a milk tea company and didn’t believe it actually wanted to buy coffee beans. Now the processing plants are far more friendly.” Chen says that orders from Mixue to his business alone have nearly doubled since 2020. “We’re delivering a lot.”

The largest buyer of Yunnan beans in 2026 has been Luckin, headquartered in Xiamen, in the eastern Fujian province. Unlike other brands, which sent teams to purchasers in the region, Luckin relied for years on trading companies to handle procurement. It wasn’t until 2024 that it built its own coffee processing plant in Baoshan.

During Luckin’s Q1 2026 earnings conference call in April, co-founder and CEO Guo Jinyi announced the company had purchased more than 30,000 tons of Yunnan coffee during the 2025–26 harvest season. According to government-run news outlet Yunnan.cn, Luckin’s target is 80,000 tons a year by 2030.

For growers, the expanding market has led to enormous orders, more flexible requirements compared with Starbucks and Nestlé, and higher prices. For domestic brands, Yunnan beans mean lower transportation costs and provide an opportunity to tell the story of China-grown coffee.

Fresh take

The challenge now is keeping up with the huge demand. Industry insiders point out that even if coffee plants were grown in every suitable place in China, there would still be a supply shortage.

Chen, who started his business in 2018, says most Yunnan growers were struggling to make a profit before the market boom. Now their beans are a hot commodity, they no longer seek his help to find buyers — he needs to beg them to sell to him.

“Many aren’t comfortable with digital communication; you have to meet them in person,” says Chen, explaining that his team had to visit countless plantations, processing plants, and even farmers’ homes to secure enough beans to fill orders. This involved traipsing across sparsely populated countryside and driving 13 hours between various counties across Pu’er and Baoshan.

The thriving local economy has also attracted many Yunnan natives to return home to open coffee farms, while Pu’er tea growers have even cut down trees to make space for more coffee plants.

Some farms are also taking a chance on rare and prestigious varieties, such as Geisha, which can command a price of up to 1,500 yuan per kilogram. However, Zhang is concerned for those rookie growers who expect to sell the beans from their newly planted trees for less than 500 yuan per kilogram.

“They are investing heavily, perhaps recklessly,” he says. Geisha plants take at least three years to bear fruit and typically reach peak production around six to eight years old. No one knows what the market will look like by then, Zhang adds.

Trouble brewing?

As the buying frenzy continues, concerns about quality also grow.

Last year, Ma had to reject a whole batch of beans delivered by one of the farms he manages. “They were so bad that I couldn’t stand looking at them,” he recalls.

Coffee cherries ripen at different times, so pickers typically make three or four passes over the three- to four-month harvest season, selecting only fully ripened cherries to ensure quality and consistency. Now, in the haste to satisfy demand, some growers are cutting corners, making only two passes and picking unripe green cherries together with ripe red ones.

“Some people are willing to buy beans like these. I just don’t understand it,” Ma says. “If people keep harvesting so carelessly, in another two or three years, Yunnan coffee will be worthless.”

Chen sees the same problem. Once the outer fruit has been removed, it’s extremely difficult to distinguish between ripe and unripe beans during sorting, increasing the risk of defects. When his company tried to enforce quality standards at the source, growers simply told him that if he didn’t buy their cherries, someone else would. “There’s nothing we can do; we have to buy them,” Chen says.

When prices were 20 to 30 yuan per kilogram, his company would take green beans classified as Grade 1 — the highest level, applying to plump, unbroken beans measuring at least 6.5 millimeters — and sort through them again to try to reduce the defect rate.

But when ripe and unripe cherries are harvested together, quality control becomes impossible. “At prices above 60 yuan per kilogram, even a 4% loss is a huge amount of money. We can’t afford to do it anymore. We have no choice but to bow to market pressure,” Chen adds.

Even with a 5% defect rate, the market average, Chen’s company had sold its entire inventory by the end of April 2025.

Nestlé originally chose Yunnan because it provided a stable, low-cost source of beans for its instant coffee factory in the southern Guangdong province. Later, domestic coffee brands came to capitalize on both the market appeal of the homegrown coffee story and the logistical advantages.

However, as prices continue to rise, Pushan’s Zhang has observed that the market is starting to look overseas for alternative suppliers.

From January to May this year, China’s coffee bean imports from Vietnam increased 76.9% year on year by volume and 87.1% by value. Unlike Yunnan, which primarily grows arabica beans, Vietnam is a major producer of robusta, a cheaper variety with higher caffeine.

With this in mind, Zhang highlights a recent shift he’s noticed in how Chinese brands market their coffee. “Previously, many would advertise that they used 100% arabica, but as costs have risen, they’re no longer making that claim. They may well be blending in robusta,” he says.

Ultimately, the effects of the influx of domestic brands and rising prices will be felt in the consumers’ coffee cups.

(Due to privacy concerns, Hao Yi is a pseudonym.)

Reported by Li Dan.

A version of this article originally appeared in The Mirror. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Carrie Davies; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: A farmer harvests coffee cherries at a plantation in Lancang Lahu Autonomous County, Yunnan province, Dec. 9, 2020. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019298/China’s Cargo Drones Take Off With Two Successful Trials
World.title: China’s Cargo Drones Take Off With Two Successful Trials
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019298/China’s Cargo Drones Take Off With Two Successful Trials
World.content:
China has successfully tested two large unmanned cargo aircraft: one with a 5-ton payload capacity and the other capable of flying 3,000 kilometers, laying the groundwork for future commercial and emergency transportation systems.

On Tuesday, the country announced that the Changying-8, a domestically developed unmanned cargo aircraft, had completed a test delivery. Three days prior, another domestically developed unmanned cargo aircraft, the W5000, also completed its maiden flight.

The milestones come as China’s drone market is expected to exceed 140 billion yuan ($19.6 billion) by the end of 2026, with the industrial drone segment alone projected to reach 84 billion yuan, up 12.5% from last year.

China began testing large cargo drones as early as 2017 and incorporated the concept of the “low-altitude economy” into government policy in 2021. The Civil Aviation Administration of China has also laid out a roadmap to establish an air transportation system for unmanned aircraft by 2035.

During its delivery test, the Changying-8, developed by China North Industries Group Corporation, released a cargo pallet at an altitude of 300 meters before returning to its base.

The aircraft, whose maiden flight took place in Zhengzhou, capital of the central Henan province, on March 31, has a maximum range of over 3,000 kilometers, measures 17 meters in length, has a 25-meter wingspan, and an 18-cubic-meter cargo compartment volume, domestic media reported.

In the event of extreme disasters such as earthquakes, floods, and mudslides destroying roads and bridges, the aircraft can be used to transport up to 3.5 metric tons of goods, equal to over 700 disaster-relief tents, the head of the Changying-8’s development team told state news agency Xinhua.

According to its engineers, future applications could include transportation of regional cargo, emergency supplies, and cold-chain deliveries, domestic media reported.

On Saturday, the W5000, an unmanned cargo aircraft developed by Chinese aviation company Air White Whale, also completed its maiden flight in northern China’s Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region.

The aircraft flew for about 30 minutes at an altitude of 1,000 meters, completing a series of test maneuvers before landing. The test focused on the aircraft’s flight stability and the coordinated operation of its propulsion, flight control, electronics, and ground-based monitoring and control systems.

With a maximum payload capacity of 5 metric tons, the W5000 is billed as one of the world’s largest unmanned cargo aircraft by payload capacity. Made of carbon fiber and weighing less than 6 metric tons, the aircraft measures over 22 meters in both length and wingspan and can fly at a cruising speed of 526 kilometers per hour, with a maximum range of 2,600 kilometers, domestic media reported.

Hu Zhendong, founder, chairman, and CEO of Air White Whale, said the W5000 could reduce logistics costs per ton-kilometer by more than 60% compared with comparable crewed cargo aircraft.

The W5000 is expected to begin commercial operation by the end of next year, according to domestic media.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: The W5000, billed as the world’s largest unmanned cargo aircraft, on display at Airshow China 2024 in Zhuhai, Guangdong province, Nov. 12, 2024. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019294/Why China’s Latest Blockbuster Game Had a Change of Heart
World.title: Why China’s Latest Blockbuster Game Had a Change of Heart
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019294/Why China’s Latest Blockbuster Game Had a Change of Heart
World.content:
One of the wildest boss fights in China’s latest hack-and-slash blockbuster game begins with a calligraphy brush. Soul, the protagonist of Phantom Blade Zero, released late last month, dots the eyes of a lion-dance head, performing a traditional Chinese ritual believed to awaken the eponymous beast.

Cue the violence. Two performers animate the lion, lunging at Soul with blades spinning on its head and flames pouring from its mouth. The fight then spills onto elevated wooden poles, where Soul and the lion-dance master leap from perch to perch, trading blows to pounding Chinese drums and screaming electric guitar.

In the game its creator originally envisioned, Soul had just 66 lives to survive this fight and every other. Use them up, and hours of progress across the campaign would be gone for good.

The restriction was meant to mirror the game’s story: Soul has just 66 days to find a replacement for his damaged heart. But Beijing-based developer S-Game eventually abandoned the compulsory death limit, introducing three difficulty settings and making the original challenge optional.

S-Game founder Liang Qiwei called the compromise “one of the countless difficult decisions we made in developing Phantom Blade Zero.” His studio spent four years and a reported 300 million to 400 million yuan ($45 million to $60 million) creating a game it hoped would introduce wuxia — Chinese martial arts fantasy — to audiences around the world.

To bring its combat to life, S-Game recruited Hong Kong action star Donnie Yen, enlisted martial arts experts, and brought traditional performers into motion-capture studios. The finished game features more than 50 bosses and 55 weapons, each offering different ways to fight.

The scale of the undertaking drew inevitable comparisons with Black Myth: Wukong, China’s breakout global gaming hit of 2024. Chinese gamers even dubbed Phantom Blade Zero “the village’s second college student,” hoping the conditions for success would align twice.

So far, it has. Video game rating site IGN gave Phantom Blade Zero a 9 out of 10, praising its “memorable boss fights, compelling combat, and limitless swagger.” Its PC version scored 88 on review aggregator Metacritic, surpassing the 81 Black Myth: Wukong received.

Released on Oct. 29, with a standard edition priced at 268 yuan ($40) and a deluxe edition at 328 yuan, the game sold more than 4 million copies in its first 72 hours, topping Steam’s bestseller chart and generating an estimated 1 billion yuan in gross sales.

Unlike Wukong, which drew on the beloved Chinese classic “Journey to the West,” Phantom Blade Zero had to win over players with a far less familiar fictional universe, one Liang had spent two decades developing.

Punk fiction

In 2006, while studying architecture at Beijing’s Tsinghua University, Liang began developing Rain Blood, an independent role-playing game inspired by Taiwanese wuxia novelist Gu Long. Built using software intended for amateur game developers, it introduced Soul, an assassin serving the Order, a secretive organization of martial artists.

Over the following years, Liang, who later earned a master’s degree in architecture from Yale University, expanded the fictional universe through a series of PC and mobile games, retaining its characters, history, and storytelling conventions. In 2017, he began developing concepts for Phantom Blade Zero.

This time, Soul is fighting for his own survival. Framed for the murder of the Order’s leader and gravely wounded, he is kept alive by a venom-infused replacement heart that will last just 66 days. He must uncover the conspiracy, clear his name, and find a way to survive.

His search takes him through a bleak, rain-soaked world where ancient Chinese temples house enormous machinery, and traditional martial arts coexist with mechanical prosthetics. Liang calls the distinctive blend of wuxia and industrial technology “kungfupunk.”

Geng Youzimin, a researcher at Peking University’s Video Game and Art Research Center who has followed the series for years, recognized much of the old Rain Blood universe in the new game, from its character names and dialogue to its cold, gray atmosphere.

While many Chinese wuxia games emphasize storytelling over action, Geng was particularly impressed by Phantom Blade Zero’s side quests and the portrayal of jianghu — the loosely governed world of wandering martial artists, rival factions, and secret societies familiar to readers of wuxia fiction.

“The jianghu often represents a world in which an existing power structure governing a region has collapsed, while a new one has yet to emerge,” he said.

In one such quest, a Shadow Warden sent to capture Soul instead seeks his help to escape the organization he serves. He even discards the numerical identity assigned by his masters and chooses a name for himself. Though he ultimately fails to break free, he secretly helps Soul defeat his enemies, even at the cost of his own life.

Yet not all of the older series’ conventions have been as warmly received. Some players mocked the game’s grandiose names as adolescent melodrama, including “Dark Demon Castle,” where Soul fights a boss portrayed by Donnie Yen. Others found its dialogue overly straightforward.

Geng, who welcomed those familiar touches as a longtime fan, said the pushback underscores how tastes have shifted since the franchise’s indie beginnings. “When this IP first emerged, these elements were popular,” he said, adding that today, the same stylistic quirks have become “baggage” that risks alienating a wider audience.

For Cao Yuan, a game content creator in his 30s who had never played S-Game’s earlier titles, the moral ambiguity of its world struck a chord. “The game incorporates many such blurred boundaries between good and evil,” he said.

Cao also found Soul’s struggle more relatable. “I have no weapons, no resources, nothing at all, but I still have to fight my way into the jianghu,” he said. “That experience feels very close to real life.”

The fire-breathing lion that confronts Soul took shape in a Shanghai motion-capture studio, where a troupe from China’s southern Guangdong province performed a traditional lion-dance routine. Combat director Yang Liu and his team used the recordings to develop the fight, exaggerating the performers’ head tosses and tail swings into attacks.

Even the vegetables suspended above the arena draw on cai qing, or “plucking the greens,” a southern Chinese lion-dance ritual in which the lion retrieves greenery symbolizing prosperity and spits it out to spread good fortune.

In the game, Soul can collect the vegetables to boost his power; later, when the lion-dance master finally breaks free of the force controlling him, he offers Soul the greens.

The music, helmed by Bo Caisheng, a composer who’s worked on animated productions and video games, draws on the same traditions, beginning with drums performed live before introducing percussion evocative of the northern Shanxi province and electric guitar. Bo described his approach as “using Chinese music as the skeleton and Western music as the flesh.”

Tang Zhi, 35, grew up in central China’s Hunan province, where he was familiar with lion dancing from neighboring Guangdong. A Beijing-based developer relations executive, he’s followed Phantom Blade Zero since its early trailers.

“When you jump around on the plum blossom poles and fight the boss, it immediately reminds you of the martial arts performances you watched as a child,” he said.

Game theory

For all the intricate martial arts choreography onscreen, pulling off spectacular moves in Phantom Blade Zero requires surprisingly few commands.

In a fight against a wooden puppet, flashes of blue signal an attack the player can block, while red warns of one that must be dodged. Each response takes a button press, though timing is crucial: dodge at precisely the right moment, and Soul executes “ghoststep,” instantly slipping behind his opponent.

Another button unleashes an elaborate finishing sequence, launching the puppet into the air before Soul slashes its neck as it lands.

Liang wanted to make such combat accessible to newcomers while giving experienced players room to test their skills and explore its depth. Those less interested in mastering the fighting system could concentrate on the story or simply enjoy the cinematic choreography.

“And in the era of livestreaming and short videos, the gameplay itself will become content for a wider audience,” Liang wrote on social media.

Players can combine 30 primary weapons and 25 secondary weapons, including broadswords and twin daggers, each with their own moves and finishing animations. A sha qi, or “killing intent” meter, replenished by well-timed blocks and weapon switches, encourages fast, aggressive combat.

For Zhang Yingshen, 35, a game content creator who works in public relations for a foreign gaming company, the combat was exhilarating without the frustration he associated with learning other action games.

“It’s a game where positive feedback practically spills out of the screen,” he told Sixth Tone.

But Zhang admitted that he eventually wanted more of a challenge. “About halfway through the game, I felt it was a little easy, so I switched to the highest difficulty setting. But even that wasn’t challenging enough,” he said.

Players can switch between three difficulty settings as they progress, but the toughest challenge is reserved for those who complete the main story. Only then can they unlock “66 Days,” a separate mode that limits them to 66 lives — the restriction Liang originally intended for every player.

But Zhang’s experience at a Phantom Blade Zero playtest in Beijing left him with reservations about the combat system’s staying power. “We (and other uploaders) were worried that players might feel exhausted after 10 to 20 hours of gameplay,” he said.

Yet he found that the game’s more than 50 bosses and interconnected, three-dimensional maps gave players plenty to explore across Liang’s sprawling jianghu world.

“Throughout the game, you constantly feel like you’re discovering something new around every corner, and you always maintain a sense of freshness about the world,” Zhang said.

He Wei, a professor at Beijing Normal University’s School of Arts and Communication, sees Phantom Blade Zero’s fusion of wuxia and industrial machinery as an attempt to create a distinctive style that international audiences can readily embrace.

But he argued that incorporating Chinese traditions was only part of the challenge. “Gameplay is the vessel, while culture is the soul. Only when the two are integrated can a game spread culture far and wide,” he said.

He nevertheless considers Black Myth: Wukong stronger in artistic vision and cultural depth, particularly in its character designs. “From the character concept art to the finished designs, the illustrated portraits of characters are more sophisticated and demonstrate greater depth,” he said.

Geng, from Peking University, cautioned against expecting other Chinese developers to reproduce Wukong’s extraordinary cultural impact. “Black Myth: Wukong was a phenomenon. The cultural discourse it carried, or the cultural responsibilities it took on, were things that neither the game itself nor its development team could ever have fully anticipated,” he said.

Nor did the commercial success of Wukong and Phantom Blade Zero resolve Geng’s doubts about the sustainability of AAA development. Such games demand enormous investment and large-scale production, and require high returns to justify their costs.

“AAA games will always represent the ultimate ideal for many game developers, the crown jewel of their ambitions. But commercially, they are increasingly more like luxury goods,” he said.

For Liang, bringing a fictional world he had spent two decades developing to a mass audience meant balancing his desire for creative expression with his responsibilities to paying players. After a playtest in Beijing, he described himself as “a service provider” who had to give players more than their money’s worth.

“Making games is a process of dissolving one’s own ego and sinking it into the earth,” he wrote on social media, “where it can grow into a flourishing tree nourished by the soil.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A scene from the video game “Phantom Blade Zero.” From @影之刃零 on Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019293/China Proposes Tougher Rules to Curb Skills Certification Fraud
World.title: China Proposes Tougher Rules to Curb Skills Certification Fraud
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019293/China Proposes Tougher Rules to Curb Skills Certification Fraud
World.content:
China has proposed its first regulation on vocational skills certifications, cracking down on fraudulent credentials and tightening oversight of certification bodies.

The Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security released the draft regulation on Nov. 12, with public feedback open until Dec. 12. No date has been set for when the rules will take effect.

China now has more than 220 million skilled workers — including electricians, AI trainers, and elderly-care workers — accounting for about 30% of its workforce, according to the ministry. Vocational skills certificates can bring benefits such as cash subsidies, children’s school enrollment, and fast-tracked residency applications.

Fraudulent vocational skills certificates have proliferated online in recent years, prompting a nationwide crackdown on bogus credentials in 2022.

The proposed regulation would tighten oversight of certification bodies, barring them from making misleading claims or leaking exam questions. In addition, certificates can be issued only to candidates who pass the required assessments, rather than those who simply pay to obtain them.

The draft also outlines that organizations responsible for vocational qualification assessments would be barred from offering related training. Institutions that issue certificates without first registering with the government, as well as those that forge, alter, or trade certificates, may face suspension, confiscation of illegal earnings, and fines of 10,000 to 100,000 yuan ($1,500 to $15,000).

The rules also outline penalties for examiners who engage in misconduct, candidates who cheat, and officials who fail to perform their duties properly. Employers will be encouraged to use workers’ certified skill levels as a key factor in determining pay.

Previously, workers obtained vocational qualifications through government-organized exams. Starting in 2020, however, China phased out most government-issued vocational qualifications, shifting responsibility to registered and supervised third-party organizations. By the end of 2025, 32,000 such organizations were in operation nationwide.

Cheng Xiezhong, a law professor at the China University of Political Science and Law, told domestic media that the shift had “helped expand the pool of skilled workers” but had also led to uneven standards among certification bodies and a widespread increase in bogus certificates.

An investigation by domestic media this June found vocational certificates openly advertised on multiple Chinese e-commerce platforms. In one case, a reporter paid just 300 yuan for a mechanical equipment installer certificate showing passing scores on tests they had never taken.

Previous reports also found that some training providers issued course completion certificates rather than recognized vocational credentials. Others lured young jobseekers into “training loan” scams, persuading them to borrow thousands of yuan for courses.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Heade image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019284/Bot, Interrupted: DeepSeek Users Report New Limits on Free Chats
World.title: Bot, Interrupted: DeepSeek Users Report New Limits on Free Chats
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019284/Bot, Interrupted: DeepSeek Users Report New Limits on Free Chats
World.content:
Chinese AI model DeepSeek has reportedly begun limiting use of its free chatbot by reducing the number of characters users can input and discontinuing inactive conversations after seven days.

DeepSeek users began reporting seeing an error message — “Due to server overload, the use limit has been reached” — on Monday when they tried to continue chats inactive for a week or when they tried to input larger volumes of text, according to posts on microblogging platform Weibo.

According to domestic media, users of the large language model (LLM) can now only enter around 40,000 characters at a time (a page of Chinese text typically ranges from 500 to 800 characters). Previously, the chatbot had no publicly stated text limit. Once users reach their daily limit, DeepSeek displays an error message.

It is reportedly the first time DeepSeek, headquartered in China’s eastern city of Hangzhou, has restricted free-user access since its launch in January 2025.

According to its official status page, DeepSeek has experienced 57 outages or performance degradations this year, without providing additional explanation. Domestic media reported that disruptions in the first half of the year mainly involved slower responses, delays in data generation, and occasional request failures. After October, prolonged global outages began to occur more frequently.

Usage caps apply only to individual users, but because DeepSeek has no related paid plan, those who hit their capacity cannot pay for more. App developers, who pay to use DeepSeek through an application programming interface, or API, a connection that shares data between their software and the AI model, are subject to separate limits and per-use billing.

As of Wednesday, DeepSeek had not announced a reason for the new rules or whether it might lift them. Developers who spotted references to a “Coding Plan” in the website’s code have speculated that the company may soon implement a paid subscription plan for individual users.

Online, users debated the new limits, with many expressing outrage and complaining that the company had not rolled out a paid plan option for individual users before the usage limit. “I feel like I’m a widow who just lost her husband,” wrote one user on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote.

Others sympathized with DeepSeek, arguing that data is costly or hypothesizing that the company was clamping down on users developing companion relationships with its AI, alluding to China’s ban on AI products designed to mimic human personalities that took effect on July 15.

Data from OpenRouter, a U.S.-based platform that provides access to numerous AI models through one interface, showed DeepSeek’s latest model processing 59.2 trillion tokens the week of Nov. 9 to 15, topping OpenRouter’s weekly token usage chart.

Long chats are more costly for LLM developers because models must parse more information with each reply. Industry watchers told domestic media that the higher costs mean DeepSeek may now have to choose between training new models, serving paying API customers, and providing free chats.

DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng has long said the company has moved toward developing its artificial general intelligence capabilities — the drive to create an AI that can match or surpass humans across a wide range of tasks — rather than consumer revenue.

Earlier this year, Liang said computing power is the biggest factor holding the company back. He also described near-term business opportunities targeting customers as “sesame seeds,” a Chinese turn of phrase describing small gains not worth chasing at the expense of a bigger payoff.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)
