World.title: Spared from Maguindanao massacre: Unnamed journalist’s 17 years of silence
World.content:
ORPHANED. Seventeen-year-old Franzitha Subang – only a one-month-old infant when the 2009 Maguindanao massacre occurred – appeals for continued scholarship aid so she can pursue college. Now living with her aunt, she continues to hope for sustained educational support for massacre survivors' families.

The journalist was flagged down but allowed to leave, in what has been described as a stroke of luck: one of the police officials who stopped the journalist was an acquaintance

MAGUINDANAO DEL SUR, Philippines – For 17 years, a journalist who witnessed the early stages of the infamous Maguindanao massacre has remained silent about what unfolded on the day 58 people were abducted and killed, including 32 journalists and media workers.

The journalist was not among those traveling in the convoy on November 23, 2009. Running late, the media worker was on the way to meet the group along the highway when an armed group flagged down the vehicle.

The journalist was eventually allowed to leave, in what Maguindanao del Sur Representative Esmael “Toto” Mangudadatu described as a stroke of luck: one of the police officials who stopped the journalist was an acquaintance. That police official was later convicted, along with several others, in connection with the massacre.

REMEMBERING. Families of Maguindanao Massacre victims, including Maguindanao del Sur Representative Toto Mangudadatu gather for a reunion-lunch to commemorate the 17th anniversary of the carnage, in Buluan, Maguindanao del Sur. Ferdinandh Cabrera/Rappler

The convoy the journalist had been trying to meet was carrying Mangudadatu’s wife, sisters, relatives, lawyers, political aides and journalists to the provincial election office to file his certificate of candidacy for governor. Mangudadatu was challenging Andal Ampatuan Jr., son of the incumbent governor and patriarch of one of Mindanao’s most powerful political clans, in the 2010 elections.

The convoy never reached its destination. In Ampatuan town, armed men seized its passengers and killed 58 people, including 32 journalists and media workers. Motorists and other civilians were also caught in the carnage, some mistaken for members of the convoy. One media worker remains missing to this day.

The Maguindanao massacre became one of the deadliest episodes of political violence in Philippine history and one of the world’s worst single attacks on journalists. It exposed the reach of powerful political clans, their armed networks and a culture of impunity in which an electoral challenge could end in mass murder.

Nearly two decades later, Mangudadatu is appealing to the journalist to break the silence, hoping that an account of what was witnessed before the killings could help fill gaps in the history of a day that continues to haunt the victims’ families.

Speaking at a gathering marking the massacre’s 17th anniversary in Buluan, Maguindanao del Sur, attended by more than 20 relatives of the slain media workers and members of the Mangudadatu family, the lawmaker said he had long wrestled with whether to disclose the existence of the journalist.

He had considered waiting until the 20th anniversary. But the uncertainty of life, he said, made him think that another three years might be too long to wait.

“I had thought of waiting until two decades, but then I realized that maybe my life wouldn’t reach that far, or maybe theirs wouldn’t either,” Mangudadatu said in Filipino, appealing directly to the unnamed journalist.

He declined to disclose the journalist’s identity or whether the media worker remained in the profession.

Mangudadatu said there were details of what happened that day known only to him and the journalist, details that had never been publicly discussed in the 17 years since the killings.

He recalled that whenever their paths crossed, including at a recent event in Cotabato City, both would fall silent, their eyes cast down, weighed by the memory of what happened.

For Mangudadatu, what the journalist saw could help fill gaps in the public account of the massacre while easing the burden of a painful memory carried for almost two decades.

“What we are fighting for here is not just one life, but many lives,” he said. “We are fighting for justice so that what happened will never happen again.”

Orphaned

Among those who gathered on November 23 was 17-year-old Franzitha Subang, now a senior high school student whose parents were both killed in the massacre.

Her father, Ian “Joker” Subang, was publisher for Socsargen Today, a small community newspaper based in General Santos City. Her mother, Eleanor “Lea” Dalmacio, was a reporter for the same publication.

Less than a month old when the killings took place, Franzitha learned about the massacre through accounts shared by her guardians and news reports. Seventeen years later, she said the pain remained, but her immediate concern was her future, particularly her education, as scholarships previously offered to victims’ families had ended.

“It’s so hard for me and my other siblings to continue our studies since there are no more scholarships, just like what happened with my older sibling,” said Franzitha, the third of her parents’ children, who was adopted and raised by her aunt.

Reflecting on the case as a senior high school student, she said: “What I learned in this life is that if you are powerful, you can easily get justice, but for us who are poor, it is next to impossible.”

Families await CA ruling

Although key figures, including former regional governor Zaldy Ampatuan of the now-defunct Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) and former Datu Unsay mayor Andal Ampatuan Jr., were convicted of murder in December 2019, the victims’ families, media groups and legal advocates continue to seek full accountability, the arrest of several dozen others still at large, and the resolution of pending appeals and payment of civil damages.

Supreme Court Chief Justice Rodil Zalameda on Monday, November 23, urged the Court of Appeals to swiftly resolve pending appeals in the massacre case.

Speaking at his first flag-raising ceremony as chief justice, held on the 17th anniversary of the killings, Zalameda called for prompt action while upholding due process and the rights of all parties.

Pending before the appeals court are challenges by convicted members of the Ampatuan clan to the 2019 regional court verdict, as well as petitions involving civil damages for the victims’ heirs.

Jergin Dela Cruz, daughter of murdered Saksi News and Mindanao Focus journalist Gina Dela Cruz, said her family had endured immense hardship over the past 17 years. Expressing hope that the appellate court would rule in favor of the victims, she appealed to journalists to continue reporting the truth.

“I appeal to journalists across the entire country to continue and be brave in telling the truth,” she said.

Ronnie Perante Jr., 25, whose father, Ronnie Sr., worked for the Cagayan de Oro-based Gold Star Daily, said the prolonged appeals process raised concerns that the outcome might not favor the victims’ families. He said financial difficulties and the termination of educational assistance had prevented him from completing college.

“The case should have ended long ago,” Perante said in a mix of Filipino and English. “If they were truly in favor of us, it would have been resolved a long time ago. So there is really a lingering fear that the appeals will not go in our favor. The compensation claims would be a big help as we move on.”

Reminder against abuse of power

Mangudadatu said the anniversary served as a reminder of the dangers of unchecked political power, even as the province sought to move forward.

“Whenever the Maguindanao massacre is mentioned, let us always remember that it was the gravest example of a leader’s abuse of power – something that must never be emulated,” he said in Filipino, referring to the impunity that led to the killings.

Although the principal perpetrators remain behind bars, Mangudadatu said his family continued to pursue full justice while trying to rebuild their lives.

“Even so, we will not stop searching for full justice. We have also moved on, because it wouldn’t be right if we didn’t, yet we continuously seek justice,” he said.

He urged the public not to hold the entire Ampatuan clan responsible for the crimes committed by its convicted members.

“So that everyone knows: not all Ampatuans are bad,” he said. “Let us not generalize, because sometimes people ask me, ‘How are things? Why are there still Ampatuans around?’ I tell them, ‘Not all Ampatuans are bad.’ There are good Ampatuans. There are young Ampatuans who had nothing to do with what happened.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Raya School brings Reggio Emilia exhibition, conference to Manila January 2027
World.content:
The event will bring together more than 200 educators from across the Philippines for a roving exhibition and a two-day conference exploring the Reggio Emilia Approach to early childhood education

This is a press release from The Raya School

This January 2027, an authentic exhibition-atelier from Reggio Children will come to Manila, offering Filipino educators a rare opportunity to engage with the research, documentation, and pedagogical thinking developed in the infant-toddler centres and preschools of Reggio Emilia, Italy.

The Raya School, in partnership with Reggio Children and the Italian Embassy in Manila, will bring together more than 200 educators from across the Philippines for a roving exhibition and a two-day conference exploring the Reggio Emilia Approach to early childhood education.

Titled Mosaic of Marks, Words, Material, the exhibition explores research on mark-making and drawing woven with narrative. It reveals how children use materials, images, words, and multiple languages to express ideas, construct meaning, and make their thinking visible.

More than an exhibition, Mosaic of Marks, Words, Material invites educators to look closely at children’s work, listen deeply to their ideas, and reconsider how children learn, communicate, and express themselves.

The exhibition will open on January 21, 2027, at the Innovation Center of Miriam College, where it will run until February 3 before moving to another venue in Metro Manila. A two-day conference will take place on January 22–23, 2027, bringing educators into deeper dialogue with the Reggio Emilia Approach through the perspectives of two experienced practitioners from Reggio Emilia.

The conference will feature Moira Nicolosi and Marco Spaggiari, who will share their expertise with Philippine educators. Nicolosi has served as a Pedagogista in the Pedagogical Coordinating Team of the Istituzione of Preschools and Infant-toddler Centres of the Municipality of Reggio Emilia since 2014. Spaggiari, the conference Atelierista, will bring the perspective of the atelier, exploring the languages of materials, making, experimentation, and children’s creative expression.

Reggio Children is the institution recognized by the Municipality of Reggio Emilia and its preschools and infant-toddler centres to disseminate the Reggio Emilia educational philosophy internationally. Through the exhibition and conference, Philippine educators will have the opportunity to encounter this work directly and consider how its ideas might inform their own educational contexts and communities.

The event is open to early childhood educators, school leaders, pedagogical coordinators, atelieristas, art teachers, education students, Reggio-inspired practitioners, parents, and other advocates of child-centred education.

The Raya School is the best progressive school in Metro Manila dedicated to helping children discover themselves, their roots, and the world around them. Drawing on the Reggio Emilia philosophy, the school views each child as an individual with many languages—unique ways of understanding the world, communicating ideas, and expressing themselves creatively.

Through this partnership, The Raya School seeks to create opportunities for Philippine educators to engage with international perspectives on children’s learning and to reflect on how these ideas can enrich educational practice in their own communities.

For more details, please email learning@raya.edu.ph. – Rappler.com

World.title: SGS 2026: Newsrooms collaboration, data safeguards a must in new AI age
World.content:
WE, THE HUMANS. Wahyu Dyhatmika, Chief Executive officer of Tempo Digital, John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation Journalism and Media Director Kathy Im, and Rappler Executive Editor Glenda Gloria discuss the challenges and crossroads that newsrooms must face amid the rise of AI platforms during the We the Humans, Social Good Summit at BGC, Taguig City, on November 20, 2026.

CEBU, Philippines – Amid the growing influence of artificial intelligence (AI) around the globe, stronger collaborations among newsrooms and safety nets on the use of new technologies must be prioritized, SunStar Cebu editor-in-chief Mildred Galarpe said during the 2026 Social Good Summit on Saturday, November 21.

Galarpe explained that Philippine newsrooms navigate a mix of challenges—ranging from a shrinking workforce to a decline in news website traffic—which are only worsened by a lack of regulation on social media platforms, hazardous working conditions due to disasters and AI data scrapers.

According to the Reuters Digital News Report 2026, the Philippines reported a 10% drop in trust in traditional media sources from the past year, marking the largest dip among countries included in the study.

“The lives of reporters are at stake in getting stories but trust in them is declining. That those who are scraping content are getting more trust is off-tangent,” the editor-in-chief added.

But this drop in media trust and website traffic isn’t just a phenomenon experienced solely by the Philippines, Wahyu Dyhatmika, chief executive officer of Tempo Digital and co-founder of IndonesiaLeaks.id, shared.

“After the AI overview lounge at the end of 2024, I think there is a zero-click phenomenon. People’s behavior in consuming news is also changing and people just don’t click through anymore,” Dyhatmika said.

The “AI disruption,” according to the Tempo Digital CEO, has pushed some Indonesian newsrooms to implement the use of digital guardrails that prevent the misuse of data by AI platforms.

“We need to protect our most important assets, our stories, our news articles, our archives and these cannot fall into the hands of other entities that can exploit it commercially without our consent and proper licensing,” Dyhatmika added.

What AI can’t replace

Despite the challenges, Galarpe emphasized that journalism remains a valued force in the community, especially during calamities.

“When disaster happens, we need reporters who can show empathy to the victims and report the pain of vulnerable communities. AI cannot do this and if we rely on AI, it will just keep on saying yes, [and give] affirmation of what you want to hear,” Galarpe said.

The Cebu-based editor noted that even while a lack of regulation in social media platforms allows users to “compete” with journalists in breaking the news, it’s still journalists who are able to explain the context and causes of issues that matter to readers.

Unlike summaries provided by AI, Dyhatmika said journalists provide the credibility and integrity needed for information to be trusted by news consumers.

“We need to be a trusted voice in this [information] ecosystem and I think once we identify that, once we agree, that that is our strongest value, let’s build our business model around it,” Dyhatmika added.

Newsroom pivots and protecting journos

Now more than ever, Galarpe said, newsrooms must collaborate with each other to combat the rise of AI-assisted disinformation networks.

“I want to stress that collaboration should strengthen, not dilute our independence. We do not need to become one newsroom. We need to become stronger newsrooms working together,” Galarpe said.

The SunStar Cebu editor-in-chief shared that a cooperation framework among regional newsrooms in the Philippines is in the works.

For Indonesia, Dyhatmika said that publishers there are now lobbying for revisions to the country’s copyright laws that would protect journalistic content from the exploitation of AI platforms.

Kathy Im, director of journalism and media at the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation, shared during the summit that the work of foundations must reach newsrooms in the global south.

“In the American context, we have philanthropy and in the European context, there is a long tradition of private foundations and donors supporting journalism and that’s one thing I don’t see across the global south,” Im said.

Over the years, Im shared that funding for journalism has gone toward the protection of journalists, adding that this has become more prevalent as journalists in the United States are beginning to experience the plight of journalists in the global south due to a rise in authoritarian leadership and inhospitable environments.

“Information does not care about borders and those who spread mis- and disinformation don’t care about and don’t honor borders so our funding of journalism should be free of the borders of the US, and we should begin to fund globally to support independent journalism all over the world,” Im said. – Rappler.com

World.title: China’s Huawei convicted in sprawling US criminal trial over Iran business
World.content:
The jury in Brooklyn federal court finds Huawei guilty on 10 of the 12 criminal counts the company faced, including bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations and conspiring to steal trade secrets

NEW YORK, Philippines – Chinese telecommunications equipment maker Huawei was convicted by a jury in New York City on Tuesday, November 24, in a sprawling US criminal case on charges that it deceived banks about its business in Iran and stole trade secrets from American companies.

The verdict came in a criminal case that began in 2018, with the US government the following year placing Huawei on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to US technology amid American concerns that Huawei posed national security risks.

The jury in Brooklyn federal court found Huawei guilty on 10 of the 12 criminal counts the company faced, including bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations and conspiring to steal trade secrets. The jury acquitted Huawei of conspiring to obstruct justice and racketeering conspiracy, a charge alleging the company had acted as a criminal enterprise.

The trial lasted more than two months, with prosecutors calling more than 60 witnesses and the defense calling 15. It was not immediately clear what penalties Huawei will face when US District Judge Ann Donnelly sentences it on September 14, 2027.

Reuters stories in 2012 and 2013 helped expose Huawei’s activities in Iran and were discussed during the trial.

“After the media started questioning Huawei’s operations in Iran, so did Huawei’s banks,” prosecutor Meredith Arfa told jurors during closing arguments in the case last week.

Brian Heberlig, a lawyer for Huawei, said the company was disappointed by the convictions but said the acquittal on the racketeering conspiracy charge vindicated its “good-faith compliance culture.”

“We fully expect to appeal,” Heberlig told reporters.

US Attorney Joseph Nocella said in a statement: “Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering US national security, violating the sanctity of US commerce, and impeding the enforcement of US laws.” China’s embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Asked how much the company may have to pay in penalties, Heberlig said it was premature to comment, but said the acquittal on the racketeering conspiracy charge could make a significant difference.

Experts have said the case did not undermine Huawei’s business, as the company diversified and emerged as a key player in China’s push for artificial intelligence.

Founder’s daughter was detained

In December 2018, Meng Wanzhou, Huawei’s chief financial officer and daughter of the company’s founder, was detained in Canada on a US warrant, prompting a diplomatic crisis involving the United States, China and Canada.

Meng had been secretly indicted on US charges of misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei’s business in Iran, so the company could move dollars in and out of Iran in violation of American sanctions. Meng fought extradition to the US for nearly three years, before entering a deferred prosecution agreement and flying home to China to a hero’s welcome. The charges against her were dropped.

Meng did not testify at trial, though an HSBC banker she met with in 2013 did testify.

The 2018 indictment alleged that Huawei misled HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas about its business dealings in Iran. Prosecutors added new charges in 2020, including allegations that Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from US technology companies over two decades.

The prosecution case

During the trial, prosecutors sought to prove that Huawei stole source code from Cisco Systems CSCO.O for its routers, stole wireless telecommunications company Quintel’s antenna technology, and hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by semiconductor company CNEX.

Jurors watched a video that, according to prosecutors, showed a Huawei employee slipping a piece of a T-Mobile testing robot into his backpack, and heard about a Huawei engineer sneaking into a Fujitsu booth at a trade show to photograph a device.

Prosecutors gave jurors a statement attached to Meng’s deferred prosecution agreement in which she acknowledged that the company illegally conducted business in Iran.

The defense argued that HSBC and the other banks knew about Huawei’s business in Iran and were competing for Huawei’s business.

Heberlig accused prosecutors during his closing argument of having “cherry-picked” a handful of disparate incidents to support their claim of a 20-year conspiracy. Heberlig said Huawei succeeded through “hard work, innovation, and investment in research and development.”

The company has more than 200,000 employees and operates in approximately 170 countries. – Rappler.com

World.title: Senators call for transparency in Pax Silica plans, flag inconsistencies
World.content:
Screengrab from Senator Bam Aquino / Senate of the Philippines / YouTube

MANILA, Philippines — Senators on Wednesday called for greater transparency in the government’s proposed Pax Silica initiative, questioning the changing details for the project.

Sens. Bam Aquino and Imee Marcos raised the concern while the proposed 2027 budget of the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) was being tackled in the Senate plenary.

BCDA, a government-owned and controlled corporation tasked with developing former military reservations and other government properties, is overseeing the proposed Pax Silica industrial hub in New Clark City in Tarlac.

Article continues after this 

“Ang kailangan din po natin ng transparency dito, ‘no? Sa mga hearing po natin nagbabago-bago rin kung ano ba talaga ‘yung itatayo po dito sa area na ito,” said Aquino, who endorsed the BCDA’s budget proposal.

(“We also need transparency on this matter, as the details of what will actually be built in this area have changed from one hearing to another,”)

“Nagsimula ‘yan with data center, marami ang umalma, kasama na ho tayo. And then suddenly in the hearing wala nang data center. Naging manufacturing pero hindi rin malinaw kung anong klaseng manufacturing,” he added.

(“It started with a data center, which many people, including us, objected to. Then, suddenly, during the hearing, there was no longer any mention of a data center. It became a manufacturing facility, but it was still unclear what kind of manufacturing would take place,”)

READ: BCDA: No gov’t financing needed for 1,600-hectare Pax Silica hub

Article continues after this 

Marcos, interpellating Aquino, also asked if there were allocations from the 2027 budget for the project and the possible displacement of families in the area.

Aquino confirmed that there is no budget allocated for the initiative while a P322 million corporate fund for all families who stand to be affected by any of BCDA’s projects, Pax Silica included.

Article continues after this 

Marcos then inquired on the number of families to be affected.

“Kasi may binigay na mga numero nung meeting natin, di ba chair? Meron silang mga binigay na numbers pero to be continued daw yung pagbibilang,” Marcos said.

(“Because they provided figures during our meeting, right, Chair? They gave us some numbers, but they said the counting was still ongoing,”)

“Lumiit nga, Mr. President e,” Aquino said.

(“It actually went down, Mr. President.”)

Aquino said the BCDA’s official count stood at 198 families, down from nearly 400 cited during an earlier hearing. He said, however, that recent reports placed the number at around 1,000.

Aquino suggested that an independent agency, such as the Department of Social Welfare, help validate the number of potentially affected families.

Marcos also questioned the project’s anticipated demand for water and electricity.

As for the funding for the generation for these requirements, BCDA, through Aquino reiterated that the Philippine government will not spend for this.

“Paiba-iba talaga yung mga press release, paiba-iba din po yung sinasabi ng mga leaders dito and we call for transparency and a clear plan before we move on toward funding this,” Aquino said.

(“The press releases keep changing, and so do the statements made by the leaders involved. We are calling for transparency and a clear plan before we proceed with funding this project,”)

READ: Tinio urges DTI to release all Pax Silica projects’ information

Marcos sought assurances that the water requirements would not affect existing irrigation systems, downstream communities, and the rights of other water users, particularly in an area considered a major rice-producing region.

BCDA categorically committed to this, Aquino said.

According to Senate President Win Gatchalian, the Senate created a Committee of the Whole to tackle the matter as the initiative may have potential effects on the economy, energy, and environment.

“We are with you in a lot of these concerns. And hopefully, Mr. President, the Senate can be the venue for transparency and to really share with the people ano ba talaga ‘yung mga nakaplano dito, ‘no? (what is really planned here right?)” Aquino said.

“Because until today Mr. President, pabago-bago rin ‘yung information, ‘no? (the information keeps changing)” Aquino noted.

World.title: Octa: 9.8M Filipino families consider themselves ‘poor’ in Q3
World.content:
FILE PHOTO

MANILA, Philippines — Around 9.8 million Filipino families considered themselves poor in the third quarter of 2026, according to a survey by Octa Research.

Based on Octa’s Tugon ng Masa survey conducted from Sept. 28 to Oct. 4, self-rated poverty stood at 37 percent in the third quarter, equivalent to 9.8 million families.

The figure was two percentage points lower than the 39 percent, or approximately 10.3 million families, recorded in the second quarter.

Article continues after this 

“The 2-percentage-point difference is within the survey’s ±3% margin of error, so self-rated poverty is statistically unchanged from the previous quarter,” Octa said.

Meanwhile, 42 percent said they “can’t say if they are poor” or not, while 21 percent said they were not poor.

READ: Rising prices remain Filipinos’ top concern — survey says

Mindanao posted the highest level of self-rated poverty at 56 percent, followed by the Visayas at 49 percent, Balance Luzon at 26 percent, and the National Capital Region (NCR) at 20 percent.

Octa Research also found that about 5.8 million families, or 22 percent, reported experiencing hunger, with 83 percent saying it happened only once or a few times.

Article continues after this 

The figure was only one percentage point higher than the 21 percent, or approximately 5.6 million families, recorded in the second quarter, indicating that “hunger is statistically unchanged.”

The survey firm also said self-rated hunger was highest in the NCR and Visayas, at 29 percent each, followed by Balance Luzon at 21 percent and Mindanao at 16 percent.

Article continues after this 

“The burden remains heaviest among Class E households, nearly half of whom (49%) experienced hunger,” it reported.

READ: PSA: PH poverty hit lowest, single-digit level in 2025

Meanwhile, 27 percent, or around 7.1 million families, considered themselves “food poor,” only one percentage point lower than the 28 percent, or 7.4 million families, recorded in the second quarter.

“Food poverty refers to situations in which individuals and households struggle to obtain sufficient and healthful food,” it said.

Mindanao recorded the highest share of food-poor families at 54 percent, followed by the Visayas at 35 percent, Balance Luzon at 16 percent, and the NCR at 10 percent.

World.title: Python captured in Tayabas City; 3 other snakes rescued earlier
World.content:
A reticulated python, locally known as “sawa,” was safely captured inside a house in Tayabas City, Quezon, on Nov. 24, 2026. (Photo courtesy of City Environment and Natural Resources Office).

LUCENA CITY — A reticulated python, locally known as “sawa,” was captured inside a house in Tayabas City, Quezon, on Tuesday.

The Tayabas City Environment and Natural Resources Office (ENRO) said the non-venomous snake was caught in Barangay Angeles Zone-IV at 11:34 a.m.

According to the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), the reticulated python is classified as an “Other Threatened Species,” meaning it faces threats like poaching or animal hoarding by collectors and could eventually be classified as “Vulnerable” if these threats persist.

Article continues after this 

READ: Philippine cobra rescued at Tayabas City school

The latest incident follows several other snake rescues in the city.

On November 17, authorities safely captured a venomous Philippine cobra found inside a house in Barangay Wakas. Another Philippine cobra was rescued on October 27 after it was spotted within the premises of a public high school.

Although venomous, the Philippine cobra (Naja philippinensis) is not a threat to humans unless disturbed, provoked, or threatened.

The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) classifies the species as “Near Threatened,” indicating that it could face a greater risk of extinction if its population continues to decline.

Article continues after this 

The Philippine cobra inhabits various environments, including tropical moist forests, agricultural areas, and urban communities.

Meanwhile, state animal experts rescued a Philippine brown rat snake on Nov. 12 inside a barangay health center.

Article continues after this 

The Philippine brown rat snake (Coelognathus erythrurus) is non-venomous and is often mistaken for the venomous Philippine cobra because of similarities in their coloration and defensive behavior.

READ: Venomous Philippine cobra rescued inside duck pen in Tayabas City

Such confusion can lead to the unnecessary killing of this harmless species, which plays an important role in controlling rodent populations.

World.title: PNP probes mastermind behind former beauty queen’s slay
World.content:
Philippine National Police headquarters in Camp Crame. File photo

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) is probing possible masterminds and accomplices in the killing of former beauty queen and public school teacher Lullete Jane Ramino-De Guzman in Isabela following the arrest of the alleged gunman.

The 30-year-old suspect was arrested by the Isabela Police Provincial Office’s Provincial Intelligence Unit and other police units in Barangay San Isidro, Rizal, on Nov. 23 under a warrant for murder with no bail recommended.

De Guzman, a 2013 Miss Philippines Earth third runner-up, was gunned down on Feb. 13 by two motorcycle-riding suspects.

Article continues after this 

READ: Gunman in slay of former Miss-Philippines Earth nabbed

Police said witness accounts and forensic findings helped establish the alleged gunman’s involvement in the killing.

Investigative units were ordered to coordinate with prosecutors and courts to strengthen the case.

“We cannot undo the tragedy or restore what was taken from you, but we will do everything within the bounds of the law to ensure that those responsible are held accountable,” PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said in a statement on Wednesday.

“The pursuit of justice may take time, and no matter how long those responsible evade authorities, the PNP will remain relentless in tracking them down and ensuring that they suffer the consequences of committing crimes,” he added.

Article continues after this 

De Guzman was inside her vehicle with her three children outside their home in Barangay Cabaritan, San Manuel, Isabela, when the shooting occurred. Her children survived.

Her partner said in social media posts that she had been speaking out against bullying in school, defending parents who were afraid to raise concerns, and challenging authorities.

Article continues after this 

“To the victim’s family and children, we assure you that the PNP will not abandon the pursuit of justice for your loved one,” Nartatez said. /mcm

World.title: LOOK: Iloilo BPO workers evacuate amid 5.1-magnitude Antique tremor
World.content:
Employees of a business process outsourcing (BPO) company along Benigno Aquino Jr. Avenue (Diversion Road) in Mandurriao District here evacuated and gathered outside their building after a magnitude 5.1 earthquake that jolted Western Visayas Wednesday morning, Nov. 25, 2026. (Photos by Ian Paul Cordero)

ILOILO CITY — Employees of a business process outsourcing (BPO) company along Benigno Aquino Jr. Avenue (Diversion Road) in Mandurriao District here evacuated and gathered outside their building after a magnitude 5.1 earthquake that jolted Western Visayas Wednesday morning.

According to Earthquake Information No. 1 issued by the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS), the tectonic tremor struck at exactly 7:29 a.m. The epicenter was located 14 kilometers southeast of Valderrama, Antique, at a shallow depth of 10 kilometers.

READ: Magnitude 5.1 earthquake jolts Valderrama town in Antique

Article continues after this 

Instrumental Intensity III was recorded in Iloilo City, prompting authorities to implement immediate safety protocols and building evacuations across business hubs in the metro.

Meanwhile, higher intensities were logged in nearby areas, reaching Instrumental Intensity V in Valderrama, Antique, and Intensity IV in Passi City, Iloilo, as well as parts of Guimaras and Negros Occidental. /coa

World.title: Task group formed to track killers of Lanao Sur town police chief
World.content:
Fellow police officers drape the Philippine flag over the remains of Capt. Razul G. Pandulo before being laid to rest on Tuesday morning, Nov. 24, 2026, in Barangay Bulit, Datu Montawal, Maguindanao del Norte. Pandulo, police chief of Bubong, Lanao del Sur, was shot dead inside his boarding house in Kidapawan City on Monday afternoon, Nov. 23, 2026. Photo courtesy of PRO-BAR

COTABATO CITY — Police authorities in the Soccsksargen (Region 12) have created a Special Investigation Task Group (SITG) to speed up the investigation and bring to justice the suspects in the killing of a police officer in Kidapawan City, North Cotabato, on Monday afternoon.

Brig. Gen. Alan Manibog, director of the Police Regional Office-12 (PRO-12), created SITG-Pandulo on Tuesday morning and named Col. Nathaniel Villegas, PRO-12 deputy regional director for operations, as its chairperson.

Col. Argie Celeste, Kidapawan police chief, and Col. Ramel Hojilla, North Cotabato police director, are among its members.

Article continues after this 

READ: PNP orders probe, manhunt over death of Lanao del Sur town police chief

Last Monday afternoon, Capt. Razul G. Pandulo, a member of Philippine National Police Academy Class of 2013, was shot dead while resting inside his boarding house in Kidapawan City.

The task group convened Tuesday morning at Kasfalah Hall inside the PRO-12 headquarters in Tambler, General Santos City, to ensure the immediate coordination, direction, and implementation of investigative measures.

Manibog condemned the attack on Pandulo, police chief of Bubong, Lanao del Sur.

“This violent attack against a fellow police officer is an affront to the rule of law and an attack on the entire Philippine National Police organization,” Manibog said in a statement, condoling with the victim’s family and friends.

Article continues after this 

“Such a heinous act will not be tolerated, and those responsible must be brought to justice,” he added.

SITG-Pandulo is made up of representatives from the Regional Investigation and Detective Management Division, Criminal Investigation and Detection Group-12, Regional Forensic Group-12, Regional Intelligence Unit-12, and PNP-12 Legal Service.

Article continues after this 

Manibog said PRO-12, in coordination with the Police Regional Office-Bangsamoro Autonomous Region (PRO-BAR) and other PNP units, was conducting hot pursuit operations to track down and arrest the perpetrators.

READ: Police chief, driver slain in Lanao del Sur ambush

World.title: Classes halted in parts of Iloilo after 5.1 magnitude Antique quake
World.content:
A magnitude 5.1 earthquake that struck Antique on Wednesday morning, Nov. 25, 2026, prompted the suspension of classes in several Iloilo municipalities and the evacuation of students, government employees, and people transacting in public offices. (Photos courtesy of Bonifacio Gaverza, University of Iloilo, Iloilo Provincial Capitol)

ILOILO CITY — A magnitude 5.1 earthquake that struck Antique on Wednesday morning prompted the suspension of classes in several Iloilo municipalities and the evacuation of students, government employees, and people transacting in public offices.

Authorities ordered the evacuation as they began inspections of buildings for possible structural damage.

Based on the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (Phivolcs)’ initial bulletin, the earthquake occurred at 7:29 a.m., with its epicenter located 14 kilometers southeast of Valderrama, Antique, at a depth of 10 kilometers.

Article continues after this 

The earthquake was felt across Western Visayas and parts of the Negros Island Region, Central Visayas, and Romblon.

READ: Magnitude 5.1 earthquake jolts Valderrama town in Antique

At least four municipalities in Iloilo province — Pototan, Cabatuan, Badiangan and New Lucena — announced the suspension of classes at all levels as a precautionary measure against possible aftershocks.

The Pototan Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (MDRRMC) directed school administrators and personnel to inspect school buildings and facilities for possible damage and immediately report their findings to authorities.

In Cabatuan, where the municipal government reported Intensity IV shaking, classes in all public and private schools were suspended to allow municipal engineering and disaster response teams to assess the structural integrity of school buildings.

Article continues after this 

Badiangan Mayor Suzette Mamon likewise ordered the suspension of classes at all levels and mobilized municipal and barangay disaster response teams to inspect public buildings, facilities, and hazard-prone areas.

New Lucena Mayor Carl “Toto” Mondejar also announced the suspension of classes at all levels in both public and private schools, with the municipal engineer and disaster risk reduction and management office tasked to inspect school facilities to ensure the safety of students and personnel.

Article continues after this 

Evacuations in Iloilo City

The earthquake also prompted evacuations in several government buildings and educational institutions in Iloilo City.

Students at the West Visayas State University (WVSU) Main Campus proceeded to the university’s football field following the tremor, according to Bombo Radyo Iloilo.

Employees and clients at the Iloilo Provincial Capitol evacuated the building and gathered in open areas while authorities conducted safety inspections.

Engineer Jeb A. Escarilla, officer-in-charge of the Office of the Provincial Engineer, said no structural damage was found at the provincial capitol after an inspection, according to a Bombo Radyo Iloilo radio report.

Iloilo City Hall and the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) building personnel also evacuated their respective offices following the earthquake.

Shaking recorded across several provinces

According to the Phivolcs bulletin, the highest instrumental intensity was recorded in Valderrama, Antique, at Intensity V (strong).

Intensity IV (moderately strong) was recorded in Culasi, Antique; Buenavista and Jordan, Guimaras; Passi City, Iloilo; and Bago City, Negros Occidental.

Intensity III (weak) was recorded in Malinao, Aklan; Pandan and Sebaste, Antique; Roxas City, Tapaz and Jamindan, Capiz; Iloilo City; and the cities of Bacolod and La Carlota in Negros Occidental.

Intensity III was also reported in Ibajay, Aklan.

Intensity II (slightly felt) was recorded in Nueva Valencia and San Lorenzo, Guimaras; Sipalay City, Negros Occidental; and Odiongan, Romblon.

Intensity I (scarcely perceptible) was recorded in Anini-y, Antique, and the municipalities of Argao and Liloan in Cebu.

READ: Phivolcs: ‘Moderately strong’ 4.3 quake felt in Iloilo City

Local authorities urged residents to remain calm, stay alert for possible aftershocks, and monitor official announcements.

World.title: UK Sanctions 5 Regime Generals Following ICJ Rohingya Genocide Ruling
World.content:
The United Kingdom on Monday sanctioned five more senior Myanmar military officers after the United Nations’ top court ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya community in 2017.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) announced its ruling in the case on November 19.

The UK stated on Monday that it formally recognized the ICJ ruling and announced a major package of measures in response, imposing sanctions against five Myanmar military officers for atrocities against civilians since the 2021 coup.

The new UK sanctions target Brigadier General Myo Htut Hlaing, Major General Myo Min Tun, Major General Myat Thet Oo, Major General Kyaw Soe and Major General Kyaw Swar Oo.

The UK announced asset freezes, travel bans and director disqualifications in response to ongoing violence and repression against civilians across the country.

“Today, we are imposing new sanctions on those suspected of involvement in repression of the civilian population and other serious abuses of human rights in Myanmar,” UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said.

The UK claimed that Brig-Gen Myo Htut Hlaing, deputy commander of Northwestern Regional Command, is responsible for serious cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment of detainees in Chin State.

Maj-Gen Myo Min Tun, Eastern Military Command chief in Shan and Karenni states, was involved in repression of the civilian and threatens the peace, stability and security of Myanmar, it said.

Former head of the Northern Command in Kachin State and ex-ambassador to Laos Major General Myat Thet Oo, who was reportedly removed and jailed in 2024, was sanctioned for his role in enabling military authorities to repress civilians.

Maj-Gen Kyaw Soe, commander of the Western Command in Rakhine State, was sanctioned for involvement in airstrikes on civilians and medical infrastructure.

The UK said Maj-Gen Kyaw Swar Oo, former head of the Western Command, was responsible for repression of civilians including through an airstrike on Mrauk-U General Hospital that killed 33 civilians, including a baby, and left many others injured.

London also intends to introduce legislation targeting the export and supply of aviation fuel to Myanmar.

Alongside the sanctions, the UK is providing £5 million (US$6.53 million) in new aid for about 350,000 people, including Rohingya and other communities in Rakhine State, while a further £3 million will go towards strengthening accountability and justice for survivors of human rights abuses across Myanmar.

The United Kingdom has already imposed sanctions on 42 individuals and 39 entities, including individuals responsible for atrocities against the Rohingya, since the 2021 coup.

The UK earlier welcomed the ICJ ruling and ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s defense attaché, Captain Soe Aung, from London.

World.title: 2 More Chinese Scam Syndicates Raided on Military-Linked Land in Yangon
World.content:
The Myanmar regime has raided two more Chinese scam syndicates operating at sites on military-owned land or believed to have military-linked ownership in the commercial capital Yangon.

The regime raided two residential houses in Mayangone Township and a Golden City Condo in Yankin Township on November 20 and November 22 respectively, arresting over 120 people, according to regime reports.

Observers believed the series of scam raids was prompted by tip-offs provided by Beijing.

On Sunday night, the regime raided Golden City Condo in Yankin Township and arrested 16 people on suspicion of involvement in an online gambling scam, the regime reported on Monday.

During raids on four condo rooms, the regime seized 15 laptops, 26 smartphones and three Wi-Fi routers. All four units were linked to Chinese national Jiang Hong Feng, who allegedly operated online casino and sports betting platform Zaw Play.Com.

Golden City condo sits on military-owned land leased in 2013 under a long-term Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) agreement with the military’s Office of the Quartermaster General.

In 2016, Singapore-based Emerging Towns & Cities Singapore (ETC) entered the development by taking a 70-percent stake. The other 30 percent is held by a military-linked local partner, Nature Link. The project generates revenue for the Myanmar military through land-use premiums and ongoing lease payments.

In 2023, two years after the coup, ETC took steps to sell its stake in a subsidiary linked to the project to Grand Ally Pte Ltd, which is owned by Li Bo, a Chinese citizen who is the vice president of sales and marketing for ETC, and the company’s regional sales and marketing director for Myanmar.

Justice For Myanmar (JFM), a rights watchdog, pointed out that ETC’s related-party sales risk maintaining ties to the military through personnel and stakeholders.

Nature Link belongs to Yangon-based Jewellery Luck, a group owned by regime crony Kyaw Sein with interests in real estate, hospitality, mining and forestry.

This scam syndicate not only sits on military-owned land, but is also just 500 meters from police housing compounds, a local resident told The Irrawaddy. The condo sheltering the scam center also shares a compound with the military-owned Myawaddy Media Center, formerly the Military Records Department. It is also located 600 meters from the regime’s No. 2 Police Security Command Headquarters located at the corner of No. 1 Industrial Road and Sayar San Road.

Following Sunday night’s raid, word spread in real estate circles, with agents warning other agents who had rented properties to Chinese nationals to flee the area, a local resident noted.

Real estate agents have a lot of incentive to rent to Chinese nationals in the Golden City condo, she added.

“To enter the condo, you have to pass a security gate and do a face scan,” she said.

Prior to Sunday’s raid, some media—citing resident accounts—had reported a previous regime raid on the condo on November 13, in which suspected scammers were also detained. But the regime has not made any public announcement about the earlier raid.

On the night of November 20, the regime raided suspected Chinese scam syndicates based in two residential buildings in Mayangone Township’s Ward No. 5, arresting 33 Chinese, two Thai and 70 Myanmar nationals.

The two compounds at 19/A and 43/1 Ma Soe Yein Street were just under 1 km from military bases including Military Intelligence Assistant Unit 1. Military defectors claimed the land housing the scam centers is linked to retired military officers and others in military circles.

A Chinese analyst claimed this raid, too, came in response to a tip-off from China.

Although the regime has pledged to keep fighting scam operations and act in accordance with the law, online critics are widely questioning how authorities could remain unaware of large numbers of people living in such compounds while Myanmar nationals face strict overnight guest registration rules and constant surveillance.

“When we register overnight guests, we have to provide the regime ward administrators with portrait photos of guests with their personal identities,” a Yangon resident said.

“Why don’t the ward administrators and authorities know about that?” he said.

Online critics urged authorities to check the many other places in Yangon where Chinese nationals live or rent together, alleging they could be running online scams.

On the night of November 12, the regime raided nine rooms at Golden River Residence condo in Thaketa Township and arrested 52 Chinese nationals, including Su Fu Quan, who was wanted by China, along with eight Vietnamese and 46 Myanmar nationals.

According to the regime’s reports, the syndicates targeted Chinese, Japanese, South Korean and Indian nationals with romance and investment scams.

The regime reported the arrest of 323 people—302 Chinese nationals and 21 Myanmar women—during a raid on a makeshift online scam and gambling compound in southern Shan State’s Kyethi Township on Monday morning.

In a January 2026 report, the Institute for Strategy and Policy-Myanmar (ISP-Myanmar) said scam syndicates in Shan State were relocating from the China-Myanmar border to central Shan State and major urban centers such as Yangon and Mandalay.

ISP-Myanmar also said crackdowns on scam compounds in Karen State had pushed syndicates to relocate to other areas.

On November 19, the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army’s Commander-in-Chief General Saw Shwe Wah and Phaya Thonezu town commander Colonel Saw A One, accusing them of operating and facilitating cyber-scam centers on the Myanmar-Thailand border.

World.title: After the Genocide Verdict, Myanmar’s ‘Foreign Intruder’ Scare Returns
World.content:
Since November 3, when the International Court of Justice (ICJ) announced the date for its judgment in Myanmar’s Rohingya genocide case, one word has surged across Burmese-language social media: “khoe win”, meaning “illegal entrant.” It is routinely paired with “Bengali,” the label Myanmar’s military establishment uses to deny the Rohingya their chosen identity. Sometimes it comes with “kalar,” a slur against Muslims and people of South Asian descent.

The message is familiar. The timing should worry anyone who remembers where it led.

On November 19, the ICJ ruled, by nine votes to six, that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during the military’s 2017 operations in northern Rakhine State.

Rather than reckon with that finding, pro-military nationalist circles are again urging Myanmar people to look for “Muslim outsiders” in their own neighborhoods.

Over the past three weeks, I have been monitoring Facebook and TikTok, Myanmar’s most-used social media platforms, and found hundreds of posts demanding that “Bengali intruders” be expelled, questioning Muslim businesspeople’s identity cards or calling for household members’ lists or guests’ lists inspections.

Some propose an Operasi-style campaign, borrowing the Malay term for enforcement operations against undocumented migrants, including Myanmar workers. An old video of former spy chief Khin Nyunt denying Rohingya identity has resurfaced on TikTok. None offers evidence of an influx from Bangladesh.

From social media to parliament

The posts are not all anonymous. On Facebook, veteran pro-military journalist Myat Khine encouraged guest-list checks, suggesting they would expose intruders.

Since November 19, the day of the ruling, Ashin Agga Dhamma, a famous nationalist Buddhist monk, has posted at least 12 interview videos featuring two Muslim businessmen. One of them, Htay Aung, claims Yangon is seeing an influx of illegal Muslim immigrants and rejects Rohingya identity. The monk and Htay Aung are widely seen as close to Ma Ba Tha, the ultranationalist Buddhist movement, and have previously appeared at anti-Rohingya rallies.

On November 15, the Burma Human Rights Network warned that Ma Ba Tha-backed groups were reportedly preparing nationwide protests against the ICJ ruling. It documented threats demanding that Myanmar Islamic organizations deny Rohingya identity, backed by calls to boycott Muslim-owned businesses if they refused.

Separately, UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar Kelley Currie warned on October 29 that groups behind earlier anti-Muslim agitation were becoming more active online and in political spaces under military control. On November 18, citing reports from inside Myanmar, she told journalists in Dhaka that authorities in Naypyitaw were acting alongside Ma Ba Tha and other Buddhist nationalist organizations previously involved in spreading hatred and inciting violence.

On November 10, before the judgment, the inflammatory language reached the military-controlled parliament. Lawmaker Hla Swe accused the Arakan Army of letting undocumented entrants cross from Bangladesh. Deputy Immigration Minister Lin Zaw Tun outlined plans for inspections and arrests of people described as undocumented “Bengali” migrants. No independently verified evidence of the alleged influx was presented, but online demands to “check papers” had acquired an official counterpart. On November 20, the regime rejected the judgment and again called Rohingya “Bengalis.”

The road to 2017

This same deadly playbook has unfolded before. A UN fact-finding mission cited a government inquiry recording 192 deaths during the 2012 Rakhine violence, which displaced more than 140,000, mostly Rohingya. Anti-Muslim mobs killed at least 44 in Meiktila in 2013, according to Human Rights Watch. False online rape allegations helped ignite Mandalay riots that killed two in 2014, according to the US State Department.

These attacks occurred under former General Thein Sein’s military-backed government. Military hardliners and nationalists exploited religious fears during the political opening, presenting the army as the country’s protector. They used the same message against Aung San Suu Kyi’s National League for Democracy before its 2015 landslide.

The violence of 2012–2014 was part of a broader campaign of hatred and discrimination that culminated in the military’s far larger assault on the Rohingya in 2017. By then, Aung San Suu Kyi led a civilian government, but the military still controlled security operations. The generals carried out the atrocities while her government bore much of the international backlash. That outcome also served the military’s political interests.

The ICJ’s judgment now shows how far the military took this approach. Citing UN investigators, it noted that 36 military-linked Facebook pages posted 10,485 anti-Rohingya hate-speech items, including repeated material, during six months of 2017.

Why revive the rhetoric now?

Min Aung Hlaing, president since April after a military-dominated election, faces pressure on several fronts. On the battlefield, while Chinese pressure helped Naypyitaw secure fragile ceasefires in parts of northern Shan State, major regime counteroffensives in Rakhine and Kachin states have stalled against fierce ethnic and resistance forces.

Diplomatically, ASEAN still bars the junta’s political representatives from summits, while Ambassador Kyaw Moe Tun, who is loyal to the pro-democracy parallel government, still holds Myanmar’s UN seat. At home, the economy is in deep distress, with the kyat plunging toward 5,000 to the U.S. dollar and driving severe inflation.

The ICJ judgment brings another humiliation for a military establishment that has long portrayed itself as the sole defender of Myanmar’s sovereignty. Inciting public anger toward supposed foreign infiltrators is a tactic used by successive generations of generals. But repeating it today carries a far deadlier risk. Myanmar is far more heavily armed than during the communal riots a decade ago. Since the 2021 coup, the military has equipped and mobilized local militias, including Pyithu Sit and Pyu Saw Htee groups, to fight the resistance. In Meiktila in 2013, mobs carried machetes and petrol bombs. Today, the same crowd has access to guns and grenades. Another massacre is not inevitable, but hatred in a country with so many armed groups could be harder to contain.

The opposition has responsibilities too. The National Unity Government and Karen National Union welcomed the ruling. Yet some democracy supporters still reject Rohingya identity. Opposing military rule is not enough if we still deny the minorities’ rights and identity.

Rohingya civilians are not the enemies of Rakhine Buddhists, nor are Rakhine civilians the enemies of the Rohingya. Neither community is the enemy of Myanmar’s people. Their grievances and rights cannot be settled by another campaign of suspicion and hatred.

Myanmar’s generals have spent decades teaching people to fear one another, and those divisions have repeatedly helped the military justify its grip on power. Myanmar’s people have seen where campaigns against supposed outsiders can lead. The genocide judgment should be a reason to confront that history, not repeat it. A demand to inspect someone’s identity card must not become the first step toward another burning village.

Nyein Chan Aye is a Burmese journalist based in Washington, D.C., who previously worked for the BBC and Voice of America. He writes on Myanmar, U.S. policy, China and regional affairs.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Battles Resistance on Irrawaddy’s Northern Banks
World.content:
Resistance forces led by the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) have captured three regime outposts on the Twin Nge–Mongmit road in northern Shan State while regime troops are busy with their offensives across the river in Sagaing.

The combined forces of the KIA, heartland People’s Defense Forces (PDF) and All Burma Students’ Democratic Front seized regime positions in three villages on the road leading from Twin Nge on the east bank of the Irrawaddy River to northern Shan State’s Mongmit, according to resistance sources.

The outposts were reportedly crucial to the defense of Mongmit, which is held by the central military regime under an uneasy truce with ethnic armed forces.

At least five regime soldiers were killed and 20 others wounded in the attacks, resistance sources said. The Irrawaddy could not independently verify the casualties.

The towns of Mogoke and Mongmit were captured during Operation 1027 by the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA), which returned them to the regime under Chinese pressure last November. But the KIA and allied resistance forces retain a presence in rural parts of the two townships.

The military has now fortified Baw Dae village in Mongmit Township at one end and is airlifting reinforcements to a military training school in Twin Nge at the other.

Just across the river in northern Sagaing, meanwhile, regime troops have taken control of the road stretch between Kantbalu and Indaw townships after fighting since early October. Twenty-five resistance fighters were reportedly killed in the clashes.

More than 700 troops from 33rd Light Infantry Division are deployed in Kawlin and Kantbalu, according to resistance forces.

Military defector Zin Yaw said the regime has recaptured northern Kantbalu and is preparing to advance on the southern part of the township.

“Troops from 33rd have reached the Armored Battalion 6006, so their objective for northern Kantbalu has been achieved,” he said.

Battles have also been raging since April in three villages opposite Katha town further upriver, where more than 300 troops from Northeastern Command previously based in Lashio are conducting an offensive.

World.title: 14 Countries ‘Acknowledge’ ICJ Ruling on Rohingya Genocide
World.content:
LONDON—The UK and 13 other countries on Monday “acknowledged” the top UN court’s ruling that Myanmar perpetrated genocide against its Rohingya minority as London announced new sanctions.

The foreign ministers of Australia, Belgium, Canada, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Estonia, Iceland, Latvia, Luxembourg, New Zealand, Portugal, Spain, the Gambia and the United Kingdom said Myanmar had “violated its obligations under the Genocide Convention.”

“We underscore that the Court’s judgment is binding upon Myanmar and call on Myanmar to comply fully with its obligations under international law, including the Court’s decision,” they said in a joint statement.

The UK separately said it “formally recognizes” genocide against the Rohingya and announced sanctions on five senior military figures.

“The horrific violence and persecution inflicted on the Rohingya cannot go unanswered,” UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said.

The sanctions include asset freezes and travel bans, a Foreign Office statement said, adding that London “also intends to introduce legislation targeting the export and supply of aviation fuel to Myanmar”.

“The UK is providing an additional £5 million [US$6.5 million] in new funding to support Rohingya and other communities with essential lifesaving and life-affirming services to approximately 350,000 people who need it most in Rakhine State, where humanitarian need is most acute,” the statement added.

It said a further £3 million would “go towards strengthening accountability and justice for survivors of human rights abuses across Myanmar.”

On November 19 in a historic verdict, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 crackdown in Rakhine State.

The ruling was the first time in the ICJ’s 80-year history that it has determined that a state committed genocide.

Myanmar’s government called the ruling unfair and a “great disappointment.”

Shortly after the verdict, Britain announced it would expel Myanmar’s defence attache.

World.title: Inside the Shadow Networks Helping Min Aung Hlaing Consolidate Power
World.content:
With the help of a Russian-trained military network led by a key aide-de-camp, a team of old spooks and the military’s security and intelligence apparatus, junta boss Min Aung Hlaing now runs Myanmar with an extraordinary degree of personal authority.

Diplomats, Naypyitaw insiders and regional security specialists say the regime’s system of governance has shifted from institutionalized military junta rule toward a highly personalistic system centered on Min Aung Hlaing.

While formal cabinet ministries, the diplomatic corps and conventional military command structures remain intact on paper, The Irrawaddy has learned that substantive authority is increasingly concentrated within a narrow circle of trusted military, intelligence and informal advisers. Sources said Min Aung Hlaing has consolidated personal control since the 2021 coup, while creating three primary networks that have sidelined formal institutions and now exercise substantial influence over state and military policy.

From institutionalized junta to personalistic rule

Historically, successive Myanmar military regimes—notably the State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) and the State Peace and Development Council (SPDC)—operated through a degree of collective leadership among senior generals and powerful regional commanders. Since the February 2021 coup, however, sources close to the military say Min Aung Hlaing has systematically dismantled those consultative norms, concentrating executive, legislative and operational authority in his own hands.

According to insiders familiar with decision-making in Naypyitaw, major political, economic and battlefield directives now originate directly from the Commander-in-Chief’s Office rather than through cabinet deliberations or collective military council meetings. They said internal mechanisms for debate and peer review among senior generals have steadily hollowed out, leaving top brass with little room to challenge or shape core regime strategy.

At the same time, cabinet ministers and senior bureaucrats have been subordinated to the role of administrative implementers tasked with executing orders rather than formulating policy, according to people familiar with the regime’s current governance in Naypyitaw.

Within this centralized structure, access to the junta chief depends heavily on personal trust, household proximity and demonstrated loyalty, which frequently outweigh seniority or formal military rank. Insiders note that Min Aung Hlaing routinely prioritizes his own strategic instincts and the counsel of trusted informal circles over professional or technocratic assessments. They said that rather than governing through the military’s established institutional machinery, Min Aung Hlaing increasingly relies on bespoke personal networks, reducing formal state organs to instruments of execution.

Who has his ear? The three circles of influence

Sources within and close to the regime point to three distinct yet overlapping circles that exercise disproportionate sway over Min Aung Hlaing’s thinking across defense technology, foreign outreach and internal security.

Influence Circle Key Figures & Entities Primary Domain Mechanism of Influence Circle 1: Technical & Russian-Trained Network Lt-Col Kyaw Zaw Ye, aide-de-camp, DSA Intakes 46 & 47 graduates Defense procurement, drone warfare, Russia ties, strategic messaging Proximity to the leadership’s household; technical specialization bypassing general staff Circle 2: Former Intelligence Network Thein Swe, Hla Min; Paragon Institute Informal political advice, discreet foreign outreach (especially China) Reactivation of legacy Khin Nyunt-era intelligence networks; track-two diplomacy Circle 3: Security-Intelligence Core Office of the Chief of Military Security Affairs (OCMSA) Regime security, internal surveillance, political & battlefield intelligence Direct institutional control over intelligence filtering; constant personal access

Circle 1: Kyaw Zaw Ye and the Russian-trained military network

One of the most striking shifts inside Min Aung Hlaing’s inner circle is the ascent of younger, technically specialized officers educated in Russia—particularly graduates of Defense Services Academy (DSA) Intakes 46 and 47. Some 21 personnel from the two intakes form a key part of the inner circle. Multiple sources told The Irrawaddy that Lieutenant Colonel Kyaw Zaw Ye, a DSA Intake 47 graduate, has emerged as an influential figure with direct access to the junta chief. He was appointed as Min Aung Hlaing’s aide-de-camp last year. Trained in Russia, Kyaw Zaw Ye belongs to a cohort of officers versed in Russian defense hardware, procurement pipelines and emerging military technologies.

Insiders say Kyaw Zaw Ye’s clout stems less from his mid-level rank than from close personal ties to Min Aung Hlaing and the leadership’s immediate household, giving him direct channels to the top that bypass senior commanders. The Irrawaddy has learned that this network plays an active role in bilateral defense dealings with Moscow, specialized arms acquisitions, and efforts to source and deploy unmanned aerial vehicles (drones) to counter resistance forces. Sources also link Kyaw Zaw Ye to military propaganda and strategic communications, reflecting the regime’s push to overhaul its information operations. By elevating Russian-educated technical officers through personal access, Min Aung Hlaing has cultivated an alternative source of military-strategic advice that routinely sidesteps conventional general staff hierarchies, people familiar with the matter said.

Circle 2: Thein Swe and the former military intelligence network

Facing severe diplomatic isolation and institutional deficits after 2021, the regime has turned to veteran operatives from Myanmar’s dismantled military intelligence apparatus—specifically figures formerly aligned with ousted prime minister and spy chief General Khin Nyunt. Both Thein Swe and Hla Min, prominent intelligence officers in the former military intelligence establishment under the previous regime, were arrested during the 2004 purge of Khin Nyunt’s faction and later released. Following the 2021 coup, they quietly returned to advise and assist Min Aung Hlaing’s regime.

The Irrawaddy has learned that the Paragon Institute, a policy and research platform run by Thein Swe and Hla Min, serves as an informal hub for former operatives. In 2024, they travelled to China ahead of Min Aung Hlaing’s trip to meet with organizations that promote Chinese foreign policy and work for policy research projects commissioned by major Chinese government departments.

Sources familiar with the group’s activities indicate operational overlap between Paragon-linked figures and the Office of the Chief of Military Security Affairs (OCMSA), particularly in managing discreet international contacts and backchannel outreach to key regional powers, most notably China. Through Thein Swe and platforms like the Paragon Institute, sources said, Min Aung Hlaing has effectively reactivated legacy intelligence networks to conduct sensitive political groundwork and foreign engagement beyond the constraints of formal diplomacy.

Circle 3: OCMSA and the security-intelligence apparatus

While informal advisers provide specialized channels, the OCMSA serves as the regime’s primary institutional pillar of control. Although the agency is now led by Lieutenant General Kyaw Ko Htike, its former chief—current Commander-in-Chief of Defense Services General Ye Win Oo—is widely regarded by insiders as Min Aung Hlaing’s closest confidant and principal gatekeeper, with a steady rise through the military hierarchy that reflects decades of close personal and professional alignment with the junta chief.

Since February 2021, the OCMSA’s reach has expanded dramatically. Sources say the agency oversees surveillance of resistance networks, monitors civilian political actors, vets state officials and conducts intensive counterintelligence policing inside the military itself to preempt defections and internal dissent. They said OCMSA has operated not merely as a counterintelligence service, but as the primary informational filter shaping Min Aung Hlaing’s political and strategic decisions.

The sidelining of ministers and formal institutions

As power has consolidated around these three circles, formal state institutions and cabinet ministries have seen their policymaking authority sharply curtailed. Sources in Naypyitaw say senior ministers and economic officials have repeatedly seen their warnings—particularly regarding foreign exchange controls, trade restrictions and diplomatic isolation—overruled whenever they clash with Min Aung Hlaing’s immediate political or security priorities.

Consequently, key ministries have been hollowed out of strategic influence. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has been largely reduced to handling protocol and consular affairs and defending the regime in multilateral forums, while substantive negotiations take place through intelligence and military channels. Economic ministries, meanwhile, operate primarily as enforcement arms for ad hoc directives rather than architects of coherent macroeconomic policy. Even within the armed forces, operational decision-making has become heavily centralized, limiting the autonomy of regional commanders and traditional staff departments while elevating security and procurement insiders.

While formal ministries no longer shape major strategic decisions, insiders note they remain useful to the regime for bureaucratic execution, day-to-day administration and projecting the outward appearance of state continuity.

Min Aung Hlaing’s reliance on the three circles described above has taken its toll on the country, analysts and diplomats said.

On the economic front, he has failed to listen to experts. Instead, he relies on advisers with military backgrounds, leading to misguided decisions and restrictive measures that have further undermined the economy.

As a result, Myanmar’s economic crisis has reached an extremely critical, if not its worst, point, sources said.

In foreign relations, Min Aung Hlaing appears to be counterbalancing China by leaning toward the United States, while also moving noticeably closer to Russia. He appears to be openly snubbing China, failing to recognize that antagonizing Beijing serves neither his own interests nor Myanmar’s efforts to resolve its ongoing crisis, some diplomats said.

His foreign trips have also failed to deliver tangible results. Despite reaching agreements and making commitments with international partners, few have translated into concrete action.

This likely reflects the limited capacity of those advising him, who appear to lack the understanding and expertise needed to turn diplomatic agreements into practical outcomes that serve the country’s interests, insiders said.

World.title: Myanmar Migrant Workers Have a Weapon Against Junta Abuses – Here’s How to Use It
World.content:
Representatives of the International Labor Organization (ILO) Workers’ Group for Asia-Pacific and Arab States met on the sidelines of the Governing Body’s 358th Session on Nov. 14 to discuss the junta’s demand that Myanmar migrant workers remit 25 percent of their salaries through official channels.

Among those attending the Geneva meet was Phyo Sandar Soe, Assistant General Secretary of the Confederation of Trade Unions Myanmar (CTUM), who represented Myanmar’s labor movement.

In addition to the remittance issue, participants discussed strengthening trade unions, challenges facing workers across the region, and the hardships confronting Myanmar migrant workers in the Middle East, Asia and the Pacific.

The ILO adopted its strongest constitutional enforcement measure (Article 33) against Myanmar in June 2025 following mass arrests of labor leaders and the dismantling of independent unions. At the latest meeting, member states were urged to enforce Article 33 measures demanding an end to violence, forced labor and conscription, and the restoration of union freedoms. The article also gives countries UN backing to impose trade sanctions while opening a UN channel for workers and unions to submit complaints of junta abuses, including passport extortion, forced remittance rules, and conscription threats.

Myanmar’s regime responded by dismissing the enforcement decision and rejecting the ILO’s monitoring mechanism.

Phyo Sandar Soe spoke to The Irrawaddy about the meeting, the junta’s labor policies, and recent developments at the ILO.

What were the key issues raised at the meeting?

The regime’s remittance rule is not only affecting workers in Thailand and Malaysia but worldwide.

We told ILO regional directors for Asia-Pacific and the Middle East that Myanmar migrant workers are facing serious rights violations and requested an emergency meeting on the issue. The ILO agreed to convene a meeting with experts in attendance.

Junta labor minister Maung Myint has dismissed the ILO’s concerns about migrant workers as exaggerated and misleading. What is your response?

Looking at his social media posts, it’s clear that despite holding the post of labor minister he has no desire to defend workers.

His comments reflect a dictatorship’s mindset. They don’t care how much suffering is endured by workers. Their repression never stops even as people sink deeper into misery.

A labor ministry is supposed to protect the grassroots, the working class of the country. The situation is quite the opposite in Myanmar, which is a shame for the country.

Normally, a country that sends out migrant workers asks the receiving countries to protect its citizens. But in this case, Thailand had to ask the ILO to help protect Myanmar migrant workers. That is deeply embarrassing. The generals should reflect on their own position.

Has the situation for both migrant and domestic workers worsened under the new labor minister?

The regime faces a severe shortage of foreign currency and needs money to fund its military and purchase weapons. So, it has imposed import-license restrictions, tightened access to foreign currency, and is now milking even more from migrant workers through exchange-rate controls and remittance requirements. Regime leaders do not see migrant workers as fellow Myanmar citizens – which is not strange given that they are already killing their own people. What we are seeing is an attempt to squeeze more money from workers to finance further repression.

What decisions were made on Myanmar during the 358th session of the ILO Governing Body in Geneva on Nov. 17?

A follow-up decision on the Article 33 resolution for Myanmar was adopted by the Governing Body. It calls for an immediate end to violence, arbitrary arrests of labor leaders, and forced military recruitment. It also demands the unconditional release of political prisoners, the repeal of laws and orders restricting freedom of association, safe access for ILO missions to Myanmar, and the establishment of a mechanism to monitor labor-rights violations.

The decision further urges member states to review their relations with Myanmar authorities and calls on governments not to forcibly return refugees to Myanmar.

We will urge the ILO to enforce these by January 2027. The ILO Director-General is expected to present an update on Myanmar and progress in implementing the recommendations of the Commission of Inquiry at the 359th session of the Governing Body in March 2027.

What message do you have for Myanmar workers inside and outside the country?

Some people think ILO mechanisms achieve nothing, but a mechanism is only effective if people use it. A knife becomes sharp only when properly sharpened. The same is true of international mechanisms: the more workers make use of them, the more effective they become in protecting Myanmar workers.

Many ask why the international community fails to act despite widely publicized abuses. The reason is simple: without complaints from victims and affected workers, cases cannot move forward.

So, if workers want action and accountability, they need to file complaints and use these mechanisms. I encourage workers to make full use of them.

World.title: Dimash Qudaibergen Holds First Solo Concert in Colombia
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakh singer Dimash Qudaibergen held his first solo concert in Colombia on Nov. 22, performing before thousands of fans at Bogotá’s Movistar Arena as part of his DIMENSIONS world tour.

The concert marked the continuation of the Latin American leg of the tour following five performances in Mexico. Colombian fans welcomed the singer with prolonged applause and chants, including “¡Se vive, se siente, Dimash está presente!” (You live it, you feel it, Dimash is here!) and “¡Dimash querido, aquí eres bienvenido!” (Dear Dimash, you are welcome here!).
