Australian author and illustrator Shaun Tan rarely shows his two children his works in progress. Occasionally, if he’s unsure whether a drawing is clear, he’ll summon one of them to take a three-second look – but that’s about as much scrutiny as he’s willing to invite. “I often wonder why I don’t,” Tan says. “I think partly because I’m very sensitive to people’s comments, and I know kids are dead honest. So if they say something negative, my feelings will be hurt and I might not be able to continue so well.” Hometown follows a young girl in a strange world. Allen & Unwin Fortunately for Tan, his latest book is finished. Four children will now help determine whether he takes home a Booker Prize. His first graphic novel in two decades, Hometown, has been shortlisted for the inaugural Children’s Booker Prize, which gives young readers a majority on its seven-person judging panel.



The award was established by the Booker Prize Foundation to recognise fiction for readers aged eight to 12 and carries the same £50,000 (about $100,000) financial reward as its adult counterpart. The eight shortlisted books comprise five novels, two graphic novels and an illustrated collection of short stories. Tan, who won an Oscar in 2011 for the animated adaptation of his book The Lost Thing, never set out to be a children’s author, and his work has always defied neat age classifications. Shaun Tan’s new book Hometown is his first graphic novel in 20 years. He started his career illustrating science fiction and fantasy for adults and was initially bemused to find his own stories being marketed as children’s books. But visits to schools and libraries opened his eyes to how perceptive young readers could be, offering their own interpretations rather than asking what the author intended. “They just ask exactly the right questions, and the most challenging questions, and they didn’t make the assumptions that adults made,” he says. “I resisted this label of being a children’s creator, and I started embracing it. If this is the audience that I have, they’re awesome and I’m going to go with that.”



Tan was also initially reluctant to return to the graphic novel form, having last tackled it with his acclaimed 2006 book The Arrival. He conceived the idea for Hometown in 2016 and, for much of the next decade, kept the project a secret from publishers so he would have the freedom to abandon it. Editor's pick Take 7 ‘I can’t survive like this’: The moment Shaun Tan’s life changed completely “Reluctant, because it takes so long,” he says. “If you talk to any graphic novel creator, they’ll just bemoan the fact that this feels like an insane way to tell the story.” Hometown follows a nameless young girl who is at home in a world of strange creatures until a human arrives and insists her home is elsewhere. Tan’s experiences as a father, particularly fielding philosophical enquiries from his then five-year-old daughter as they walked around their neighbourhood during Melbourne’s lockdowns, inspired the book in ways he hadn’t anticipated. “She’d be asking all these questions: ‘Why is this the way it is?’ and ‘What happens when you die?’ Small kids ask very big questions, very casually,” he says. “The book is about coming to terms with a strange world for the main character, and finding a home in a strange world. And I realised that’s exactly what’s happening with my kids.”



Editor's pick Literature So you think you’re well-read? Take the 2026 Great Book Quiz The shortlist was selected by three adult judges: children’s author Frank Cottrell-Boyce, actor and comedian Lolly Adefope and bookseller Sanchita Basu De Sarkar. They will be joined by four children, aged eight to 12, selected from more than 4000 applicants. “The genius of Tan is to take readers to a different universe and illuminate it with the most human dilemma, which he does here with more than a touch of magic,” the judges said. Tan is particularly interested in hearing what the young judges make of his book. “Their idea of value is very personal,” he says. “They don’t care who the author is or where they come from. They just want to know if the story’s good, if the characters resonate with them.”



Tan plans to travel to London for the announcement of the winner on February 2. As for the prospect of adding a Booker to his Oscar? “Well, that would be nice,” he says. “I’m not too concerned about winning or not winning. I’m just so chuffed to be shortlisted. To be among a group of other really good books, that’s the most exciting part for me.” The other seven shortlisted books The Worst Thing That Could Possibly Happen by Guy Bass, illustrated by David Roberts

Tadpole Summer by Catherine Bruton

War by Eoin Colfer and Andrew Donkin, illustrated by Giovanni Rigano

The Night I Borrowed Time by Iqbal Hussain

The Teller of Tall Tales by Liz Hyder, illustrated by Tom de Freston

The Rambler’s Curse by Mikey Please

Séamus Almost Famous by Jessica Scott-Whyte, illustrated by Becka Moor What else is happening in the book world? She wrote seven novels about one day. Now she never wants to write again

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has touted the government’s new pact with the Solomon Islands in front of the largest ever visiting delegation to Parliament.

Albanese said the agreement, which includes banning China from building military bases in the Pacific Island nation, marked a great day for the region and made Australia the Solomon Islands’ primary security partner.

Prime Minister of the Solomon Islands Matthew Wale (right) and his delegation during question time. Dominic Lorrimer

“This relationship and this agreement brings us a new chapter of friendship, advancing our shared interest and the interests of our region,” Albanese said.

“Australia’s prosperity and security is simply inseparable from our Pacific family. When our neighbours are stronger, Australia is stronger as well.”

Albanese personally welcomed his Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale, and said he had probably also set a record. “I doubt whether 17 members of the cabinet of any government apart from Australia’s, have been present here on the floor of the parliament”.

Speaker Milton Dick confirmed: “This is the largest parliamentary delegation ever to sit on the floor of the House of Representatives”.

World.title: ‘Multiple queens’: More fire ants detected as Sydney nest part of rare colony
World.content:
Updated PoliticsNSWBiosecurity ‘Multiple queens’: More fire ants detected as Sydney nest part of rare colony Jessica McSweeney Updated November 25, 2026 — 2:24pm ,first published 12:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A discovery of red imported fire ants in Sydney’s west has been identified as a rare colony with multiple queens never detected before in NSW. The NSW government has established a specialised taskforce after further surveillance of the Auburn site discovered a larger and more complex infestation than first realised, with more alive ants detected after the site was treated on the weekend. The fire ant nest at Auburn has been identified as a rare colony with multiple queens. NSW Government Unlike nests with one queen, the colony discovered in Auburn contains multiple queens which can support a higher concentration of ants and nests in a smaller area. The type of colony is rare in Australia. Imported materials are believed to be the source of both the Enfield discovery two months ago and the Auburn nest, although the two locations are not believed to be connected. The government is yet to identify the country of origin of both incursions.



A new taskforce will trace high-risk products transiting through the businesses around the Auburn site, which mostly includes shipments from Asia, Agriculture Minister Tara Moriarty said. “I was able to check it out myself yesterday, and even though the area is not geographically big, the types of ants that we have here do spread in a different way … we’ve not seen ants spread in this way ever like this in NSW before,” Moriarty said. More than 900 members of the public have called the fire ant hotline, but no ants have been detected at other sites. Fire ants are one of the worst invasive species to reach Australia. Invasive Species Council A Biosecurity Control Order will be in place on Friday to formally limit the transport of high-risk materials from the area, including mulch, soil and building materials.



The fire ants found in Auburn are believed to have been there for about 12 months before it was reported by a member of the public. “At this stage, we’ve found all of these queens in this one particular zone, but the tracing will help us to determine if other colonies have set up elsewhere,” Moriarty said. Related Article Updated

Biosecurity New fire ants’ nest found near Sydney importers may have been there for a year Known as polygyne fire ant colonies, these groups of ants can establish new nests when a queen and workers move away from the existing colony in a process known as budding. The ants are native to South America but have spread internationally, particularly into the United States, thanks to freight shipping.



Their painful bites cause burning sensations that can last for an hour, and kill pets, native wildlife and humans sensitive to insect bites. Red imported fire ant nests appear as small mounds of dirt with no obvious exit holes. Suspected sightings should be reported on 1800 680 244 or via an online form. World.title: Why boom Blues draftee thinks he could have played AFL this season
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2027 Why boom Blues draftee thinks he could have played AFL this season Jon Pierik November 25, 2026 — 2:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Prized Carlton draftee Cody Walker has declared he is all but a “ready-made” AFL player and has his mind set on a round one debut against Richmond – the club which also bid for him. Walker, the No.3 overall selection in the national draft, and his fellow influx of draftees – Harvey Spawton-Guy, Jackson Watkins, Ethan Herbert and Marcus Prasad, the latter the shortest listed player in the AFL – are dealing with their first week of pre-season training along with other first-to-fourth-year players. Stepping up: Prized Carlton draftee Cody Walker believes he is ready to play AFL senior football. Getty Images On a warm Wednesday morning, Walker sparkled when working with fellow midfielders, including young star Jagga Smith and George Hewett, the veteran opting to return a week ahead of schedule. Walker, whose father Andrew played 202 games for the Blues, has had the benefit of spending much of the past 18 months at the club. He has been likened to Patrick Dangerfield for his power and speed out of stoppages, and even suggested he could have been ready for the big league last season.



Related Article Draft AFL draft, all the picks: Pandemonium at year 12 graduation as three schoolmates drafted on same night “I definitely would have liked to have, you know, challenged myself to do that [to have played AFL football in 2026], and I see myself as a pretty ready-made player,” Walker said. “And that’s all thanks to the Carlton footy club as well for giving me a gym program for so many years, and then also getting me training with AFL players for … a year and a half now. So, I think I definitely would have liked to have challenged myself, but I am ready this year.” Walker spent time in the VFL last year on a wing and at half-forward, but his long-term future is likely more as an inside midfielder. The Echuca product, who played senior football for his home club aged 16, keen fisherman and former Bendigo Pioneer said his game differed to his father’s more high-flying and outside running role.



What is clear is that Walker was a wanted man. The Tigers made a strong pitch to recruit Walker, who was tied to the club’s next-generation academy. They also bid for him on draft night, but the Blues matched. Walker has embraced life as a professional player for some time, and already considers himself a leader among his rookie teammates, some of whom are still settling in after shifting from interstate. Father and son: Cody Walker is presented with his guernsey by his dad Andrew, who played 202 games for the Blues. The Age He said it had been a touching moment when his father presented him with the No.1 guernsey he used to wear. “It’s pretty special, to be honest,” Walker said. “When I got handed it the other day, when Dad presented it to me, I didn’t actually know I was getting it until Dad said turn around, and I saw it. And yeah, it was a little bit emotional to me and Dad.



“It’s a pretty cool number as well. The first locker in the change room.” Related Article AFL 2026 More than 60 players were picked in the AFL draft. Here’s who your club selected, and what they said about it Walker said his father had offered a simple piece of advice heading into his first pre-season campaign. “Just attack my first year like this is my 13th … don’t really hold back. At the end of the day, that’s your team now, and yeah, just really attack it,” Walker said. It’s been a week of adjustment for the new crew. Spawton-Guy, a West Australian key forward who had Nick Riewoldt as his idol, fell asleep at the cinema watching a movie with teammates on Monday night, so exhausted was he after a demanding first day of training.



Prasad, taken in the rookie draft, has modelled his game on Hawthorn star Nick Watson – and for good reason. Prasad is listed at 167cm, shorter than Fremantle’s Isaiah Dudley (168cm), Watson (170cm), with whom he shares the same management team, and North Melbourne’s Caleb Daniel (171cm). World.title: Baking bad: Political brawl erupts over tradwife social media videos
World.content:
PoliticsFederalSocial media Baking bad: Political brawl erupts over tradwife social media videos Brittany Busch Updated November 25, 2026 — 2:04pm ,first published 11:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Shadow Attorney-General Michaelia Cash has attacked a Labor senator’s claim that women should be shielded from tradwife content online, as the Coalition shapes up to follow One Nation and promise to repeal the government’s digital duty of care. The opposition frontbencher wielded WA senator Ellie Whiteaker’s recent comments on social media linking tradwife content – which promotes traditional family values – to subservience to men, and clashed with Housing Minister Clare O’Neil on Wednesday morning, who rejected the claim that Labor wanted to ban baking videos. Senior Labor and Liberal frontbenchers have clashed over whether tradwife content will be captured by the digital duty of care laws. Marija Ercegovac In the social media clip in question, Whiteaker points to a video of a woman baking a “spicy snack” for her husband as leading to content in which a woman says her husband and God are her bosses. Whiteaker said a conversation needed to be had about what women were seeing online: “Being told to give up their independence, to submit to a man, to obey their husbands – things that women just shouldn’t be exposed to online in 2026.”



The Labor senator went on to say: “Our digital duty of care bill puts responsibility on the platforms. It holds them accountable for what you see in your feeds, and it makes sense. They make money off it. They should be accountable for it. “It also gives the power back to you to decide whether you want the algorithm or not. And if you do, great, you can keep it. But if you don’t, you can switch it off.” Loading Appearing on Seven’s Sunrise on Wednesday morning, Cash said: “Since when did a woman choosing to bake for her husband ... choosing to stay at home, or a traditional view of marriage, become a problem for the Labor Party?” O’Neil responded that “of course there’s nothing wrong with baking”.



“That is completely made up, and the type of content that Michaelia is talking about, of course it doesn’t create harms,” she said. The stoush erupted after Labor struck a deal with the Greens to legislate the next pillar of its online safety agenda, which the opposition has branded as censorship. The laws passed the Senate on Wednesday. Conservatives have seized on Whiteaker’s comments as evidence for their argument. Opposition communications spokeswomen Sarah Henderson described the remarks as an insight into the government’s “insidious” online agenda in a social media post last week. O’Neil insisted on Wednesday that tradwife content would not be banned and challenged Cash to justify voting against reforms that would prevent children from terrorism and eating disorder content. “Michaelia and her colleagues are howling at the moon trying to come up with any way that they can think of to oppose this legislation,” she said, as she and Cash shouted over each other. “I just can’t fathom it … how can you defend your position?”



Related Article Social media Tech giants to face billion-dollar fines for breaching Labor’s digital duty of care laws Asked what her concerns were given O’Neil’s response, Cash said the prime minister had a track record of lying. “Labor have made it very, very clear the type of content they believe should be included,” she said. “The minister and the regulator under this bill ... have sweeping powers to define what harm is. Take that section out of the act. For God’s sake, Clare – read your own legislation.” O’Neil replied: “No … you read the legislation, Michaela, and you go back to Western Australia and you explain to the people who elected you to parliament why you are voting against a bill that actively protects Australian children.”



Labor removed a controversial power in the laws that would have allowed the communications minister to designate new harms, but concerns remain around how the harms identified in the legislation will be defined. The digital duty of care lists content deemed harmful to children, including pornography, promoting eating disorders and bullying. But other definitions of harm have been criticised as too broad and open to interpretation, particularly encouraging “hostile attitudes towards women or gender equality” and “any other material or conduct, or combination of material and conduct, that may cause serious harm to children”. Constitutional law expert Anne Twomey has also raised concerns that the bill is too vague because in practice it means removing content that could be harmful to children from all publicly available platforms that children can access. “Is this what is intended, or have I missed something?” she asked in a submission to a parliamentary inquiry into the digital duty of care.



Coalition frontbencher Andrew Hastie said on Wednesday morning the digital duty of care was “heavy-handed censorship”, and “our instinct and our posture will be to repeal it”. Communications Minister Anika Wells dismissed censorship concerns on Wednesday, including from the newly appointed United States ambassador who attacked the laws and said protecting free speech was a US priority. View post on X “Vaguely defined ‘harms’, backed by penalties of up to 5 per cent of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech,” David Brat said in a post on X. “As Australia’s largest foreign investor, the US is concerned with regulations that impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors.”



Asked whether Australia expected retaliation from the Trump administration, Wells told Radio National: “It’s not for me to hypothesise what another nation and nations administration might want to do.” She said she had a useful first meeting with Brat on Tuesday, and that each party understood that position of the other. “We’re ironing out where there are points of difference,” she said. “We won’t take a backward step from protecting Australian kids and helping Australian parents, and they won’t take a backward step from their position.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Golden Dragon hits 27g/t gold as WA discovery deepens
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Golden Dragon hits 27g/t gold as WA discovery deepens Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Andrew Todd November 25, 2026 — 2:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Golden Dragon Mining has struck the deepest gold yet at its Coodardy prospect in Western Australia’s Murchison region, with a 4-metre hit grading 7.84 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 70m downhole, confirming gold continues into the fresh rock at depth and requires deeper probing. The company says the latest 17-hole, 1871m reverse circulation (RC) drilling program has confirmed the key northeast-trending mineralised structure now extends for more than 500m of strike and, importantly, remains open to the north, south and northeast. Drilling crews on site at Golden Dragon’s Coodardy prospect in WA’s Murchison region. The latest results from Coodardy arrive as exploration activity gathers pace across the white-hot Murchison region, with several explorers, including Golden Dragon, looking to ramp up drilling assaults across new targets to take advantage of the region’s hungry existing processing infrastructure and historically high-grade gold operations. Golden Dragon says its latest standout hit at Coodardy came from the northernmost drill line tested to date and represents the company’s deepest high-grade intersection into fresh rock. The result suggests the mineralisation is not simply a shallow, weathered feature, but continues at depth into the Murchison greenstones.



‘(This) represents another important step towards our longer-term objective of advancing Coodardy towards resource development.’ Golden Dragon Mining managing director Simon Buswell-Smith It joins a growing list of solid intercepts at the prospect, including a previously reported 8m at 10.82g/t gold from just 25m and another hit of 11m at 6.42g/t gold, containing a spectacular one-metre section at 59.20g/t. Geological interpretation indicates a shallow, east-dipping mineralised system where gold is hosted within quartz veining, altered dolerites and chlorite schists. The company believes higher-grade zones occur within stacked quartz vein arrays, forming structurally controlled shoots that could point to a much larger, stacked system. Golden Dragon Mining managing director Simon Buswell-Smith said: “This is an excellent result for Golden Dragon and represents another important step towards our longer-term objective of advancing Coodardy towards resource development.” Coodardy lies within the broader Cue project outside of Meekatharra, where Golden Dragon has been busy consolidating a prolific gold acreage. The strategy recently attracted a significant vote of confidence from Shanghai-listed heavyweight Chengtun Mining Group, with the gold miner tipping in $2.2 million at a premium for a cornerstone 19.9 per cent stake in the company.



Once all of its new applications are granted, Golden Dragon will control a dominant landholding of roughly 619 square kilometres in the same region that hosts Westgold’s 2.3-million-ounce Big Bell gold mine. To keep the exploration ball rolling, the company recently launched into a major aircore assault at Cue to test two sizeable anomalies in its gold corridor that stretch for more than three kilometres. The program, totalling 6000 to 9000 metres, will probe gold-in-soil targets around the Coodardy-Behring Bore area, where recent surface work has suggested the company’s known gold footprint could be considerably bigger than previously thought. If successful, the program could effectively link Golden Dragon’s Curtis Find, Behring Bore, Coodardy and Piston prospects into a single, big mineralised system rather than a series of isolated targets, a substantial prize for any major looking to muscle into the Westgold, Ramelius-dominated terrain. With deeper drilling set to resume in early December and the northern extensions still wide open, Golden Dragon has plenty of room to chase more high-grade ounces. The pieces look to be falling into place at Coodardy, with the next campaign set to test whether the growing discovery can deliver the scale needed for a maiden resource. World.content:
NationalQueenslandTragedy US father drowns while saving children at popular Gold Coast swimming spot Courtney Kruk November 25, 2026 — 1:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. An American influencer has shared a candid video of her despair after a family “trip of a lifetime” turned to tragedy when her husband drowned saving their children on the Gold Coast. Patrick Rohde, 41, was unresponsive when he was pulled from the water at Tallebudgera Beach about 1.15pm on Monday. He was declared dead at the scene by attending emergency services. Thais Rohde (right) says her husband Patrick (left) died saving their two children from drowning. BookTok creator Thais Rohde, known online as “ChaptersWithThais”, posted a tearful video on social media on Tuesday. She said he died saving their two children, aged seven and eight, after they were swept away in a current.



“My husband died, less than 12 hours ago, and I don’t know what to do,” she said. “We are in Australia, for a trip – me, him and the kids. And he drowned, at the beach … holding my kids. “I am lost … how am I going to survive the rest of our lives?” Rohde said the family would return to Pennsylvania this week, but her husband’s body would remain in Australia for now.



“My kids are devastated [and] traumatised. “I am in a foreign country, and I just have so much that I need to do. “This was supposed to be a trip of a lifetime and a dream to come to Australia, and my husband is dead. What do I do?” Rohde later updated a fundraiser launched to support the family and return Patrick’s body to the United States, and said she had been overwhelmed by the response to her candid video, intended to “share heartbreaking news with my small community”.



“I never imagined that video would reach millions of people and I am truly humbled and overwhelmed by the outpouring of love, prayers and messages from strangers all over the world,” she wrote. “Thank you for holding us in your hearts during the hardest moment of our lives.” A spokesperson for City of Gold Coast confirmed lifeguards were on patrol at Tallebudgera Creek on Monday and were among the first responders, performing CPR until paramedics arrived. “Our thoughts are with the family at this time, and we are also providing support to our lifeguards,” the spokesperson said. “During the warmer months (September to May), Tallebudgera Creek is patrolled every day, with city lifeguards on duty Monday to Friday, and volunteer surf lifesavers on weekends and public holidays.



“The city regularly reviews the areas we patrol to ensure patrols are conducted in the right locations and are appropriately staffed based on visitation, incident data, a location’s risk profile and conditions.” A report was being prepared for the coroner. World.title: ‘We’re interested in him’: Bennett confirms Munster is on Souths’ radar
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘We’re interested in him’: Bennett confirms Munster is on Souths’ radar Adrian Proszenko November 25, 2026 — 1:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. South Sydney coach Wayne Bennett has confirmed the club’s interest in Cameron Munster, but has no intention of turning the Melbourne playmaker into a halfback. Speculation that next year could be Munster’s last at the Storm has ramped up after this masthead revealed he had knocked back their latest offer, an increase from $750,000 to $850,000 per season. That figure is well below the $1.1 million contract he is on, at a time when the salary cap is increasing and there are new teams jockeying the signatures of marquee men. Loading For the first time in his career, the 32-year-old is seriously considering a move to Sydney, just as the Rabbitohs have flagged their interest. “We will meet up with him in the future,” Bennett said. “He’s coming off contract and we’re interested.



“He doesn’t look like he’s staying in Melbourne. That’s his decision, whether he makes the decision to stay in Melbourne … We’re talking 2028, not 2027. We’ve got our squad for 2027 … “He’s a quality football player, that’s what I will say.” Wayne Bennett and Cameron Munster. Aresna Villanueva Bennett’s pursuit of Munster is an indication there is no bad blood after the Kangaroos five-eighth knocked back an approach to work with him at the Dolphins. They worked together for Queensland in the 2020 State of Origin series: the Maroons won it 2-1 and Munster earned the Wally Lewis medal as the player of the series. Souths have also met with out-of-favour Rooster Sam Walker, in a sign they are chasing an elite playmaker. Cody Walker has re-signed for 2027 – the club has an option on his services for the following year – while Ashton Ward, Bud Sullivan and Jonah Glover are South Sydney’s other halves options.



Asked about chasing Munster while also being in the hunt for Walker, Bennett said: “It’s nothing to do with anyone else. If we approached Cameron Munster, it means we want him to play with us. “There’s an opportunity to do that, if we get to that stage. I certainly haven’t met with him, no one at the club has met with him at this stage … “We’re happy with what we’ve got for a seven. It will all be played out with who is coming and going over the next 12 months.” Munster began his career as a fullback before transitioning into the five-eighth role. Bennett has no intention of turning him into a halfback. “He’s a six, he won’t be playing seven at this stage of his career,” Bennett said.



On Tuesday, Munster said he was open to all offers after feeling he had been lowballed by Melbourne. “I’m not saying I’m going to leave Melbourne, just, obviously, with the terms and conditions that they put out to me was probably something I was a little disappointed in,” Munster said. “But I guess it’s a business.” Storm veteran Cameron Munster. Getty Images It is a testing time for the Storm, given they have yet to name a replacement for coach Craig Bellamy when he finishes up at the end of next year and a host of other superstars – including Harry Grant and Stefano Utoikamanu – are weighing up big offers to sign elsewhere. The Rabbitohs have their own rostering issues to work through, including whether to retain Latrell Mitchell. This masthead reported that some club powerbrokers were happy to let him go, while Bennett has long been a supporter.



Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 Munster to tour Sydney clubs despite Storm’s improved contract offer “Nothing has changed,” Bennett said. “There will be talk about Latrell, but he knows where he stands with us, and where we stand with him. “We would love Latrell to finish his career with us. That’s what we’re intending to do.” Bennett said the current off-season was the messiest yet from a player movement perspective.



“We just need to have a look at it, our transfer system and player movement system,” he said. “We need to look at it a bit harder, that’s what we need to do.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Shaun Tan could win a Booker Prize. Four children will help decide
World.content:
CultureBooksLiterature Shaun Tan could win a Booker Prize. Four children will help decide Melanie Kembrey November 25, 2026 — 1:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australian author and illustrator Shaun Tan rarely shows his two children his works in progress. Occasionally, if he’s unsure whether a drawing is clear, he’ll summon one of them to take a three-second look – but that’s about as much scrutiny as he’s willing to invite. “I often wonder why I don’t,” Tan says. “I think partly because I’m very sensitive to people’s comments, and I know kids are dead honest. So if they say something negative, my feelings will be hurt and I might not be able to continue so well.” Hometown follows a young girl in a strange world. Allen & Unwin Fortunately for Tan, his latest book is finished. Four children will now help determine whether he takes home a Booker Prize. His first graphic novel in two decades, Hometown, has been shortlisted for the inaugural Children’s Booker Prize, which gives young readers a majority on its seven-person judging panel.



The award was established by the Booker Prize Foundation to recognise fiction for readers aged eight to 12 and carries the same £50,000 (about $100,000) financial reward as its adult counterpart. The eight shortlisted books comprise five novels, two graphic novels and an illustrated collection of short stories. Tan, who won an Oscar in 2011 for the animated adaptation of his book The Lost Thing, never set out to be a children’s author, and his work has always defied neat age classifications. Shaun Tan’s new book Hometown is his first graphic novel in 20 years. He started his career illustrating science fiction and fantasy for adults and was initially bemused to find his own stories being marketed as children’s books. But visits to schools and libraries opened his eyes to how perceptive young readers could be, offering their own interpretations rather than asking what the author intended. “They just ask exactly the right questions, and the most challenging questions, and they didn’t make the assumptions that adults made,” he says. “I resisted this label of being a children’s creator, and I started embracing it. If this is the audience that I have, they’re awesome and I’m going to go with that.”



Tan was also initially reluctant to return to the graphic novel form, having last tackled it with his acclaimed 2006 book The Arrival. He conceived the idea for Hometown in 2016 and, for much of the next decade, kept the project a secret from publishers so he would have the freedom to abandon it. Editor's pick Take 7 ‘I can’t survive like this’: The moment Shaun Tan’s life changed completely “Reluctant, because it takes so long,” he says. “If you talk to any graphic novel creator, they’ll just bemoan the fact that this feels like an insane way to tell the story.” Hometown follows a nameless young girl who is at home in a world of strange creatures until a human arrives and insists her home is elsewhere. Tan’s experiences as a father, particularly fielding philosophical enquiries from his then five-year-old daughter as they walked around their neighbourhood during Melbourne’s lockdowns, inspired the book in ways he hadn’t anticipated. “She’d be asking all these questions: ‘Why is this the way it is?’ and ‘What happens when you die?’ Small kids ask very big questions, very casually,” he says. “The book is about coming to terms with a strange world for the main character, and finding a home in a strange world. And I realised that’s exactly what’s happening with my kids.”



Editor's pick Literature So you think you’re well-read? Take the 2026 Great Book Quiz The shortlist was selected by three adult judges: children’s author Frank Cottrell-Boyce, actor and comedian Lolly Adefope and bookseller Sanchita Basu De Sarkar. They will be joined by four children, aged eight to 12, selected from more than 4000 applicants. “The genius of Tan is to take readers to a different universe and illuminate it with the most human dilemma, which he does here with more than a touch of magic,” the judges said. Tan is particularly interested in hearing what the young judges make of his book. “Their idea of value is very personal,” he says. “They don’t care who the author is or where they come from. They just want to know if the story’s good, if the characters resonate with them.”



Tan plans to travel to London for the announcement of the winner on February 2. As for the prospect of adding a Booker to his Oscar? “Well, that would be nice,” he says. “I’m not too concerned about winning or not winning. I’m just so chuffed to be shortlisted. To be among a group of other really good books, that’s the most exciting part for me.” The other seven shortlisted books The Worst Thing That Could Possibly Happen by Guy Bass, illustrated by David Roberts

Tadpole Summer by Catherine Bruton

War by Eoin Colfer and Andrew Donkin, illustrated by Giovanni Rigano

The Night I Borrowed Time by Iqbal Hussain

The Teller of Tall Tales by Liz Hyder, illustrated by Tom de Freston

The Rambler’s Curse by Mikey Please

Séamus Almost Famous by Jessica Scott-Whyte, illustrated by Becka Moor What else is happening in the book world? She wrote seven novels about one day. Now she never wants to write again

World.title: Hamilton streets reopen after suspicious item found
World.content:
An item that prompted police to close streets and evacuate buildings in Hamilton has been confirmed as not suspicious.

Police said the item was discovered on Fifth Avenue near Five Cross Roads around 1.10pm on Wednesday.

Surrounding streets were closed and nearby buildings were evacuated as a precaution.

People were also asked to avoid the area and expect delays, but there was no risk to public safety.

Police said the item was examined by specialist staff, including the New Zealand Defence Force's Explosive Ordnance Disposal Team.

World.title: Man arrested after joining RNZ staff protest
World.content:
A man has been arrested after joining in among protesting RNZ staff this afternoon.

Union members gathered outside the RNZ offices in Auckland and Wellington on Wednesday in protest over the plan for job cuts after organisational failures ran up an $11.8 million deficit.

As members in Auckland chanted and waved signs, a man joined the crowd.

He picked up a Public Service Association flag and began chanting alongside protesters.

Shortly after, a police officer arrived at the scene, speaking to the man.

He was led away and arrested.

E tū union delegate Melanie Earley said it was disappointing the man disrupted the protest.

Police confirmed the man was not related to any protest and instead had been arrested over a dispute between two parties.

World.title: Missing Canterbury man found safe and in 'remarkably good health'
World.content:
A 72-year-old man earlier reported missing near Timaru has been found safe after spending the night out in the open..

Steven Pringle was reported missing on Tuesday afternoon after leaving for an hour-long bike ride about 11am.

His e-bike was found on Monavale Road in the Albury area near the town of Cave on Tuesday afternoon.

Inspector Matt Scoles said he had now been found.

"He has been located in remarkably good health, given his overnight ordeal out in the open, and he is being checked over by medical professionals," Scoles said.

"We would like to thank the community for coming together and putting in a great effort to locate him. We could not do this alone and this amazing, happy, outcome is a testament to the skills and commitment of Land Search and Rescue volunteers, and the support of members of the community and the man's own family, many of whom were part of the search efforts from first-light this morning.

"We are delighted to been able to bring him home safely."

World.title: Gloriavale Christian School to lose registration after High Court ruling
World.content:
Gloriavale Christian School will lose its registration following a decision by the High Court.

The Secretary for Education Ellen Macgregor-Reid has twice tried to close the West Coast Christian community's school over student safety concerns.

The 80 student school had remained open due to the High Court challenge by the school's board, who said its closure would be unlawful and an overuse of state power.

In a judgement issued on Wednesday, Justice Karen Grau dismissed the board's application and said the cancellation of the school's registration would now take effect.

She said the timing of the school's closure was yet to be determined.

"There may remain an issue about whether the interim order keeping the school open should remain in place to enable an end to the school year without unnecessary disruption.

"I ask the parties to confer and attempt to reach an agreed position."

Months of dispute

Wednesday's High Court decision followed a year of legal dispute over the future of the West Coast Christian community's school.

MacGregor-Reid informed the school's board in October last year that she was considering cancelling the school's registration after a second failed Education Review Office (ERO) audit in as many years.

The July ERO report found Gloriavale Christian School had not met three of eight registration criteria and was not a physically and emotionally safe space for students.

Documents released to RNZ under the Official Information Act show the board wrote to MacGregor-Reid on 14 November last year.

In a letter, it said it was deeply concerned that the Ministry of Education's approach was legally flawed and procedurally unfair, and the school's closure would be a disproportionate response.

"It is an overuse of state power on a religious and cultural minority," the letter said. "There are significant flaws in the proposed decision to close the school such that it is unlawful."

A month later, in December 2025, the Secretary confirmed the school's registration would be cancelled, taking effect from 23 January 2026. MacGregor-Reid said the board had provided insufficient evidence to assure the ministry that student safety concerns had been addressed.

The school board said it was deeply disappointed by the decision.

"We believe this decision is unjust and does not reflect the significant efforts we have made to address concerns raised."

A High Court challenge by the school's board prevented the school's closure, pending a judicial review.

Then, in September 2026, MacGregor-Reid again confirmed the move to cancel Gloriavale Christian School's registration, after considering the findings of another ERO review, with the ministry applying to lift interim court orders preventing the school's closure.

ERO's special review pointed to safety concerns, saying the school was not providing a physically and emotionally safe place for students.

In October 2026 in the High Court at Wellington, Gloriavale counsel Richard Raymond KC told a courtroom packed with community members, that the decision to close the school was unlawful and flawed to such an extent it should be dismissed.

It was revealed during the two days of hearings that the Ministry of Education had been critical of the school board's response to an allegation of an historical sexual assault.

The ministry confirmed how the board responded to a recent complaint was one of the aspects considered by the Secretary.

MacGregor-Reid said Gloriavale Christian School will close no later than December 18.

In a statement, she said her focus was on ensuring the 80 school students have a safe place to learn.

"The Ministry has other schooling options ready, and my staff will work directly with families to help them decide what best meets their child's needs. We want to make that move as straightforward as possible for every student, with as little disruption to their learning as possible.

World.title: Wellington businesses gear up for Black Friday
World.content:
By Eva Perese-Wood, RNZ intern

Wellington businesses are gearing up for the major sales period but some shoppers say they're having a leaner Christmas this year.

Retailers were hoping to attract customers with Black Friday sales.

Wallace Cotton Lambton Quay was one of them, promoting a storewide discount.

Store manager Mindy Dalzell said the period was extremely important for the shop's survival.

She said despite the cost-of-living crisis, Wallace Cotton had surprisingly maintained growth.

"The fact that Wellington has still been able to maintain two stores shows that Wellington isn't as sad as the rest of the country thinks," she joked.

Many told RNZ the Black Friday shopping period was a chance to make a start on Christmas shopping.

Pedestrian John Keith said he would be making the most of that opportunity.

"I'm going to spend every single dollar I have to try and make a saving."

He said while the cost-of-living was something to consider, Christmas shopping was always worth it in the long run.

Local Megan said she had already done some Black Friday shopping online.

"The more we prepare now, the more money we'll have later to have a nice Christmas day."

According to Westpac data, Black Friday spending was rising year-on-year, with spending in 2025 being 48 percent higher than the average Friday.

However, not all retailers were sold on the craze.

Co-manager of Unity Books Wellington Susanna Andrew said that while Black Friday had become a fixture in the retail calendar, it did not always make sense for booksellers.

"Independent bookshops have very little margin to give away.

"We're offering free delivery across New Zealand on online orders over $100 through the Unity Books website and instore. It's not really a Black Friday sale but Black Friday has become the starting pistol for all the craziness of Christmas spending."

She said Unity was focused on keeping books alive and people engaged with reading.

Andrew said the lead up to Christmas was a thrilling time of year for the shop, and that she believed the store would "definitely" see an uptake in sales anyway.

"The shopping tills are ringing everywhere around town.

World.title: All Black Beauden Barrett reportedly signs deal with Bristol Bears
World.content:
After a prolific All Black career, Beauden Barrett is reportedly set to sign to English club Bristol Bears.

English newspaper The Times is reporting that the veteran will depart New Zealand at the end of the 2027 Rugby World Cup in Australia.

The 35-year-old has reportedly been offered a two-year contract worth more than £1 million per season ($2.4 million), which would make him the highest paid player in the English competition.

Making his debut in 2012, Barrett has racked up 150 caps, scored 858 test points including 51 tries, and won consecutive World Rugby Player of the Year awards in 2016 and 2017.

After falling significantly down the All Blacks pecking order under Dave Rennie on the back of a poor Super Rugby season, Barrett reignited his career when an injury crisis struck the side, winding back the clock with some vintage performances.

World.title: Person critical after serious crash on Auckland's Southern Motorway
World.content:
One person has been critically injured in a serious crash on Auckland's Southern Motorway.

The crash involving three vehicles was reported to police at 1.19pm near Takanini.

A police spokesperson said one person was critical and a second had minor injuries.

Two southbound lanes were blocked and delays were expected.

World.title: Solomon Islands, Australia sign new treaty to keep foreign military bases out
World.content:
Solomon Islands has signed a sweeping new treaty with Australia that will ensure there is "no foreign military or security base" in the island nation.

The Australia-Solomon Islands Treaty, signed by Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale and Australian PM Anthony Albanese in Canberra on Wednesday, will also ensure the Melanesian nation's "sensitive infrastructure will remain free from militarisation, foreign interference and unauthorised access".

In a joint statement following the signing, the two leaders said the treaty would make Australia, Solomon Islands and the region "safer and more prosperous".

They said Australia and Solomon Islands would work to advance joint economic, development and security priorities, including through new investments and resources aimed at building on Australia's long-standing and substantive relationship as Solomon Islands' largest development partner.

"The Treaty includes substantial support towards the Solomon Islands Government's free education policy, so that every child can reach their potential."

The two leaders said the pact affirmed Solomon Islands' sovereignty and capacity to determine its own security needs and partnerships.

Australia and Solomon Islands share the view that Pacific security is the collective responsibility of Pacific Islands Forum members, they said, adding that Solomon Islands would look to Forum members for future security cooperation needs.

Australia will continue to support the expansion and development of a stronger, modern, and self-reliant Royal Solomon Islands Police Force through enhanced cooperation, the joint statement read.

"We will also continue to support the development of the Solomon Islands border management system."

The treaty comes after Solomon Islands told China that it was ditching its 2022 security pact with Beijing.

According to ABC sources, Wale's government informed Beijing that it would not renew the security agreement when it expires in April next year.

On Monday, Solomon Islands opposition leader Manasseh Sogavare warned Wale against scrapping the China deal.

"We must be able to work with China, Australia, the United States and other countries without losing our ability to make independent decisions in the interests of our people," Sogavare, who was prime minister when the country signed the Framework Agreement on Security Cooperation with China in April 2022.

World.title: Indian teen wonder breaks List A record with 200 from 52 balls
World.content:
Indian cricket prodigy Vaibhav Sooryavanshi has broken yet more records, this time with the fastest century and double century in men's List A competitions.

The 15-year-old smashed a century in 28 balls, then 150 in 40 balls, and finally crossed 200 in 52 balls while playing for India A against the United Arab Emirates in the Asia Cup Rising Stars 50-over tournament.

All of those are records for List A competitions, the International Cricket Council confirmed, adding that Sooryavanshi's 200 was nearly twice as fast as the previous record of 103 balls.

The teen was caught soon after on 204 to end an innings boasting 28 sixes. India easily chased down the target of 250 set by the UAE to finish on 3-254. More than 80 per cent of the team's runs came off Sooryavanshi's bat.

List A cricket is the level below one-day international cricket. It covers the top level of one-day domestic cricket around the world as well as international games involving a top nation's development team, such as India A.

The records continue a spectacular year for Sooryavanshi. He scored 175 to win the Under-19 World Cup final for India in February, lit up the Indian Premier League and became the youngest player to represent India in a full international game, beating the record held by all-time great Sachin Tendulkar.
